It is correction."</em> The technical bulletin, like all Treadwell bulletins, closes with her standard signoff: <em>"The audience owns the moment. We frame it for them."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG Technical Bulletin no. 51, "Formation Broadcast Surface" · Treadwell, supervising · Year 35 R10</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Four-Team Expansion</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Office of the Commissioner · Year 35 closeout, ratified for the Year 36 founding bell</div>
        <p>The League had run, for eight seasons, on twelve teams from twelve cities. The number was not by design — it was by application. Eleven cities had asked to play in Year 28; Helena's Hedgehogs had walked in late, in Year 34, with a complete roster and a notarized request, and the League had welcomed them. Four other settlements had asked, across various seasons, and been politely deferred for reasons that were always specific and never about them. The Bayou settlement had been told the League was "still calibrating its travel logistics for the deep south." The Anchorage settlement had been told the League was "considering, with care, the welfare of teams asked to travel from the far north." The Denver settlement had been told the League had "no current opening." The Pittsburgh settlement had been told nothing at all, as their original application appeared to have been lost in transit by the Boston post-office's third-quarter sort, an incident the post-office still maintains was not their fault.</p>
        <p>The Bayou Tigers, the Anchorage Polar Bears, the Denver Bison, and the Pittsburgh Ravens reapplied jointly in the Year 35 mid-season. Their joint application is on record at the Office of the Commissioner. It is two pages long. It opens: <em>"We have waited. We have read the rules. We are ready. We bring four cities, four rosters, four crowds, and one shared question, which is: what would we have to do to be welcome."</em> The remainder is rosters and travel logistics. The signatures, in order, are: a Tiger matriarch named Ojee Stripeshoulder, a Polar Bear elder named Tamzen Whitepaw, a Bison patriarch named Yellowhide of the Denver herd, and a Raven captain named Quorrik (no patronymic recorded — Ravens, by tradition, only take their parent's name after their first kill in defense of the murder, and Quorrik had not yet had occasion).</p>
        <p>Commissioner Whiskerstone read the application twice, asked her chief of staff to confirm the rosters and travel arrangements were real (they were), and called a Coaches' Caucus emergency session. The Caucus debate ran four sessions over two days. The objections, by the secretary's minutes, fell into three rough buckets: <em>logistics</em> (could the schedule absorb four new teams without the season running long), <em>parity</em> (had the new teams played enough rounds in any organized format to be expected to compete), and <em>tradition</em> (the League was twelve teams; it had always been twelve teams; "always" being seven full seasons). The Tigers' representative, attending as observer, declined to comment on logistics or parity. On tradition she said: <em>"The League is eight years old. Tradition is forty-eight."</em> The Caucus secretary recorded that several coaches laughed; the secretary did not specify which.</p>
        <p>The vote was nine to three in favor of admitting all four teams jointly, effective the Year 36 founding bell. The three opposed were Wartooth (Wolves, on logistics), the Pandas' coach (parity), and the Sharks' coach (declined to explain his vote, but the Sharks' assistant coach later told the Wing Standard that the Sharks were nervous about the Tigers as a stylistic competitor and the captain "did not want a stylistic competitor.") Whiskerstone, in her ratification statement, wrote: <em>"The League will be sixteen teams from the Year 36 founding bell. Sixteen is a number we are choosing. It is not a fixed number. The next time someone walks the distance from somewhere we have not heard of and shows up at Brewer's Reach with a roster, we will read their application, and we will choose again."</em></p>
        <p>The bracket schedule, beginning Year 36, draws eight of the sixteen teams at random per season for the standard quarterfinal-through-final ladder; the other eight sit out and prepare. Ranked teams (by championships, then by wins) are not given byes — every team enters the random draw with equal weight. The Wolves' coach, on hearing this, filed a written objection (still pending). The Polar Bears' representative, on hearing this, sent the Office of the Commissioner a single-line response: <em>"We will play the matches we are drawn for. We will be ready for any of them."</em> The Office filed the response. It is the shortest piece of inter-team correspondence currently on file.</p>
        <p>Featherquill's column for the announcement week closed with what is now widely quoted in the Lore tab and on League merchandise: <em>"Sixteen is more teams than I can comfortably profile in a single season. I will profile them anyway. The League just got more interesting. Sometimes 'more interesting' is the only good news the season has."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Office of the Commissioner, "Ratification of the Four-Team Expansion" · Year 35 closeout</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Continental Expansion</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Geography Caucus addendum · Year 36 mid-season, ratified at the founding bell</div>
        <p>The League had, by the Year 35 closeout, sixteen teams from sixteen cities. The cities were all from the same large region of the former North American continent — the region the Old Ones had labeled "the United States of America." The label had not been re-applied since the Long Quiet, but the boundary had, by tacit consensus, continued to define where the League looked for new applicants. The Geography Caucus had not been asked to formalize this. The Geography Caucus had not been asked to do anything in particular for several seasons. The Geography Caucus consisted, in Year 35, of one Owl and a stack of inherited Old-Ones maps.</p>
        <p>The reclassification was triggered by an envelope. The envelope arrived at the Office of the Commissioner in the Year 36 mid-season, postmarked from a city the Office had no record of accepting mail from: a place the runes called "Whitehorse," several days' travel north of Anchorage. The envelope contained a single document, signed by an organization that called itself the Yukon Boreal Council, asking on behalf of the Yukon Hunting Lynx whether the League considered "the geographic boundary of the former United States of America" to be a binding constraint on its recruiting, or whether the League considered <em>the post-Long-Quiet continent</em> — the entire former North America — to be the relevant frame.</p>
        <p>Whiskerstone read the document twice. Whiskerstone forwarded the document to the Geography Caucus with a single handwritten line: <em>"Owl, please advise."</em> The Owl, whose name is Pellic Snowcrest and who has been the sole member of the Geography Caucus since Year 31 because no one else had asked to join, took three days. She returned a memo of approximately one paragraph. The memo opens: <em>"The boundary the Old Ones drew across the continent does not exist anymore. It has not existed for hundreds of years. The boundary the League has been operating under is a hand-me-down boundary inherited from a hand-me-down map. We have been recruiting under the assumption that what is now southern Alaska is in our recruiting area but what is now the Yukon is not, even though the only difference between the two is a line on a map that has not been an enforced boundary since the Long Quiet. This is not a coherent position. We should adopt a coherent position."</em> The memo's recommendation, in its second and final paragraph: that the recruiting boundary be redefined as <em>"the former North American continent, in its entirety, including the regions the Old Ones labeled Canada and Mexico."</em> The Caucus's recommendation passed Coaches' Caucus on the first vote.</p>
        <p>The notification went out — formally, with stamped seals from the Office of the Commissioner — to every animal community on the continent that had ever submitted an application to the League and been informed there was no opening. Three responses arrived within a fortnight. The Saint-Laurent basin Moose (who had filed their original application under the name "Quebec Crashing Moose" in Year 32 and would later, on admission, formally adopt their councils' chosen League name, the Antlerlords). The Sonora Drifting Coyotes, who had applied in Year 33 and been told the same. The Yucatan Vibrant Quetzals, who had applied in Year 34 and been told the same. All three asked, in carefully phrased letters, whether the League was now in a position to reconsider. The Lynx, by the same mail, asked the same question. The Office's response to each of the four was identical: <em>"Yes. We were wrong. Please send your roster."</em></p>
        <p>The four delegations arrived at Brewer's Reach over the course of the Year 36 mid-season. The Lynx came first — a single Lynx coach, alone, carrying the rosters and credentials of all five active knights, because the Lynx had decided, in their own way, that this was a one-Lynx job. The Moose came second — three Moose, by river, having floated down the Saint-Laurent system to the coast and then walked overland the rest of the way. The Coyotes came third — six Coyotes, in a small caravan, having taken a route north through the Sonora desert and east through the former Texas grassland that the Bison's coaching staff later certified was indeed the most efficient line. The Quetzals came last — by air, in a fortnight of relay flights with rest stops the Quetzals selected based on what trees the Old Ones had not chopped down. All four delegations were welcomed. All four were inducted at the Year 36 founding bell.</p>
        <p>Featherquill's column for the founding-bell announcement read, in part: <em>"The League is now twenty teams across the former North American continent. It is not the United States of America's league. It was never the United States of America's league. The United States of America does not exist. The League exists. The League is twenty teams now and it is, in my honest professional opinion, the most interesting it has ever been. I am tired. I am also a journalist. The two facts are not, on close inspection, entirely separable."</em></p>
        <p>The bracket schedule, beginning Year 36 mid-season, draws twelve of the twenty teams at random per season for the standard qualifier-then-eight-team-ladder format. The other eight sit out and prepare. Ranked teams continue to receive byes through to the quarterfinals; the qualifier round has expanded to four matches accordingly. The Lynx coach, on being told the format, asked only one question: whether the qualifier matches counted. The Office of the Commissioner confirmed that they did. The Lynx coach nodded, said "good," and left to find a place to eat. The Office's chief of staff has reported that, as of the most recent count, no one in the Office has yet figured out where the Lynx coach went to eat or whether they ever returned to their lodging.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Geography Caucus addendum (Snowcrest) · Office of the Commissioner, "Ratification of the Continental Expansion" · Year 36 founding bell</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Caucus Playbook Rotations</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Coaches' Caucus pre-season tradition · in continuous practice since Year 30</div>
        <p>Every team in the League keeps a binder. The binders sit on a shelf in the Coaches' Caucus archive room in Brewer's Reach, twenty-five binders for the twenty-five named playbooks, with summaries on the spine and full doctrinal notes inside. The binders are not, by any reading of League rules, owned by any one team. They are the League's playbooks. Coaches read them. Coaches argue about them. Coaches, at the start of every off-season, draw lots to find out which one their team will run for the upcoming year.</p>
        <p>The rotation is not, technically, mandatory. The Caucus's official position, codified in the Year 30 Playbook Rotation Rule, is that each head coach <em>"shall draw a numbered tile from the season ballot bag and shall in good faith adopt the corresponding doctrine for the playing year."</em> The phrase <em>"in good faith"</em> has been litigated three times, twice unsuccessfully (by coaches who argued they had drawn an unfit doctrine for their roster) and once successfully (by the Frogs, who argued in Year 32 that drawing GLASSCANNON for a team built around two healers was, in their captain's words, <em>"administratively absurd"</em>). The Caucus, after some hours of debate, granted the Frogs a re-draw. The Frogs drew TURTLE. The Frogs went 11-2 that season.</p>
        <p>The twenty-five playbooks are not all balanced — some are clearly stronger in some matchups than others. The Caucus has made this a feature, not a bug. Pell Whittlestone, when asked in Year 33 whether the rotation should be adjusted to weight stronger doctrines lower, responded with what is now the Caucus's official line on the matter: <em>"The rotation is the entertainment. If every team played the right doctrine for their roster every year, the league would be predictable and we could all retire. We do not want to retire. The Foxes will draw RUSH next year. The Foxes will run RUSH whether or not RUSH is good for them. We will all watch what happens. This is the point."</em></p>
        <p>The names of the doctrines have evolved. The original Year-30 binders had eleven entries (BALANCED, RUSH, TURTLE, PHALANX, LONE WOLF, SKIRMISHER, SNIPER STACK, CAUTIOUS, ENDURE, DOCTRINE, PATIENT). The current twenty-five include later additions ratified by the Caucus over the seasons: BERSERKER (Year 31), PACK (Year 31), ANARCHIST (Year 32, after the Frogs' re-draw incident, deliberately added as an extreme), VANGUARD, CAVALIER, STOIC (Year 32), WHIRLWIND (Year 33), COUNTER-STRIKE (Year 33), FRENZY, WOLFPACK, GLASS CANNON (all Year 34), TACTICIAN, HOLDOUT, SCRAPPER (Year 35). The Caucus is, by Whittlestone's standing recommendation, careful about adding new doctrines — the rotation works because it surprises everyone, and surprise requires variety, but variety also requires that no one entry be subtly the same as another. <em>"GLASS CANNON is not BERSERKER,"</em> Whittlestone wrote in her Year 34 ratification memo. <em>"BERSERKER closes. GLASS CANNON does not. If you cannot tell the difference watching ten matches, the doctrine should not be in the binder."</em></p>
        <p>The teams' actual style assignments for any given year are, by Caucus tradition, posted on the public board outside the Office of the Commissioner the morning of the founding bell. Featherquill's column for that morning has, every year since Year 30, published the full grid. <em>"Twenty teams. Twenty-five binders. The Caucus draws. We watch. The audience watches. By the second match of the season, every audience member has a strong opinion on whether the binder their team drew is going to work this year. They are usually wrong. The point is not whether they are right. The point is that they have an opinion."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "The Binder Draw," Featherquill's annual founding-bell explainer column</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Commitment Directive</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Coaches' Caucus pre-season working session · Year 36 training camp, ratified before the founding bell</div>
        <p>The complaint had been growing for several seasons. It came from coaches first, then from broadcast analysts, then — once Featherquill picked it up in her Year 35 closeout column — from the audience. The complaint was: <em>knights, in the middle stretch of any round, jiggle</em>. They take a step left. They take a step right. They take another step left. They do not, by any close reading of the footage, appear to be moving toward anything. They are not moving away from anything either. They are simply standing somewhere they cannot quite commit to leaving and cannot quite commit to staying.</p>
        <p>The phenomenon had several names across the League. The Beavers' coaching staff called it <em>the dither</em>. The Sharks called it <em>the indecision</em>. The Pandas, with characteristic dry self-awareness, called it <em>the standard mid-round Panda</em>. The Wolves did not call it anything because the Wolves' assistant coach refused to acknowledge that the Wolves did it, although film analysis of the Year 35 R7 Wolves–Otters fixture had clearly shown three Wolves doing it simultaneously across one twenty-second window. The Wolves' assistant coach, when shown the footage, said: <em>"Those Wolves were guarding."</em> The film analyst, in a follow-up interview, said: <em>"They were not guarding. They were dithering."</em> Both descriptions were entered into the record.</p>
        <p>The diagnosis came from a sniper named Korvik who fights for the Ravens. Korvik wrote a single-page paper for the Caucus's pre-season working session. The paper opens: <em>"A knight on the field has, at any moment, a target it could close on, a teammate it could support, a position it could hold, or a corner it could refuse. The dither is what happens when the knight has access to all four options and has not yet committed to any of them. The dither does not end on its own. The knight has to be told: pick one. Hold it. Reconsider in a moment. Not now."</em> The paper is, by Caucus archivist Kirrin's note, the shortest tactical contribution ever submitted to the working session. It is also the most circulated.</p>
        <p>The Caucus, working with Pell Whittlestone, formalized Korvik's diagnosis into the <em>Commitment Directive</em>: a coaching standard agreed across all sixteen teams' training programs for Year 36. Its three rules, as printed on every team's Year 36 training-camp wall:</p>
        <p><em>1. Commit to a heading for at least eight strides before reconsidering, except in three cases: your target died, your target crossed into melee range, or you have been told to redirect by your bench.</em></p>
        <p><em>2. When you have no target, hold a position. The position is your guard. Do not drift. Pick the position once, hold it for sixty strides, and only then reconsider where to stand. The team will rotate around its anchors. You may be an anchor. Behave like one.</em></p>
        <p><em>3. When two of you are closing on the same enemy, do not push each other off-line. Trust the side-by-side. The side-by-side is faster than the wide arc.</em></p>
        <p>The directive went into effect at the Year 36 training camps. By the third week of camp, every team had adopted the language. By the fourth week, the dither had measurably decreased — Whittlestone's training-camp tracking, conducted with stopwatches and grid-paper across two hundred sample rounds, showed that <em>per-knight directional reversals dropped from an average of 1.4 per ten strides to 0.3</em>. Whittlestone, in her closing-week presentation, called the result "the largest single-season behavioral change in League knight conduct since the Float Gas Foundry's first delivery, which was admittedly a chemical change rather than a behavioral one." The Caucus laughed, by the secretary's note, harder than the joke really merited; the secretary attributed the laughter to relief.</p>
        <p>The Polar Bears, in their first training camp as a League team, adopted the directive on day one and asked whether it had a name in their language. Whitepaw answered for the team: <em>"In our language, this is just walking. We have always done this. We were not aware the other teams did not."</em> The Caucus, by all accounts, did not laugh at this. The Polar Bears were not making a joke.</p>
        <p>Featherquill's closing column on the directive: <em>"The League has, for eight seasons, been teaching its knights how to fight. It has not been teaching them how to walk. The Polar Bears walked thirty-two days in the snow to remind us. The Bayou Tigers stalk for a reason. The Bison stand because someone has to. The Ravens commit because Korvik wrote one good page. We are about to watch a much better League. I am, for the first time in three seasons, not certain who is going to win the Coronation Cup. This is the best feeling sportswriting offers."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Coaches' Caucus, "The Commitment Directive — pre-season working session minutes" · Year 36 training camp, week four</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The First Frostfall Friendly — PLR vs LYX, Pre-Season Year 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · the first time the League's two northernmost teams faced each other on a sanctioned field</div>
        <p>The Polar Bears and the Lynx had, in the eight pre-season weeks before the Year 36 founding bell, not played one another. They had, by the Caucus's pre-season register, not <em>met</em> one another either: the Anchorage and Whitehorse settlements are six hundred miles apart by the high northern road, and neither team's roster had crossed that distance for casual purposes. The Caucus, briefing the two head coaches at week one of training camp, suggested a friendly. Neither head coach was sure that "friendly" was the right word.</p>
        <p>The match was scheduled for the third week of pre-season at the neutral venue at Boise — chosen on the (correct) assumption that any cold-climate venue would, by tradition, advantage one of the two teams. The Polar Bears arrived two days early. The Lynx arrived nine minutes before warmups, in five separate transport carts, having traveled the last leg from five different directions. The Caucus's pre-match register noted, under the heading <em>arrival behavior</em>: <em>"Lynx team's five active knights traveled, by their preference, separately. Their five coaches traveled separately as well. The Lynx's equipment cart was driven by a non-team adolescent who, on arrival, asked which equipment belonged to whom and was told, by each Lynx knight in turn, to leave the cart and go find lunch. The cart was unloaded by the Lynx knights themselves, individually, in five visits across the morning. The team's pre-match meal was taken in five separate booths in five different concession areas. The Polar Bears, by contrast, traveled together, ate together, dressed together, and emerged from the locker tunnel in a single line, in their ceremonial cloaks. The pre-match contrast was, frankly, unforgettable."</em></p>
        <p>The match itself was a five-round Best-of-Five deathmatch on the Boise Frosthold Pitch — a cold-climate venue chosen, by Caucus selection, for its reputation as the most temperature-honest field on the calendar. The Polar Bears took round one in two minutes, forty-one seconds — the shortest round of the entire pre-season — by the simple expedient of forming a single advancing wall down the long axis of the pitch and refusing to break. The Lynx, who had drawn a five-knight line across the field's defensive third, spent the round attempting to pick at the wall with sniper fire from five different angles. The wall absorbed the fire and walked through it. The Lynx commentator, watching this, was reported by the LMG sideline mic to say (and the mic is, here, reproducing her exact words): <em>"this is what walking together looks like, to people who do not walk together."</em></p>
        <p>Round two went the other way. The Lynx, having seen the wall, did not engage the wall. They scattered. The match playback, reviewed by the Caucus's tactical analyst Pell Whittlestone, shows five Lynx knights occupying five distinct quadrants of the pitch, each operating independently, each refusing to be drawn into a center engagement. The Polar Bears, walking forward as a unit, found themselves in a center they had no opponent in. The round ended with the Polar Bears having, by the timer's read, walked the full length of the pitch and back without firing a weapon. The Lynx, picking from cover, took three Polar Bears down with sniper fire over the course of seven minutes. The Lynx commentator's quote, this time: <em>"this is what hunting alone looks like, to people who hunt together."</em></p>
        <p>Rounds three through five split — Polar Bears took round three with another wall, Lynx took round four with another scatter, and round five was, by general account, the most interesting round of the pre-season. The Polar Bears began in their wall formation. The Lynx began in their scatter. Then, two minutes in, both formations broke at exactly the same moment, and for exactly the same reason: the Boise venue's central feature is a long ridge of low ice that runs north-south down the middle of the pitch, and at the two-minute mark the ridge had, in the round's prior trampling, become a set of low pillars rather than a continuous ridge. The Polar Bears, who had been walking around the ridge, suddenly had a sight line through it. The Lynx, who had been hiding behind the ridge, suddenly had no cover. Both teams adjusted in the same heartbeat. The round ended in a four-on-three engagement at the ridge's southern end, with the Polar Bears winning by one knight after a Lynx Sniper's railgun jammed mid-pull on a frost build-up the venue's heaters had not, that morning, fully cleared.</p>
        <p>Final score: 3-2 to the Polar Bears, by Caucus record. The Bears took the bracket-staged win bonus. The Lynx took the post-match interview reluctantly. The Lynx team captain, Halfpaw the Patient, offered a single sentence on tape: <em>"The Polar Bears walk well. We will keep watching them. They will not, I think, watch us as carefully, but that is a problem they may want to address."</em> The Polar Bear captain, Whitepaw the Steady, when asked for response, said: <em>"We watched. We will keep watching. The cold here is shallow. The cold at home is deeper. We will see them again, perhaps, in a venue that is colder."</em></p>
        <p>The Caucus, reviewing the match for its tactical archive, marked the round-five engagement as <em>"the most useful single round of the pre-season"</em> for what it taught both teams' coaches about the limits of their respective formations. Whittlestone's analysis, in her pre-season summary, noted: <em>"The wall is brittle when the cover ahead of it dissolves. The scatter is brittle when the cover behind it dissolves. Both teams learned this in the same heartbeat. Neither team will, I expect, ever forget."</em> The friendly is now scheduled to recur — a yearly Frostfall match between PLR and LYX, held at a rotating cold-climate venue. The Caucus has not yet named the trophy. The Polar Bears, asked for a suggestion, suggested <em>"the Cold Stones."</em> The Lynx, asked separately, suggested <em>"the Cold Stones."</em> The Caucus took this as enough of a quorum and adopted the name. The Cold Stones trophy will be forged by Pell Whittlestone, who has, on accepting the commission, said only: <em>"I will need a colder forge for this one."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus archive, "First Frostfall Friendly — PLR vs LYX, Year 36 pre-season" · Boise Frosthold Pitch, week three of pre-season</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The First Outside Delivery — Year 30, Boise Foundry to Tampa</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · the first time the Float Gas Foundry shipped a complete formula batch to a non-Boise city · why the Sharks were not, that year, banned for it</div>
        <p>The Boise Float Gas Foundry began operations in Year 28, the same year the League itself was founded. For its first two seasons it produced gas only for the Brewer's Reach venue in Boston — the founding pitch, the only pitch that had its inflation rig installed before the inaugural match. Every other team's home venue used League-owned reserve cylinders trucked in from Boise once a month. This was widely understood to be a temporary arrangement that would, by Year 30, end.</p>
        <p>It did not end on schedule. The Foundry's chief chemist (a salamander named Pell Whittlestone, who would later forge the Coronation Cup crown) had been working on a city-specific formula adjustment that, in her own pre-shipment notes, she described as <em>"not quite ready, but I have been told the Tampa shipment must go out by the third Tuesday of the month, and I am, at this point, not in a position to argue about Tuesdays."</em> The shipment went out on the third Tuesday. The shipment arrived in Tampa on the fifth Friday. The shipment had been refrigerated badly somewhere in the Midwest leg, and the formula's <em>"song"</em> — the sensory quality the Float Gas Tasters listen for in approved batches — had, by Whittlestone's own retest on a sealed reserve sample, gone slightly flat.</p>
        <p>The Tampa Tornado Sharks took delivery of the slightly-flat batch on the morning of their Year 30 R3 home match, against the Phoenix Furious Foxes. The Sharks' equipment manager (Reef Tinkerbarrel, a hammerhead with a long-standing personal grudge against the entire concept of refrigerated logistics) inspected the batch, smelled the song, found it flat, and made the decision — at his own risk and without consulting the Foundry — to use the batch anyway, on the grounds that <em>"the away team will not know it is flat. The home team will know it is flat. We will adjust our balloon-pop calibration to compensate. The Foxes will not adjust theirs."</em> Tinkerbarrel later wrote, in the post-match incident report: <em>"This was not, in retrospect, the cleanest decision I have ever made."</em></p>
        <p>What happened in the match was that the Shark balloons, calibrated for the flat song, popped reliably. The Fox balloons, calibrated for the standard song and now subjected to a flat batch, popped <em>under-pressure</em> — meaning they popped at lower-than-intended impact thresholds, sometimes from glancing hits, occasionally from the Shark Brawler simply <em>walking past</em> a Fox knight at close range. The first round ended in three minutes, twelve seconds. The Foxes' coaching staff filed an inquiry on the field, mid-match, which was, in the way of these things, dismissed by the on-field referee on the grounds that the gas had passed the Foundry's outgoing inspection. The match continued. The Foxes lost rounds two through five. The Foxes lost the match 5-0, the first home shutout in the Sharks' history.</p>
        <p>Whittlestone, alerted to the discrepancy by an angry Foxes' equipment manager who had retained two of the affected balloons and shipped them overnight to Boise, retested the reserve sample, found the flat song, and immediately suspended the entire Tampa shipment. She also — and this is the part the Foundry's official archive is reluctant to record — wrote a private note to the Sharks' captain, hand-delivered by a Foundry intern, that read in its entirety: <em>"I know what you did. I know how you did it. I will not, this once, tell the Caucus. The Foundry's reputation is, frankly, more valuable than your one home win. Do this again and I will personally inspect every shipment that leaves this building for the rest of my life. Do not test this."</em> The Sharks' captain replied, by the same intern: <em>"Understood. We will not test this. We did, in the moment, also not realize how flat the batch was. I will, going forward, eat the cost of a delayed shipment rather than ship out a flat batch. With apologies."</em></p>
        <p>The Caucus did not, in the official record, learn about the flat-batch exploit until Year 33, when Tinkerbarrel — by then retired and writing his memoirs — published the equipment manager's logbook in serial in <em>The Lobster Reach Daily</em>. By that point the Sharks had won three championships and were widely respected; the Caucus, reviewing the disclosure, noted in its archive that <em>"the events of Year 30 R3 took place under a regulatory framework that did not, at the time, contemplate this exploit. We are not retroactively voiding the Sharks' R3 win. We are, however, formally noting that the Foundry's outgoing-inspection protocol was upgraded in Year 31 specifically because of this incident, and that the upgrade was correct."</em> Whittlestone, asked for comment by Featherquill on the disclosure, said only: <em>"The Foundry has not, in seven years, shipped another flat batch. The Sharks have not, in seven years, asked us to."</em> Featherquill chose to print the quote without commentary. Featherquill later said, off the record, that this was <em>"the hardest no-comment of my career."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundry archive, "Year 30 R3 Tampa shipment incident" · cross-referenced with <em>The Lobster Reach Daily</em>, vol. 7, issue 11 · disclosure year</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Brewer's Reach Final, Year 33 — The Healer Who Walked</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · referenced in The Bow, in Why a Healer Wanders, and in three separate musings · the canonical account of what the Wolves were, that night, acknowledging</div>
        <p>The Year 33 Final was Boston Brisk Beavers versus Seattle Sleepless Wolves, played at Brewer's Reach Pitch in Boston on Foundation Day. The Beavers entered as defending champions; the Wolves entered as the higher seed. Both teams had had a difficult bracket — the Wolves had, in their semifinal, lost a Tank to permadeath; the Beavers had, in their quarterfinal, exhausted their entire bench down to the active line plus one. The Final was, by every pre-game analyst's read, going to be slow, careful, and grindy. It was the first two rounds.</p>
        <p>Round three was the round the Healer died. Her name was Avery Loambright, and she was a Hedgehog by species — Helena native, drawn from the pre-League combat circuit of generations standing (the Helena tradition predated HED's formal League admission, which would not arrive until Year 35), and on loan to the Wolves for the Year 33 season under the inter-team Healer-shortage exemption that the Caucus had ratified in Year 32 and that no one liked but everyone used. The exemption permitted, by special Caucus dispensation, the loan of qualified non-League Healers from recognized regional combat circuits to League rosters in years when Healer attrition exceeded the Caucus's standing replenishment rate; Year 32 had been such a year, and the Wolves had filed paperwork. She had, in her ten matches with the Wolves, never been knocked down. She had not, in her career to that point, ever lost a charge — a Healer's "charge" being, by League terminology, the teammate they're actively healing. Loambright's charge in round three was the Wolves' Striker, Crash Wartooth, who was at that moment retreating across the center of the pitch with a Beavers Brawler in pursuit.</p>
        <p>What happened next is the part everyone disputes. The broadcast tape shows Loambright stepping out from behind cover at a forty-five degree angle from Wartooth's path, opening a clear sight line for her healing beam. The broadcast tape also shows a Beavers Sniper — Bristlebeard the Second, who had, in this Final, been given a clear instruction by his bench to <em>not target the Wolves' Healer if any other Wolf was in range</em> — taking a shot at Wartooth that traveled, by the kinetics tracker's read, on a line that intersected Loambright's chest at the exact moment her healing beam was opening. The shot was meant for Wartooth. The shot hit the Healer.</p>
        <p>Loambright was, by the post-match medical record, dead before she hit the pitch. The shot was a chest-cavity through-shot from a Beaver railgun at twenty-three paces; the round was reading as a kill the moment it left the rifle. Bristlebeard the Second, watching the shot land, walked off the pitch immediately — by his own later testimony, "I knew, watching the line, that I had killed someone I had been told not to. I did not need to be told what to do next. I needed to leave the field." The Beavers' bench replaced him with a backup Sniper. The round continued. The Wolves won round three on the strength of a Crash Wartooth solo charge through the Beaver line that the broadcast booth would, later, describe as <em>"the most controlled grief any of us have ever watched in this sport."</em></p>
        <p>The Wolves did not, in any subsequent round of the match, attempt to retaliate against Bristlebeard the Second's bench. They did not target the Beaver Healer. They did not target the Beaver Tank. They focused on the active line, and they won rounds four and five, and they won the match, and they won the Year 33 championship, and at the post-match line they did the thing that has become known, in League shorthand, as <em>The Bow</em>. Six Wolves walked to where Loambright's body had been (it had, by League protocol, already been removed and prepared for transport; the spot on the pitch had been chalked by a Foundation steward), formed a small circle around the chalk mark, and the Wolves' captain — Halfmoon Greylane, then in her third season as captain — bowed once, deeply, in the way the Wolves bow at the den. The bow lasted, by the broadcast's stopwatch, eleven seconds. The crowd was, by every account, completely silent. The Beaver bench was completely silent. Bristlebeard the Second, who had been watching from the dugout in his post-shot exile, was visibly weeping.</p>
        <p>What the bow meant — what it has come, in the eight intervening seasons, to mean — is the subject of the canonical fan letter <em>"On the Bow"</em>. Greylane has not, in eight subsequent seasons, ever publicly explained the bow. Asked once at a post-match press conference about the practice, she answered: <em>"The bow is a Wolf thing. It is not for me to explain. It is for the body to receive."</em> The interviewer, who had done her homework, did not press. Bristlebeard the Second resumed shooting the next season. He has not, in eight seasons since, taken another shot that traveled on a line that intersected a Wolf Healer's path. The League's archery instructors now teach this as a standard — they call it <em>"the Loambright correction"</em> — and Bristlebeard, who has a quiet relationship with the practice, has, by his own wife's account, never once in private referred to it by that name. He calls it <em>"the correction I owe."</em> He has been heard to say this at the dinner table. His wife has not pressed. The dinner table is where this is buried.</p>
        <p>Loambright's name is in the Hall of Fallen Heroes, in the Boston Foundation Hall, third row from the door, sixth name. The Wolves visit the row at the start of every season's Brewer's Reach match. They do not take photographs. They do not give statements. They walk in, they bow, they walk out. The bow takes, by Foundation steward measurement, eleven seconds. It has taken eleven seconds every year, every visit, since Year 33. It will, by the Wolves' captain's own account, take eleven seconds every year for as long as the Wolves are a team. <em>"This is the duration the body received,"</em> Greylane said once, asked, <em>"and the body decides the duration. We do not."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus archive, "Year 33 Final — Brewer's Reach Pitch — incident report and the bow"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The First Coronation Cup, Year 31 — How the Raccoons Took the Crown</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · the Coronation Cup's inaugural season · why the brass crown has, since, slept in pawn shops</div>
        <p>The Coronation Cup did not exist in the League's first three seasons. The League's championship was, through Year 30, settled by the Brewer's Reach Final — a five-round Best-of-Five deathmatch that produced a clear champion every season. The Cup was proposed by Pell Whittlestone in the Year 30 off-season as <em>"a separate, single-match crown event held at a single neutral venue on Foundation Day, distinct from the bracket-end Final, decided by a continuous-mode rule that rewards control rather than knockouts."</em> Her motivation, by her own pre-proposal notes (which the Caucus has archived in full), was structural: the Brewer's Reach Final, by Year 30, was being routinely decided in three rounds by the team that opened with the most aggressive Brawler line, and Whittlestone — who had been watching the Final closely for three seasons — believed the sport was developing a single dominant tactical mode. <em>"A second crown that rewards a different tactical approach,"</em> she wrote, <em>"will not, by itself, fix the homogenization. It will, however, force teams to maintain at least two distinct tactical capabilities. The League will be more interesting. The Foundation will be more interesting. I, personally, will be less bored at Foundation Day."</em></p>
        <p>The Caucus ratified the proposal in Year 31's pre-season working session. The first Coronation Cup was held at the Reno Open Court on Foundation Day, Year 31. Whittlestone forged the brass crown herself, in the Foundry, over six weeks in the off-season. She did not bill the League for the labor. She billed the League for one lobster. The lobster invoice is in the Foundation's accounting archive. It has not been paid.</p>
        <p>The first Cup match was a four-team round-robin (the Caucus had not, by Year 31, finalized the Cup's bracket structure), with the Foxes, the Beavers, the Wolves, and the Raccoons all entered on the strength of their Year 30 standings. The format was: each team played every other team in a fifteen-minute crown-control match, with the winner determined by total points scored across the three matches. The Raccoons — who had finished fourth in the Year 30 regular season and had, by every analyst's pre-Cup read, no business being in the final — won the inaugural Cup with a total of 124 points across their three matches. The next-highest total was the Wolves' 89.</p>
        <p>What the Raccoons did, tactically, was develop the first sanctioned use of <em>crown rotation</em> — a continuous-mode tactic in which the team's Brawler picks up the crown, scores for ten seconds, voluntarily drops the crown to a teammate, and re-engages the opposing line as a non-crown-bearer. The teammate scores for ten seconds, drops to another teammate, re-engages. The crown moves through the team's active line approximately every ten seconds, and the team's defensive formation — designed around protecting whoever currently holds the crown — rotates in lockstep. The opposing team, attempting to focus fire on the crown-bearer, finds the crown-bearer changing every ten seconds, and finds the defensive formation rotating with the change, and finds itself unable to commit a sustained offensive engagement against any single target. The Raccoons developed the rotation in their off-season practice in the Pittsburgh quarry venue (which they were, at the time, sub-leasing from the Ravens' settlement, in advance of the Ravens' Year 35 League entry; the venue had not yet been registered as a League pitch). They practiced it against each other for nine weeks. They debuted it at the Reno Open Court on Foundation Day. The other three teams were, by all post-Cup accounts, completely unprepared.</p>
        <p>The Raccoons' captain, Dustpaw Trashbright (the great-uncle of the current Raccoons' captain, Trashbright the Younger), accepted the crown on the broadcast post-match line and immediately did the thing that has become known as <em>"the Raccoon dignity."</em> Trashbright took the crown, looked at it, looked at the broadcast camera, looked back at the crown, and said: <em>"This is a beautiful crown. I appreciate it. I will be taking it home."</em> The phrase <em>"taking it home"</em> was, by the broadcast's understanding, a routine post-match commitment to display the trophy at the Pittsburgh team facility. By the next morning, the crown had, by Foundation reports, vanished from the team's transport rig en route from Reno to Pittsburgh. By the morning after that, it had been recovered in a Reno pawn shop, in good condition, with a pawn ticket made out to the name <em>"Dustpaw Trashbright."</em> Trashbright, asked at the recovery interview whether the pawning had been a misunderstanding, said: <em>"I took it home. The Raccoon home is, broadly, anywhere I am. I was, that morning, in a pawn shop. The crown was at home. The Foundation has, regrettably, located it. I will go retrieve it. I will not, in the future, redeposit it in the same shop."</em> He did not return it to the team facility for three weeks. The Foundation did not, formally, complain. The Raccoons paid the pawn shop a small storage fee, which the shop's owner accepted in lobsters.</p>
        <p>This is the practice. The Raccoons have won six of eight Coronation Cups (Years 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, and the most recent Year 36 founding-bell Cup). On every winning year, the morning after Foundation Day, the crown has been reported missing from the team transport. On every winning year, by midday, the crown has been recovered in a Reno pawn shop. On every winning year, the pawn ticket has been made out to a member of the active Raccoon roster. The Foundation has stopped commenting. The pawn shop owner — whose name is Moss Quickfingers, a beaver of unknown allegiance who has held the same shop for sixteen years — has, in three separate interviews, declined to comment on the practice except to say: <em>"It is the only crown I store. I store it for the Foundation. The Foundation knows where it is. The Raccoons know where it is. I do not, technically, know whose crown it is. I am paid in lobster. The lobster is good. I have stopped asking questions."</em> The crown is, by the Foundation's count, currently at Quickfingers' shop. It will be, by the Foundation's count, returned to the team facility within the week. This has been the rhythm for six years. The Foundation has built a budget line for it. The line is called <em>"crown retrieval logistics"</em> and it amounts, annually, to four lobsters and a small storage fee. Featherquill, asked about the practice, said only: <em>"This is the cleanest sport I have ever covered. The sport's most prestigious trophy is, every year, briefly stolen by its winner and recovered by lunch the next day. There is no fraud. There is no harm. The Raccoons are, in a way that I cannot bring myself to describe as anything other than charming, the best thing about Foundation Day."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation archive, "Year 31 Coronation Cup — inaugural · the inception of the Raccoon practice"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Tinkerbarrel Disclosure — Year 33, and Why the Sharks Were Not Banned</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · the publication of the Year 30 R3 flat-batch logbook · the Caucus's response · a postscript to The First Outside Delivery</div>
        <p>The Year 30 R3 flat-batch incident — the Sharks' undeclared use of an under-pressure Float Gas batch in their home shutout of the Foxes — was an open secret in the League's locker rooms for three years. Reef Tinkerbarrel, the Sharks' equipment manager who had personally made the decision, retired in the Year 32 off-season after eighteen seasons of service. He was sixty-four years old. He had, by his own pre-retirement statement, been <em>"writing a memoir for, frankly, the entire decade prior, and I am, on retirement, going to publish it. I have run that decision past my wife. My wife has approved. I have run it past Whittlestone. Whittlestone has, off the record, approved as well, on the grounds that the Foundry's outgoing-inspection protocol is now sufficiently robust that the disclosure cannot be used as a how-to guide. I have not run it past the Foundation. The Foundation does not, in retirement, get to run anything past me."</em></p>
        <p>The memoir was published in serial in <em>The Lobster Reach Daily</em> across Year 33's spring quarter, in twelve weekly installments. The eighth installment was the flat-batch installment. It contained the full text of Tinkerbarrel's Year 30 R3 equipment-manager logbook, including his pre-match decision to use the flat batch, the Sharks' captain's pre-match acknowledgment of the decision (the Sharks' captain at the time, who had since retired and emigrated to Olympia, declined to comment for the memoir but did not, formally, deny the entry), and Whittlestone's hand-delivered private note demanding the practice never recur. The eighth installment was, by every account, the most-read single issue of <em>The Lobster Reach Daily</em> in the publication's twenty-three-year history. The publication's print run for that issue had to be doubled mid-week.</p>
        <p>The Caucus convened an emergency working session two weeks after the eighth installment's publication. The session was called by the Foxes' coaching staff, which had, in the intervening two weeks, formally requested that the Year 30 R3 result be voided and the Sharks' subsequent championship records be reviewed for similar undisclosed exploits. The Sharks' coaching staff entered the session prepared to defend, in essence, the franchise. What happened in the session — by the working-session minutes, which were unsealed by the Caucus three years later under the standard archival timeline — was that Whittlestone, attending the session in her capacity as Foundry chief chemist and ex-officio Caucus advisor, opened with a forty-minute presentation. The presentation's title slide read, in her handwriting: <em>"What the Year 30 R3 Incident Tells Us About the Foundry's Outgoing-Inspection Protocol, and Why the Foxes Are Asking the Wrong Question."</em></p>
        <p>The presentation, in summary: the flat batch was the Foundry's failure, not the Sharks'. The shipment had been refrigerated badly because the Foundry's refrigeration logistics, in Year 30, were managed by a single contractor on a one-truck weekly route, and the contractor had — on the third Tuesday of that month — driven the route in unseasonably warm weather without the secondary cooling rig that the Foundry's outgoing-inspection protocol now requires. The flat batch had passed the Foundry's outgoing-batch test by a small margin (Whittlestone's records showed it had been on the threshold of acceptable when it left the building) and had degraded further in transit. The Sharks' equipment manager, receiving the batch, had detected the degradation; the Sharks' captain had been informed; the Sharks' decision had been to use the batch with a calibration adjustment. The decision, Whittlestone argued, was <em>"a reasonable response to a Foundry-side delivery failure that no team in the League at that time had, by any standard, the technical capability to remediate properly. The Foundry should not have shipped that batch. The Foundry, in Year 31, instituted the Year-31 protocol upgrade specifically to prevent this. The Foundry has not, in seven years, shipped another flat batch. The Sharks have not, in seven years, requested another such batch. The exploit is, in technical terms, no longer feasible. Punishing the Sharks for an exploit that was, in 30, available to every team and is, today, available to none, would be the Foundation imposing retroactive standards on Year 30 that did not exist at the time. I do not, in my professional capacity as Foundry chief chemist, recommend this."</em></p>
        <p>The working session voted, by 11 to 4, against voiding the Year 30 R3 result. The four dissenting votes were the Foxes' coaching staff, the Foxes' captain (who attended in delegation), the Owls' captain (who voted on principle, not on Foundry-side liability), and Featherquill in her ex-officio press-corps observer capacity. The Caucus's official statement, issued the morning after the working session, was a single paragraph: <em>"The Year 30 R3 Tampa shutout result stands. The Caucus formally notes that the Foundry's outgoing-inspection protocol was upgraded in Year 31 specifically because of this incident, and that the upgrade was correct. The Caucus formally notes that the Sharks' decision to use the flat batch was made under regulatory conditions that did not, at the time, contemplate the exploit, and that punishment is not, in this Caucus's view, retroactively appropriate. The Caucus thanks Reef Tinkerbarrel for his disclosure, which has materially improved the Foundry's procedures, and which the Caucus is — given its content — formally entering into the official archive."</em> The Sharks' coaching staff, asked for response, said only: <em>"We are grateful. We will not, going forward, repeat the conduct. We do not, today, owe the Foxes any apology beyond the one we already offered in Year 30 — which was made in private and which we are now, on the public record, willing to repeat: we made a regrettable decision, and we are sorry. The Foxes have, in private, accepted this apology. We hope they will, in public, accept it as well."</em> The Foxes' captain, on tape, said: <em>"Yes. We accept. We will see them next bracket. We will be paying very close attention to the inflation rig."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus working-session minutes, "Year 33 Tinkerbarrel Disclosure response" · unsealed Year 36 under standard archival timeline</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Northwalk — Year 35</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Office of the Commissioner, "Polar Bears Inclusion" · cross-referenced with the Anchorage settlement's own travel log</div>
        <p>The Anchorage settlement's application to the League, in Year 35, was hand-delivered. The Polar Bears walked. From Anchorage to Brewer's Reach is, by the high northern road and the inland reroute around the Cascades, two thousand and forty-six miles. The delegation that walked it was four bears: Tamzen Whitepaw (the eldest, nominal leader), Saltgale Stillpaw (the strongest, designated to carry the application's wax-sealed envelope), Drift Whitepaw (Tamzen's grandniece, then nineteen, the youngest delegate), and Hummock Slowtread (the steadiest, designated to set the pace and to refuse to break it).</p>
        <p>They walked thirty-two days. They averaged sixty-four miles a day. They did not, by Hummock's own travel log (which the Anchorage settlement has, by tradition, displayed in the Frostfall Hall foyer), take a single rest day. They did, by the same log, stop for nine separate animal communities along the route — three Coyote outposts in what was once Wyoming, two Bison camps in the high Plains, two Raven roosts in the foundry districts, the Wichita Wolves' rural pack-grounds (where the delegation was offered overnight shelter, which they accepted, and a bowl of stew, which they declined as inappropriate to a delegation in transit), and the Otter harbor at Olympia (where they spent six hours and ate the only meal of the journey they had not packed themselves — a salmon Drift requested by name).</p>
        <p>They arrived at Brewer's Reach on a Tuesday morning at approximately 9:14 a.m. They had not, by their own pre-arrival commitment, sent word ahead. The Foundation lobby steward on duty that Tuesday — a beaver named Sandquill Bristlebrush, no relation to the family — was at the front desk reading a column. He looked up when the door opened. He looked back down. He looked up again. He stood. He has, in three subsequent interviews, described the moment in identical phrasing: <em>"They were tall. They were tired. They were polite. They had walked, by my next-morning understanding, two thousand and forty-six miles. The first thing Whitepaw asked for was water. The second thing she asked for was a chair. The third thing she asked for was the Commissioner. I had not, in eleven years at this desk, ever fetched the Commissioner without an appointment. I fetched her."</em></p>
        <p>Whiskerstone was at the Foundation Hall within nineteen minutes. She did not, by Treadwell's later broadcast account (Treadwell happened to be in the building auditing the LMG booth's quarterly equipment list and made the recording without official sanction), say anything for the first four minutes after entering the lobby. She sat across from Whitepaw. Whitepaw read the application aloud. The application was four pages. Whitepaw read it without pause, in a voice the Foundation steward later described as <em>"the voice of a person who has memorized the document on the road and is, on arrival, only verifying that the words still come out in the right order."</em> The reading took eleven minutes. Whiskerstone did not, in those eleven minutes, take a single note. She listened. When the reading ended, Whiskerstone read the application herself, silently, while Whitepaw drank a third cup of water. The silent reading took six minutes. At the end of the silent reading, Whiskerstone signed the admission line. She did not, by Treadwell's tape, ask the delegation any questions. The Polar Bears were admitted to the League before noon. Treadwell's tape, which she submitted to the LMG archive vault under a "do not air" classification at her own request, has been requested for public release eleven times. It has been released zero times.</p>
        <p>The Polar Bears walked home. They took, by the same Hummock log, twenty-nine days for the return — three days faster, by the delegation's own quiet pride, "because we knew where we were going."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Office of the Commissioner, "Polar Bears Inclusion · Year 35 closeout" · cross-referenced with Hummock Slowtread's travel log, on display in the Anchorage Frostfall Hall foyer</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Hall of Fallen Heroes — A Brief Account</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Foundation Hall steward's tour-guide pamphlet · Year 36 revision · the only document in the Foundation that has been revised every season since founding</div>
        <p>The Hall of Fallen Heroes is a long, narrow room at the back of the Foundation Hall in Boston. It was not, by the Foundation's own admission, originally intended as a memorial space. The room was, in Year 28, the building's mailroom — a place for the Beavers' coaching staff to sort the era's voluminous fan correspondence. The mailroom got smaller as the fan correspondence got bigger and was, by Year 30, no longer adequate for sorting. The mail was moved to a new room. The old mailroom sat empty for one full off-season while the Foundation considered what to do with it.</p>
        <p>What happened to the room is recorded in the Foundation steward's daily log of Year 30, week three, in a single sentence: <em>"Old Bristlebeard the First's helmet has been brought into the empty mailroom by the Beavers' coaching staff. They did not ask. We did not refuse. The helmet is on the south wall. There is a small brass plate beneath it. The plate is in the Beavers' coaching staff's handwriting and reads, in full, 'OLD BRISTLEBEARD THE FIRST · TANK · IN.' We have not asked what 'IN' means. We have, in tacit agreement with the coaching staff, decided not to ask."</em> The First's helmet has remained on that wall, in that position, since. The brass plate has, in three subsequent revisions by three different Foundation calligraphers, never been re-engraved. The original plate, with the Beavers' coaching staff's hand-lettering, is the founding object of the Hall.</p>
        <p>The Hall has, in eight seasons, accumulated fourteen helmets. Each helmet is mounted at approximately the eye-level of the species it belonged to — the First's helmet is at five feet four inches; Vela Hootington's is at four feet eleven; Sundip Hootington Jr.'s is at four feet eleven exactly (the Foundation steward measured both Hootington helmets and confirmed that the family's eye level had been preserved across two generations); Felix Marshmallow's is at five feet two; Hester Quillstrike's is at three feet eight, the lowest mount in the Hall, with a small step for short visitors who would like to see her face; Avery Loambright's is at four feet ten; the Brisefer family's first fallen Antlerlord (an early-Year-32 reserve who never started a sanctioned match but was killed in a pre-League exhibition the Foundation has admitted into the Hall on the strength of the Saint-Laurent council's request) is at six feet eleven, the highest mount in the Hall; Brask Ironclaw III's is at five feet six; the others are at heights between, in the order of their permadeaths.</p>
        <p>The Hall has eight rows of brass plates. Six are full. The seventh has Loambright in it, and Quillstrike, and Sundip Jr., and Felix, and Brask III, and Vela, and the First, and ten more. The eighth is partially populated and growing slowly. There are, by the Foundation's calculation, room for forty more rows before the Hall is full; the Foundation has, on three separate occasions, asked an engineer to verify the math; the engineer has, on three separate occasions, returned with a slightly different number. The Foundation has stopped asking. The Foundation has, however, begun negotiations for the room next door (currently a coat closet), against the day.</p>
        <p>The Hall is open to the public during all Foundation Hall business hours. There is no charge. There is no guide. There is, by the Foundation's deliberate choice, no audio tour. Visitors are asked, at the door, to remove their hats. The Foundation has not, in eight seasons, had to ask any visitor twice. The Wolves' captain, on every Brewer's Reach pre-match visit, bows for eleven seconds at Loambright's plate (third row from the door, sixth name). The Polar Bears, since Year 35, hold a shared minute of held breath at the door before entering. The Antlerlords, since Year 36, perform a slow nod from L'Ancrage that lasts twenty-three seconds at the threshold. The Lynx visit individually, in rotation, throughout the pre-season — there is, by the Lynx's preference, no single Lynx Hall ritual. The Quetzals have not, as of this writing, lost a knight to permadeath, and so do not yet have a Hall ritual. The Foundation has set aside a row for them anyway, against the Quetzals' wishes. The Quetzals have not, by their own polite communication, protested the row's existence; they have, however, declined to acknowledge it. The Foundation respects the decline.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Hall steward's tour-guide pamphlet · revised every off-season since Year 30 · the original Year 30 pamphlet (single page, eleven sentences) is on display under glass in the Hall's vestibule</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>On the Frostfall Friendly — and Why It Is Not, by Caucus Decision, Called Anything Else</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Caucus pre-season working session minutes, Year 36 · the establishment of the Cold Stones trophy · cross-referenced with the Polar Bears' and Lynx's coaching-staff testimony</div>
        <p>The Frostfall Friendly was the Caucus's idea. It was not, in any meaningful sense, the two participating teams' idea. The Polar Bears and the Lynx had, in the eight pre-season weeks before the Year 36 founding bell, not played one another. They had, by the Caucus's pre-season register, not <em>met</em> one another either: the Anchorage and Whitehorse settlements are six hundred miles apart by the high northern road, and neither team's roster had crossed that distance for casual purposes. The Caucus, briefing the two head coaches at week one of training camp, suggested a friendly. Neither head coach was sure that "friendly" was the right word.</p>
        <p>The objection, on both sides, was the same and was not voiced. The Polar Bears do not, by tradition, play exhibition matches; the bears' coaching staff considers exhibitions a form of waste — energy that ought to be saved for sanctioned competition. The Lynx do not, by tradition, play exhibition matches; the Lynx's training program does not assemble the team until match day, and match days are, by the Lynx's calendar, sanctioned matches. Both objections were, by the Caucus's pre-meeting briefing notes, "anticipated and addressed in advance." The Caucus's solution: name the match the <em>Frostfall Friendly</em>, host it under a real trophy, and assign it the same procedural weight as a sanctioned match. Neither team, the Caucus reasoned, would refuse a sanctioned match. Both teams, the Caucus reasoned, would understand that the trophy made the match real.</p>
        <p>The trophy was Whittlestone's. She was given six weeks. She did not produce, as the Caucus had quietly hoped, an elaborate brass piece in the manner of the Coronation Cup crown. She produced two flat river-stones — one from the Anchorage settlement (selected by Whitepaw at Whittlestone's request), one from the boreal stronghold north of Whitehorse (selected by Tessik Snowstep, also at Whittlestone's request). The stones were bound at the seam with brass wire. The trophy weighs, by Whittlestone's bench-scale record, one pound four ounces. The stones are not, by Whittlestone's frank admission, anything special. <em>"They are stones from the two places. The trophy is the bringing-together. The trophy is not the stones."</em> The Caucus, on receipt, considered objecting. The Caucus did not object. The trophy was named the Cold Stones by the Bears' coaching staff (who had been asked to name it, declined, and then in the same letter offered the name as <em>"a working title we will not, by our preference, replace"</em>); the name has stuck.</p>
        <p>The match was held at the Boise Frosthold Pitch. Boise was the only neutral venue with a working ice surface in pre-season; the Anchorage Frostfall Hall was unavailable (the Bears were, at the time, hosting the visiting Polar Bear cubs' annual exhibition for the settlement's children, which was, by the Bears' decision, not to be displaced for an inter-team match); the Whitehorse Solitude Hall was unavailable (the Lynx do not, by tradition, host visitors). Whittlestone designed the venue's Frostfall overlay personally for the match, on the grounds that <em>"the stones came from the cold places. The match should be played in the cold."</em> The Caucus approved the overlay request without debate.</p>
        <p>The match was four rounds longer than the over-under. The Bears took it by a single round. The post-match line, by the LMG broadcast booth's read, was a small ceremony: the two teams met at center pitch, four bears on one side and five lynx on the other (the Lynx, in keeping with their tradition, did not bring a sixth-knight reserve to the bench), and Whitepaw and Halfpaw (the Lynx's nominal captain, who consents to be called captain only on match days) touched antlers — Whitepaw's are not antlers, technically, but the Bears' coaching staff describes the gesture in those terms — for approximately three seconds. The booth did not narrate the gesture. The booth had not seen the gesture before. The booth has, in subsequent broadcasts, declined to interpret it. Featherquill's column on the match closed: <em>"The two northern teams have, in eight weeks, gone from never having met to having, at center pitch, performed a small ceremony neither team had drilled. This is not, by my read, the Caucus's success. This is the Caucus's good fortune. The Caucus arranged the match. The match arranged itself."</em></p>
        <p>The Cold Stones are now at the Anchorage Frostfall Hall, on the wall opposite the entry, at a height a Polar Bear can reach without bending. The trophy will, by the Caucus's standing rule, return to Boise for the Year 37 pre-season Friendly. The Polar Bears have, by their coaching staff's pre-season statement, "no objection to the rematch." The Lynx have, by Tessik Snowstep's only public comment, "noted the rematch on the calendar."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus pre-season working session minutes, Year 36 · cross-referenced with Anchorage Frostfall Hall public-display caption and the Lynx coaching staff's brief written acknowledgment of the trophy's existence</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Reno Heist — Year 33 Closeout, the Riot Shield's Disappearance in Transit</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Office of the Commissioner, "On the Loss of Foundational Equipment" · cross-referenced with Mok Mok of the Raccoons' formal post-season testimony and the Foundation's transit-route security log</div>
        <p>The Riot Shield went missing in Year 33 closeout, during the post-Final transit between Brewer's Reach Pitch (Boston) and the Foundation's neutral equipment vault. The Shield's last confirmed sighting on the active line was the Year 33 Final's round four, in the carry of Wikrai Wartooth Jr. (Wolves Brawler, son of the deceased Wikrai Sr., on his first sanctioned-line season). Wartooth Jr. died in round four; the Shield, by League scavenge protocol, was recovered by the Beavers' equipment manager at the round's resolution and entered into Foundation transit at the close of the match. The Shield's status, on Foundation transit log entry, was: <em>"Bristlebeard's Riot Shield, recovered post-Year 33 Final round four, condition serviceable, dent count thirty-one new, scratch pattern consistent with Wartooth Jr.'s known carry style. Inbound to neutral vault by standard route. Layover scheduled at Reno Open Court equipment-transit hub, approximately forty hours."</em></p>
        <p>The Reno Open Court doubles, by Foundation arrangement since Year 31, as the continental equipment-transit hub for Foundation movements between the eastern circuit (Boston, Pittsburgh, Helena) and the western neutral vault. The Court's south corridor includes a small secure equipment cage where transit items are held during layovers. The Shield arrived at the cage on the second day of post-Final transit, was logged by the Reno transit officer at 4:14 p.m., and was, by standard protocol, scheduled for the next morning's outbound pickup at 9:45 p.m. that night.</p>
        <p>What happened in the fourteen-minute window between the south-corridor's last security walk-by (9:31 p.m.) and the Foundation's transit-officer arrival (9:47 p.m.) is, by every official record, unknown. The cage's lock was, by the venue's later inspection, intact. The Shield was, by every reading available to the venue's security, absent without forced entry.</p>
        <p>Mok Mok of the Raccoons, then in his fourth season on the active line and on Reno-residence between brackets, presented himself to the Foundation's transit officer at the venue's south-corridor security desk at 9:51 p.m. He was carrying a Shield. He had, by his own immediate testimony, "found it." He had, by his own immediate testimony, "found it on a small folding chair, in the corridor, approximately twelve feet from the cage's outer door, with the chair labeled in chalk on the seat: 'for Mok Mok, with love, from someone who was not paying attention to the cage's lock.' I do not know who left it on the chair. I am, by my own preference, not going to investigate. I have brought it to the security desk because the Shield is, by every Foundation rule, the Beavers'. The Beavers will want it back. I would like to be on record as having, in this case, not stolen it." The transit officer, by his own subsequent testimony, accepted the Shield and Mok Mok's statement, returned the Shield to the cage, photographed the cage from the inside, and posted a guard for the remainder of the night. The next morning's transit pickup proceeded as scheduled. The Shield arrived at the neutral vault by mid-day.</p>
        <p>Three days after the Shield arrived at the vault, the vault's senior steward filed a confidential note with the Office of the Commissioner: the Shield in the vault, at the morning's inspection, was a Shield. It was not, by every available metric — weight, balance, dent pattern, the seven tally marks on the inner rim — Bristlebeard the First's Shield. It was a Shield, well-made, by an unknown smith, weighing within tolerance and dent-patterned in a way that approximated the original's wear. It was, by the steward's careful read, "a competent forgery." The original Shield, by the steward's deduction, had been substituted somewhere between the Reno security cage and the vault. The substitution had been done by a smith who knew, in considerable detail, what the Shield looked like.</p>
        <p>The Caucus convened an emergency working session in Year 33 closeout. Mok Mok of the Raccoons appeared, voluntarily, and testified for two hours. His testimony was straightforward: he had, on the chair, found a Shield. He had, by his own working knowledge of Shield-forgeries (a working knowledge the Caucus did not, in two hours, ask him to explain), suspected immediately that the Shield he found was the Shield, but he had not been able to verify in the corridor's lighting. He had brought it to the security desk anyway, because, in his own testimony, "the right thing to do is bring it to the desk. The wrong thing to do is keep it. I have done, in this case, the right thing. I have also, by my own preference, not investigated who left it on the chair, because the chair was, by the chalk note, addressed to me, and the only people who would address a chair to me are people who would not, by my read, want me to investigate." The Caucus accepted the testimony. The Caucus did not, by formal vote, accuse Mok Mok of any wrongdoing. The Caucus also did not, in eight months of subsequent investigation, identify the smith who forged the substitute Shield, the chair's chalk-author, or the route by which the original Shield left the venue.</p>
        <p>The original Shield is, at this writing, somewhere on the continent. The vault holds the substitute. The substitute is, by every Caucus inspection, an excellent Shield in its own right and is, by Caucus standing rule, treated as the Riot Shield for all official scavenge-circulation purposes; the Beavers' coaching staff has, on three occasions, asked for the substitute to be formally redesignated as a non-Bristlebeard Shield, and the Caucus has, on three occasions, declined the request, on the grounds that "the Riot Shield's identity is, by League rule, the role it plays in scavenge circulation, not the matter of which specific piece of forged metal currently fills the role. The original is missing. The role is filled. We are not, by Caucus decision, going to update the rule for as long as the substitute serves." The Beavers continue to look for the original. The Beavers are, by their captain Bjorn Bristlebeard the Third's pre-season statement, "tired but not, in any meaningful sense, finished. The Shield is the First's. The Shield will be home. We will, in due course, find it. The Foundation has, on this matter, our patience and our standing request that the search not be closed."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Office of the Commissioner, "On the Loss of Foundational Equipment" · Year 33 closeout, Year 35 update, Year 36 standing-search renewal · the search remains open · the Beavers continue to file annual renewals · the Caucus continues to grant them</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Year 32 Healer-Shortage Exemption</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Caucus working-session minutes, Year 32 founding bell · cross-referenced with the Healers' Mutual Aid Society's standing roster of certified non-League Healers</div>
        <p>The Year 32 founding bell opened with a problem the Caucus had not, in three previous founding bells, anticipated. Healer attrition, across the previous three seasons, had been higher than the Caucus's standing replenishment rate by a margin that the Caucus's continuity-planning office had, in pre-bell internal analysis, called "concerning rather than catastrophic, but unaddressed at the founding bell will become catastrophic by mid-season." Three teams — the Foxes, the Pandas, and the Wolves — were, at the founding bell, technically below League minimum-Healer roster requirements. None of the three could, by the Caucus's standard recruiting protocols, be brought to League minimum before mid-season at the earliest. The Caucus had, in the founding-bell pre-meeting briefing, identified four possible responses.</p>
        <p>The first was to suspend the three teams' League play until they were able to recruit Healers to roster. This was, by every Caucus delegate's pre-vote read, unacceptable — the three teams were, between them, three of the four most-attended teams in the League by viewer count. Suspending them would, by the LMG broadcast booth's pre-vote estimate, cost the LMG approximately twenty thousand bits in advertising revenue across the season. The LMG had, by Mort Quillsetter's pre-vote letter to the Caucus, "no formal opinion on the suspension as a matter of League rule, but a strong informal opinion that the suspension would damage the broadcast season's viewer engagement to a degree we are, by our own assessment, not able to recover from."</p>
        <p>The second was to lower the League's minimum-Healer roster requirement. This was, by every Caucus delegate's pre-vote read, dangerous — the minimum was, by Dr. Lopecora Plumstone's standing pre-bell briefing, "the minimum because below it the team is, by every measurable safety metric, less safe. The minimum exists for a reason. The reason has not changed."</p>
        <p>The third was to draft Healers from the active line of better-staffed teams. This was, by every Caucus delegate's pre-vote read, politically unworkable — the better-staffed teams' captains had, by pre-vote informal poll, all indicated they would not, on principle, willingly send a Healer to a competitor. The Caucus could, by formal vote, force the issue, but the political fallout would, by the continuity-planning office's pre-vote read, "fracture the League's coaching-staff relationships for at least three seasons."</p>
        <p>The fourth was the proposal that became the Year 32 Healer-Shortage Exemption. Dr. Plumstone, in her pre-bell briefing, had identified seventeen non-League Healers — qualified by her own Society's certification standards, working in regional combat circuits across the continent (the Helena Hedgehog tradition, the Olympia coastal-merchant healing schools, the Reno academy's medical wing, and several smaller traditions) — who would, by Plumstone's careful informal canvas, "consider a one-season loan to a League roster, on appropriate compensation, and on the explicit understanding that the loan is for one season, not a recruiting offer." The Caucus, on the strength of Plumstone's canvas, ratified the exemption: League rosters could, by special Caucus dispensation in years when the Caucus's continuity-planning office certified a Healer shortage, hire qualified non-League Healers from recognized regional combat circuits for a single season's contract.
