The contract would, by Plumstone's standing condition, include a return-clause: at the season's end, the loaned Healer returned to her circuit unless both parties, in writing, agreed otherwise.</p>
        <p>The exemption was used four times in Year 32. Three of the four loans worked exactly as Plumstone had hoped — the loaned Healer played a season, returned to her circuit, and the borrowing team recruited a permanent Healer in the off-season. The fourth was Avery Loambright, who would, in Year 33, become the only loaned Healer to die on a sanctioned field. The exemption was, on Loambright's death, briefly suspended; Plumstone testified at the Caucus's emergency working session that the suspension would, in her professional judgment, leave at least two League rosters below minimum-Healer requirements within four months. The Caucus reinstated the exemption, with one modification: the loan contract now included a Healer's standing right to refuse engagement on a target-line that, in her professional judgment, presented an unacceptable risk to the loaned Healer's own life. The modification was, by Plumstone's pre-amendment statement, "the Loambright correction, in contract form. The Loambright correction was already taught at the snipers' workshop. It is now also written into the contract every loaned Healer signs. We have done, by my read, what we can do."</p>
        <p>The exemption remains, as of Year 36, on the books. It has been used in two additional seasons since Year 33 — both quietly, both successfully, both with the Loambright clause preserved. The Healers' Mutual Aid Society maintains the standing roster of certified non-League Healers; the roster, by the Society's last public statement, has thirty-one names on it. The Caucus's continuity-planning office tracks Healer attrition closely. The exemption has, in eight years, prevented exactly one season-suspension and one mid-season cascade. The Caucus considers this an acceptable trade. The Society considers it a workable arrangement. The roster of names is, by Plumstone's pre-retirement note, "the most important single document in my professional career. I will, on my retirement, hand it personally to my successor. The successor has not, in eight years, been chosen. I am, on this matter, in no rush."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus working-session minutes, Year 32 founding bell · revised Year 33 emergency session · maintained on standing review by the Caucus continuity-planning office · cross-referenced with the Healers' Mutual Aid Society's roster (thirty-one names, as of Year 36)</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Pawington Cup's Founding — A Dropped Kerchief</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Caucus founding-event archive · "Pawington Cup, codification" · cross-referenced with the Olympia Outlaw Otters' team archive and the Foundation's flag-event ratification minutes</div>
        <p>Mira Pawington — the Scavenger Queen, deceased Year 32, the Otters' founding captain — invented the Pawington Cup format by accident. The accident was: a dropped kerchief, in a Year 31 exhibition match against the Kits, in the third round of the second half. Pawington had been carrying her team's standard exhibition kerchief (the same black wool, eighteen inches square, embroidered otter-in-the-corner — the kerchief that would, after her death, hang in the Olympia Harbor Pitch's locker corridor) through what was meant to be a routine Long Snatch run. She tripped on a Kit Speedster's outstretched paw at approximately the field's mid-point, dropped the kerchief, and continued running. The Kits' Speedster, who had been engaging the rest of the Otter line in the standard Long Snatch escort-block, broke off, picked up the kerchief, and ran it back across the field in the opposite direction. The Otter line, by reflex more than tactics, pursued. The match was, at that point, formally scored on a different metric — round wins by combat resolution, not by kerchief carry — but the field's collective attention, by every spectator's account, had pivoted onto the kerchief. The Kits' Speedster delivered the kerchief to the Kit captain, in the Kit corner, eight seconds before the round's clock expired. The crowd cheered.</p>
        <p>Pawington, asked at the post-match interview what had happened, said: <em>"the kerchief got away from me. the Kit got it. the Kit ran it home. it is, by my read, a more interesting use of the kerchief than the Long Snatch was. we should, on this matter, stop running the Long Snatch and start running this. the new run does not, by my read, need a name yet. the run is the run."</em></p>
        <p>The Caucus, watching the post-match interview, took it seriously. The Caucus's flag-event committee — which had been informally exploring a flag-style format for the bracket for two seasons without finding the right ruleset — invited Pawington to draft a working format. Pawington declined. Her stated reason: <em>"the rules are the rules. the run is the run. i do not, by my own preference, want to write the rules. i would rather, by my own preference, run the kerchief. someone else can write the rules. i will, when the rules are written, run them."</em> The Caucus's flag-event committee drafted the rules without her, over the course of Year 31's off-season; the format was ratified at the Year 32 founding bell. The committee named the event the Pawington Cup, against Pawington's mild objection. Pawington, on the naming, said only: <em>"if you are going to name it after me, do not, by my preference, name it after the wrong run. the run that got away from me on the field is the run. the Long Snatch is the run that did not. name it after the run that got away from me. that is, by every reading, the correct run."</em> The committee accepted the clarification.</p>
        <p>The Pawington Cup format, as ratified: a colored kerchief spawns at center pitch. Each team must carry the kerchief, in continuous physical possession, from one corner of their opponent's half to the opposite corner of their own half. The kerchief may be dropped (intentionally or by accident); a dropped kerchief reverts to neutral status and may be picked up by either team. The kerchief may not be thrown; an attempted throw is, by League rule, an automatic forfeit of possession. First team to deliver the kerchief, intact, to the prescribed final corner, wins the round. Best of five rounds wins the match.</p>
        <p>Pawington played the inaugural Pawington Cup match in Year 32 R5. She dropped the kerchief in round one — by her own subsequent statement, "intentionally, on principle, to demonstrate that the rules accommodate the dropping" — and the Otters lost the round. She did not drop it again. The Otters won the match three rounds to one. Pawington carried the kerchief in two of the four rounds, including the deciding round five. The Cup is, by Caucus archival record, the only inaugural-event championship that has been won by the format's namesake.</p>
        <p>Pawington died, in a non-League hunting accident in the Olympia harbor coastal range, in late Year 32. The Olympia Outlaw Otters' coaching staff did not, in the immediate post-death interviews, accept the standard League grief protocol; they declined the Foundation's offered Hall-of-Fallen-Heroes induction (Pawington had not, by Foundation rule, died on a sanctioned field), and they organized, on their own initiative, a small private ceremony at the harbor at sunset, attended by approximately sixty Otters, no other team's representatives, and one (uninvited but quietly tolerated) Featherquill. Featherquill's column on the ceremony — the only public account — closed with the only line that has, in five subsequent Pawington Cup seasons, been quoted by the LMG broadcast booth at every Cup-final post-match line: <em>"The Cup is hers. The kerchief got away from her once. The kerchief, in five subsequent seasons, has been carried by Otters who knew her, and Kits who beat her, and the Raccoons (twice) who scavenged the kerchief mid-round in a way Pawington would have, in her time, deeply admired. The Cup belongs to whoever runs it. Pawington's only contribution was the dropping. The dropping was the contribution."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus founding-event archive, "Pawington Cup, codification" · cross-referenced with the Olympia Outlaw Otters' team archive entries on Mira Pawington and the Year 32 inaugural Cup match · Featherquill's column on the harbor ceremony has, by general agreement, never been reprinted in full and is, by the Otters' coaching staff's preference, available only to Otter coaching staff and Foundation Library staff with appropriate clearance</div>
      </article>
      <article class="history lore-wide">
        <h3>On the Pittsburgh Visiting Perch and the First Northbound Arrival</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau filing · Year 36 mid-season · cross-published with the Pittsburgh Murder's Roost minutes (where authorized by Roost vote) and the Federación's Cartagena bulletin (in Spanish translation, by the Bears' bureau)</div>
        <p>The Pittsburgh Visiting Perch sits on the foundry-side ledge of the Pittsburgh harbor wall, twenty-three feet above the Allegheny's high-water line, on a cantilevered iron arm that the Murder's master arrowsmith Slate Wirethorn forged across the Year-36 founding-bell off-season. The arm is the only piece of Wirethorn's working life that has, in his thirty years at the foundry, been built for a non-Murder occupant. The Roost commissioned it on the ratification of Inkbeak Sr.'s standing proposal — the proposal Inkbeak had drafted on Flight 6, three years before the ratification, and which the Roost had voted slowly on through the entire intervening period in the way the Roost votes slowly on every proposal that asks the Murder to extend hospitality outside its own line. The Roost approved unanimously in the Year 36 mid-season. The construction began the morning after.</p>
        <p>The perch is not, by design, equivalent to the senior perch the Bears wax at Cartagena. The Bears' perch is on a stone tower; ours is on iron, set into the foundry-quarter brick, because iron is what Pittsburgh has and what Pittsburgh knows. The Bears, on receiving the relay news from Inkbeak Sr.'s Flight 8, sent a sealed jar of the Cartagena-perch wax northward with a note in Doña Inés's hand reading <em>"para el día"</em> — for the day. Wirethorn examined the wax, examined the iron, examined the Pittsburgh harbor air, and produced a written reply (in his standing pencil, on Roost letterhead): <em>"the wax is excellent. the wax is, by every honest read, not for our iron. our iron asks a different finish. i am, on this matter, going to apply the wax to the perch's small ledge, where the visiting bird will rest a wing on landing. the rest of the perch will be finished as the iron asks. the wax will be where the bird touches first. that is the part of the perch that owes the wax. the rest of the perch owes Pittsburgh."</em> The Roost approved without amendment. The Bears, on receiving the reply (relayed by Inkbeak Sr. on Flight 9 southbound), are reported to have said, in the Cartagena working session at which the reply was read aloud: <em>"el herrero ha entendido. la cera estará donde tiene que estar. el resto del posadero es Pittsburgh, y debe ser Pittsburgh. esto es, por toda lectura honesta, lo correcto."</em> Doña Inés is reported to have agreed without further comment.</p>
        <p>The perch was completed on the third afternoon of the Year-36 mid-season. The Bears' wax was applied to the small ledge — a six-inch arc of cured wax, set against the cantilevered arm's underside, polished to the exact finish the Cartagena senior perch carries — and the rest of the perch was finished in the standard Pittsburgh foundry-quarter blacking. Wirethorn applied the blacking himself, over four working days, in a paste he mixes from foundry-floor coal-dust and basin water in a proportion that is, by every Murder elder's pre-publication acknowledgment, his own and his alone, and which he has not, in thirty years, written down. The Roost held a brief ceremony at completion. Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. attended in his standing capacity as the Murder's senior flying Raven. He spoke briefly, in the standing format the Roost uses for ceremonies of perch dedication: <em>"the perch is here. the perch is for the visitor. the visitor will, in due course, arrive. the perch will, on that day, do the work the perch was built to do. on that day we will, as the Bears asked us to remember, be the place that is, by every Federación read, the harbor that asked questions of visiting birds. we are not yet that place. the perch will, on the day the visitor arrives, make us that place. we wait."</em> The Roost adjourned without further comment. The perch stood empty for forty-six days.</p>
        <p>The first northbound arrival landed on the morning of the forty-seventh day, an hour after dawn, in light fog that was lifting off the river in slow stages — a working condition the Pittsburgh harbor watch describes as <em>"the kind of morning the harbor uses for its own work; the visiting bird is, by tradition, the harbor's guest, but the harbor is also doing what the harbor does, which is rising into a clear day from a wet night."</em> The arriving bird was a senior Andean Condor scout named Marisol Cumbralta, twenty-nine years old, with sixteen years of high-cordillera scouting experience and three previous southbound Caribbean-basin crossings to her record. She was, by Federación standing description, <em>"la voladora de larga distancia con el récord más completo de cualquier Cóndor activo en la Federación, y la exploradora a quien la Federación ha acordado, en sesión, encargar el primer arribo norte, por la razón de que el primer arribo debe ser hecho por la Cóndor cuyo registro resista la clase de escrutinio que la Manada de Pittsburgh aplica a todo testimonio de aves visitantes."</em> Doña Inés signed the dispatch authorization three weeks before the flight. Cumbralta departed Cartagena on the third morning of the seventh week of the Federación's calendar year. The crossing took, by her own pocket-log, eleven days and four hours, with three rest stops on the standard Caribbean-basin route the Murder's Inkbeak Sr. had documented across his eight prior southbound flights.</p>
        <p>Cumbralta touched the perch at six minutes past dawn-plus-one-hour. She rested her right wing on the small wax-finished ledge — the ledge the Bears had asked us to build, the ledge Wirethorn had finished to the Cartagena standard — and she held the rest position for the standard four-second visiting-bird acknowledgment that the Murder uses when receiving its own flying Ravens at the foundry quarter on return from Boston scouting flights. The Roost, who had been watching from the harbor wall in their standing reception formation since first light, completed the four-second acknowledgment in unison. The acknowledgment is, by Roost convention, the moment the visitor has arrived. Cumbralta had arrived. The Roost had received her. The work the perch had been built for had, on the forty-seventh day, been done.</p>
        <p>Cumbralta stayed four days. She was interviewed, by long-standing arrangement with the Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau, on the first afternoon by the bureau's senior curator (Sigridweave, the Owl, who holds the curatorship since Year 31). The interview lasted six hours across two sittings. Cumbralta declined fish-scraps; she accepted Roost-standard hospitality water from a clay vessel Inkbeak Sr. had fetched from the Murder's archival roost; she answered every question Sigridweave asked her in what the bureau's pre-publication notes describe as <em>"careful Federación-Spanish, with a Quechua-creole register Sigridweave's translator (an Owl-side junior bureau scribe named Pellic Snowcrest, recently rotated in from the LMG translation booth) rendered into League Common with what was, by every cross-reference, equivalent care."</em> The interview transcript runs to one hundred and forty-one pages. The bureau has filed it, in ink, in the Northeast Coast Bureau's senior-archive drawer. The transcript is available to scholars by formal request. The bureau's curator's standing pencil-annotation on the file's flyleaf reads, in full: <em>"this is, by my own honest read, the second careful entry the file has received in six years. we have, on this entry, more institutional vocabulary for the receiving than we had for the first. we are, on the matter, no longer the bureau that did not have the vocabulary. we are the bureau that has it now. — sgw."</em></p>
        <p>Cumbralta departed Pittsburgh on the morning of her fifth day, southbound, in fair flying weather. The Roost completed the standard departure acknowledgment. Inkbeak Sr. flew with her as far as the Atlantic shelf — a Pittsburgh-side courtesy not previously offered to any visiting bird, agreed by Roost vote on the second afternoon of her stay — and turned back at the shelf's edge. He returned to Pittsburgh the same evening. He filed his standard post-flight report. He noted, at the end, in his own pencil: <em>"the visitor was a careful narrator. the bureau was correct, by my read, to send the senior curator for the interview. the bureau will, in due course, file the interview's pages. the pages will, by my best read, be the most-cited pages in the Old World File's six-year operating record by the close of the next archival quarter. the file is, by this arrival, no longer a file with one careful entry. the file is a file with two. we are, by this arrival, the place the Bears said we were. we have, on this matter, the work to keep being it."</em></p>
        <p>The wax on the small ledge — the wax the Bears had sent for the day — was, by Wirethorn's standing rule, not refreshed after Cumbralta's departure. Wirethorn's rule, written on the same Roost letterhead as his earlier reply: <em>"the wax was for the day. the day has been. the wax remains where the day left it. we will, in due course, when the next visitor arrives, finish the ledge as that day asks. the wax will, on this matter, settle into the iron as the iron settles around the wax. the perch will, on every visitor's arrival, carry on its small ledge the trace of every prior arrival. that is, by my read, what the perch is. the perch is the harbor's memory of what arrived. the iron remembers. the wax remembers. we, on this matter, do not need to."</em> The perch stands. The wax is, as of this filing, two months into its settling. The next northbound visitor's date of arrival has not, by either league's working calendar, been scheduled. The perch waits. The Roost waits with it. The harbor is, as Inkbeak Sr.'s Flight-6 pocket-diary entry described from the other end of the route four years ago, the place that has now begun to do, on its own ledge, the work the Cartagena perch has been doing for four years on its.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau filing, Year 36 mid-season · the bureau has, in two subsequent working sessions, agreed to file Cumbralta's interview transcript in ink rather than pencil, on the grounds that the transcript is, by every available standard, finished work; the senior curator's standing dissent on this point is preserved in pencil at the bottom of the filing slip and reads, in full: <em>"the transcript is finished. the work is not. the work, by my own read, will not be finished in our lifetime. the file should, by my preference, be kept open in pencil for as long as the work requires. i have signed in ink because the bureau's standing rule asks ink for filings of this type. the dissent is, on this matter, in pencil, and is, by my preference, preserved. — sgw."</em></div>
      </article>
    
      <article class="history">
        <h3>The First Lobster</h3>
        <div class="meta">Mid-Year-26, Boston · two seasons before the inaugural bell · Concession Row commercial archive</div>
        <p>The vendor (a Beaver, fourth-generation lobsterer, name on the License Wall but not in any League broadcast) sold the first lobster on Concession Row two seasons before the inaugural Year 28 bell. The match was a friendly. The vendor's stand, by her own log, took six lobsters that day. By Year 27 she was taking three hundred per match-day. By Year 28 she had, in the meantime, set the price.</p>
        <p>The price has not, in eight seasons, changed. The lobster has not, in eight seasons, decreased in size. The vendor has, by my best read, not been seen smiling at a customer except on the Year 32 R6 morning Mira Pawington died — and that smile was, by every cleaner's account on Concession Row that morning, a smile of recognition rather than welcome. The vendor knew Mira's order. The vendor said, on the matter, exactly nothing. The vendor handed Mira a cup of water and refused payment. Mira drank it standing up. The cup was returned. The day went on.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Boston Concession Row Commercial Archive, vendor file 26-A-002</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>On the Naming of "Float Knights"</h3>
        <div class="meta">League etymology · the Caucus's third Year-28 minute · Office of the Commissioner</div>
        <p>The name was settled on the third minute of the third Caucus session, by the third margin of the third vote. The contenders were, in order of their final tallies: <em>"Float Knights"</em> (12), <em>"Balloon Combat League"</em> (11), <em>"Aerial Honors Tournament"</em> (8), and three further entries that the Caucus's secretary, by long-standing tradition of not embarrassing the rejected, has declined to release.</p>
        <p>The deciding vote was cast by Commissioner Whiskerstone, who has, on the matter, given exactly one public answer: <em>"The knights are knights and they float. The other names were either accurate or evocative but not both. We needed both."</em> The matter has not been re-opened. The Caucus has, by the secretary's own preference, kept the rejected names sealed.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— League Office, foundational documents, sealed minute</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Marshmallow Protocol's Adoption Process</h3>
        <div class="meta">Year 34, between R5 and R6 · the seven-day grenade-safety push · Foundation safety archive</div>
        <p>Felix fell on the Wednesday. The Marshmallow Protocol was on every team's bench by the Tuesday following — a six-day turnaround that the Foundation safety committee has not, in any subsequent grenade incident, matched. The committee has, in interviews, explained the speed by reference to two factors: every team had already met Felix at least once in the post-match Concession Row queue, and Felix's family had, before the burial, asked only that the protocol be named after him. The committee did not have, by their own admission, the heart to delay.</p>
        <p>The protocol's text is six paragraphs. The teams' coaching staffs have memorized them. The Pandas' coach Yu Cobblepad has, by reliable bench account, recited paragraph four ("the grenade does not, by its design, distinguish between teammate and opponent") at every Pandas' grenade-safety drill since Year 34, in Felix's voice — which Yu reports learning by listening to a single recording, three times, the night Felix died.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Safety Committee, year-end report, Year 34</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Brass Crown's Pawn Tickets</h3>
        <div class="meta">An accounting curiosity · the Coronation Cup, Year 30 onward · Foundation budget archive</div>
        <p>The Coronation Cup brass crown has, in eight seasons of being awarded to the Reno Rascal Raccoons, been pawned at Moss Quickfingers' Reno pawn shop a documented eight times — once after each victory. The pawn ticket is, on every occasion, made out to the active Raccoon roster's captain. The ticket is, on every occasion, redeemed by the Foundation by lunch of the following day for a fee of <em>"four lobsters and a small storage charge."</em></p>
        <p>The Foundation budget line for crown retrieval was added to the books in Year 31, by the second tournament's morning, after the first retrieval was paid out of the Commissioner's discretionary fund. The line item is, by the budget secretary's preference, on the books permanently. The Raccoons have not, on the matter, been asked to stop. They have, on the matter, occasionally implied that they would consider stopping, in exchange for an additional lobster annually. The Foundation has not, on the matter, blinked.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation budget archive, line item 31-CRWN-001 through current</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Gauge That Lied</h3>
        <div class="meta">Boise Float Gas Foundry · the Year-33 41-day shutdown, abbreviated · Foundation incident summary</div>
        <p>What is publicly known: the Foundry shut down for forty-one days in the autumn of Year 33, ostensibly for "maintenance." Production resumed without incident. No League team's reserves were affected. The Foundry's quarterly safety review for that year was filed on time, with no irregularities noted. The Foundry's master Bristlebeard the Second declined comment.</p>
        <p>What is privately known, per the burned-page document recovered the following season (item 33-EPH-012, partial): the fourth tank's gauge had, for six weeks, been miscalibrated. The product in the fourth tank's batch was discovered, by the Foundry's own honest account, to be off-spec. The Foundry shut down before any of that batch reached customers. The shutdown was, by the burned page's anonymous author, "the right handling." The League agreed, in the only way the League agrees to such things — by saying nothing about it for a year, and then by not asking again.</p>
        <p>The fourth tank's batch is, on the matter, not in any League team's reserves. The fourth tank works now. The League does not, on the matter, need to know more. The League, by my read, will not.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation incident summary, Year 33, shutdown file</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Translator Booth's First Day</h3>
        <div class="meta">Year 36 R1 · the LMG broadcast booth · Foundation broadcast archive</div>
        <p>Estelle Roiseau-Manchot took the booth at 14:02 on the morning of the Year 36 inaugural Continental Expansion match. The booth had, in eight prior seasons, never employed a translator. The Caucus had, the previous winter, ratified the hire on the strength of two factors: Antlerlords on the bracket, and a Quebec creole that the LMG's senior commentator (by his own admission) could not, in any honest reading, follow.</p>
        <p>Estelle's first sentence, by every booth recording in the archive, was clean: she repeated Marc-Olivier Brisefer's pre-match line ("we move when we choose") in League Common, with the cadence intact. The senior commentator, off-mic, was heard to whisper <em>"oh, thank god."</em> Estelle's career as the booth's translator has, on the matter, never been threatened.</p>
        <p>Her contract, by Foundation accounting record, includes a clause that pays her in lobster — at her own insistence, and at a rate that exceeds the Concession Row vendor's daily take on a busy match-day. The Foundation has not, on the matter, complained. The Foundation has, on the matter, occasionally bragged.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG broadcast archive, Year 36 R1, booth log</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Gate-Three Tradition</h3>
        <div class="meta">An undocumented courtesy · multiple venues · approximately Year 34 onward · Foundation usher's discretion</div>
        <p>Gate Three, by Foundation venue convention, is the back overflow gate at most League stadiums — a gate that opens onto whatever embankment, sidewalk, or grassy slope the architect could provide for fans without tickets. Sight-lines are partial. The audio comes through the stadium walls. The price is, on the matter, free.</p>
        <p>The Gate-Three Tradition began, by the best Foundation reconstruction, with a single Owls Striker (name retained in the Foundation file but withheld from broadcast at the Owl's request) who, after winning the Year 34 R3 home match, walked her gear-bag out Gate Three on the way to the dressing-room and handed a still-folded matchday program to a young fox kit who had been, by usher's report, watching matches from the embankment for at least six matchdays running. The program was, by Foundation record, the kit's first.</p>
        <p>The next match, three Knights from three different teams quietly handed Gate-Three programs to whoever was on the embankment that afternoon. By Year 35, the tradition had spread to four venues. By Year 36, it is, by Foundation usher's quiet count, a standing convention — not League policy, never written down, but practiced.</p>
        <p>The Foundation has, on the matter, declined to formalize it. The Foundation has, on the matter, also declined to interfere. The senior usher at Brewer's Reach, asked once by a young deputy whether the tradition should be regulated, answered: <em>"the gate is the gate. The kids are the kids. The programs are not, on the matter, doing anyone any harm."</em> The deputy filed the answer, on the matter, exactly as recorded. The matter has not, on the matter, been re-opened.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation usher's manual, addendum, Year 36 · "Convention, not policy"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>Section 14, Row M</h3>
        <div class="meta">An oral history, in two voices · Brewer's Reach Pitch · the seat that does not, on the matter, sit empty</div>
        <p>The seat is, by Foundation broadcast staff convention, the loudest single point in any League stadium. The seat is also, by long-standing Section 14 tradition, where the regulars seat new arrivals on their first match — under the firm understanding that the new arrival will, on the matter, learn to holler within three matches or be re-seated.</p>
        <p>The senior Section 14 usher's quieter version, given in private to a young Foundation deputy: <em>"the seat is the seat. The Ewe owns the seat in spirit. The seat is, by my read, the only piece of stadium real estate that has, in eight seasons, never sat empty for an entire match. Even the bench at the post-match line empties out when the team goes back to the dressing-room. Section 14 Row M does not, on the matter, empty. There is always somebody hollerin' from there. There has always been."</em></p>
        <p>The young deputy's follow-up question, by his own subsequent memo: <em>"is the Ewe ever going to write down what the cheering is for?"</em> The senior usher's answer: <em>"the cheering is for the cheering. The Ewe knows. The seat knows. We do not, on the matter, need it written down."</em> The deputy filed the answer, on the matter, exactly as recorded.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Brewer's Reach senior usher's oral history · transcribed Year 36 mid-season</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Year 33 Closeout — A Voice Arrives at Section 14</h3>
        <div class="meta">Brewer's Reach Pitch · the closeout match against the Sharks · Y33 R7 · Foundation usher's archive, refreshed in Y36 mid-season after the third Featherquill column</div>
        <p>The senior usher of Section 14 has, in his archive, a single dated note from the morning of the Year 33 closeout: <em>"new fan, Row M seat 3, female sheep, green wool scarf, very loud. Has, on the matter, hollered "PEW PEW" at every Sharks Sniper draw for two consecutive rounds. The regulars have, by their own informal vote, accepted her. The seat is, on the matter, hers as long as she keeps purchasing it weekly. I will, on the matter, refresh this note if anything changes."</em></p>
        <p>The note has, on the matter, been refreshed exactly twice. Once at the Year 35 mid-season letter (<em>"the new fan has written to The Wing Standard"</em>), and once at the Year 36 R5 morning (<em>"the new fan has been on the matter for thirty-three matchdays. The regulars have, on the matter, given her a handle. The seat is, on the matter, permanent in spirit if not in lease."</em>). The first note's original ink is, by Foundation archive convention, kept legible by careful re-tracing every five seasons. The senior usher has, on the matter, performed the re-tracing personally each time it has come due.</p>
        <p>The senior usher's quieter aside, in the same archive: <em>"by jingo, on the matter, she does not, on the matter, stop. I do not, on the matter, want her to stop."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Section 14 senior usher's archive · Y33 closeout, original note · re-traced Y34 mid-season, Y35 closeout, Y36 mid-season</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>Gate Three's First Program — Y34 R3</h3>
        <div class="meta">Brewer's Reach Pitch · the back overflow gate · the morning of the Owls' Y34 R3 home match · Foundation usher's reconstruction</div>
        <p>The Owls Striker walked her gear-bag out Gate Three because Gate Three was, on the matter, the closer route to the Foundation parking lot. The boy was, on the embankment, ten feet from the gate. He had been there, by usher's count, since the third match before; the embankment was, by Foundation convention, free for any animal who could climb the slope.</p>
        <p>The Striker stopped. The Striker had, by her own subsequent quiet account, noticed the boy on his second matchday and had been, on the matter, thinking about him since. The Striker handed him the matchday program. She did not, on the matter, speak. The boy, by usher's report, did not speak either. He took the program with both paws. The Striker waved once, briefly, and continued toward the parking lot. The boy waved back at her retreating shoulders. The wave was, on the matter, also a program — a phrase the boy would write down, in his own pencil, two seasons later.</p>
        <p>The Foundation usher present at the gate that afternoon recorded, in his standard daily log, only the line: <em>"Gate Three regular received first program. Striker did not, on the matter, identify herself. The boy will, in due course, return tomorrow."</em> The boy returned tomorrow. He has returned every tomorrow since. The Striker has, on the matter, never been formally identified to the boy or to any reporter. The Owls' bench staff have, by long-standing internal convention, declined every Foundation request to confirm or deny the Striker's identity. The Foundation has, on the matter, decided not to press.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation usher's daily log, Brewer's Reach Pitch, Y34 R3 · "Convention preserved by silence"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Year 34 Mid-Season — When the Tradition Spread to Reno</h3>
        <div class="meta">Reno Open Court · the Y34 mid-season match · the second documented Gate-Three handoff · Foundation usher's archive, Reno bureau</div>
        <p>The second venue to see a Gate-Three handoff was, by Foundation timestamp, Reno — not Brewer's Reach again. The match was Y34 R5, RCC vs OWL, and the gear-bag walk-out was, by every Reno usher's account, deliberate. The Owls Striker who had handed the original program at Brewer's Reach R3 had, by her bench staff's quiet confirmation, told three teammates about the embankment kid. Two of those teammates were on the Year 34 R5 Owls roster. One of them was, on the Y34 mid-season Reno trip, the Owls' second-year Sniper Bramblepaw Hootington (no relation to Vela, by the standard inquiry).</p>
        <p>Bramblepaw walked her gear-bag out the Reno Open Court's Gate Three after the match (a 6-2 Owls win — Bramblepaw had, on the matter, recorded three of the kills) and handed her matchday program to the first kit she saw on the embankment. The kit was a Raccoon kit, age uncertain, by the Reno usher's note "perhaps eight." The kit took the program. The kit did not, on the matter, speak. Bramblepaw did not, on the matter, speak either. The kit's family was waiting at the bottom of the embankment. The kit ran down the slope with the program. The family looked at the program, looked back up at the gate, and waved. Bramblepaw waved back.</p>
        <p>The Reno usher's note, in his daily log: <em>"the Brewer's Reach thing has, on the matter, traveled. The kit will, in due course, return. The mother looked, on the matter, like she might, on the matter, also return. We will, on the matter, see."</em> The mother did, on the matter, return. The kit did, on the matter, also return. The Reno embankment had, by the Y34 closeout, three regulars. The tradition had, on the matter, traveled.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation usher's archive, Reno bureau · Y34 R5 · the second documented handoff</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Pamphlet's Year 35 Revision</h3>
        <div class="meta">League Office · the annual Pamphlet for New Fans · Year 35 mid-season revision · the only revision in eight seasons not authored by Whiskerstone</div>
        <p>The Pamphlet for New Fans is the League Office's annual orientation document — six pages, printed in Reno, distributed at every venue's main concourse for free. It has been, since Year 28, authored by Commissioner Whiskerstone personally. The Year 35 mid-season revision is, by the Office's own quiet record, the only revision in eight seasons authored by someone else: the Office's senior deputy, a Tabby cat named Linnet Stripewhisker, who has held the post since Year 31.</p>
        <p>Whiskerstone's reason, by Stripewhisker's own subsequent memo: <em>"the Commissioner is, on the matter, traveling. The Commissioner has, on the matter, asked me to handle the revision. The Commissioner has, on the matter, also asked me to add a paragraph about Gate Three. I have, on the matter, done so."</em></p>
        <p>The Year 35 Pamphlet's added paragraph reads, in full: <em>"the League's stadiums have main gates and back gates. The back gates are, on the matter, free. If you cannot afford a ticket, you may watch from the back-gate embankments at Brewer's Reach (Pitch), Reno (Open Court), Olympia (Harbor), and Helena (Glacier Rink). The view is, on the matter, partial. The audio comes through the walls. The League is, on the matter, glad you are here. The seat, on the matter, is the seat — and the embankment is, on the matter, also a seat."</em> The Pamphlet has, in subsequent annual revisions, retained the paragraph verbatim.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— League Office archive · Pamphlet for New Fans, Y35 mid-season revision · Stripewhisker as author of record · "the seat is the seat"</div>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Year 35 Closeout Auction Incident</h3>
        <div class="meta">Reno · the post-Coronation-Cup auction floor · Y35 closeout · the lot that did not, on the matter, sell</div>
        <p>The annual Coronation Cup auction floor, held the morning after the Cup match, sells off the year's accumulated lost-and-found ephemera — programs, bench notes, broken whistle-tags, the occasional unclaimed gear piece. Lots are sold to fans, archivists, and (twice in eight seasons) the League Office for its own archive. The Year 35 auction floor included, by lot register, eighty-six items.</p>
        <p>Lot 47 was a single sheet of butcher paper. It was, by the auctioneer's read, "an annotated ticket-stub scrapbook page, twenty-six stubs, signed in green crayon — the Pew-Pew Ewe." The auctioneer — a senior Foundation accountant named Pip Quickfingers (no relation to the Reno pawn-shop Quickfingers, by his own quiet preference) — opened the lot at one lobster. The bidding stalled at one lobster. No one would, on the matter, raise. The auctioneer waited. After ninety seconds of silence, a small voice from the back of the room said, in cadence the auctioneer would later identify as the Pew-Pew Ewe's own: <em>"that page belongs in Section 14, by jingo. WITHDRAW THE LOT, FOLKS!"</em></p>
        <p>The auctioneer withdrew the lot. The page was, by his own subsequent decision, returned to the Brewer's Reach Pitch lost-and-found. It has, in two seasons since, never been re-auctioned. It is, by Foundation tradition, no longer eligible for auction. Lot 47 has been, since Y35 closeout, formally annotated in the auction register with the line: <em>"Section 14 property. Not for sale. Refresh weekly."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation auction floor register · Reno · Y35 closeout · Lot 47, retired</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Lost-and-Found Wall</h3>
        <div class="meta">Brewer's Reach Pitch · the senior usher's office · the wall that grew from one frame to nine · Y34 onward</div>
        <p>The Brewer's Reach lost-and-found wall is, by Foundation venue convention, a single corkboard at the senior usher's desk on which un-claimed ephemera of cultural value are pinned for indefinite display. The wall has, by usher count, grown from one frame in Year 28 (a single Hardvein Quickstep training note, Y28) to nine frames as of Y36 mid-season.</p>
        <p>The senior usher's annotated map of the wall, refreshed annually:</p>
        <p>Frame 1 (top-left, original): the Y28 Quickstep training note. Frame 2 (Y29 addition): a Boston Concession Row receipt with the lobster vendor's first written annotation. Frame 3 (Y31): the Cultural Office's pre-leak draft of Project Neon Inheritance, returned to Brewer's Reach at the senior usher's request. Frame 4 (Y32): a Mira Pawington post-match note, "for the next polite scavenger." Frame 5 (Y34): the boy's traced pencil sketch of his first matchday program. Frame 6 (Y34 closeout): a Pew-Pew Ewe scribble, framed without removal because the regulars petitioned for it. Frame 7 (Y35): the lost-and-found's own copy of the auctioned-and-withdrawn Section 14 scrapbook page (Lot 47, the original). Frame 8 (Y36 mid-season): the program-in-a-program transcription, by Foundation cleaner. Frame 9 (Y36 closeout, current): the two-hand pencil-and-crayon page, the Boy and the Ewe.</p>
        <p>The senior usher has, on the matter, declined every Foundation request to dismantle older frames to make room for newer ones. The wall is, on the matter, expandable — he has, every two seasons, added a section to it himself, with screws and a small saw. The wall is, by his own quiet read, the most accurate single document of Brewer's Reach's cultural year-by-year accumulation. The Foundation has, on the matter, agreed.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Brewer's Reach senior usher's office · the wall · refreshed annually, expanded biennially</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Whittlestone Annual</h3>
        <div class="meta">Boise Float Gas Foundry · Pell Whittlestone's published yearly report · Y28 onward · the Foundry's only commercially circulated document</div>
        <p>Every winter, Pell Whittlestone — chief chemist of the Boise Float Gas Foundry since Year 28 — publishes a six-page document she calls, in her own copy, "the Annual." It is, by every Foundation cross-reference, the Foundry's only commercially circulated publication. It contains: a full-year quality summary (one page), the off-season pricing schedule for the following season's float gas (one page), the Foundry's commitment-statement on safety (half a page, unchanged in eight seasons), and four pages of what Whittlestone calls "essays on the work."</p>
        <p>The essays vary in subject. The Y29 Annual's essay was on the proper pour rate for Tank-grade float gas (technical). The Y31 Annual's essay was on the philosophy of inspection (philosophical). The Y33 Annual's essay was, by Foundation cultural-archive cross-reference, the only public-facing acknowledgment Whittlestone has ever issued of the 41-day shutdown — the essay does not name the shutdown, but it discusses, at considerable length, the relationship between a chemist and a gauge that is, in her words, "no longer telling the truth." The Y36 Annual's essay was titled, in her own words, <em>"On the Wax Jar — A Chemist Looks At Diplomacy."</em></p>
        <p>The Annual has, by Foundry archive count, been printed at a circulation of exactly 2,400 copies every year since Year 28. The print run has, in eight seasons, never sold out — Whittlestone's own quiet preference is that fans who want one can have one without competition. The Foundry's archive holds, by Whittlestone's standing arrangement, a numbered copy of every Annual (numbered #1, by her own pen, on the inside front cover). The Caucus has, on the matter, requested copy #1 of the Y36 Annual for the League archive. Whittlestone has not, on the matter, yet sent it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Boise Float Gas Foundry · the Whittlestone Annual · Y28-Y36 series · "the gauge that is no longer telling the truth"</div>
      </article>
</div>
