      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Boston Brisk Beavers · BVR · founded Year 28</h3>
        <div class="meta">The oldest team in the League · Brewer's Reach Pitch (the founding venue) · the team that built the venue before the venue was a venue</div>
        <p>The Beavers founded the League the way a beaver founds a dam: by deciding, in advance, where the dam would go, and then quietly building it. The Brewer's Reach venue was built by the Beavers' coaching staff in Year 26 and 27, two years before the inaugural match, on the assumption that a venue would, eventually, be needed. The first opponent the Beavers played was their own backup line, in a five-week pre-season scrimmage that had no audience and no broadcast. The first sanctioned match, the founding match of the League itself, was Year 28 R1 against the Wichita Wild Wolves, who had, at that point, been a team for six weeks. The Beavers won by three rounds. The Beavers then helped the Wolves' coaching staff plan their off-season, on the grounds that <em>"the League will be better when there are at least two teams that know what they are doing, and we are willing to teach. We will not, on the field, take it easy on you. We will, off the field, give you our notes."</em> The Wolves' coaching staff still has the notes. The notes are, by the Wolves' own report, in a binder in the Olympia training facility, on the second shelf of the head coach's office. The binder has been added to since. The binder is now thicker than the Wolves' own training manual.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Wichita Wild Wolves · WLF · founded Year 28</h3>
        <div class="meta">The pack arrives · Olympia rural training grounds · co-founders of the inaugural match</div>
        <p>The Wolves are, by their own internal record, older than the League. The pack — the Olympia rural pack, which descended from a single den-line that survived the Long Quiet in the upper Cascade foothills — has been holding match-style sparring engagements for at least five generations. The League's Year 28 founding gave the pack a venue, a regulation, and a broadcast. The pack treated the League's regulations the way the pack treats most things — quietly, attentively, with no public dispute. The Wolves did not win the inaugural match (the Beavers did). The Wolves did not win the Year 28 championship (the Beavers did). The Wolves did, in Year 29, win their first championship, and the Wolves' captain at the time — Hardvein Quickstep, then in his third season as captain — accepted the trophy without comment, walked off the post-match line, and went home to Olympia. The pack does not, by tradition, celebrate. The pack's only on-record celebration is the Bow, which did not exist until Year 33.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Tampa Tornado Sharks · SHK · founded Year 30</h3>
        <div class="meta">A coastal salvage operation that became a sport · Tampa Bay venue · three championships in five seasons</div>
        <p>The Sharks were not, in their pre-League years, a team. They were a coastal salvage crew that operated out of the Tampa Bay flooded warehouse district, recovering Old-Ones marine equipment and metalwork from the bay floor. The team's founding captain — a hammerhead named Tideglass Splashfang — petitioned the Caucus for League inclusion in Year 29, on the strength of a single argument: <em>"We have, on the salvage crew, twelve animals who have spent their entire working lives moving heavy objects underwater under time pressure. We are, by skill profile, the best Brawler-class line you are ever going to find. The Caucus should test this. We will, in the test, win."</em> The Caucus tested it. The Sharks won. The Sharks were admitted in Year 30 and won their first championship in Year 31. The Sharks' aggressive close-quarters style is, by every Caucus tactical analyst's read, a direct descendant of the salvage-crew working method: identify the heavy object, get to it before the tide turns, get it secured, get out. The Sharks have, in seven seasons, never lost a Brawler engagement at less than three meters' range. The Sharks' captain is reported to sleep in chainmail. The reporting on this comes from Tideglass's grandniece, who wrote a school paper about it; the paper has been quoted by every sportswriter in the League and the grandniece is, at this writing, twenty-seven and runs the Tampa Bay tourist office.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Boise Brawling Badgers · BDG · founded Year 30</h3>
        <div class="meta">The Foundry's hometown team · slow, grindy, oldest-line average tenure in the League · the wide draw debuted Year 36</div>
        <p>The Badgers were founded the same year the Float Gas Foundry began commercial production. This is not, by every account, a coincidence. The team was, in its first season, sponsored almost entirely by Foundry workers — the Foundry's break-room betting pool funded the team's equipment kit, and the Foundry's chief chemist (Pell Whittlestone, who would later forge the Coronation Cup crown) personally wrote the team's first equipment-spec sheet. The Foundry's sponsorship was disbanded in Year 32 when the Caucus formalized rules against in-League cross-sponsorship; the Badgers, by that point, had a fan base of their own and did not need the subsidy. The team's tactical style — which has been, in every season since founding, the slowest in the League by an average forty-percent margin — is, by Coach Slatebrush's own description, <em>"a Foundry tactic. The Foundry knows that the floor is the floor. The floor does not move. The floor is, in every match, the most reliable thing on the field. We hold the floor. We are the floor. The floor is us."</em></p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Phoenix Furious Foxes · FOX · founded Year 31</h3>
        <div class="meta">A desert raider crew that became, by accident, a respectable sports franchise</div>
        <p>The Foxes were, in their pre-League years, a desert raider crew that operated out of the Phoenix dust basin. They were not popular with their neighbors. They were not unpopular either. They were, by their own retired captain's account, <em>"a thing the desert had. The desert has us. The desert has scorpions. The desert has tortoises. The desert has the Foxes. We are part of the desert."</em> The team joined the League in Year 31 after the Foxes' founding captain, Bask Ironclaw the First, was challenged to an honor duel by an Owls captain (the Owls' founding captain, in his pre-Owls career, had been a Foxes-affiliated freelance scout who had a personal disagreement with Ironclaw the First about a salvage-rights issue; the disagreement had simmered for six years before producing the duel). Ironclaw the First won the duel. The Owls captain, on losing, said: <em>"Then come into the League with us. We will take this off the field. The field is, frankly, a more appropriate venue for what we have been doing in alleyways."</em> The Foxes accepted. They have, in six seasons of League play, never lost a match against the Owls. The Owls have, in six seasons, never publicly complained about this fact, on the grounds that they consider the Foxes' inclusion to have been their idea.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Kansas Kicking Kits · KIT · founded Year 31</h3>
        <div class="meta">Acrobatic Strikers · Hardwood Hall venue · zero championships, beloved anyway</div>
        <p>The Kits were founded by a single litter — five sibling rabbits born to the same Kansas warren in Year 22 — who decided, at age nine, to start a sports team. Their original team had no League affiliation, no venue, no rules, and no opposing teams; they played each other in a converted hayloft for six years before approaching the Caucus for inclusion in Year 29. The Caucus declined the first petition on the grounds that the team was, technically, all five members of one extended family and that this presented potential issues with roster turnover. The Kits' captain (Mira Pawington, the eldest of the litter) wrote a single-page response that read in its entirety: <em>"We are a litter. The litter is the team. The team has been the team since age nine. The litter is willing to add non-litter members. We are not willing to disband the litter. The Caucus may make of this what it will. We will continue training in the hayloft."</em> The Caucus, by working-session minutes, took two years to deliberate. The Caucus admitted the Kits in Year 31 with the litter intact and a formal exemption from the family-roster-overlap rule. The Kits have, in seven subsequent seasons, won zero championships. The Kits have, in seven seasons, never had a season-ending record below .500. The Kits are, by every fan poll the League runs, the most-loved team in the League. Mira Pawington died in Year 32 R7 holding her opponent's Power Cell, and the team named the Pawington Cup after her while she was still alive. The four surviving Pawingtons are still on the active roster as of Year 36.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Seattle Sleepless Owls · OWL · founded Year 32</h3>
        <div class="meta">Nocturnal pit-fight champions, gone legitimate · 24-hour training schedule · the Reno catwalk specialists</div>
        <p>The Owls were, before the League, the most successful nocturnal pit-fight circuit in the former Pacific Northwest. The pit-fight circuit was — by every available account, and despite repeated and sincere denials from the Owls' coaching staff — not entirely above-board. The circuit dissolved in Year 30 after a series of regulatory pressures from the Olympia council that the Owls' coaching staff has declined to elaborate on. The Owls' founding captain, Hawkeye Hootington (the great-uncle of current OWL captain Sundip Hootington Sr., whose son Jr. died in Year 35 climbing the Reno Power Core), petitioned the Caucus in Year 31 with a roster of twelve former pit-fight champions and a single line of argument: <em>"We are very good at fighting. We have, for ten years, been doing it in places we should not have been. The League is a place where we should be. Let us be there."</em> The Caucus admitted them in Year 32. The Owls' first match was a four-round shutout. The Owls won the Year 33 championship. The Owls have, in five seasons since, finished top-four every year. The 24-hour training schedule rumor is, by Coach Bristlewren's own confirmation, true, but the schedule is rotating — no individual Owl works more than nine hours of any twenty-four — and the team's medical staff considers this less unhealthy than it sounds. The black coffee rumor is also true. The spite rumor is, by Bristlewren's careful statement, "professionally insulting; we are powered by discipline; the spite is a side effect."</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Fresno Frantic Frogs · FRG · founded Year 32</h3>
        <div class="meta">Speed-archetype specialists · Mississippi River Run circuit alumni · coached by a very angry tree frog</div>
        <p>The Frogs were assembled in Year 31 from the surviving competitors of the Mississippi River Run, an informal long-distance river-swim circuit that had operated from Year 12 to Year 30 and which, by Year 30, had become functionally inviable due to upstream salinization in the Old-Ones-era levee system. The Run's organizing committee — a board of seven retired river champions — approached the Caucus in Year 31 with a proposal: the Run's competitors would, as a unit, transition to the League's Speedster archetype, on the grounds that <em>"river-running selects for the same physical attributes as Speedster combat: speed, agility, lung capacity, and the ability to read terrain three seconds ahead of where you currently are."</em> The Caucus agreed. The Frogs were admitted in Year 32. The team's head coach is, by registry, a tree frog named Slickleaf the Furious, who has not been seen by any LMG broadcast camera in five seasons (he coaches from a hidden spot in the Fresno venue's rafters; the team's bench staff relays his instructions). Slickleaf is reportedly, by every mid-season scouting report, "extremely angry about something" — but no one has ever asked him what. The Frogs' tactical style is, by Caucus analyst's read, "the closest thing to a river current the League has ever produced. It does not stop. It does not reverse. It does, eventually, win."</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Portland Punching Pandas · PND · founded Year 33</h3>
        <div class="meta">Tank specialists · the heaviest armor in the League before the Antlerlords arrived · slow, calm, methodical</div>
        <p>The Pandas were the League's first explicitly engineered expansion team. The Caucus, in Year 32 off-season, formally announced that the Year 33 founding bell would include a new team built around a single archetype the existing twelve teams underused — Tank specialization. The Caucus solicited applications. The Portland community — a settled bamboo-grove cooperative in the foothills of what the Old Ones called Mount Hood — submitted a roster of eight pandas, all of whom met the Caucus's Tank-class physical specifications by the relevant margin. The Pandas were admitted in Year 33. Their first season's regular-season record was 9-3, the best founding-season record in League history at that point. Their first championship came in Year 35, in a four-round Final against the Sharks that took, by stopwatch, the longest cumulative match-time of any Final ever recorded — sixty-seven minutes, one second. The Pandas won 3-1 and walked off the pitch in the same column they walked on. They did not, in their celebration, raise their voices. The Pandas do not, by tradition, raise their voices. The crowd was, by the broadcast booth's read, the quietest championship-winning crowd in League history. The Pandas considered this respectful. The other teams, in their post-season reviews, considered it terrifying.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Olympia Outlaw Otters · OTR · founded Year 33</h3>
        <div class="meta">River pirates with a fluid combat style · gear-scavenging specialists · the only team to have won a Final after every starting weapon was traded</div>
        <p>The Otters were a river-piracy crew operating out of the Puget Sound delta who, by Year 32, had developed a reputation for non-violent salvage — they would board moving vessels, take what they wanted, and leave without raising a fin. The League's Year 33 founding bell coincided with a dispute between the Otters' crew and the Olympia harbor authority over a year of unpaid mooring fees. The crew's leader, an old otter named Sandbark Trickwater, proposed to the Caucus and the harbor authority simultaneously: <em>"Forgive the fees. Admit the crew to the League. We will, in League play, donate fifty percent of our match purses to the harbor authority for the next ten years. The harbor will be made whole. The League will gain, frankly, a very good team. The crew will be made law-abiding by direct funding agreement."</em> Both parties agreed. The Otters were admitted in Year 33. They have, in six seasons of League play, donated, by harbor accountancy, exactly fifty percent of their match purses every season. The Olympia harbor's long-term mooring fees have not increased since. The Otters' on-field tactical style — which has, in every season, produced the highest mid-match gear-trade rate in the League — is a direct descendant of the salvage-piracy tactic. They are, by Trickwater's own retirement statement, <em>"a good crew. The League made us a good crew. We were always going to be a good crew. The League just gave us the right kind of work."</em></p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Reno Rascal Raccoons · RCC · founded Year 34</h3>
        <div class="meta">The newest founding-era team · the highest scavenged-gear ratio in the League · six Coronation Cups in eight</div>
        <p>The Raccoons were the last of the founding-era teams. They were admitted in Year 34, after a four-year-long lobbying campaign by the Reno community council and a single decisive testimonial from Pell Whittlestone (who had, in her capacity as Foundry chief chemist, observed the Reno raccoons' off-season scavenging at the Brewer's Reach equipment lockup and concluded that <em>"these animals have, by every measurable standard, a more refined understanding of equipment value than any of the existing twelve teams. The League will be more interesting with them in it. They will, on the field, be very difficult to play against. The League should admit them. They will not, in any case, stop coming to Brewer's Reach to look at the equipment."</em>). The Raccoons accepted admission with the practical caveat that they would, on every winning match, take the trophy home — meaning, in practice, that the trophy would visit a Reno pawn shop on the way. The Caucus accepted the caveat informally, on the grounds that the Foundation had, by that point, already noticed the pawn-shop pattern and developed a standing recovery protocol. The Raccoons have, in five subsequent seasons, won six Coronation Cups (Years 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, with the Year 36 founding-bell Cup their most recent). The pawn shop has, in every winning year, stored the crown overnight. The Foundation has, in every winning year, recovered it by lunch the next day. The Raccoons consider this the cleanest possible expression of the Reno spirit. The Foundation, after eight years, agrees.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Helena Hidden Hedgehogs · HED · founded Year 35</h3>
        <div class="meta">The Year 35 closeout expansion's first team · spike armor · two referees have filed grievances</div>
        <p>The Hedgehogs were the first of four expansion teams admitted in Year 35's closeout cycle. The Caucus, having determined that the founding twelve had stabilized into a competitive equilibrium, opened Year 35 to four new teams from the upper continental range. The Hedgehog community of Helena — a settled colony in the high glacial valleys of what the Old Ones called the Northern Rockies — applied with a single tactical demonstration: their lead Sniper, an aging archer named Hester Quillstrike, took, on a clear morning at the Helena Glacier Rink, a shot that traveled four hundred and twelve paces along the rink's diagonal and popped a balloon at the far end. The Caucus admitted the team that afternoon. Quillstrike died in Year 35 R3 setting the same shot in her League debut. The Year 35 R3 shot is, by Caucus record, the longest single-shot kill in League history. It has been tied once, posthumously, by Sundip Hootington Jr. of the Owls, who carried Quillstrike's Rifle to the Reno Open Court and matched the distance exactly. The Rifle has been at large since.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Bayou Tigers · TGR · founded Year 35</h3>
        <div class="meta">Delta-basin stalker line · the matriarch hand-paints every helmet · stalk for half the round, then commit explosively</div>
        <p>The Tigers descend from the cats who survived the Long Quiet in the flooded warehouse district of what the Old Ones called New Orleans. The community, before League admission, had been a settled bayou cooperative for at least eleven generations, run by a continuous matriarch line — the current matriarch, Stripeshoulder, is the eleventh in unbroken descent from the founding matriarch (a tabby named Jasper, who established the New Orleans warehouse stronghold in the second generation after the Long Quiet). The Tigers' League application was filed in Year 33 and held in Caucus deliberation for two years before admission in Year 35. The deliberation centered on the Tigers' bayou-only home venue, which the Caucus had concerns about regarding broadcast logistics; the Tigers' coaching staff offered, as a compromise, to play half their home matches at neutral northern venues. The Tigers were admitted on the compromise. They have, in two subsequent seasons, exercised the compromise twice and otherwise played at home. The Bayou Walk — their pre-match ritual perimeter walk in single column led by the matriarch — was first observed at their Year 36 founding-bell home opener. It is now considered required at any Tigers home match.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Anchorage Polar Bears · PLR · founded Year 35</h3>
        <div class="meta">The League's only true northern team · walked thirty-two days to petition for admission · never lost a Frostfall match</div>
        <p>The Polar Bears trekked south from the Anchorage settlement to petition for League admission in Year 34. They walked the entire distance, on foot, for thirty-two days, in winter conditions, with a delegation of seven (six adults and one yearling who, by the delegation's leader's later account, <em>"insisted on coming and would not be persuaded otherwise; we let her come because she is, frankly, the toughest of us"</em>). They arrived in Boston on the morning of the Year 34 closeout meeting. They petitioned in person. The Caucus admitted them on the spot, on the strength of the petition's first sentence: <em>"We have, walking, demonstrated the only quality your League requires of us. We will not test this further. We will, however, play in your tournament."</em> The Polar Bears were inaugurated in Year 35. Their armor is, by the Caucus's mass register, the heaviest in the League excluding the Antlerlords. They have, in two subsequent seasons, never lost a match held in Frostfall conditions. They are, by Whitepaw the Steady's account, <em>"in this for the long walk. We are not in a hurry. The League will be the League. We will be in it."</em></p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Denver Drifting Bison · BSN · founded Year 35</h3>
        <div class="meta">Herd-rotation specialists · the Yellowhide tradition · never less than three knights inside a twenty-meter circle</div>
        <p>The Bison applied for League admission in Year 33 on the strength of a single tactical document — a forty-page treatise on herd-rotation combat written by Yellowhide the Elder, the founding patriarch of the Denver herd, who had, in his pre-League career, been the most-decorated combat instructor in the post-Long-Quiet Denver militia. The Caucus took the document seriously. The Caucus's working session minutes from the Year 33 deliberation note that <em>"the Bison have, in their submitted treatise, articulated a tactical framework that the existing twelve teams do not, in the aggregate, possess. The Bison should be admitted. We are not, today, ready. We will be ready in two seasons."</em> The Bison were admitted in Year 35. Yellowhide the Elder retired from the active line at admission (he was, at that point, eighty-one) and was named Patriarch-in-Residence; he attends every home match in full ceremonial harness and has not, by herd record, missed one. The current Bison captain is his great-grandson, Yellowhide the Younger.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Pittsburgh Plundering Ravens · RVN · founded Year 35</h3>
        <div class="meta">Salvage corvid clan turned arrow-makers · the most-decorated archery class in the League · the Beavers refuse to discuss this</div>
        <p>The Ravens were originally a salvage clan running steel reclamation across the Allegheny basin — a working corvid network with twenty-three members at the time of their League admission, descended from a continuous foundry-ruin community that had occupied the Pittsburgh foundry district since the second generation after the Long Quiet. The Ravens approached the Beavers' coaching staff in Year 33 with a request to purchase League-specification archery equipment, on the grounds that they intended to apply for League admission and wanted to enter the application process pre-equipped. The Beavers' coaching staff declined the sale, on the grounds that — by Coach Splinter Tooth's stated reasoning — <em>"the Ravens should learn to make their own equipment. We will not, on principle, sell finished gear to a team that has not yet manufactured anything in our own discipline. The Ravens have a foundry. The Ravens should use the foundry. We will, on the field, see them when they are ready to be seen."</em> The Ravens used the foundry. The Ravens manufactured their own archery equipment over the next eighteen months. The Ravens applied for admission in Year 34 and were admitted in Year 35. The Ravens' first sanctioned match was a five-round Best-of-Five against the Beavers, which the Ravens won 3-2, on the strength of their Snipers' arrow-grouping accuracy at every range above forty paces. The Beavers' coaching staff has not, in five subsequent regular-season meetings, formally discussed the loss. The Ravens, asked about it, said only: <em>"The Beavers were correct. We did learn to make our own equipment. We make better equipment than they do. The lesson stands."</em></p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Yukon Hunting Lynx · LYX · founded Year 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">The Year 36 Continental Expansion · the most thoroughly solitary team in the League · they only form up on match day</div>
        <p>The Lynx are an exception to most of the League's organizational assumptions. Their settlement, in the boreal stronghold north of what the Old Ones called Whitehorse, has no central hall, no continuous council, and no single elder. The community is — by its own internal description — <em>"five hundred and forty individuals who, when necessary, agree on things."</em> The Caucus took six years to negotiate Lynx admission, against the resistance of the Lynx themselves, who consistently and politely informed the Caucus that they did not, as a community, have a way to send delegations to a continental sports league. The negotiations succeeded in Year 36 only because the Caucus agreed to two unprecedented accommodations: the Lynx team would be coached by five separate coaches (one per active knight, drawn from the knight's own training relationship), and the Lynx team would not be required to assemble for any non-match-day team activity. The Caucus's working-session minutes note that <em>"these accommodations are not modifications of the Lynx by the League; they are modifications of the League by the Lynx. We are aware of this. We are admitting them anyway. They are, by tactical assessment, the best Sniper roster on the continent. We will adapt."</em> The Lynx have, in their inaugural season, lived up to the assessment.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Saint-Laurent Antlerlords · MOS · founded Year 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">The largest knights in the League by mass · Quebec creole-speakers · L'Ancrage at center, the rotation around him</div>
        <p>The Antlerlords were the slowest of the Year 36 Continental Expansion teams to apply for admission and the most thoroughly negotiated to admit. The Saint-Laurent moose community is one of the largest continuous animal populations on the continent — by the Caucus's pre-admission census, over four thousand individuals, spread along the basin from the Old-Ones-Montreal ruin all the way down to the freshwater outflow. The community's organizational structure had no equivalent of a sports team before the League's approach. The Brisefer family — the line that produced both the founding captain Marc-Olivier and the current L'Ancrage Théodred III — proposed the team's formation in Year 33 and spent three years building consensus across the basin's six elder councils. The team was inaugurated in Year 36 with a thirteen-knight roster (the League's standard active line is five plus eight reserves) and a coaching staff that included two translators, one cultural liaison, and a single elder council member who attends every match in ceremonial dress. The Antlerlords' inaugural sanctioned match was the Year 36 founding-bell debut against the Pittsburgh Ravens, which they won 1-0 in round one and 4-1 across the match. Théodred III did not, in round one, swing his antlers. He has, in subsequent rounds, swung them sparingly. He prefers to stand. The team is, by every account, comfortable with this.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Sonora Drifting Coyotes · CYT · founded Year 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">The drift-and-bait team · the most travel-hardened roster in the League · la borradura, el sexto</div>
        <p>The Coyotes' application for League admission was filed in Year 35 by Coach Reyes himself, who at the time was a fifty-year-old desert traveler with no prior coaching credentials and a single-page application that opened with the line <em>"We have, in the Sonora basin, twenty-eight years of practice running the only tactic that has ever beaten a wall. Your League has been building walls for eight seasons. We are willing to come north and demonstrate."</em> The Caucus invited Reyes to a private demonstration at the Boise venue. Reyes brought five Sonora coyotes. The five coyotes drifted around an eight-Caucus-member observation panel for twenty minutes; at the end of twenty minutes, the panel had counted seven distinct coyotes on the field and could not, by photographic review, account for the sixth. Reyes had, in fact, brought five. The panel admitted the team. The Coyotes have, in their inaugural season, finished every match they have played within their projected win-rate band, with one notable exception (the Year 36 R7 BDG vs MOS match, which the Coyotes were not in but which produced, in the Boise Highland Pitch parking lot the next morning, a single hand-delivered envelope addressed to Coach Reyes containing the postcard that has become known, in the Coyotes' team facility, as <em>"the well-drifted card."</em>).</p>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Yucatan Vibrant Quetzals · QTZ · founded Year 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">The League's only two-color team · canopy snipers · the trees' language</div>
        <p>The Quetzals are the southernmost team the League has ever admitted, and (as of Year 36) the southernmost in the League's foreseeable future. The Yucatan jungle community — which descended from a continuous quetzal population that survived the Long Quiet in the upper canopy of the Yucatan basin — applied for admission in Year 34 and was admitted in Year 36, after a two-season negotiation that resolved, primarily, the question of whether the Quetzals' habitual canopy nesting could be accommodated in non-Yucatan venues. The Caucus's resolution: every venue must provide at least one elevated nesting position for the Quetzals' Sniper, with the position registered as terrain rather than equipment. The Quetzals' captain, Cintzli, brings her own moss to every venue. The Quetzals have, in their inaugural season, fielded the highest aerial-shot accuracy rate in the League by a margin no other team has approached. They have not, as of this writing, lost a match to a non-Continental-Expansion team. The League's tactical analysts believe this is because the existing twelve teams have not yet learned to play against an opponent whose Sniper is, by registered terrain, in the rafters. The Quetzals believe the same. The Quetzals are, in their patient way, willing to wait for the existing teams to catch up.</p>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Whittlestone Address — Year 31 founding-bell convocation, Boston</h3>
        <div class="meta">A speech · delivered by Pell Whittlestone (then Foundation Counsel; now Caucus chair-emeritus) · 14 minutes · transcribed from the LMG broadcast feed and the Foundation's archival recording · the speech is, by Caucus standing convention, the only public address required in the League's bylaws · it is delivered at the founding-bell convocation of every season the League adds a new team or changes the standing rule book · the canonical version below is from Year 31, the season the Foxes joined</div>
        <p>Whittlestone was thirty-eight years old at the Year-31 convocation. She had been Foundation Counsel for two seasons. The address — which was, by her own pre-delivery account, "the second speech I have ever written and the first I have not, in any way, expected to be remembered" — was delivered at the Brewer's Reach mid-pitch, on the standard founding-bell platform the Foundation Atlas Committee assembles for each season's opening, in front of approximately fourteen hundred attendees and the LMG broadcast feed. The Foxes' incoming line stood in formation to the speaker's left; the founding twelve teams stood, in their alphabetical-by-city order, behind. Whittlestone wore the standard Counsel's slate-gray robe, no insignia. She read from a single sheet of unbleached paper, hand-folded twice, which she did not return to her pocket after speaking. The paper is, by her donation in Year 35, in the Foundation Drawer.</p>
        <p>The speech opens with the standard Caucus convocation salutation ("the bell is rung; the season is begun; the Knights are on the field") and proceeds, without further preamble, to its three numbered points. The first: <em>"the League is, by the bylaws we have ratified, a tournament. the League is, by the bylaws we have not ratified and never will, also a covenant. the tournament is the part you can see. the covenant is the part the bell rings for. when the bell rings, the tournament begins. the covenant has, by my reading, been ringing since before the first bell, and will, by my reading, ring after the last."</em> The second: <em>"every team that joins this League brings, with them, a thing they did before the League existed. the Foxes' thing is the heat. the Foxes have lived in the heat for as long as Foxes have lived. the heat is, by no reading available to the League, the League's. the heat is theirs. when the Foxes play in Boston, the heat does not come with them, but the heat-knowledge does. that knowledge is what they bring. that knowledge is what we, by accepting their admission, have agreed to honor."</em> The third — the line that became the Address's most-quoted: <em>"a League that does not, by its own standing rules, make room for what each team brought before it joined is not a League. it is a competition. competitions have winners. Leagues have, in addition to winners, knights. we are, on this matter, building a League."</em></p>
        <p>The speech's middle passage — eight minutes — is a per-team enumeration of "what each team brought before they joined." Whittlestone names the founding twelve, in their alphabetical-by-city order, and gives, for each, a single short sentence describing the pre-League tradition the Caucus has formally agreed to honor. The Beavers: their bench-built rifles. The Sharks: their first-contact-wins doctrine. The Owls: their patience. The Hedgehogs: their counter-attack. The Frogs: their hit-and-fade. The Foxes (then incoming): their heat. The Pandas: their plate. The Raccoons: their scavenge. The Wildkits: their vertical mobility. The Wolves: their pack tactics. The Badgers: their floor-hold. The Otters: their fluid trade. Each sentence is, by Whittlestone's drafting choice, exactly fourteen words long; the count was set by her at the speech's drafting and has been preserved by every subsequent Caucus chair who has adapted the address for the Continental Expansion seasons, with eight new fourteen-word sentences added (Tigers, Polar Bears, Bison, Ravens; Lynx, Moose, Coyotes, Quetzals).</p>
        <p>The speech closes with a four-line coda the Caucus has, by standing rule, never altered: <em>"the bell is rung. the season is begun. the Knights are on the field. let us, on this season, be worthy of what each of them brought."</em> Whittlestone, in the Year-31 delivery, paused approximately two seconds between the third and fourth lines. The pause is, by Caucus archival convention, included in every subsequent broadcast of the convocation regardless of which Caucus chair is delivering the speech that year. The four lines, plus the pause, are timed by the Foundation Library at exactly eleven seconds. The eleven-second close is, by Featherquill's column "On The Bell," the second canonical eleven-second silence in the League's traditions, the first being The Bow.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library archival transcript · Year 31 founding-bell convocation · the Whittlestone Address · the eleven-second close has been preserved by every subsequent Caucus chair through Year 36 · the original folded-paper draft is in the Foundation Drawer · Pell Whittlestone has, in five years since stepping down from active Counsel work, declined three publication offers for the speech's drafting notes · her stated reason: <em>"the speech is the speech. the drafting was, by my read, mine to do and not mine to share. the speech is, by every read since delivery, the League's. that is, by my read, the right division of property."</em></div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Loambright–Wartooth Friendship — Year 32 to Year 33</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · cross-team · documented across thirteen extant sources, the most important of which are the Helena Glacier Rink concession-stand steward's nightly log (Year 32 R3 onward), the Olympia Pack Grounds' visiting-team locker assignment records (Year 33 pre-season), and Avery Loambright's three letters to her parents during her Year-32 inter-team Healer-shortage loan to the Wolves · the friendship lasted approximately forty-one weeks before the Year-33 final · this article does not describe the final's events, which are covered in the canonical Match Log and in The Bow's glossary entry</div>
        <p>The friendship began at the Helena Glacier Rink concession stand on the evening of the Year 32 R3 match between the Hedgehogs and the Wolves. The match itself ran short — the Wolves took a 3-0 sweep in fifty-seven minutes, the third-fastest result of the Year-32 regular season — and the Hedgehogs' starting Healer Avery Loambright, who had been substituted out in round two and had not returned, found herself with approximately ninety minutes of post-match downtime before the team bus departed for the airport. She walked, alone, to the concession stand to buy a hot drink. The Wolves' starting Brawler, Crash Wartooth, had also walked, alone, to the concession stand, for the same reason. The concession stand had, that evening, exactly one staff member on duty: the Helena venue's senior steward, who has, in nineteen years of service, kept a nightly log of "interactions of note." Wartooth and Loambright's first meeting is the third entry in the Year-32 R3 log.</p>
        <p>The steward's entry, in his characteristically dry hand: <em>"Wartooth (Wolves, Brawler) and Loambright (Hedgehogs, Healer) arrived at the booth within thirty seconds of each other, in opposite directions, both looking for hot tea. The booth had, at this point in the evening, two cups of hot tea remaining. They each ordered one. Wartooth, on receiving his cup, paid in clams. Loambright, on receiving hers, paid in clams. They stood, side by side at the booth's standing rail, and drank in silence for approximately four minutes. Wartooth then said, by my best reconstruction: 'you fix bots. that is good work.' Loambright then said: 'you break them. that is also work.' Wartooth said: 'we should not, by our own standing positions, like each other.' Loambright said: 'no, we should not.' They drank for another two minutes, in silence. Wartooth left first. He left, by my count, three additional clams on the standing rail beside Loambright's empty cup. Loambright did not, on leaving four minutes later, take them. The clams were, on closing the booth, mine to keep. I did not keep them. I left them at the standing rail for the next match. They were, by my best read, not mine."</em> The three clams remained at the rail for the Year 32 R7 match between the Hedgehogs and the Wolves, which Wartooth and Loambright both attended in the active line. They each, on arrival at the venue, walked to the concession stand and silently picked up one clam each. The third clam remained. The third clam is, as of the Year-36 mid-season Foundation audit, still on the rail.</p>
        <p>The forty-one weeks of the friendship, between Year 32 R3 and the Year-33 final, are documented across the thirteen sources. Loambright was loaned to the Wolves for the back half of Year 32 (R5 through R12) under the inter-team Healer-shortage protocol, the first such loan in League history; the Wolves' Healer (Mossleaf Underbrush) had been permanently retired in R5 of Year 32 by an unrecoverable spinal injury sustained at the Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue, and the League's Year-32 mid-season Caucus voted, on a 14-1 ballot (the 1 against being the Hedgehogs' standing delegate, who voted against on procedural grounds and not on the loan's merit), to allow the loan. Loambright accepted. The Hedgehogs' coaching staff, by their own pre-loan account, "accepted the loan with the same grace the species has accepted, in three pre-League centuries, every loan we have ever been asked to make. the Healer is what we are. we will, by long-standing tradition, give a Healer when a Healer is asked for. we will, by the same long-standing tradition, expect her returned at season's end. she will be returned. she has, by every prior loan's record, always been returned." Loambright was returned at season's end. She did not, in the eight remaining months of her life, ever speak to her Hedgehog teammates about the loan. She did, in three letters to her parents, write extensively about Wartooth.</p>
        <p>The three letters — donated by Loambright's parents to the Foundation Drawer in Year 35, on the second anniversary of her death — describe a cross-team friendship that, by the parents' own characterization, "should not, by every locker-room rule we are aware of, have been possible." The letters describe shared meals at the Olympia Pack Grounds visitors' locker hallway. They describe Wartooth teaching Loambright the proper way to grip a stun baton, a technique she would never use in active play because Healers do not, by League rule, wield batons, but which she wanted to know "because Crash, by his own laughing account, has been gripping it wrong for nine seasons and would like one person, at least, in the League to know what wrong looks like before he retires." They describe Loambright teaching Wartooth the harmonic frequency at which a Healer's beam stops being audible to non-Healers, a frequency Wartooth could hear because Wolves' species hearing extends slightly higher than the Healer-class average. They describe, in the third letter (dated three weeks before the final), a small private agreement: <em>"if we ever meet across the line in a deciding round of a deciding match, we have agreed, in advance, to play it the way the line tells us to. neither of us, by this agreement, is owed anything by the other in such a moment. we have agreed because Crash, by his own honest words, said: 'i do not want this thing we have to be a thing that lessens the work. the work is the work. you fix bots. i break them. if it ever falls that you are fixing one i am breaking, you fix yours and i break mine and the field is, on that evening, the field.' i agreed."</em> They met across the line in a deciding round of a deciding match in the Year-33 final. The match log records what happened. The Bow describes what came after.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library archival history · Year 36 mid-season filing · the thirteen extant sources are itemized in the Library's master index · the steward's nightly log is in his ongoing custody and remains, by his standing personal preference, unpublished beyond the three entries that are in the public record · the third clam is, as of the Year-36 audit, still on the rail · the Helena venue has not, in the four seasons since, swept the rail · the rail is, by every venue staff member's standing acknowledgment, "to be left as it is, on this matter, indefinitely"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history lore-wide">
        <h3>The Federación Sudamericana — a parallel league, a separate continent</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · drawn from sixteen Foundation Library sources, the most foundational of which are the four Inkbeak Communiqués (Year 33–36, by Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. of the Pittsburgh Murder, the only confirmed-trustworthy Raven correspondent who has flown the Caribbean basin), the Cintzli Letters (Year 36, three letters from the Yucatan Quetzals' captain to the Quetzal-Federación liaison in Cartagena), and the surviving fragments of the Year 33 Bogotá-League Bylaws (carried north folded into the lining of a Hedgehog's medical kit during the Year 35 inter-team Healer-shortage exchange) · this article is the canonical North American summary; the Federación maintains its own canonical record, in Spanish and the Inca composite-creole, which the Foundation Library has not, by Federación-Caucus standing rule, been authorized to translate</div>
        <p>The Federación Sudamericana de Caballeros Flotantes (the Federation of Floating Knights of South America; in colloquial League Common usage, "the Federación" or "the Sur League") is a sport organization parallel to and contemporaneous with the North American League. The two leagues do not share rosters, scheduling, or governing bodies. They do share the rules of the sport, in their substantive form — five-knight teams, balloon contracts, perma-death, position archetypes broadly recognizable as Tank/Striker/Speedster/Brawler/Sniper/Healer/Grenadier with regional variation — and they share, by every available account, the canonical Whittlestone Address as their convocation speech, in a Spanish-and-Inca-composite-creole translation drafted by the Federación's first general counsel and ratified at the Federación's founding-bell convocation in Year 12. The two leagues' founding bells were not coordinated. They rang in the same season by, on every available analyst's read, mutual ignorance.</p>
        <p>The Federación was founded in Year 12 (League Common dating) at the Bogotá Cordillera Pitch, in a founding-bell convocation attended by representatives of seven communities: Bogotá's Spectacled Bears, Manaus's Capybaras, Cusco's Vicuñas, Buenos Aires's Maned Wolves, Caracas's Sloths, La Paz's Chinchillas, and Iquitos's Lowland Tapirs. The seven were the original Sur League's founding teams. The Federación has, in the twenty-four seasons since, expanded to eleven teams (the original seven plus Asunción's Howler Monkeys, Belém's Giant Anteaters, Montevideo's Coatis, and Santiago's Pampas Foxes — the last admitted in the Federación's own Year-22 Continental Expansion, which they call <em>la Expansión del Cono Sur</em>, "the Southern Cone Expansion"). The Federación's eleventh team is, by Federación standing rule, also its current configuration; the Federación has not announced plans for a twelfth.</p>
        <p>The Federación's founding bell was rung at Bogotá by Mateo Espinaobscura, a Spectacled Bear of the Cordillera Bear-Council and the Federación's first commissioner, who served from Year 12 through Year 19. Espinaobscura's pre-League career — which is, by every account the Foundation Library has gathered through Inkbeak's communiqués, the most-cited single biography in Sur League records — included a decade as a regional combat circuit organizer in the Andean foothills, in a circuit the Bear-Council called <em>el Circuito de las Cumbres</em> ("the Summits' Circuit"). The circuit's rules were broadly similar to the pre-League regional combat circuits the North American teams emerged from; the Spectacled Bears of the Cordillera, by their own historical record, claim the circuit's founding date is approximately three centuries pre-Long-Quiet, which would make it older than the equivalent North American pre-League traditions by a margin no analyst has, on either continent, attempted to dispute. The claim is, by every Sur historian's account, a matter of cultural pride. The claim is, by every North American historian's available scholarship, untested. The Foundation Library's filing note: <em>"the claim is, by my read, what the Bears say. the Bears have, in twenty-four seasons of correspondence, said it consistently. consistency is not, by my read, evidence; consistency is, by my read, a thing we should respect even when we cannot, by our own methods, verify it."</em></p>
        <p>The two leagues are connected primarily by the Pittsburgh Murder's flying-Raven correspondence program, established in Year 33 when Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. — the senior flying Raven of the Murder, then in his twenty-second year — undertook the first sanctioned northbound-southbound oceanic flight in modern League history. The flight took eleven days each way. Inkbeak landed at Cartagena, on the Federación's Caribbean coast, where he was met by a delegation of the Bogotá Spectacled Bears' coaching staff, who had been pre-warned of his arrival by a Quetzal-relay operating out of the (then-prospective) Yucatan canopy community. Inkbeak spent forty-one days in Federación territory, observed twelve sanctioned Federación matches, and returned with a folded-paper communiqué of seventeen pages handwritten in the Murder's archival shorthand. The communiqué is the canonical first-contact document. It is on display, by the Murder's standing donation, in the Foundation Library's archival roost — though not in any North American venue, by the Roost's standing preference that "the document is the Murder's, and is also, by our reading, the Federación's, and should not be hung in any venue that does not have, in its own institutional record, a relationship to both."</p>
        <p>The Federación and the North American League have not, as of Year 36, scheduled a sanctioned cross-continental match. The Caucus has discussed the possibility, in three closed-door working sessions across Years 34, 35, and 36; the Federación's parallel deliberations are, by Inkbeak's reports, similarly cautious. The principal obstacles, in both leagues' deliberations, are: (1) the journey itself, which is not, by any non-bird species' reasonable assessment, navigable in either direction within a tournament-friendly window; (2) the rules-divergence that, while small, is consistent — Federación matches use a six-balloon contract rather than three, with three popped by the standard popping rule and three reserved as <em>balones de honor</em> ("honor balloons") that may not be popped except in the deciding round of a deciding match, a rule the Federación argues "preserves the dignity of the visiting line by making certain forms of midmatch elimination impossible"; (3) the question of which league's commissioner, in the event of a match, has standing authority over rule disputes. The Caucus and the Federación have, in three working sessions each, declined to resolve any of the three. The leagues remain parallel. The Pittsburgh Murder remains the bridge.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library archival history · Year 36 mid-season filing · the canonical North American summary; the Federación's own canonical history is held in Bogotá and is not, by Federación-Caucus standing rule, available to non-Federación archivists in translation · Inkbeak Sr. continues to fly the Caribbean basin annually and has, in the four years since the first communiqué, made seven additional flights · the Murder's Roost has, on three subsequent Roost-vote questions of expanding the program, voted unanimously to keep it as a one-Raven program · their stated reason: <em>"one Raven is, by our reading, the Murder. multiple Ravens are, by every Federación-side report, a delegation. we are not yet, on this matter, a delegation. we will, in due course, be a delegation. we are not yet."</em></div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Land-Bridge Problem — why the two Leagues are not, despite geography, one</h3>
        <div class="meta">A history · drawn from the Foundation Atlas Committee's Year-34 cartographic survey, the Cintzli Letters (which are the most reliable Quetzal-side account of post-Long-Quiet Central American conditions), and the four Inkbeak Communiqués · this article addresses the question that, by every Caucus working-session minute since Year 33, the Caucus has been asked at least once per session: "the continents are connected. why are the leagues not?"</div>
        <p>The North American and South American continents are, by every pre-Long-Quiet geographic record the Foundation Library has access to, connected by an isthmus running approximately twelve hundred kilometers from southern Yucatan through what the Old-Ones called Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, to the northern terminus of the Andean cordillera in modern-day Colombia. By the same pre-Long-Quiet records, the isthmus was, in the centuries before the Long Quiet, traversable on foot in approximately forty-two days by a moderate-pace walker, and by various forms of pre-Long-Quiet transit in considerably less. The isthmus, in modern conditions, is not traversable in any reasonable interpretation of that word. The Foundation Atlas Committee's Year-34 cartographic survey — which is, by every committee member's pre-survey account, "the most thorough survey we are able to conduct without sending anyone we are not, by our consciences, willing to send" — establishes the modern isthmus as a discontinuous chain of seventeen separate land-segments separated by, in order from north to south: a flooded basin in southern Belize, a series of three volcanic-active high-temperature exclusion zones in Guatemala and Honduras, an unbridged river system in central Nicaragua that the survey describes as "approximately as wide as Lake Superior in pre-Long-Quiet measurements and as deep, by sonar samples taken from Cintzli's flight at minimum altitude, as anything short of an actual ocean," a coastal swamp belt across Costa Rica that the survey did not, by committee resolution, attempt to cross, and a final isthmus segment in Panama that is, by Cintzli's flight observation, "geographically intact but chemically altered in ways the canopy elders are not, by our own diagnostic ability, prepared to characterize for non-Quetzal species. it is fine for us. it is, by every read we have of pre-Long-Quiet bear and capybara physiology, very much not fine for them."</em> The committee's resolution: <em>"the isthmus is, in modern terms, an ocean. it is not, by our cartography, the same ocean as the Caribbean or the Pacific. it is its own ocean. the ocean has, by our naming, no name."</em></p>
        <p>The practical consequence of the Land-Bridge Problem is that the two Leagues are connected only by air, and by air only via the Caribbean basin's eleven-day Raven crossing route, which is — by every honest account on either continent — survivable only by long-distance flying birds with documented ocean-flight conditioning. The Pittsburgh Murder's flying Ravens are the only confirmed North-American-side survivors of the route to date. The Federación's side has its own fliers — three Andean Condor scouts who occasionally make the reverse trip, but who are, by Federación standing description, "less reliable narrators than our Bears would prefer," for reasons consistent with the broader birds-as-narrators caution the Federación shares with the North American Caucus and the Pittsburgh Murder. (See the Murder's Year-35 commentary on bird testimony, which the Federación's general counsel has, by formal letter, endorsed in full.) Cintzli of the Yucatan Quetzals has flown the Caribbean basin twice — once in Year 35, on the Quetzal-Federación liaison's first formal mission to Cartagena, and once in Year 36 on a personal visit she has, by her own pre-publication explanation, declined to characterize further. Cintzli is, by every Federación bear's pre-publication characterization, "not, by our reading, an unreliable narrator." She is, by her own pre-publication acknowledgment, also not a Raven, and is, by her own pre-publication acknowledgment, "willing to be considered the exception that confirms the rule, on the matter of which birds the Federación trusts on continental matters."</em></p>
        <p>The Caucus and the Federación have, in three working sessions each, considered the question of whether the Land-Bridge Problem is, on long enough timescales, soluble. The Caucus's working answer (drafted by Whittlestone in Year 35): <em>"on the timescale of the League's institutional memory — on the order of decades — the answer is no. on the timescale of the species' presence on this continent — on the order of millennia — the answer is, by every honest read available to us, also no, but the question becomes a different question. on the timescale of the planet — on the order of millions of years — the answer is yes. the planet has been, in pre-Long-Quiet geological record, both isthmic and oceanic across the gap multiple times. the gap will, on its own schedule, be both again. we will not, by any reasonable read, be present for the next transition. we are operating in a window. the window is, by every honest measurement, a very small slice of the planet's history. the work of the Leagues is to play, in the window, with the dignity that is owed to the work. the work is the work. the gap is the gap. neither, by my read, owes the other a resolution we are not, in our lifetimes, capable of providing."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library archival history · Year 36 mid-season filing · the canonical Caucus-side answer to the question · the Federación's parallel answer (drafted by Espinaobscura's successor, current Federación commissioner Doña Inés de la Niebla, also a Spectacled Bear) is, by Inkbeak's communiqué report, similar in conclusion but somewhat different in framing — the Federación frames the Problem as <em>"un problema del continente, no de la liga"</em> ("a problem of the continent, not of the league"), and considers the leagues' parallel existence to be, in itself, an honest response to the problem · the Foundation Library files both framings in the same drawer, by the curator's standing instruction</div>
      </article>
    </div>

        <h3>The League's Stadium Atlas</h3>
        <div class="meta">A field guide · Float Foundation Atlas Committee · live previews</div>
        <p>The complete Atlas, as of the Year 36 founding bell: 20 cities across the former North American continent, 8 sports, 12 effect overlays — 1,920 venue configurations across 160 physical buildings. Each card shows a faithful preview of the surface, its court markings, and (when an overlay is selected) the thematic effect applied. The picker bar at the top of the grid lets you browse every variant of every overlay; "Stock" shows the 160 venues in their natural state, while the other eleven effects re-skin them with their thematic dressing.</p>
        <p>The naming convention follows Whittlestone's three-axis "prefix-and-suffix model": <em>City / Adjective / Effect / Sport Venue</em>. So a Phoenix soccer pitch with the Foundry overlay reads "Phoenix Sandstone Foundry Pitch"; a Reno tennis court at default reads "Reno Neon Court"; a Helena ice rink with Hallowtide overlay reads "Helena Glacier Hallowtide Rink"; a Yucatan badminton hall with Petalfall reads "Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Petalfall Net Hall." The names are long. The names are also accurate. The Saint-Laurent Antlerlords' home venue is, by its own translator, "the only venue in the League whose name reads correctly in both League Common and Old-Ones French."</p>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Boston Concession Row</h3>
        <div class="meta">A field guide companion · Brewer's Reach Pitch · the License Wall is on the south corridor, behind the lobsterer's stand</div>
        <p>Concession Row is, by Foundation Atlas Committee designation, the only piece of stadium architecture in the League that is also a small functioning city. There are 26 vendors. The senior vendor's stand has been at the same address since Year 24, four seasons before the inaugural bell. The newest stand opened mid-Year 36 and sells, by sole discretion, three things: cider, dressed crab, and a small wedge of cheese the vendor has refused, on the matter, to name.</p>
        <p>The License Wall hangs in the south corridor, behind the lobsterer's stand. There are 47 names on the Wall — 26 active vendors and 21 retired or moved. By Foundation tradition, no name is removed; retired vendors' names are simply not lit. The Wolves have, on the matter, taken to bringing their annual cedar plank delivery to the License Wall first, and the lobsterer's stand second. The lobsterer has, on the matter, never complained about being second.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Atlas Committee, Concession Row companion entry</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall's Rafters</h3>
        <div class="meta">A field guide companion · the Quetzals' home venue · Cintzli's personal nest is, by Caucus declination, not registered as terrain</div>
        <p>The Hall is the only League venue with an active in-rafters habitat. Cintzli's personal nest is, by Caucus ruling (three separate declinations), not registered as terrain — the Quetzals' captain may, by League rule, retreat to the rafters during a match without forfeiting position. She has, in five seasons, done so exactly three times: two for tactical retreat, one for a stuck Tank teammate she had, on the matter, decided to coach in real-time from above.</p>
        <p>The rafters are not, by venue rule, accessible to the opposing team. This is not because the Caucus has ruled them off-limits — they have not — but because the rafters' construction (woven canopy fiber over a 28-foot ceiling) does not, by structural engineer's report, support any knight heavier than a Quetzal. The Antlerlords have, on the matter, never tested the rule. The Antlerlords have, on the matter, also never made eye contact with the rafters during a match. Marc-Olivier Brisefer's pre-match brief, on the Yucatan visit, is by team transcription a single sentence: <em>"on this match, the ceiling is the ceiling. Move on."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Atlas Committee, Yucatan companion entry</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Pittsburgh Visiting Perch's Empty Days</h3>
        <div class="meta">A field guide companion · the Allegheny Foundry · Slate Wirethorn's perch, two years' notice</div>
        <p>The Visiting Perch is the only piece of stadium architecture in the League that was, on commission, intended to stand empty. Slate Wirethorn forged the cantilevered iron arm in the autumn of Year 34, two seasons before the Andean Condor's arrival. The Bears sent a wax jar with a note that read, in full: <em>"para el día"</em> — "for the day." The jar sat sealed for 46 days before the perch was first occupied.</p>
        <p>The Foundry has, by tradition, kept the perch swept clean every morning regardless of whether a flying scout is in residence. The morning Marisol Cumbralta landed, the perch had been swept three hours before her arrival. The cleaner who swept it that morning was, by Maurin Brushpaw's own preference, Maurin's apprentice — a young Capybara whose first season on the Foundry staff was, on the matter, the season the perch was, on the matter, occupied. The apprentice's name is, by Maurin's own request, withheld from the broadcast roster. The apprentice will, by Maurin's own assurance, get her own line in the archive when she has, on the matter, earned one.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Atlas Committee, Pittsburgh companion entry</div>
      </article>

    <div class="lore-section lore-grid" data-loresection="bios">
      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Commissioner Margaux "Fang" Whiskerstone</h3>
        <div class="meta">Maine Coon · b. uncertain · League Office, head</div>
        <p>The Commissioner has been the Commissioner since Year 31. Before that, the Commissioner was, in order: a port-authority arbitration officer in Boston, a syndicated columnist in Tampa, the proprietor of a moderately successful tea shop in Olympia, and (briefly) a competitive sleeper. None of this should be relevant. All of it has come up.</p>
        <p>Whiskerstone is famous for her dispute resolution method, which is to physically sit on the contested object until both parties agree to a settlement. This works because the Commissioner is a Maine Coon, and Maine Coons are extraordinarily heavy when they want to be. The Office has documented at least two cases where she sat on a stadium's title deed for the better part of a fortnight before either city blinked.</p>
        <p>In a rare interview, the Commissioner once said: "I do not enforce the rules. I am the rules. Please do not test this." The interviewer's follow-up question is recorded in the League archives only as the word <em>laughter</em>, written in the margin by the recording clerk.</p>
        <p>Her chair is famously raised on a small dais. The League Office insists this is "for visibility." Everyone in the Office knows it is because Maine Coons hate not being the tallest creature in the room.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— "Who's Who in the League," updated annually</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Old Bristlebeard the First</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver · Tank · BVR · in the Hall · died Year 28 R5</div>
        <p>The first martyr. The first true Beaver. The patriarch of a name that has now been retired twice and re-fielded three times.</p>
        <p>Old Bristlebeard the First was, by all accounts, slow. He moved at the speed of an unloaded freight wagon. He was the worst Tank in his rookie cohort by the metric of footwork; he was the best by the metric of "still standing at the end of the round." He led the Beavers in damage absorbed for the inaugural season's full bracket, never won a single match's MVP award, and did not seem to mind.</p>
        <p>He died in the inaugural championship final of Year 28, holding a position that did not need to be held. He took three Beavers with him in the blast — a friendly-fire call that was, in his case, a strategic call: he ate the grenade so the Wolves could not use it on his squad. The League has classed it as <em>tactical self-sacrifice</em> and the Wolves still complain about it.</p>
        <p>His Riot Shield is the most-traveled item in League history. His Plasma Mace returned to a Bristlebeard exactly once, for one round, before being lost in the same match.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Hall of Fallen Heroes plaque, BVR</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Vela Hootington</h3>
        <div class="meta">Owl · Speed · OWL · in the Hall · died Year 35 R7</div>
        <p>The fastest Owl to ever hold a weapon. Vela Hootington's 22-kill streak still stands; the next two knights to break it both died trying.</p>
        <p>Hootington was a paradox. She moved like fog and spoke like she had a clock running. Her teammates loved her and resented her in roughly equal proportion, because she would lap them mid-engagement, and because she would refuse to repeat instructions she'd already given. She was famous for two pieces of equipment: her Plate Cuirass, which she handed to a teammate for a single round (her last) and which has since become known as Vela's Plate Cuirass, and her Stun Baton, which her killer (a Shark named Tomik Splashfang) carried for the rest of his career and then died holding.</p>
        <p>The "Vela's Plate Cuirass" item — the legacy item, in scavenge circulation — is currently believed to be on a knight in Olympia, though that knight has refused to confirm. The teammate she gave it to never spoke about her again. He retired after that season and bought the tea shop the Commissioner used to own. He still works there.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Owl Hall, Sundip Memorial Wing</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Mira Pawington, "The Scavenger Queen"</h3>
        <div class="meta">Kit · Speed · KIT · in the Hall · died Year 32 R6</div>
        <p>Mira Pawington holds the league record for scavenges in a career: eleven. She held the record for scavenges in a single match (four) until a Raccoon broke it; she does not particularly mind.</p>
        <p>She specialized in <em>polite</em> scavenging. Pawington was not a thief. She would walk up to a fallen knight, kneel, ask the body's permission (a Kits tradition), and then take the gear. League officials documented this in Year 31, when an opposing knight watching from the bench claimed Pawington had spent a full eight seconds in conversation with a corpse. The bench knight insisted, on record, that the corpse <em>responded</em>. The bench knight was sent home.</p>
        <p>Pawington died with her opponent's Power Cell in her hand, two animation frames from completing the steal. The opponent was a Raccoon. The Raccoon survived the round. The Raccoon kept the Power Cell. The Raccoon did not apologize. The Kits hold a moment of polite silence for Pawington in their pre-season retreat every year, and the Raccoons hold a moment of slightly less polite silence at the same time.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— "Quiet Hands: A Memoir of Scavenging," posthumous</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Felix Marshmallow</h3>
        <div class="meta">Panda · Tank · PND · in the Hall · grenade-safety drill namesake · died Year 34 R5</div>
        <p>Felix Marshmallow was the kind of teammate every team wants. He brought baked goods to practice. He learned everyone's siblings' names. He was famous for being the slowest Panda on a roster of slow Pandas, and proud of it.</p>
        <p>He died in Year 34, Round 5, of a fragmentation grenade thrown by a teammate from approximately seven feet away. The teammate had been aiming at an Otter. The Otter was, in fairness, on the other side of Felix Marshmallow.</p>
        <p>The League's grenade safety drills are now mandatory in pre-season for all teams. They were not mandatory before Year 34. The drills are, on the books, called the "Marshmallow Protocol." On the field they are called "Felix Drills." The teammate who threw the grenade has refused to grenade since. He has refused to grenade so emphatically that the Pandas now have a roster carve-out for him: he is <em>not allowed</em> to handle explosives, and his contract specifies it.</p>
        <p>Felix Marshmallow's family receives a benefit from the Float Foundation. The benefit is paid in lobster, at his family's request, sourced from Boston.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Pandas Roster Memorial, Portland Greenhouse</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>"Splinter" Tooth (allegedly)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver · disputed historical figure · "the Balloon's Father"</div>
        <p>Did Splinter Tooth exist? No one alive can confirm.</p>
        <p>League folklore credits Splinter Tooth with proposing the Balloon Contract in the League's first year — three balloons, three lives, popped publicly so the scoreboard could be read by the audience. The story is repeated by every Beaver coach to every Beaver rookie. The story has minor variations. In some versions Splinter Tooth was a champion who later retired to the lobster trade. In others, Splinter Tooth was a drunk who proposed the system on a bet and then forgot. In one version, recorded by a Reno historian who is not trusted, Splinter Tooth was a <em>Wolf</em> who infiltrated the Beavers' first roster.</p>
        <p>No League roster from Year 28 lists a "Splinter Tooth." This is taken, by Beavers, as proof of how good Splinter was. It is taken, by everyone else, as proof that Splinter Tooth never existed. Both interpretations agree that the Balloon Contract is real, valid, and binding.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— "Founding Myths," League Library Reading Room</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Hester Quillstrike</h3>
        <div class="meta">Hedgehog · Sniper · HED · in the Hall · died Year 35 R3 · 412-pace record co-holder</div>
        <p>Hester Quillstrike was a finished sniper before her League career began. She grew up shooting at painted plate targets in the foothills of Helena, where Hedgehog kids learn ranged combat the way Boston kids learn to use a hammer — quietly, daily, without ceremony. By the time HED was admitted to the League in Year 35, Hester was already, in any meaningful sense, the best sniper alive.</p>
        <p>She debuted in HED's inaugural season at the Helena Glacier Rink. Her first League kill was a 290-pace shot through a Wolf's helmet visor in Round 2 of HED's opening match. Three matches later, in HED's third match, she made a 412-pace rail shot across the full diagonal of the Rink, into a fleeing Otter Speedster. The League officials sent calipers to verify the distance. They confirmed. They apologized for asking. Hester said nothing.</p>
        <p>In Round 3 of that same match — the match where she set the record — she was killed by a coordinated four-Otter rush who had clearly identified her as the threat. She fell at her sniper position, her quiver still half-full, her Railgun Rifle still in her hand. The Rifle was scavenged by a Sundip Hootington Jr. shortly afterward. Sundip went on to match her record exactly, posthumously, before his own death at the Reno Open Court later in Year 35.</p>
        <p>The 412-pace mark is now co-held by Hester and Sundip. Neither one is alive to claim it. The Hedgehogs consider this fitting.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Hall of Fallen Heroes, Helena annex</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Tomik Splashfang the Bold</h3>
        <div class="meta">Shark · Brawl · SHK · in the Hall · died Year 30 R2 · grenade-fumble pioneer</div>
        <p>Tomik Splashfang was the kind of Brawler the league used to have — heavy, loud, charging, and immune to any form of strategic thinking that lasted longer than four seconds. He was the captain of the Sharks' inaugural roster (SHK was founded Year 30) and held that role until his death later that same year.</p>
        <p>His final match was Round 2 of SHK's third game ever. The Sharks were up 2-0 in rounds against the Beavers. Tomik had picked up a Frag Grenade — possibly his own, possibly Bristlebeard the First's, accounts differ — and was preparing to throw it at the Beavers' back zone. He was, at the time, two seconds into a stun applied by a Beaver Sniper. The stun ran out exactly when his throw arm would have completed.</p>
        <p>It did not complete. The grenade exploded in his hand. He took two Beavers with him; he also took himself. The Sharks, in fairness, won that match anyway, but they retired Tomik's number for the season and required all Brawlers to undergo a one-week stun-recovery course before handling explosives. The Marshmallow Protocol of Year 34 cites the Splashfang Incident in its preamble.</p>
        <p>Tomik's Stun Baton entered circulation after his death and was carried by, in order, Brask Ironclaw III and Vela Hootington. Vela died holding it. The Stun Baton is now believed to be in private retirement, somewhere on the Boise mountain pass.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Hall of Fallen Heroes, Tampa wing</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Crash Wartooth</h3>
        <div class="meta">Wolf · Brawl · WLF · in the Hall · died Year 33 R3 · Crash Rule namesake</div>
        <p>Crash Wartooth was, by Wolf standards, average. By every other team's standards he was terrifying. The Wolves are a hard grading curve.</p>
        <p>He played five seasons as the Wolves' lead Brawler, accruing 41 kills and an 11-kill streak. His pack-coordination instinct was excellent — the Wolves under his roster had a 70% match-win rate during his tenure. He was not personally famous; he wasn't a face-of-the-team kind of knight. He was reliable in the way load-bearing beams are reliable, and the Wolves liked him for it.</p>
        <p>He died at the Brewer's Reach Pitch in Round 3 of a Wolves vs. Beavers match in Year 33. The Beavers had brought three Stun Batons. Crash, doing what Brawlers do, charged. The Beavers stunned him. Crash stayed standing through the first stun (Wolves are tough). The Beavers stunned him again. Crash stayed standing through the second. The Beavers stunned him a third time. Crash, by this point, was unable to defend himself. A Beaver Brawler closed the kill. The full sequence, including all three stuns, took twelve seconds.</p>
        <p>The Wolves spent the next month re-engineering their Brawler kit. The "Crash Rule" — heavy plate is mandatory for any Wolves Brawler — was adopted in pre-season of Year 34 and has been honored ever since. No Wolf Brawler has died to a stun-volley since the Rule was adopted. Three Stun Batons have been thrown at Wolf Brawlers and bounced off without effect; the Beavers consider this insulting and the Wolves consider it correct.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Hall of Fallen Heroes, Wichita wing</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Sundip Hootington Jr.</h3>
        <div class="meta">Owl · Sniper · OWL · in the Hall · died Year 35 R8 · 412-pace record co-holder</div>
        <p>Sundip Hootington Jr. was the son of Sundip Hootington Sr., who was a journeyman Owl Brawler who died unspectacularly in his fourth season. The Junior was, by the family's accounting, supposed to be a Brawler too. He was not. He was a Sniper. The family did not approve until he tied the league's longest-shot record posthumously, by which time the family was no longer in a position to disapprove.</p>
        <p>His career was sparse and excellent. 36 kills across 4 seasons, 13-kill streak, 4 scavenges. He was famously methodical, disliked by his own teammates for refusing to call shots in advance, and feared by Healers for the obvious reason. He took his job seriously enough to make weekly visits to the Hall of Fallen Heroes' Hester Quillstrike memorial — he had carried her Railgun Rifle for two seasons after her death and considered it a debt.</p>
        <p>His final match was at the Reno Open Court in Year 35. He fired a 412-pace rail shot across the diagonal of the tennis court — exactly tying Hester's record — into a fleeing Frog Speedster. He climbed the Power Core to celebrate. The Power Core, which had been quiet for eight seasons, picked that moment to overload. Sundip did not survive the celebration. The League patched the overload that off-season.</p>
        <p>The Frog Speedster, in fairness, also died of the overload. The Frogs were given partial credit for posthumously denying Sundip his celebration. Hester's Rifle, which Sundip had been carrying, fell at the base of the Power Core and was scavenged in the post-match cleanup by a vault steward who has since requested unpaid leave.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Hall of Fallen Heroes, Sundip Memorial Wing, Seattle</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
