        <h3>Kor Wartooth</h3>
        <div class="meta">Wolf · Brawl · WLF · alive · Hallowtide Tag champion (Year 34, Year 35)</div>
        <p>Kor Wartooth is no relation to Crash Wartooth. The shared surname is solidarity — most Wolves who served on the Year 34 roster legally took on the Wartooth surname after Wikrai Wartooth Sr. fell in the Boise Final of Year 33, in the way some pack-Wolves take on the surname of a fallen pack-elder. Crash, who survived his own Year 34 R3 career-threatening injury and is still on the active line, was the family's other living elder at the time and consented to the broader adoption. The Commissioner's office accepted the paperwork without comment. There are now eleven living Wartooths and one dead one.</p>
        <p>Kor's career is unusual because most of it has happened in <em>melee-only</em> matches. In standard play he is a journeyman Brawler — competent, never spectacular, 14 kills across two seasons, no streaks longer than 4. In Hallowtide Tag he is an apex predator. He won the inaugural official Hallowtide Tag in Year 34 with one balloon remaining, the only living knight at the end of the seventy-eight-second match. He won it again in Year 35 with all three balloons intact.</p>
        <p>Asked by an LMG interviewer how he does it, Kor said: "I run faster when there are no guns." The interviewer asked if he was being literal. Kor said: "yes." The interviewer asked the team coach. The team coach said: "yes." The Wolves' kit-design office has, on three occasions, attempted to verify this claim with stopwatch trials in the off-season. The trials were inconclusive. The Wolves have stopped trialing.</p>
        <p>Kor will not enter the Coronation Cup. The crown's no-fire rule does not, on its face, prevent a melee Brawler from playing — but Kor has refused every entry the Wolves have offered. When asked, Kor says: "the crown is not for me." The Wolves do not press.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— "Profiles," LMG broadcast week of Hallowtide Year 35</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Reka Pawington</h3>
        <div class="meta">Kit · Speed · KIT · alive · Pawington Cup record-holder (3 caps in a single match, Year 35)</div>
        <p>Reka Pawington is Mira Pawington's first cousin once removed. She entered the league in Year 35 as a rookie Speedster on the Kits' roster and announced, in her debut interview, that she had two career goals. The first was to win the Pawington Cup. The second was to <em>not</em> die in the same way Mira did, which she described as "with someone else's stuff in my hand and someone else's elbow in my back."</p>
        <p>She has not yet won the Cup. She has, however, set the single-match capture record in her debut Cup appearance: three captures in one match, against the Sharks, who finished with zero captures and several complaints about the carrier-speed rule. Reka's cap rate is widely attributed to her unusual tactical preference: instead of running directly back to base after a flag pickup, she runs in a long arc that takes her near the field's edges. The arc is approximately 30% longer than the direct route. Defenders consistently fail to anticipate it.</p>
        <p>Asked why she runs the arc, Reka has given different answers in different interviews. The most-cited is: "Mira always said the corners watch you. The middle doesn't care." League historians do not know what this means. Reka has refused to elaborate.</p>
        <p>The arc is now informally known as the Pawington Arc. Three other Speedsters across the league have attempted to copy it. None have replicated her cap rate. The Pawington Tradition's third clause — <em>announce the take</em> — is still observed by the Kits when Reka caps. The announcement is a single yip that echoes off Hardwood Hall's ceiling. The crowd has learned to wait for it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— "Profiles," LMG broadcast week of Foundation Day Year 35</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Talia Featherquill</h3>
        <div class="meta">Owl · journalist · The Wing Standard · ethics columnist · Year 33–present</div>
        <p>Talia Featherquill has never been a knight. She has never trained as one and has, on more than one occasion, declined invitations to the rookie-tryouts week sponsored by the Owls' civic affairs office. She is, instead, the longest-serving ethics columnist at The Wing Standard, the Seattle-based weekly that began publishing in Year 33 and has not yet missed an issue.</p>
        <p>Her column appears in the Quarterly section, four times a year, and is widely read by knights, coaches, and the Commissioner's staff alike. She is famously hard to please. She has criticized the Personal Sandbag, the Power Core's overload latency, the Long Marketing Group's broadcast contract, and the Hallowtide Tag rule that allows the It knight to use a fallen prey's body as a tagging surface. She has also defended unpopular positions: that the Commissioner is right to refuse a sandbag-notification system, that the wider field is a structural improvement and not a betrayal of tradition, and that knights should be allowed to wear any color they want during the off-season.</p>
        <p>Her actual title at the paper is "staff columnist (ethics)." She also covers stadiums and obituaries when the regular reporters are unavailable. Her obituaries are widely considered the best in the League, in part because she refuses to write them in advance — she insists on hearing the news the same day everyone else does, and writes from the same first-shock state the readers will be in. She has written eleven knight obituaries since Year 33. She remembers all of them.</p>
        <p>Featherquill lives in Seattle near the Briarway Roost. She does not give interviews. She has, however, been the subject of one — an LMG broadcast profile in Year 35 that she declined to participate in, and which was therefore composed entirely of secondhand quotes from her colleagues, her editor, and one Otter Speedster who had once asked her for advice on accepting an endorsement deal. The Otter said Featherquill had told her: "if you have to ask me, you already know."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard staff page · author bio · Year 35 print edition</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Pell Whittlestone</h3>
        <div class="meta">Badger · journeyman knight, then artisan · BDG (active Year 28–Year 31, retired) · forged the Coronation Cup crown</div>
        <p>Pell Whittlestone played four seasons as a Boise Brawling Badger Brawler before retiring at the end of Year 31 to take up metalwork full-time. Her career stats are modest: 18 kills across 4 seasons, no streaks longer than 5, never killed in a match (she retired ambulatory, with all her balloons intact, which is unusual). She is not in the Hall. She does not need to be.</p>
        <p>What she is known for is the crown. When the League formalized the Coronation Cup at the end of Year 31 and the Commissioner's Office solicited bids for a brass crown to be delivered to whichever team won the inaugural Cup, Whittlestone submitted a single page in response: a sketch of the crown she would make, a list of materials she would need, and a price quoted in lobster instead of bits. The Commissioner's Office — staffed at the time by an intern who did not know how unusual the lobster quote was — accepted the bid. The crown was forged at Whittlestone's workshop in Boise across six weeks.</p>
        <p>The crown weighs four pounds. It is brass, hand-hammered, with a rim engraved by Whittlestone in a script that the League's calligraphers have identified as Boise vernacular but cannot decode beyond the obvious team-emblem motifs. The League has asked Whittlestone, on three separate occasions, to translate the engraving. Whittlestone has, on three occasions, declined. "It is not for the League," she has said, in three slightly different versions. "It is for the head that wears it."</p>
        <p>The crown is reported missing the morning after every Coronation Cup. The crown is recovered, in some manner, before the next Cup. The crown's engravings have grown, over the years — there is a new sigil added each season, and Whittlestone is the only person known to have access to the workshop where the engravings happen. She receives the crown by mail, returns it by mail, and bills the League in lobster. The Foundation pays in lobster. The Brewer's Reach lobster vendor supplies it. The accounting is, by every reasonable measure, sealed.</p>
        <p>Whittlestone lives in Boise. She does not coach. She does not train. She will, however, accept an apprentice — there is a current apprentice, an unnamed Badger pup, whose first independent piece (a brass match-medal, presented at the Year 35 Wichita Open) was widely admired. The apprentice is not yet doing crowns.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Day program, Year 35 — "The Hands That Make the Crowns"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Wikrai Wartooth Jr.</h3>
        <div class="meta">Wolf · Speed · WLF · alive · son of Wikrai Wartooth Sr. (deceased Year 33)</div>
        <p>Wikrai Wartooth Jr. is the only living knight in the League whose father was also a knight in the League. Most knight bloodlines, by the third generation, have at least one living parent — usually a coach, sometimes a vendor. Wikrai Jr.'s father, Wikrai Sr., died on the field in Year 33, taken in the Boise Final by an opportune Power Cell. Wikrai Jr. was eleven years old. He decided, at the funeral, that he would become a Wolf. He decided, the same week, that he would not adopt the Wartooth surname through legal solidarity (which his cousins did the next year) but would inherit it patrilineally, as the original Wartooths had done. The Pack accepted the decision. The Pack rarely refuses a grieving cub.</p>
        <p>His career is mid-tier and steady: 22 kills across three seasons, longest streak 7, two scavenges. He is not the most spectacular Wolf on the WLF roster. He is, however, the most-petitioned Wolf on the roster — meaning that fans send him more letters than anyone else, mostly thanking him for something his father did. He answers all of them. The replies are short. The replies are, by all accounts, kind.</p>
        <p>His most consequential off-field act was the Hallowtide petition. After the Year 33 informal pack-bonding ritual went well, the WLF coaching staff filed paperwork to make the ritual a formal League event. The paperwork went nowhere for two years. In Year 34, Wikrai Jr. — then 17, in his rookie season — refiled the petition under his own name, with one new sentence: <em>"My father did not get to play this. The next generation should."</em> The Commissioner approved the formalization within a week. Hallowtide Tag has been an official League event since Year 34. Kor Wartooth has won it twice. Wikrai Jr. has not yet won it. He has, in both years, made the bracket's quarterfinals and lost to Kor in matched-Wolf finals. He is at peace with this. The Pack notices that he is at peace with this. The fanbase loves him for it.</p>
        <p>He does not bow after kills. The Pack ritual is observed by older Wolves; Wikrai Jr. was raised on it and considers it sacred enough that he will not perform it casually. He is reported to have said, in a late-night LMG interview that the producer cut for length: "the bow is for fathers. I don't have one."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG late-broadcast interview, Year 35 Hallowtide eve · uncut transcript filed at WLF press office</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Old Bristlebeard the Third</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver · Tank · BVR · alive · current Year 35, third Bristlebeard, first to survive a season</div>
        <p>The Beavers have had three Bristlebeards. Old Bristlebeard the First died defending the inaugural championship final in Year 28. Old Bristlebeard the Second walked into Otter fire on the opening kickoff of Year 32 and was felled before the round's first minute. The Third, currently active, has survived eight matches. This is unprecedented. The Beavers are nervous about it.</p>
        <p>Bristlebeard the Third — Bjorn, in private — is twenty-two years old, the youngest Tank in League history at his debut, and an outlier in nearly every Beaver tradition. He does not, as the First and Second did, charge straight at the first enemy he sees. He does not, as Beaver Tanks have for eight seasons, lead the field. He plays a defensive position, holds the back line, and lets his Brawlers commit first. The fanbase is split. The older fanbase wants him to charge. The younger fanbase wants him to live.</p>
        <p>His coach, when asked about the unconventional play style, has said: "Bjorn is the first Bristlebeard who watched the previous Bristlebeards die. We do not coach him out of that." The coach was photographed saying this. The photo is in the Boston press office. Bjorn does not comment on it.</p>
        <p>He carries Old Bristlebeard the First's Riot Shield. The Shield has had seven carriers across six seasons. Bjorn is the seventh. He acquired the Shield in Year 35 R3 — it was scavenged from Wikrai Wartooth Sr.'s carrier in a gear exchange that the LMG broadcast missed and the next morning's papers had to reconstruct from witness reports. The Shield does not, by Bjorn's account, weigh more than any other Riot Shield. The Shield does, however, attract attention. Crowds cheer it. Photographers track it. The Foundation has made an offer to vault it; Bjorn declined the offer. "It's not done yet," he said, declining.</p>
        <p>If Bjorn survives this season — and the betting markets, after eight matches, currently put the odds at 3-to-1 favor of survival — he will be the first Bristlebeard in League history to play a second season. He will also, statistically, become the longest-serving Beaver Tank ever. The Beavers, who are still nervous, are also quietly proud.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— "The Survivor's Burden," Wing Standard feature, Year 35 mid-season</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Jossi Treadwell</h3>
        <div class="meta">Owl · LMG production director · Reno academy head instructor · never played a match</div>
        <p>Jossi Treadwell is, by any reasonable accounting, the most important person in the League's broadcast apparatus. She is also, by her own consistent insistence, the least photographed. The Wing Standard ran a feature on the LMG production team in Year 34; Treadwell agreed to be interviewed but declined to be photographed. The article ran with a photograph of her empty operator's chair at Hardwood Hall, the camera dolly behind it visible, the chair turned to face the action. It is, by the photographer's account, the photograph she preferred.</p>
        <p>She was not a knight. This fact gets repeated in every short reference to her in League records — <em>the LMG production director, an Owl, who has never been a knight</em> — because it is rare. Most of the League's adjacent professionals (referees, statisticians, broadcast crew) come from washed-out or retired playing careers. Treadwell never had a playing career. She apprenticed at the Beaverwell Heritage Studio — a five-room cinder block building in Boston's salvage-warren that had been continuously operated by Owls for at least seven generations, kept running on Old-Ones equipment that had been inherited, refurbished, and re-inherited so many times the equipment's provenance was, by the studio's own records, indistinguishable from the studio's identity. There was a sign on the door that read NO FOOTBALL FOOTAGE WITHOUT WRITTEN CONSENT, painted in latex compound on a slab of metal the studio's own founder had taken from an Old-Ones street-sign three centuries ago and hung above the door for reasons the studio's records describe only as <em>"because she liked it."</em> Treadwell has reportedly kept the sign and now hangs it in her Reno office. She arrived at the studio at sixteen. The studio's last director, an older Owl whose name has not survived in League records, taught her the dolly rig, the framing protocols, the timing-call protocols, and the ethics of broadcast (the older Owl's stated rule, which Treadwell has quoted in every academy lecture she gives: <em>"You do not own the moment. You frame it. The audience owns it. If you frame it wrong, you have stolen it from them."</em>) over the course of three years. The studio closed when the older Owl died in Year 22; the Heritage Studio's tools were absorbed by the Boston Cultural Office and are, to this day, available to League broadcast staff on request. Treadwell took the camera dolly with her under a separate inheritance arrangement made in writing before the older Owl's death.</p>
        <p>She arrived at Brewer's Reach in Year 28, week one, with the dolly in the back of a salvaged truck and a written request to be allowed to film the inaugural match. Old Bristlebeard the First, then the Beavers' coach, granted permission on the condition that she not photograph any individual knight without written permission from the knight first. Treadwell agreed in writing. The agreement, by League records, has been honored every match since. Knights who have asked, in subsequent seasons, whether they were filmed during a particular play have always received an honest answer; knights who have not asked have not been filmed individually, only in wide shot. The League has, on three occasions, asked Treadwell to deviate from this rule for legal-evidence purposes (the Year 31 Phoenix incident, the Year 33 Coalbroke truck-stop investigation, and an unspecified third matter the records have sealed). She has declined all three times. The League has, all three times, accepted her decline.</p>
        <p>She moved the LMG production booth to Hardwood Hall in Year 33 when the dynamic-camera prototype was being tested; she has lived in Kansas since. Her Reno academy is run remotely. She returns to Reno four times a year for the Cup-cycle finals and the academy's intake week. Her assistant production directors — there are three of them now, all from the Reno academy, all Owls — handle the regular-season broadcasts she does not personally cover. She still operates the camera personally for every Coronation Cup, Pawington Cup, and Hallowtide Tag final.</p>
        <p>Featherquill, who has known Treadwell since Year 29, has profiled her exactly once and closed the profile with the only sentence Treadwell has ever publicly co-signed: <em>"Treadwell will not be remembered as a great owl. Treadwell will be remembered as the owl who watched."</em> Treadwell, reading this, is reported to have nodded once, said "that's correct," and gone back to looking at the field.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "The Owl in the Booth" — Featherquill, Year 34 mid-season feature</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Brask Ironclaw III</h3>
        <div class="meta">Fox · Tank · FOX · deceased Year 31 · son of Brask Sr. (head coach FOX, retired)</div>
        <p>Brask Ironclaw III was the third generation of his family to play Tank for the Phoenix Foxes. His grandfather served on the founding-era roster of Year 28 in a supporting role and never started a match; his father, Brask Sr., started fourteen matches across Year 29 and Year 30 before transitioning to coaching when Brask III made the active roster. The handoff was, by every account from the Foxes' bench, deliberate. Brask III was eighteen years old when he debuted. His father stepped behind the boards within the same week.</p>
        <p>His career lasted six and a half matches. He was the second-youngest Tank in League history at debut (the youngest is now Bjorn Bristlebeard, who has the additional distinction of having survived his rookie season). Brask III's stats at his death were not remarkable: 9 kills, longest streak 4, average lives remaining at round-end 1.7. The numbers do not reflect what he was. What he was, by general agreement, was a Tank who would walk into a corridor he knew was a kill zone if his Healer was on the wrong side of it.</p>
        <p>He died at home, at the Phoenix Sandstone Bowl, in a R5 against the Wichita Wolves. The match was a Coronation Cup qualifier. The death was a Crash Wartooth pin — three Wolves on Brask, two of them carrying Plasma Maces, no clear shot for Brask's own teammates. He held the corridor for eleven seconds. His Healer reached him at the eight-second mark and was killed by the second Mace. Brask III's last balloon popped at the eleventh second. The Wolves did not, by tradition or by witness account, bow.</p>
        <p>His father coached the entire match from the boards. Brask Sr. did not call for a substitution. Brask Sr. did not call for retreat. After the round, Brask Sr. stood up, walked around the boards, and sat next to his son's body on the field for the seven minutes the field crew needed to clear it. He has not commented publicly on those seven minutes. The Foxes' assistant coach, who had to step in to manage the rest of the bracket, said only: "He was the head coach. He was also the father. He sat with his son. There was nothing else to coach in those seven minutes."</p>
        <p>Brask Sr. retired from coaching at the end of the Year 31 season. The Foxes hired the assistant. Brask Sr. is, as of the current League Year, working as a metalsmith in Phoenix's old industrial quarter. He has not attended a Foxes match since his son's funeral. He has, however, been seen at Olympia matches when the Foxes were in the bracket — not as a coach, not in colors, just as a fan in the back rows. He pays for his ticket. The lobster vendor at Brewer's Reach has, at least once, been seen at a Phoenix–Olympia road game, sharing his row, saying nothing.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Phoenix municipal archives, "Foxes Roster Histories Vol. III," compiled Year 33</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>The Lobster Vendor of Brewer's Reach</h3>
        <div class="meta">Crustacean · vendor · Brewer's Reach concession booth · uncertain age · possibly canonical</div>
        <p>The lobster vendor of Brewer's Reach is a real person. This is the most that can be said with certainty. Beyond it, the record is contradictory in almost every direction — and the contradictions are themselves part of the canon, repeated faithfully and gravely across eight seasons of attempted profiles.</p>
        <p>What is agreed: she runs a single concession booth on the south concourse of the Brewer's Reach Pitch in Boston. She has run it since the inaugural match of Year 28, every match the Pitch has hosted, including the bracket-bye matches when no Beavers were playing. She sells four things — lobster bisque, lobster rolls, lobster claws (steamed), and a small cup of clarified butter she calls "the dip." She sells nothing else. She has, on three documented occasions, refused to sell food to specific patrons; in two of those cases the patron was a Wolf, and in the third the patron was a former Beavers Tank who had publicly criticized her bisque the prior season. The record does not say whether she relented.</p>
        <p>What is contested: her age, her species (a clade of lobster-adjacent crustaceans is documented in the early-League rosters but the vendor herself has never been registered as a player or staff member of any formal League body), her residence, and the precise mechanism by which she travels to road games. She has been documented at Phoenix in Year 31, sitting silently with Brask Ironclaw Sr. in the back rows of the away stand. She has been documented at Reno, weeping in the concession area on the night of Sundip Hootington Jr.'s death — though the dispatch reporter took care to clarify that the Reno vendor was a different person, suggesting either the Brewer's Reach vendor was also there, or the dispatch reporter was being cautious about a thing he could not explain. She has been documented at Helena Glacier Rink on the night of Hester Quillstrike's death. The pattern, by every reading of the documents, is that she appears for the deaths.</p>
        <p>What is folklore: she is older than the League. She was the first vendor at the first match because she was at the site before the Pitch was built, in a small wooden cart she pulled herself. She does not age. She has never been photographed clearly enough for any reporter to confirm the same vendor across two adjacent seasons, but the vendor at the booth always says, when asked, "I have been here." She bills the Foundation in lobster, of course. The Foundation pays in lobster. The accounting, as Whittlestone's accounting does, makes its own internal sense.</p>
        <p>What is true: the bisque is excellent. Reporters who have profiled her over the eight seasons of the League's existence universally agree that the bisque is excellent. The bisque has been the same recipe since Year 28, by the vendor's account; she has, on one occasion, agreed to share the recipe with a culinary journalist from Olympia who ran the recipe in a small culinary quarterly. The recipe, when followed precisely, does not produce the bisque. The journalist tested it three times. The journalist reported, in a follow-up column, that "there is something in the bisque that is not in the recipe, and the vendor has not lied — the recipe is hers — but it is not all of it." The vendor, when asked about the column, said: "I have been here." She did not elaborate.</p>
        <p>An anonymous BVR season-pass holder, in a notebook entry covering the Year 31 funeral of Brask Ironclaw III, recorded the following: "The lobster vendor was at the funeral. I do not know how she got to Phoenix." It is the most honest sentence anyone has written about her.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard cultural feature, "Standing Witness," Year 34 — author declined attribution</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Ojee Stripeshoulder</h3>
        <div class="meta">Tiger matriarch · Bayou Burning Tigers · signatory of the Four-Team Expansion application · Year 35 closeout</div>
        <p>Ojee Stripeshoulder did not, by any account that has reached the League, set out to be the matriarch of the Bayou Tigers. She set out to be a respected Striker, broke her left hind leg in a salvage-warehouse accident at age twenty-six, lost the playing speed that had been her livelihood, and decided — three months into a forced rehabilitation she has never described publicly — to spend the rest of her career teaching tigers half her age how to stalk an opening. The Bayou roster, on the day she became matriarch, had four registered players. The roster on the day she signed the joint Expansion application had thirty-four. Twenty-eight of them learned to play under her.</p>
        <p>Her stripe-painting practice — she paints every helmet on the active roster before every match, by hand, with a pigment she mixes herself from cypress-bark resin and a closely-guarded second ingredient — is widely believed by the team to be ceremonial. It is not entirely. The pigment is also a slow-curing antifungal. Bayou helmets, in the delta humidity, would otherwise mold within four matches. The ceremony is real <em>and</em> the helmet is preserved. Stripeshoulder, when asked whether the ceremony or the antifungal was the more important purpose, said: <em>"I do not separate things that have arrived together."</em> She has not elaborated on this answer in any subsequent interview, and reporters have stopped asking.</p>
        <p>Her opening line in the joint Expansion application — <em>"We have waited"</em> — was, by the Office of the Commissioner's records, written first by her, then quietly co-signed by the other three signatories before the document was sent. Whitepaw is reported to have read it twice, said "yes, that is correct," and signed. Yellowhide is reported to have grunted approval, then offered to add a sentence that was politely declined by the other three. Quorrik is reported to have asked whether the Tigers were sure about the word "waited" — Ravens, by tradition, do not wait for invitations — and Stripeshoulder is reported to have said, after a long pause: <em>"You waited too. You did not call it that."</em> Quorrik signed without further comment.</p>
        <p>Stripeshoulder will not, by her own statement, play in any Year 36 match. She is an active matriarch, not an active knight. She will be in the stands. She will paint the helmets. She will, her assistant coach has confirmed, not coach from the bench during matches — the Tigers run a deliberately non-shouting bench, in keeping with their stalking style — but she will be visible to her knights from the stands at all times. Her chair, in every Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue, is in the same row as the field marshal's. She watches.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "The Matriarch of the Cypress Hollow" · Year 35 R12, by Talia Featherquill</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Tamzen Whitepaw</h3>
        <div class="meta">Polar Bear elder · Anchorage Avalanche Polar Bears · signatory of the Four-Team Expansion application · Year 35 closeout</div>
        <p>Tamzen Whitepaw walked from Anchorage to Brewer's Reach. So did the rest of the Polar Bears' delegation, but Whitepaw, by every account, walked first — at the front of the column, breaking trail through the late-spring snow, for the first eight days of what became a thirty-two-day journey. The other elders rotated the lead through the remaining twenty-four days. Whitepaw did not. She walked the entire trail at the front. When asked, on arrival, whether she was tired, she answered: <em>"I am the same amount of tired I was when we left. The walk is what tired looks like."</em></p>
        <p>She is, by the Anchorage settlement's records, ninety-one years old. The Polar Bears do not, as a species, retire from civic responsibility — Whitepaw has been the chief elder of the Anchorage settlement since Year 29, when the previous chief elder died of old age at one hundred and four — and she has stated, in writing, that she will continue to lead the team's elder council "for as long as the council finds my judgment useful." The council has not held a vote on this matter. The Polar Bears do not, by tradition, take votes on whether their elders should still be elders.</p>
        <p>Her armor, custom-forged in Anchorage by the settlement's lead smith Bjorgun Whitemane, is widely believed to be the heaviest functional armor in the League. Whitemane will not disclose its weight on the record but has, off the record, told visiting reporters that "you would not be able to lift it. You would not be able to lift the helmet alone. The helmet alone is not the heaviest part. The helmet is the lightest part." Whitepaw wears it in matches. She moves slowly. She does not move quickly even when the round demands it. The Polar Bear style, by Whitepaw's own description, is: <em>"slow the storm. outlast it."</em> Polar Bear Tanks have, in the team's pre-League barnstorming exhibitions, soaked thirty consecutive close-range hits without falling. Stripeshoulder, after attending one of these exhibitions, sent Whitepaw a brief note: <em>"We will not stalk you. We do not have time."</em> Whitepaw kept the note.</p>
        <p>She has, by the application's record, exactly one stated worry about the Year 36 season: that the bracket draw will pull the Polar Bears in their first season more often than the random distribution should. She mentioned this, conversationally, to Whiskerstone after the application was ratified. Whiskerstone is reported to have said: <em>"The draw will be the draw. If you are drawn often, you are drawn often. We will not adjust."</em> Whitepaw nodded. She has not raised the subject again.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "The Bear Who Walked First" · Year 35 R13, by Talia Featherquill</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Yellowhide of the Denver Herd</h3>
        <div class="meta">Bison elder · Denver Driving Bison · ceremonial lead, attends every home match in full harness · Year 35 closeout</div>
        <p>Yellowhide is twenty-two years old, which is old for a bison and is not, by Denver custom, the kind of age a fighting elder reaches. He fought competitively from age four to age fourteen — ten seasons of plains-circuit matches, no League affiliation, no records the Float Foundation can verify, only the testimony of Denver knights who saw him fight and who all describe his style identically: <em>he stood where he stood, and the other team adjusted around him, and then we won</em>. He stopped fighting after a horn fracture in his eleventh year that did not heal cleanly. He has, since, served as the herd's lead elder.</p>
        <p>His ceremonial harness — leather, worked with copper and stained with Denver red dust — was made for him by the herd's saddler in Year 29 and has been resized twice as he has aged. He wears it to every Bison home match. He stands at the south end of the Highland-Plains pitch in full harness for the duration of every match the Bison play in Denver. He does not coach. He does not heckle. He stands. The Bison knights, by the herd's coaching staff's account, do not need him to coach — they need him to stand. The Bison's herd-rotation tactical style requires every knight to know, at any moment, where the herd's center of gravity is. Yellowhide is, by tradition, that gravity. The knights orient on him without thinking about it. The opposing teams, by the third match against the Bison in the Bison's pre-League exhibitions, learned to orient on him too.</p>
        <p>He signed the Four-Team Expansion application with a hoof-print in red dust, the way Denver elders sign formal documents. The print is on file at the Office of the Commissioner. The Office's records-keeper, an elderly otter named Kirrin, has reportedly photographed it for the archive and added a single annotated note in his hand: <em>"This is a signature. We have accepted other signatures that meant less."</em></p>
        <p>Yellowhide, asked whether he intended to attend Bison away matches as well in Year 36, said: <em>"I attend the matches the herd plays at home. I am the herd. The herd cannot leave the home. The herd that travels is a delegation. They will be fine."</em> Whiskerstone, on hearing this, is reported to have agreed without comment.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Float Foundation Atlas Committee, "On Yellowhide" · Year 35 closeout, internal note circulated to coaching staff</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Quorrik</h3>
        <div class="meta">Raven captain · Pittsburgh Plundering Ravens · signatory of the Four-Team Expansion application · Year 35 closeout</div>
        <p>Quorrik — recorded only by single name in League documents because Ravens, by tradition, only take their parent's name after their first kill in defense of the murder, and Quorrik has not yet had occasion — is twenty-six years old, the youngest of the four Expansion signatories, and the only one who is also, by team designation, an active knight. Quorrik's roster position is Sniper. The Ravens' Sniper class is the most-decorated archery class in the League's pre-League barnstorming records. Quorrik, by their own coach's account, is the second-best Sniper in the Ravens' active roster. The best Sniper, an older Raven named Skell, has declined to comment on Quorrik's ranking. Skell has, however, declined to take the captaincy when offered, on the grounds that "Quorrik should hold it. Quorrik will hold it longer than I will need to."</p>
        <p>Quorrik writes left-handed. This matters because the Ravens' Snipers, by long custom, all draw the bowstring with the right hand and the arrow-rest is set up accordingly on every Ravens-issue Sniper bow. Quorrik's bow, custom-made by a Pittsburgh fletcher named Erris who has served the murder for thirty years, is a left-handed mirror of the standard Ravens bow with a mirrored arrow-rest. Erris, when asked whether the bow was harder to make, said: <em>"It was the same difficulty. The bow does not have an opinion. The fletcher had to remember to turn the workshop the other way around."</em></p>
        <p>The Ravens, as a team, do not bury their dead. They cremate, the way they have always cremated, in the foundry-fires of the Pittsburgh ruins. Quorrik will, as captain, lead the cremation ceremony for any Raven knight who falls during the Year 36 season. They have stated, in writing, that they are prepared for this. They have stated, also in writing, that they hope not to perform it more than once.</p>
        <p>Quorrik attended the Caucus's ratification meeting in Boston. They flew. The flight from Pittsburgh to Boston took six days with three rest stops. Quorrik arrived two hours before the Caucus opened its session. They did not, by Whiskerstone's record, sleep before speaking. When asked, after the ratification, whether they were tired, they answered: <em>"I will be tired in Pittsburgh. Not here."</em> They flew home. The Ravens' fletcher Erris is reported to have met them at the perch with a fresh-strung bow, said nothing, and walked them home.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "The Captain Who Flies" · Year 35 R13, by Talia Featherquill</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Tessik Snowstep</h3>
        <div class="meta">Lynx coach · Yukon Hunting Lynx · sole delegate of the Year 36 Continental Expansion · arrived alone</div>
        <p>Tessik Snowstep is the only person in League records to have personally hand-carried five active knights' rosters and credentials across the entire continent without bringing any of those knights with them. Tessik did this because the Lynx considered it inappropriate for the knights to travel together. The Lynx, by tradition, do not travel in groups larger than two; the knights would have come, but they would have come in five separate parties along five separate routes, and would have arrived at five different times across approximately a six-week window. The Office of the Commissioner did not, in its initial reply to the Yukon Boreal Council, fully understand this. The Office of the Commissioner suggested the Lynx send a delegation. Tessik replied, in a single sentence: <em>"I am the delegation. The knights will play the matches."</em></p>
        <p>Tessik is, by Yukon Council records, fifty-three years old, retired from active competition since Year 31 (a knee injury sustained on a hunt that the Council records do not specify the species of), and has been the senior coach of the Lynx team since the team's formation in Year 34. Tessik holds the rare distinction of being one of the only Lynx in known living memory to be photographed: there are exactly three photographs of Tessik in the League's records, all three taken at the Year 36 Caucus's ratification meeting, all three taken with Tessik's prior written consent, all three taken from approximately the same angle. Tessik does not consider this a personal preference. Tessik considers it a professional accommodation. <em>"The League's audience needs to be able to recognize the coaches,"</em> Tessik said when asked. <em>"I will be in five photographs over the course of my coaching career. We have agreed in advance which five. I have already used three."</em></p>
        <p>Tessik's coaching style does not, by their own description, involve a great deal of speaking to the players. The Lynx training program is constructed around solitary preparation: each knight is assigned a coach for their position class (the team has five coaches, one per position) and trains alone with that coach for the bulk of the season. Tessik's role as senior coach is to <em>review</em> the training, not to <em>direct</em> it. They write notes. The notes are short. The longest note, on file in the Yukon Council records, is forty-one words long; it concerns a Sniper named Kell who, by Tessik's observation, was holding their breath wrong before each shot. Kell adjusted. The note has not been needed again.</p>
        <p>Tessik, asked at the founding bell what their hopes were for the Year 36 season, answered: <em>"I hope my knights play well. I hope they come home. I hope I can return to the Yukon by mid-season — I have been away for some time, and I am tired of being among so many people."</em> The interviewer pointed out that the Lynx's first scheduled match was eight weeks out and Tessik would, presumably, have to remain in Boston until at least then. Tessik said: <em>"Yes. I will be very tired by then."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Yukon Boreal Council, "Coach Profile: Tessik Snowstep" · Year 36 founding bell</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Bertaud Antlerwood</h3>
        <div class="meta">Moose patriarch · Saint-Laurent Antlerlords · senior delegate · 9'2" at the shoulder, antler span 6'4"</div>
        <p>Bertaud Antlerwood is, by physical measurement, the largest knight in the League. He stands nine feet two inches at the shoulder. His antler span is six feet four inches at full racks (the antlers shed and regrow seasonally; the Year 36 spring rack is, by the Quebec roster's measurement, the largest he has ever grown). Bertaud is also, by his own assessment, the slowest knight in the League. He moves, he says, "at the speed I move. The other knights have agreed not to ask me to move faster, because they have, on multiple occasions, tried to ask, and have not enjoyed the experience."</p>
        <p>The Moose, as a species, are not native French speakers — French was the prior species' language, and the Moose simply continued to use it after the prior species was gone, in the way the Pittsburgh ravens continued to use the foundry. Bertaud, however, speaks a dialect that has descended further than most: a creole of Old-Ones French and an animal-tongue the Moose call, simply, <em>la langue</em>. The LMG broadcast booth has, for the Year 36 season, hired a dedicated translator — an Owl named Pellic Snowcrest, formerly the Geography Caucus, now part-time interpreter — to render Bertaud's match-time observations into League Common. Snowcrest's working notes describe Bertaud's speech as <em>"slower than League Common, more poetic than League Common, and, by my preliminary count, requiring approximately three League-Common sentences to render each Moose sentence accurately. I will need a larger notebook."</em></p>
        <p>Bertaud's antler rack is, under League rules, an attached weapon. The Moose argued for this designation in their original Year 32 application; the Caucus had, at the time, ruled that the rack was not an attached weapon because the rack was not <em>removable</em>. The Moose's revised Year 36 application addressed this point directly: <em>"The antler is not removable. This is correct. The antler is also lethal. We are confident the audience would prefer to know the antler counts as a weapon, rather than be surprised by the antler when the Moose reaches a Brawler at melee range. We are flexible on the wording. We are not flexible on the audience knowing."</em> The Caucus, on a 12-3 vote, classified the antler as an attached weapon for the Year 36 season forward. The Moose did not comment.</p>
        <p>Bertaud, asked at the founding bell whether he was looking forward to playing in front of a non-Quebec audience, answered (through Snowcrest's translation): <em>"The audience is the audience. I have always played in front of an audience. The audience in Quebec speaks Moose. The audience in Boston speaks League Common. The audience in Anchorage will, I am told, speak Polar Bear, which I am told sounds approximately like the wind makes when it is cold and tired. I will be all right. The audience will be all right. We will all be all right."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG Broadcast Brief, "Translator's Notes" · Snowcrest, supervising · Year 36 founding bell</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Yara of the Sonora pack</h3>
        <div class="meta">Coyote captain · Sonora Drifting Coyotes · pack leader since Year 32</div>
        <p>Yara of the Sonora pack does not, by Coyote tradition, have a surname. The Coyotes do not take surnames. Coyotes identify themselves by their pack — Yara of the Sonora pack is one Yara; there is also (by Sonora roster records) a Yara of the Mojave pack who is unrelated, a Yara of the Apache pack who is also unrelated, and at least two further Yaras whose packs are not currently in League records. The disambiguation system is functional within the Coyote community. The League's broadcast booth has, by Treadwell's recommendation, agreed to refer to Yara on first reference as "Yara of the Sonora pack" and on subsequent references simply as "Yara," with the understanding that any other Yaras who later enter League records will receive equivalent first-reference framings.</p>
        <p>Yara has been the Sonora pack's leader since Year 32. The transition from previous leader (a Coyote whose name does not appear in League records but whom the Sonora pack remembers as <em>"the one before Yara"</em>) was, by all accounts, peaceful. The previous leader walked into the desert one evening and did not return. Yara walked out the next morning to find the previous leader's tracks, followed them for half a day, found a single coyote-print pointing west, and turned around. The pack accepted Yara's leadership on her return. The previous leader has not been confirmed missing or dead by any Coyote authority — the Sonora pack considers the previous leader to be <em>"out there, somewhere, doing what they are doing"</em> — but the previous leader has also not, by League records, been seen since.</p>
        <p>Yara's tactical signature, the so-called <em>desert pattern</em>, was first documented in pre-League exhibition matches in Year 33 and has been the Sonora pack's primary engagement style since. The pattern, as Featherquill described it: <em>"A coyote will appear to retreat, then appear to retreat again, then appear to be alone, then six coyotes will engage from positions the opposing team had thought were already cleared."</em> The pattern requires the entire pack to commit to misdirection in the same beat — and the same precise timing. The Sonora pack has, by their training records, drilled the pattern eleven thousand times. They do not, by Yara's own account, ever expect to drill it ten thousand more.</p>
        <p>Yara, asked at the founding bell whether she was confident the desert pattern would translate to non-desert venues, answered: <em>"The pattern is not about the desert. The pattern is about <em>asking the desert</em>. The desert is what we have been listening to. We can listen anywhere. The Sonora is the desert that taught us how to listen. The other venues are other deserts that have not yet been told they are deserts. We will tell them."</em> Featherquill's marginal note on the interview transcript: <em>"I think she means it."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "Asking the Desert" — Featherquill, Year 36 founding bell preview feature</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy</h3>
        <div class="meta">Quetzal captain · Yucatan Vibrant Quetzals · sniper · plumage measurement on file with the Caucus</div>
        <p>Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy is the smallest active knight in the League by mass. She is also, by her own coach's measurement, the most distinctively colored: her crest is brilliant emerald, her breast is deep crimson, her wing-coverts are a shifted iridescent green that the Caucus's official plumage record describes (with apparent reluctance) as <em>"approximately the color of a particular kind of moss reflected through a particular kind of water; we have not been able to fix this color in pigment"</em>. The Quetzals, as a species, do not consider their coloration unusual. The other species in the League consider it remarkable. The Foxes' captain, on first seeing Cintzli at a pre-season inter-team meet, is reported to have said: <em>"I have just learned that we have been playing the wrong sport this whole time. The sport should be the kind that this Quetzal wins."</em></p>
        <p>Cintzli is the Yucatan team's sniper. Her preferred shooting position is in the rafters of the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy venue, in a nest she has personally maintained since the team's formation. The nest is not, by League records, registered as terrain. The Caucus has discussed registering it. The Caucus has, on each occasion, decided not to register it, on the grounds that "the rafters were here before the team was; the nest was here before the team was; the Quetzal was, by her own account, here before the rafters were; we cannot retrofit the venue around the player's nest, but we are also not in a position to ask the player to relocate her nest."</p>
        <p>Cintzli speaks four languages: Quetzal native, League Common, what the Yucatan refers to as <em>"the trees' language"</em> (which is, by Cintzli's own description, <em>"a way of asking the trees to keep being trees while we sit in them"</em>), and a working Old-Ones Spanish she learned from the runes around the Yucatan basin. She has been, on three occasions, asked to translate Spanish runes for visiting League archivists. She has, on each occasion, said yes. On each of those occasions she has charged a fee of one fresh fruit. She has been paid in fruit she selected each time. The Spanish translations she has provided are reported to be excellent.</p>
        <p>Cintzli, asked at the founding bell whether she was concerned the Year 36 schedule would put her in venues without rafters, answered: <em>"Every venue has a high point. Every high point can be a nest if I bring my own moss. I have brought my own moss. The League will see what I do with it."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Plumage Records, "Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy" · Year 36 founding bell</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio lore-wide">
        <h3>Théodred Brisefer III, "L'Ancrage"</h3>
        <div class="meta">Moose tank · Saint-Laurent Antlerlords · founding-bell roster · the largest knight in League history by mass and by a wide margin</div>
        <p>Théodred Brisefer III — known on the Saint-Laurent ice as <em>L'Ancrage</em> ("The Anchor") — is the heaviest knight to ever take a sanctioned League field. The Caucus's mass register, updated at every founding bell since Year 28, lists his weight at <em>"approximately one and three-quarters of an Old-Ones cargo lorry, fully loaded; we have not measured him precisely because the measuring scale we possess goes only to one Old-Ones cargo lorry"</em>. The previous record, set by his grandfather Théodred the First in Year 30, stood at one and one-quarter cargo lorries. The intervening generation, Théodred II, played four exhibition matches in Year 33 before retiring with a knee complaint that the Antlerlords' medical staff described, in their report, as <em>"the inevitable consequence of being two cargo lorries"</em>. Théodred III intends to play through Year 40 if his knees will allow it. They probably will not. He intends to play anyway.</p>
        <p>The Antlerlords' tank class is, by League rule, technically just a Moose. The position has no shield assignment, no plate kit, and no separate weapon — the Moose's antler rack <em>is</em> the Tank's weapon under the Year-36 ratified armor exemption. Théodred III's antler rack is, by the Caucus's plumage and antler register, the broadest active rack in the League: ninety-seven inches tip-to-tip, fourteen tines on the left, sixteen on the right, palmation that registers, by the Caucus's measurement plate, as <em>"the size of a tabletop on each side; we are not certain how the knight passes through doorways and we are choosing, formally, not to ask."</em></p>
        <p>The Antlerlords' captain, Marc-Olivier Brisefer (Théodred III's elder cousin and the team's founding captain), describes Théodred's tactical role in the Saint-Laurent native creole of Old-Ones French and animal-tongue: <em>"L'Ancrage est l'ancrage. C'est tout. Si l'ancrage bouge, l'équipe bouge. Si l'ancrage ne bouge pas, l'équipe ne bouge pas. Et l'ancrage ne bouge presque jamais."</em> The LMG broadcast booth's translator, asked to render this for the broadcast feed, supplies: <em>"The Anchor is the anchor. That is all. If the anchor moves, the team moves. If the anchor does not move, the team does not move. And the anchor almost never moves."</em></p>
        <p>Théodred III's first sanctioned match — the Antlerlords' Year 36 founding-bell debut against the Pittsburgh Ravens, played at Boise — saw him stand in the center of the pitch for the entire round-one duration of nine minutes, twelve seconds. He moved, by the Caucus's tracking grid, twenty-three feet over those nine minutes. His four teammates rotated around him in three concentric arcs, taking shots, holding cover, and engaging Ravens at the perimeter. The Ravens, who had attempted to drift around the Moose at distance, found that the Moose's stationary presence had divided their pitch into two halves; they could be on one side of him or the other, but they could not, by the field's geometry, be on both sides at once. The Antlerlords took round one 1-0 on a single Brawler kill. Théodred III did not, in the entire round, swing his antlers. The Ravens, in their post-match write-up, listed his contribution as <em>"the kind of contribution one tries to keep one's own team from making and which is, regardless, sometimes the deciding factor in a match. We do not know what to call this. We are calling it 'L'Ancrage' until we think of a better word. We will not think of a better word."</em></p>
        <p>Théodred III, asked at the post-match interview whether he had a strategy he would like to share, responded (the translator working in real time): <em>"My strategy is to be where I am. The teammates know where I am. The opponents learn where I am. The pitch decides. I do not decide. The pitch decides. I am, frankly, glad of this."</em> The interviewer, off-camera, asked the translator to confirm. The translator confirmed. The interviewer thanked Théodred III. Théodred III nodded, slowly, in the way of his species — a single deep nod, executed over several seconds, that the broadcast camera held on for its full duration because nothing else was happening. The viewer letters that came in over the following week — and the LMG mailroom received, by their count, six hundred and forty-two letters, the largest single-match response of the early founding-bell schedule — were almost uniformly about the nod. The most-quoted letter, from a viewer in the Olympia colony: <em>"I have never seen a knight nod like that. I have never seen a knight do anything like that. I want to watch every match this Moose plays for as long as he is able to play. I am moving my season schedule around to accommodate this and I want the League to know that this is what their broadcasts have done to me. Thank you, sincerely. Please tell L'Ancrage that I will be at his next home match."</em></p>
        <p>Théodred III's next home match is at the Saint-Laurent venue (a converted ice-fishing settlement on the river's southern shore) in week six of the Year 36 regular season. The home gate, by the Antlerlords' pre-sale, is already at capacity. The viewer in the Olympia letter has, the Antlerlords' ticketing office confirms, been issued a complimentary front-row seat with the team captain's compliments. The viewer's name is, by request, withheld from the public roster, but the seat will be reserved.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Mass and Antler Register, "Théodred Brisefer III, L'Ancrage" · Year 36 founding bell · entry verified by the Antlerlords' captain</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Halfmoon Greylane, Wolf Captain</h3>
        <div class="meta">Timber wolf · b. Year 11 (Olympia rural · pre-League) · Wolves' captain since Year 31 · the originator of the Bow</div>
        <p>Halfmoon Greylane is, by the Caucus's continuous-tenure register, the second-longest-serving captain in League history. She took the Wolves captaincy in Year 31 from her predecessor (Hardvein Quickstep, who retired with a knee injury that the team's medical staff declined to discuss in any detail) and has held it through six seasons. She has been on the active line for every one of those seasons. She has lost four teammates to permadeath, including Avery Loambright in Year 33 — the loss that produced the Bow. The Wolves have not lost a player to permadeath in any season since Year 33. The team's coaching staff is reluctant to say this is because of Greylane. Greylane has never said it is because of her. Featherquill, in a column the Wolves did not request, said it is because of her.</p>
        <p>Greylane plays Striker by archetype. She does not play Brawler, despite being, by the Wolves' coaching staff's frank admission, "easily the strongest melee fighter on the active line." She does not play Brawler because the Wolves' brawl-class spot has, since Year 32, been held by Crash Wartooth, who is older than Greylane by four years and was Greylane's mentor in the den-training years before her first League season. Greylane will not, by personal commitment, take Wartooth's spot until he retires. Wartooth, asked about this once at a post-match interview, said: <em>"She is faster than me now. She has been faster than me for three seasons. I am still here because she has chosen to let me be still here. This is an arrangement I am, frankly, embarrassed about. I will retire when I retire. The decision is, technically, mine, but it is also, in the Wolf way, hers."</em> The Wolves' coaching staff has not commented on Wartooth's framing of the arrangement. Featherquill, asked off the record what she thought of it, said only that the Wolves are <em>"the kind of team where you cannot read a single roster decision without reading the whole pack into it."</em></p>
        <p>Greylane is famous, beyond the Bow, for two things. The first is her pre-match silence — she does not speak, on match day, from the moment she enters the locker tunnel until the moment the round-one bell rings. Not to teammates, not to coaches, not to the LMG sideline reporters who have, on three occasions, asked her a question while she was actively walking down the tunnel. The Caucus has been told (by the Wolves' coaching staff, off the record) that the silence is part of the den-training preparation that all senior Wolves observe before a hunt; the Wolves do not, by their own term, "fight matches" — they "run hunts." The silence is the hunt's beginning. The first word she speaks every match is <em>"now"</em> — said, by stopwatch measurement, an average of 0.4 seconds before the round-one bell.</p>
        <p>The second thing she is famous for is the Year 35 quarterfinal in which she carried a downed teammate (a Healer named Pinedrift, who had been hit by a stray Sniper round) across forty-eight paces of open pitch under sustained fire from two opposing Snipers and a Brawler. Pinedrift survived. Greylane took fourteen separate hit registers in the carry, three of which dropped her HP into the red. She did not, at any point, drop Pinedrift. She did not, at any point, return fire. She walked. She delivered Pinedrift to the Wolves' bench medical strip. She turned around. She walked back into the engagement. She killed both opposing Snipers in the next twelve seconds, in melee, with a sidearm she had drawn during the carry but not fired. The match playback is in the Caucus's tactical archive under the file name <em>"Greylane carry — do not edit."</em> The footage has, by Foundation steward measurement, been viewed more times than any other match playback in the archive. The Wolves' coaching staff has refused to use it as a training video. Greylane, asked, said: <em>"That was not a teaching moment. That was the only thing I knew how to do. The Healer's name is Pinedrift. The Healer is alive. That is the lesson, if you need a lesson. I would prefer you did not need a lesson."</em></p>
        <p>Greylane will, by her own publicly stated intent, retire when Crash Wartooth retires. The Wolves' coaching staff has, in the Year 36 pre-season, formally registered the captaincy succession — a Brawler named Quickbreath Cinderpaw will take the captaincy when Greylane steps down. Cinderpaw is twenty-four years old. Greylane is, in her own words, <em>"raising her properly. The pack will be in good paws. I will not be ready to leave when I leave. None of us ever are. The pack decides anyway."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Continuous-Tenure Register, "Halfmoon Greylane, captain · Seattle Sleepless Wolves" · Year 36 founding bell update</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio lore-wide">
        <h3>Bristlebeard the Second — and the Correction He Owes</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver sniper · b. Year 9 (Boston · Brewer's Row, the original Bristlebeard household) · the shooter who took the Year 33 Loambright shot</div>
        <p>Of the Bristlebeard line, the Second is the only one to survive his first season. The First died in Year 28, R5, in the inaugural championship final against the Wolves' line, eating a grenade in tactical self-sacrifice rather than letting the Wolves use it on his squad. The Third — Bjorn, currently active — has, as of this writing, broken the Bristlebeard pattern by playing a defensive back line and reaching his eighth season in the active roster. The Second is, between them, the survivor who was supposed to be the rule-breaker — and who became, in his second season, the shooter who took the worst shot in League history.</p>
        <p>The Second is a sniper. The Second has been a sniper since the Beavers' Year 30 founding-bell roster, when he was eighteen and the Beavers' coaching staff had, against considerable internal objection, opted to cross-train a Bristlebeard out of the family's traditional Tank lineage. The decision was made on the strength of a single tactical assessment by Bristlebeard the First's widow (Lyla Bristlebeard, a former Olympia archery champion who had married into the Beaver line and who watched her husband die in his first match), who said, on the night of the Year 30 founding bell, only this: <em>"The Bristlebeards have, for two generations, charged into a line and died. The Second has, since he was old enough to draw a bow, never been comfortable charging into anything. He shoots. He is a sniper. We will not lose another Bristlebeard to a Tank's death. The boy is a sniper. Sign him as a sniper. Do not test this."</em> The Beaver coaching staff signed him as a sniper. The Second has not, in seven seasons of subsequent League play, ever been asked to play Tank.</p>
        <p>What the Second is, by every analyst's measurement, is the most-disciplined Sniper in the League. His fire-sequence selection — the order in which he prioritizes targets — is taught at the Caucus's annual sniper-class workshop as a model for the role. He has the highest opposing-Brawler engagement rate in the League. He has the lowest opposing-Healer engagement rate in the League. The latter statistic is, by Caucus record, the consequence of the Year 33 Loambright shot. He has not, in eight seasons since, taken another shot that traveled on a line that intersected an opposing Healer's path. The archery instructors call this <em>"the Loambright correction."</em> The Second, in private, calls it <em>"the correction I owe."</em></p>
        <p>The shot itself, in the Year 33 Final's round three, was not — by every available analysis — the shot the Second intended to take. He was firing at the Wolves' Striker, Crash Wartooth. The line he chose, at twenty-three paces, was a clean railgun shot at Wartooth's chest. The line passed through the spot Loambright stepped into at the moment the shot was leaving the rifle. The kinetics tracker's read showed an intersection time of nineteen frames between the trigger pull and the line-cross. The Second could not, by mechanical possibility, have aborted the shot. The shot landed. Loambright died. The Second walked off the pitch.</p>
        <p>What the Second's bench did, watching this, was substitute him out — not as punishment but as a recognition that he was, in the immediate moment, no longer capable of taking another shot. The Beaver coach, Bristlebeard's uncle, walked to the dugout and put a paw on the Second's shoulder and said (the dugout mic captured this, and the broadcast did not air it but the Caucus archive has the audio): <em>"You did the work. You took the shot you were told to take. The line was the line. The line went where it went. We will not, ever, ask you to explain this. We are also not going to send you back out tonight. Go to the trainer's room. Sit. We will come find you when the match is over."</em> The Second went to the trainer's room. He sat. He did not, by any subsequent account, weep — not at the trainer's room, not at the post-match line, not at the bow. He has, by his own wife's account, wept exactly once about the shot, three years later, alone, in the kitchen of their Brewer's Row home, on the third anniversary of the match. The wife (Marin Bristlebeard, a Boston schoolteacher) has not described the weeping in any detail. She has said only: <em>"It was the kind of weeping that does not, by its nature, get easier with rehearsal. He has rehearsed it for three years. It got worse, that night, not better. Then he stopped. Then he went to bed. Then he was, the next morning, the man he had been, except slightly. I do not, when asked, attempt to describe the slightly. I will not now."</em></p>
        <p>The Second is in his eighth season. He has never been a captain. He has never asked to be a captain. He is — by Caucus continuous-roster register — likely to play through Year 40 if his form holds. He has not, in eight seasons, taken a single shot the Wolves' coaching staff has formally objected to. The Wolves have not, in eight seasons, formally requested that the Beavers retire him. The Wolves and Bristlebeard have, twice, played each other in the post-Loambright era; in both matches, the Second's team has lost, and in both matches, at the post-match line, the Wolves' captain has walked the long way around the pitch to shake his paw. The Second has nodded, once, each time. He has not, in either case, said anything. The Wolves have not asked him to.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Sniper Register, "Bristlebeard the Second" · Year 36 founding bell · cross-referenced with the Beavers' coaching staff and Marin Bristlebeard's permission</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio lore-wide">
        <h3>Estelle Roiseau-Manchot, LMG Booth Translator</h3>
        <div class="meta">Saint-Laurent goose · multilingual broadcast translator · LMG hire, Year 36 founding bell · the only translator the Antlerlords trust</div>
        <p>The LMG broadcast booth, in pre-Year-36 seasons, did not have a translator. The League's matches were called in League Common, which the Caucus had — over the League's first eight seasons — quietly established as the lingua franca by the simple expedient of paying every team's coaching staff in Common-language documents and not, at any point, providing translations. The teams adapted. The League functioned. The LMG's broadcast feed was, for eight seasons, monolingual. The viewer letters did not, in eight seasons, complain.</p>
        <p>This worked until Year 36, when the Continental Expansion brought in the Saint-Laurent Antlerlords, the Yukon Hunting Lynx, and (most acutely) the Yucatan Quetzals — three teams whose coaching staffs, captains, and most of their active line did not speak League Common as a primary language. The Antlerlords spoke a slow Quebec creole of Old-Ones French and animal-tongue. The Lynx spoke a language they called <em>"the language we use when we have to speak"</em> and otherwise refused to speak. The Quetzals spoke a Yucatan composite of Quetzal native, an old Spanish creole inherited from the Old-Ones runes around the basin, and what their captain Cintzli called <em>"the trees' language."</em> The LMG's first three Continental-Expansion-era broadcasts were, by every viewer-letter account, almost completely unintelligible. Teams' captains were interviewed in their native tongues; the booth's commentators attempted to summarize; the summaries were, in two of three cases, factually wrong. The viewer mailbag spiked. The LMG's broadcast manager, Mort Quillsetter (a corvid, Pittsburgh-born, twelve seasons in the booth) called an emergency hire.</p>
        <p>Estelle Roiseau-Manchot was, at the time of the hire, employed by the Saint-Laurent settlement's port authority as a multilingual log-keeper. She had been recommended to the LMG by the Antlerlords' captain, Marc-Olivier Brisefer, on the strength of two qualifications: she spoke the Saint-Laurent creole as a native, and she spoke League Common (per Brisefer's quote in the recommendation letter) <em>"with the calm, slightly bored precision of a person who has, for thirty years, been writing log entries in a language she did not personally enjoy. This is, by my read, the ideal translator's voice. She does not get excited. She does not editorialize. She translates. She is the right hire. Do not test this."</em> The LMG hired her on the strength of the recommendation. They have not, in the four months since, regretted the hire.</p>
        <p>Roiseau-Manchot's working method, by her own description in a Featherquill interview, is: <em>"I do not translate. I move the meaning from one language to the other and I let the meaning do the talking. I do not editorialize. I do not summarize. If a captain says something that is, in the source language, ambiguous, I render the ambiguity in the target language. I will not, on the broadcast feed, tell the viewer what a captain meant. The captain will tell the viewer what the captain meant. I will, in the meantime, tell the viewer what the captain said."</em> This — the refusal to disambiguate — is, by Quillsetter's account, the quality the LMG most appreciates. The previous attempts at translation had been, in essence, summaries. The summaries had been wrong because the summarizers had been guessing. Roiseau-Manchot does not guess. She renders. The viewer gets the captain's words, in League Common, with the captain's own ambiguity intact. The viewer figures it out. The viewer does, by every account, figure it out.</p>
        <p>She handles, in her current rotation, all Antlerlords matches (Saint-Laurent creole), all Lynx matches (the one Lynx language, on the rare occasions a Lynx captain consents to be interviewed at all), and approximately half the Quetzals' matches (the half conducted in the Yucatan Spanish creole; the other half — conducted in the trees' language — Roiseau-Manchot has, on the record, declined to translate, on the grounds that she does not speak it. The LMG has not yet hired a trees-language translator. The trees-language matches are currently broadcast with subtitles supplied by the Quetzals' coaching staff, which are, by every account, unreliable). She does not, by her own preference, ever translate live during the round itself — only at pre-match and post-match interviews, and at coach-side sideline conversations the booth flags for translation. She has, in four months, refused exactly one translation: a Lynx captain's pre-match comment that, by Roiseau-Manchot's professional judgment, <em>"contained a private threat that the Lynx captain should not, by Lynx tradition, have spoken aloud, and which the broadcast feed should not, by my professional judgment, have aired. I omitted it. I told the producer I had omitted it. The producer thanked me. The Lynx captain, asked later, did not deny that the threat had been made and was relieved to hear that I had not aired it. We have an agreement. I am, by my read, doing my job."</em></p>
        <p>Roiseau-Manchot is paid in mixed currency — bits and lobster — at her own request. The lobster portion, by Foundation accounting, is the largest individual lobster-payment line item in the Foundation's books. She is, as of the Year 36 founding bell, the only person in the entire League hierarchy whose monthly compensation includes more lobster than the lobster vendor at Concession Row sells in a busy match-day. The vendor, asked about the arrangement, said only: <em>"She earns it. The translation is good. The League needs her. The lobster is going to a person who is doing right by the sport. I have no complaint."</em> The Foundation's accounting office has, on three occasions, attempted to convert the lobster portion to bits for streamlining. Roiseau-Manchot has, on three occasions, declined the conversion. The Foundation has, on three occasions, accepted the decline. The lobster line in the books is, by Featherquill's read, <em>"the most stable single line in the entire Foundation budget. It does not vary. It does not get questioned. It is paid every month. It will be paid every month for as long as the LMG broadcasts the Antlerlords. This is a thing the Foundation has, at long last, learned to live with."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG Booth Personnel Register, "Estelle Roiseau-Manchot, translator" · Year 36 founding-bell hire · cross-referenced with Antlerlords' captain's recommendation letter</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Mort Quillsetter, LMG Broadcast Manager</h3>
        <div class="meta">Corvid · Pittsburgh-born · twelve seasons in the booth · the voice the booth uses when the booth needs to be quiet</div>
        <p>Mort Quillsetter has been in the LMG broadcast booth since Year 25 — three seasons before there was a League to broadcast. He started as a junior audio engineer for the Tampa coastal salvage crew that would eventually incorporate as the LMG, helping run cable from the recovered Old-Ones broadcast tower to the salvage warehouse where the crew was, at the time, transcribing every working frequency they could pick up. He was nineteen years old when the salvage crew picked up its first Brewer's Reach exhibition match by accident on a southern band, and twenty when the crew, by his own quiet recommendation, decided that an AI-simulated cute-animal fighting league with perma-death was, on his read, "the kind of thing people will watch." The crew agreed. The LMG was incorporated the next spring. Quillsetter has been with the LMG ever since.</p>
        <p>He took the broadcast manager's chair in Year 31, after the previous manager (a hawk named Spirelka, by every account excellent at the job and by every account also retiring on time) flew north for the off-season and did not return. Quillsetter inherited a booth that had, by Spirelka's quiet preference, been run as a single-voice operation — one play-by-play, no color, no sideline. Quillsetter inherited it, kept it that way for one season, and at the close of Year 31 hired a color commentator, a sideline reporter, and a translator-in-waiting (the position Roiseau-Manchot would, five seasons later, fill). He has, since, hired no further full-time positions, on the grounds that <em>"the booth is the booth. Four voices is the booth. We are not, by my professional judgment, a five-voice operation."</em></p>
        <p>His on-air contribution is sparing. He is not a play-by-play voice. He is not a color voice. He is, by his own role description, <em>"the voice the booth uses when the booth needs to be quiet."</em> He takes the open mic during scheduled silences — the sixty seconds before the founding bell, the half-minute between rounds, the post-match line — and uses these windows for short, factual transitions that the rest of the booth has, in twelve seasons, never been asked to fill. His voice is, by general agreement, the voice that announces a knight's permadeath at the Hall of Fallen Heroes' annual induction. He has, in twelve seasons, announced fourteen permadeaths. He remembers all of them.</p>
        <p>The LMG's editorial discretion — the matter the Beavers' coaching staff have, in private, accused the consortium of abusing — is, by Quillsetter's working description, the broadcast manager's responsibility. Quillsetter does not, by his own statement, decline matches lightly. He does decline them. He has, in twelve seasons, declined sixty-three sanctioned matches for what he calls <em>"format coherence reasons,"</em> a term he has not, in any subsequent interview, defined further. The Sharks have lost three of those declined matches. The Beavers have won two. The standings reflect what the LMG broadcast. Quillsetter's only public comment on this, given to Featherquill in a Year 35 piece that ran in the Wing Standard's weekly: <em>"The standings are what we broadcast. The matches are what was played. These are not, by my read, the same thing. I have made my peace with the difference. The Beavers have not. The Beavers are not, on this matter, going to. I do not blame them. I am, on this matter, the one in the wrong, by every measure I can think to apply, and I have not, by my own decision, changed the practice. The booth is the booth. I will retire one day. The next manager will, perhaps, decide differently. Until then, this is what the booth is."</em></p>
        <p>He is, as of Year 36, fifty-five years old. He has not announced a retirement date. The LMG's succession-planning office has, in three separate years, asked him for one. He has, in three separate years, declined to give one. Featherquill's profile of him closes with a sentence that has, by general broadcast-booth agreement, become his unofficial epitaph-in-waiting: <em>"Quillsetter does not own the booth. The booth, in twelve seasons, has come to belong to him anyway. The booth will belong to whoever comes next, on the day he leaves. Until then, the booth is his. He has earned the booth. The booth has, in its way, earned him."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard, "The Voice the Booth Uses When the Booth Needs to Be Quiet" · Featherquill, Year 35 · subject declined to be photographed for the column</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio lore-wide">
        <h3>Halfmoon Greylane, Wolves Captain (the Carrier)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Wolf · Brawler · WLF · alive · Wolves' captain since Hardvein Quickstep's retirement in Year 34 · the carry · the bow · the eleven-second instruction</div>
        <p>Halfmoon Greylane is the Wolves' fourth captain in League history. The captaincy passed to her from Hardvein Quickstep at the end of Year 33, in a transition the pack negotiated entirely without paperwork — Quickstep walked off the post-Year-33-Final pitch, did not return to the bench, and laid a single scent-mark on the Olympia training facility's gym wall on his way out of the building.
