The mark, by Briarwing Hootington's later professional rendering (in the Foundation Drawer's "Scent-mark transcription" found-paper entry), was a four-layer notice: territorial, personal, a date-stamp on the day of his retirement, and a single short instruction addressed to Greylane that Briarwing's best translation rendered as <em>"the pack will be heavier than you expect; carry it anyway."</em> Greylane, on being shown the rendering during her first off-season as captain, did not, by Briarwing's account, comment. She did, by Briarwing's account, nod once. The nod is, by every Wolf Briarwing has spoken to since, the closest a Wolf comes to an "I have read the will and I will execute it."</p>
        <p>Her career as a Brawler, before the captaincy, was distinguished but not flashy. 47 kills across five seasons, longest streak 9, three scavenges. She was, in every season she played as a non-captain, the quietest knight on the Wolves' active line — the Wolf who took the position the captain pointed to, held it for the duration of the round, and walked off when the round was over. She did not, in five seasons, lose her position to an opposing engagement. She did not, in five seasons, advance from her position without a captain's signal. She was, by every Wolves' tactical analyst's read, the most reliable single piece of geometry on the field. The pack noticed. Quickstep noticed. The captaincy passed to her because the pack had, by an internal process the pack does not narrate, agreed in advance.</p>
        <p>The carry happened in Year 35 quarterfinal at Olympia. The Wolves' Healer, Pinedrift, was downed by Sniper fire forty-eight paces into open pitch. Greylane was at center pitch when it happened. Greylane crossed the forty-eight paces, picked up Pinedrift, and walked back across the same forty-eight paces under sustained Sniper fire. She took fourteen hit registers during the carry. She did not return fire. She did not, by the LMG kinetics tracker's read, increase her pace at any point during the carry. She walked. The match playback is in the Caucus's tactical archive under the file name <em>"Greylane carry — do not edit."</em> Greylane has, on three separate Caucus requests, refused permission for the playback to be released as a training video. Her stated reason, in a single sentence each time: <em>"It was not a tactic. I will not let it be taught as one."</em> The Caucus has, on three occasions, accepted the refusal.</p>
        <p>The bow has been the Wolves' post-kill ritual since Year 33's final, but Greylane's bow is, by every observer's read, distinct. It is, in duration, identical to every other Wolf's bow — eleven seconds, the duration set on the bow's first observation and never since varied. It is, in posture, fractionally lower than the other Wolves'. The Foundation steward who measured the bows for the Year 35 Foundation Day program (an unusual project the steward took on at her own initiative) reported a difference of approximately six degrees between Greylane's bow and the second-deepest Wolf's. The difference has not been formally noted. The Wolves do not, by their own preference, discuss the depth of any individual Wolf's bow. The pack is the pack. The depth is, by Wolf custom, what the pack chooses for itself.</p>
        <p>Greylane is, as of Year 36, forty-one years old. She has not, by her coaching staff's pre-season statement, announced a retirement plan. The Wolves are, by their internal succession process, already in soft conversations about the next captaincy — the pack does not, by tradition, wait for a captain to announce retirement to begin the conversation. The candidates are, by general locker-room consensus, two: Wikrai Wartooth Jr. (Speedster, son of the fallen Wikrai Sr.) and a younger Brawler named Sapphire Pinedrift (no relation to the Healer of the same surname; Wolves naming traditions are, by long-standing personal practice, not always genealogical). The pack has not, by any external indicator, indicated a preference. Greylane has, by her own pre-season public statement, said only: <em>"The pack will choose. The pack does the choosing. I will, on the day of the choosing, accept the choice. I will, on the day after, train the choice. The pack is the pack. I am, this season, the captain. That is enough."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Captain Register, "Halfmoon Greylane, WLF" · cross-referenced with the Wolves' coaching staff's transition statement and Briarwing Hootington's scent-mark rendering · Greylane has, in five seasons of captaincy, given exactly one televised interview, and the transcript has been, by her preference, never reprinted</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Cintzli of the Yucatan Canopy, Quetzals Captain</h3>
        <div class="meta">Quetzal · Sniper · QTZ · alive · Quetzals captain · the smallest active knight in the League by mass · the rafter-nest at Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall · speaks four languages, refuses to translate three of them</div>
        <p>Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy is the smallest active knight in the League by mass, by the Caucus's pre-season measurement: nine and a half ounces in fighting weight (her own crest plumage included). She is also, by her own coach's measurement, the most distinctively colored knight on any active roster — emerald crest, deep crimson breast, wing-coverts in the shifted iridescent green that the Caucus's official plumage record describes (with apparent reluctance) as <em>"approximately the color of a particular kind of moss reflected through a particular kind of water; we have not been able to fix this color in pigment."</em> She is, by every measurement that exists, the most photographable knight in the League. She has, in her inaugural season, been photographed three times, all three at her own pre-photograph consent.</p>
        <p>Her career stats, as of Year 36 mid-season, are extraordinary by every available metric. 31 kills in 14 matches. Eleven scavenges. Highest aerial-shot accuracy in the League by a margin no other Sniper has approached. Lowest body-mass-per-kill ratio in the League by a margin no other Sniper has approached, the same statistic. She has not, in fourteen matches, lost a one-on-one Sniper duel. She has, in the Caucus's tactical archive, been the subject of a single technical paper (titled, in the archive's filing, <em>"On the canopy advantage — and what teams without a canopy can, theoretically, do about it"</em>) that opens with the sentence: <em>"The Quetzals are, in their inaugural season, in the rafters. The other teams are not in the rafters. This is not, by any reading, a parity question. This is a geometry question. The Caucus is, on this paper, asking: do we change the geometry, or do we tell the other teams to climb."</em> The Caucus has not, on the paper, made a recommendation.</p>
        <p>The rafter-nest at Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall is hers personally. She built it before the venue was registered, in the rafters that were already there, with materials she gathered herself. The Caucus has, on three separate occasions, discussed registering the nest as terrain. The Caucus has, on each occasion, declined — on the grounds that doing so would imply the League had built it, which the League did not. The Quetzals have not asked for the registration. The matter is, by mutual silent agreement, not a matter. Cintzli brings her own moss to away venues. She has, in fourteen matches, not lost an aerial shot for lack of an appropriate elevated nesting position; she has, in two matches, declined to take a shot for lack of an appropriate moss substrate. She has not, in either case, explained the decline. The Quetzals' coaching staff does not press.</p>
        <p>Her language situation is delicate. She speaks four: Quetzal native (the canopy language, used among Quetzals only), the Yucatan Spanish creole (used in pre-match and post-match interviews), what she calls <em>"the trees' language"</em> (used in private conversation with members of her own roster, and in her broadcast post-match interview when she is, by her own pre-match commitment, willing to speak it), and League Common (used reluctantly, with a slight delay, when no other option is available). She has, by her own statement, declined to render the trees' language into League Common on the grounds that the language is not, by its nature, renderable. The LMG's broadcast booth handles trees-language matches with subtitles supplied by the Quetzals' coaching staff, which Roiseau-Manchot has, in writing, certified as <em>"unreliable in the way the source language is unreliable; this is not a translation problem; this is a language problem; the language is what it is."</em> Cintzli, on hearing this characterization, said only: <em>"the goose understands. she is, on this matter, my friend."</em></p>
        <p>She is, as of Year 36, twenty-three years old. She has not, by her own pre-season statement, set a career goal beyond the one she has already accomplished — to take the captaincy of a Yucatan team that is, in her own words, <em>"a team. before us, the Yucatan was a place. now it is also a team. the place is still the place. the team is, this season, the team. both are real. neither is the other. this is enough."</em> The drawing the child ZUNUN sent to the Foundation Hall corkboard — <em>"Cintzli is in the tree. The tree is in her."</em> — is, by Cintzli's own quiet account, the most accurate description of her she has read in any language.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Captain Register, "Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy, QTZ" · cross-referenced with the Quetzals' coaching staff's pre-season statement and ZUNUN's drawing on the Foundation Hall corkboard · Cintzli has not been photographed for this entry, by her own preference</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Tessik Snowstep, Lynx Senior Coach</h3>
        <div class="meta">Lynx · senior coach · LYX · the only delegate to walk the entire Yukon Boreal Council application personally · one of three living Lynx ever photographed · review-not-direct coaching method</div>
        <p>Tessik Snowstep is, by Yukon Council records, fifty-three years old. They retired from active competition in Year 31 after a knee injury sustained on a hunt that the Council records, by Lynx tradition, do not specify the species of. They have been the senior coach of the Lynx team since the team's formation in Year 34 — two full seasons before the team's League admission. The team trained under Tessik's senior coaching for two complete pre-Continental-Expansion seasons; by the time the Caucus admitted the team, the active line had been training under their respective position-coaches for, in some cases, more than a hundred individual sessions. The team had not, before its first sanctioned League match, ever assembled as a five-knight unit.</p>
        <p>Tessik's coaching method, by their own description, is <em>"reviewing without directing."</em> They write notes. The notes are short. The longest note on file in the Yukon Council records is forty-one words long; it concerns a Sniper named Kell who, by Tessik's observation, was holding their breath wrong before each shot. Kell adjusted. The note has not been needed again. Tessik does not, in their working method, attend training sessions in person; they rely on the position-coaches' weekly summaries, which they read in their cabin in the boreal stronghold, twelve days' hike from the nearest postal hub. The summaries arrive once every fortnight by Yukon Boreal Council courier. Tessik responds, when response is warranted, by the same courier, two weeks later. The method has, in two seasons of pre-League training and one half-season of League play, produced exactly seven written responses. Each response was, by the receiving position-coach's account, <em>"the right thing to have said, said in the right number of words, at the right moment."</em></p>
        <p>The decision to walk the application personally to Brewer's Reach in Year 36 was Tessik's, against the Yukon Boreal Council's mild preference that they send a younger delegate. Tessik's stated reason, in a Council meeting that was, by Council tradition, not formally minuted: <em>"I am the senior coach. The application is from my team. The application is the team's word. The word should be carried by the senior coach. The Council does not, in this matter, get to choose which Lynx walks. The Lynx who walks is the Lynx who, on the morning of the walking, is the right Lynx to walk. That morning, the right Lynx is me. The Council will, by the next morning, agree."</em> The Council, by the next morning, agreed.</p>
        <p>Tessik is one of three living Lynx ever photographed. The three photographs in the League's records were taken at the Year 36 Caucus's ratification meeting, all three with Tessik's prior written consent, all three from approximately the same angle. Tessik does not consider this a personal preference. Tessik considers it a professional accommodation. <em>"The League's audience needs to be able to recognize the coaches. I will be in five photographs over the course of my coaching career. We have agreed in advance which five. I have already used three."</em> The remaining two are, by Tessik's pre-statement to the Yukon Council, reserved: one for the Lynx team's first sanctioned championship victory, if and when one occurs; one for the day Tessik retires from coaching, if and when that occurs. The order in which the two will be used is, by Tessik's preference, not announced.</p>
        <p>They returned to the Yukon by mid-season. The Lynx team's match-day assembly works, by Caucus accommodation, without their on-site presence. The position-coaches assemble the line; the line plays; the position-coaches debrief; Tessik reads the summaries by Council courier two weeks after the fact. The arrangement is, by every Caucus tactical analyst's read, "unusual but not, by any measurable performance metric, suboptimal." The Lynx have, in their inaugural half-season, finished within their projected win-rate band. The position-coaches are, by general accommodation, considered the team's day-to-day coaching staff. Tessik is, by every formal record, the senior coach. The arrangement holds. Tessik is, by their own pre-retirement statement, "tired of being among so many people, but not yet tired of the work. The day I am tired of the work is the day I will use the fifth photograph."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Yukon Boreal Council, "Coach Profile: Tessik Snowstep" · cross-referenced with the Caucus's Year 36 ratification minutes and the position-coaches' weekly courier-delivered summary archive · Tessik has not, since their return to the Yukon, given an interview to any League-affiliated publication, and is by Yukon Council policy unreachable except by courier</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio lore-wide">
        <h3>Pell Whittlestone, Boise Float Gas Foundry Chief Chemist</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver-born, Boise-resident · forty-three years old · Foundry chief chemist since Year 30 · forger of the Coronation Cup brass crown (Year 31) · designer of the Cold Stones trophy (Year 36) · architect of the twelve-overlay venue catalog · the most-bylined non-press figure in the Foundation Archive</div>
        <p>Pell Whittlestone is, by the Foundation's working register, the single most-cited figure in the League's institutional record outside of active-line knights and the Commissioner herself. She is cited, by the Drawer's curator's running tally, in 47 separate documents across the Lore Archive. The 47 citations span: the Year 30 R3 flat-batch incident (in which Whittlestone shipped, accidentally, an out-of-spec batch to the Sharks and rewrote the Foundry's outgoing-inspection protocol the next year as a personal commitment); the Year 31 forging of the Coronation Cup brass crown (forged in her off-season, billed to the League for one lobster, which has not been paid); the Year 32 designing of the Old-Bristlebeard helmet replica that hangs in the Hall of Fallen Heroes' founding wall; the Year 33 Tinkerbarrel Disclosure response (in which Whittlestone testified, in person, at the Caucus working session and argued — successfully — against retroactively voiding the Year 30 R3 result); the Year 34 venue-overlay catalog development (twelve overlays, designed in two weeks, plus three follow-up additions); and the Year 36 Cold Stones trophy commission for the Frostfall Friendly.</p>
        <p>She started at the Foundry as a junior chemist in Year 28 — the same year the League was founded, though the Foundry would not formally exist as a commercial entity until Year 30. The Foundry was, in Year 28, a Beaver-clan workshop in the Boise highlands run by Whittlestone's mother and three of her mother's sisters, all of whom were, by family tradition, addressed as "Auntie" regardless of biological relationship. Whittlestone joined the workshop the year she turned fifteen, which is, by Boise highland Beaver tradition, the age at which a young Beaver chooses her trade. She chose chemistry. She has not, in twenty-eight years, chosen otherwise.</p>
        <p>Her chief contribution to the League's standing infrastructure is the Float Gas itself — the proprietary lifting-gas formula that fills League-spec balloons and that is, by League rule, the only gas permitted on a sanctioned field. Whittlestone inherited the formula from her mother and has, in twenty-eight years, refined it five times. The five refinements are documented in the Foundry's chemical-process archive under file numbers PW-001 through PW-005; the file numbers are, by Foundry tradition, the only place Whittlestone has ever signed her own work. The teams' team-specific gas variants — the heavy regulator-laced batch for Boise, the lightest batch for Olympia, the desert high-altitude formula for Phoenix — are, by Whittlestone's quiet personal commitment, hand-tested by her at every batch's outgoing inspection. She has not, since Year 30, missed an outgoing-batch test. She has not, since Year 31, shipped another flat batch.</p>
        <p>She is, by every Caucus committee's pre-meeting briefing notes, the only non-Caucus figure who is invited to every Caucus working session as an ex-officio observer. She has, in eight years of working sessions, voted in zero — Caucus rules permit her presence but not her vote. She has, in eight years of working sessions, spoken approximately eleven times. The Caucus's procedural archivist has noted that Whittlestone's eleven contributions, when she has made them, have, in nine of eleven cases, been the deciding factor in the working session's eventual ratification. The two cases in which she did not change the outcome were the Year 33 Tinkerbarrel response (in which she argued for non-voiding and won, but the Caucus would, by the procedural archivist's read, likely have ruled the same way without her) and the Year 36 Antlerwood Rule (in which she argued for a more permissive definition of "attached weapon" than the rule eventually took, and lost; her preferred definition would have included tooth-class implements, which the rule does not).</p>
        <p>The Coronation Cup brass crown is, by every Foundation staffer's read, her most-public single object. The Cold Stones, for the Frostfall Friendly, are her most-private. The crown is brass, ornate, formally engraved, three pounds even. The Stones are two flat river-rocks bound in brass wire, one pound four ounces, with no engraving. Asked, off the record, in a Featherquill profile, why the two trophies were so different, Whittlestone said: <em>"the crown is for the Cup. the Cup is a regular event. the Cup happens every year. the crown should look like a crown. the Stones are for the Friendly. the Friendly is, by every team's read, an unusual event. the Friendly happens because the Caucus made it happen. the Stones should look like the two places. the trophy is the bringing-together. the trophy is not the trophy. it is, on this matter, fine."</em> Featherquill's column ended with the sentence: <em>"Pell Whittlestone has, in fourteen years at the Foundry, said about three thousand sentences on the record. None of them, by my count, has been a sentence that did not, on careful re-reading, mean exactly what it said. This is, by every reading, the rarest skill in any field. We should, on this matter, be grateful she chose chemistry."</em></p>
        <p>She is, as of Year 36, forty-three years old. She has, by her own pre-retirement statement, "approximately fifteen years of useful chemistry left" before her hands stop being steady enough for outgoing-batch tests. She has not, by the same statement, identified a successor. The Foundry's chemistry-staff register lists six candidates. Whittlestone has, in eight years, declined to rank them. Her stated reason: <em>"the chemistry will pick the chemist. the chemistry has, in my own case, picked correctly. it will, in fifteen years, pick again. i will, on the day it picks, retire to the Boise highlands and finish the small painting i have been working on for nine seasons. the painting is, by my own admission, not very good. the painting is, also by my own admission, mine. that is enough."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundry chemistry-staff register, "Pell Whittlestone, chief chemist" · cross-referenced with the Caucus procedural archive's working-session attendance log · Featherquill's profile (Wing Standard, Year 35) is the only long-form interview Whittlestone has given in fourteen years and is, by her own preference, also the last</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Hester Quillstrike, HED Sniper (the 412-Pace Mark)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Hedgehog · Sniper · HED · deceased Year 35 R3 · the longest-shot record holder in League history (412 paces, the diagonal of the Helena Glacier Rink) · the lowest mounted helmet in the Hall of Fallen Heroes (three feet eight inches) · rookie, half-season</div>
        <p>Hester Quillstrike was twenty-three years old when she took the shot that set the 412-pace record. She was, by every measurable metric, a rookie — fewer than ten matches of sanctioned League play, no prior bracket appearances, no prior media training. She was, by the Helena combat-circuit's senior Hedgehogs' shared assessment, the most accurate Sniper the Helena tradition had produced in three generations. The Helena tradition, by the elder Hedgehogs' best account, predates HED's formal League admission by six generations. The math holds: Quillstrike was, by every read available to the Helena combat circuit's record-keepers, the best Hedgehog Sniper in approximately ninety years of Hedgehog snipers.</p>
        <p>She debuted at HED's R1 against the Pandas (the team Quillstrike had, by her family's pre-debut interview, been studying for the previous six months in the Helena combat-circuit's away-team-tape archive — the archive being, in Helena's tradition, a single ledger of opposing-team observations passed informally between snipers). She took two shots in the R1 match. Both connected. Neither was a kill. The Pandas' coaching staff, on the post-match line, said only: <em>"the Hedgehog rookie is, by our best read, the best rookie any of us have seen in three years. we will, on the next bracket, pay attention."</em></p>
        <p>The 412-pace shot, in HED's R3 match at the Helena Glacier Rink, was a single shot taken across the diagonal of the home venue. The kinetics tracker's read: 412 paces from the Sniper's mark to the impact point. The shot connected with an Otter Brawler in mid-engagement and registered a kill at the impact-frame. The Otter Brawler was, by the LMG broadcast's post-match medical reconstruction, dead before falling. The shot was, by every Caucus archery analyst's read, technically the longest sanctioned-field shot in League history by a margin of approximately twenty paces. The previous record (Sundip Hootington Sr.'s Year 31 mark at the Reno Open Court — 391 paces, since superseded by the 412-pace mark) had stood for four seasons.</p>
        <p>Quillstrike died in the same match, in the round immediately following the 412-pace shot. The Otters, by general post-match analysis, organized a coordinated rush at the next round's open — three Otter knights closing on Quillstrike's nest position simultaneously, with a Sniper's covering fire from the south stand. Quillstrike took two of the three Otter rushers down. The third reached her position. She did not have time to redraw. The third Otter — a Brawler named Kelp Tideturn, on his own debut season — engaged her at point-blank range and made the kill before her own bench could call a substitution. Tideturn, on the post-match line, was visibly weeping; he had not, by any pre-match indication, intended to be the knight who killed the rookie who had just set the record. Tideturn has, in two subsequent seasons, retired from the active line and become an Otter junior coach. He has, on three occasions, been asked about the shot. He has, on three occasions, declined to comment.</p>
        <p>Quillstrike's helmet is in the Hall of Fallen Heroes, mounted at three feet eight inches — the lowest mount in the Hall, with a small step beside it for short visitors who would like to see her face. The step was, by the Foundation steward's record, requested by Quillstrike's grandmother (a Helena combat-circuit elder named Bryony Threadspine, who would later, in Year 35 closeout, write the final entry in the seventh circuit notebook) on her first Hall visit. The Foundation built the step in the off-season. The step has, in twelve months of service, been used by four hundred and fifty-six visitors who would not otherwise have been able to see Quillstrike's face. The Foundation does not, in any other case, count step-uses by individual visitors. The exception was, by the Foundation steward's pre-counting note, "because Threadspine asked us to count, and we agreed, and we are not, by any measure, going to renege."</p>
        <p>The 412-pace mark stands. It was, in Year 35 R8, tied by Sundip Hootington Jr. at the Reno Open Court (Sundip Sr.'s grandson, taking the shot at his own home venue, then dying in the celebration's Power-Core overload). It has not been broken. The Caucus's archery instructors have, in two subsequent seasons, drilled snipers on the geometry of the 412-pace shot as a teaching exercise. None of the snipers in two seasons of drill has, in practice conditions, replicated the shot. The shot was, by every read, an outlier — the right Sniper, the right venue, the right wind, the right rookie season. Quillstrike was, by every read, the right Sniper. The League has not, in two seasons, found another.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Hall of Fallen Heroes, third row from door, fourth name (the row also containing Loambright, Sundip Jr., Felix Marshmallow) · helmet mounted at three feet eight inches · the step is, by Foundation policy, the only physical accommodation in the Hall, and is, by the Foundation steward's standing instruction, never to be removed</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Commissioner Margaux Whiskerstone</h3>
        <div class="meta">Mouse · Commissioner of the Float Knights League since Year 31 · the only Commissioner in League history · author of the Geography Caucus reclassification (Year 36) · settles her Concession Row booth tab personally, in lobster, on the Tuesday after Foundation Day</div>
        <p>Margaux Whiskerstone took the Commissioner's office in Year 31, after three seasons during which the Office had been informally administered by a rotating committee of Caucus delegates. The committee was, by every member's later admission, "not equipped to make Commissioner-grade decisions" — the most-cited example being the Year 30 contested deed for the Reno Open Court, which the committee had been unable to resolve in three rotating-chair attempts. Whiskerstone took the office, sat on the deed for two weeks, and produced a settlement by the simple expedient of refusing to leave the conference room until both parties agreed. The settlement gave the Court to the Reno municipal authority, with a long-term League lease at a rate the lobster vendor would consider reasonable. The committee disbanded the next month. Whiskerstone has been the Commissioner since.</p>
        <p>She is, by species, a mouse — the smallest Commissioner in any League's history, by every pre-League and Old-Ones-era reference the Foundation Library has been able to locate. (The Foundation Library has, on three occasions, attempted to confirm this against pre-Long-Quiet records; the Library's archivist, on each attempt, has reported back: <em>"there are not, in our holdings, sufficient records of pre-Long-Quiet sports leagues to make a categorical claim. there are also not, in our holdings, any records of a non-mouse Commissioner of any League we can identify, which is, by my read, also a kind of categorical claim. we have stopped trying to verify."</em>) Whiskerstone stands four inches at the shoulder, in formal harness; her ceremonial chair at Foundation Hall is mounted on a small platform that brings her eye-level to roughly the height of a standing Beaver's chest, which is, by her own quiet preference, the height she prefers to negotiate at.</p>
        <p>Her two most-cited public acts as Commissioner are the Year 33 ratification of the Crash Rule (the rule prohibiting overhead-stun-volley targeting on Speedsters in solo retreat, named for Crash Wartooth's Year 34 R3 career-threatening injury — the rule was actually ratified in Year 34 and is misattributed to Year 33 in approximately half the Caucus archive's secondary documentation) and the Year 36 Geography Caucus reclassification (the formal ruling that the League's recruiting boundary was no longer "the former United States" but "the former North American continent," which opened the door for the Lynx, the Antlerlords, the Coyotes, and the Quetzals). The reclassification ruling is, by every Caucus delegate's pre-vote read, the single most-consequential decision Whiskerstone has made in office. She has, in five subsequent interviews, declined to comment on this assessment except to say: <em>"the ruling was overdue. we should, by the Office's own internal review, have made it in Year 32. we did not. we made it in Year 36. the four teams that were waiting were patient with us. they should not have had to be."</em></p>
        <p>Her relationship with the lobster vendor is, by every Foundation staffer's pre-mention warning, a sensitive subject. Whiskerstone has, by long-standing personal practice, eaten her Foundation Day bisque at the Concession Row booth — paid for in mixed currency at the vendor's standard rate, settled (when the bill is settled late, which it usually is) on the Tuesday after Foundation Day, in lobster, the way the Foundation settles all its booth accounts. The vendor has, in eight seasons, never raised the price for the Commissioner. The Commissioner has, in eight seasons, never offered to pay more. The relationship is, by every Foundation staffer's quiet read, "the only relationship in the entire League in which the Commissioner is, demonstrably, not the senior party." Whiskerstone has, on this characterization, said: <em>"the Vendor was here before me. the Vendor will be here after me. i am, on this matter, the temporary tenant. the Vendor is the building."</em></p>
        <p>She is, as of Year 36, fifty-two years old. She has not announced a retirement plan. The Caucus's continuity-planning office has, in three separate years, asked her for one. She has, in three separate years, declined to give one. The Office's standing pre-vacancy protocol — the procedure that would, in the event of a sudden Commissioner vacancy, be activated to choose a successor — has been drafted, redrafted, and re-ratified in every off-season since Year 32. Whiskerstone has, by her own pre-statement at every off-season ratification, "no objection to the protocol's existence and no intention of triggering it on any timeline that is not the Office's own to set." The Caucus has, on three occasions, requested clarification of "the Office's own to set." Whiskerstone has, on three occasions, declined to clarify. The protocol remains drafted. The Office remains hers. The League continues.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Office of the Commissioner, "Commissioner Profile" · the only authorized profile in League records · cross-referenced with the Reno Open Court deed settlement, the Crash Rule and Geography Caucus reclassification ratifications, the Concession Row booth-tab register, and Whiskerstone's standing pre-vacancy protocol</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Doña Inés de la Niebla</h3>
        <div class="meta">Spectacled Bear · b. uncertain (Bogotá Cordillera high country) · Federación Sudamericana, Commissioner since Year 28</div>
        <p>Doña Inés has been the Federación's commissioner for nine seasons. Before that, she was the Cordillera Bear-Council's senior archivist for, by Bogotá-side records, "approximately as long as the Council had had archives." Before that, she was a working scholar at the Bogotá High Library, the third-largest pre-Long-Quiet-document collection on the South American continent. Before that, by every account that has reached the Foundation Library through Inkbeak's communiqués, she was a young Bear who was, in her cohort, "the one who asked the unanswerable questions and waited politely for an answer."</p>
        <p>The Federación's records keep her age in the same way the North American League's records keep Whiskerstone's: in a column called "uncertain." The Bears of the Cordillera, by their species' standing custom, do not formally count years. They count seasons-in-the-cordillera. Doña Inés has, by her own self-described count, lived "many cordillera-seasons." A cordillera-season is, by Bear-Council convention, "the time between one snow-clear at the upper passes and the next." This is not, by any measurable standard, a unit. It is, by every Bear's standing acknowledgment, a unit anyway.</p>
        <p>She took the commissioner's office in Year 28 (Federación dating) following the death of her predecessor, Espinaobscura, in a flash flood at the Manaus venue's outer concourse during a heavy-rain match. Espinaobscura had named her his preferred successor, in writing, in his Year-26 personnel file; the Federación's transition protocol allowed the named-successor to assume the office without a vote, by Federación rule, provided the eleven team commissioners' standing assemblies registered no formal objection within sixty days. None did. She has been the office since.</p>
        <p>Her tenure has been characterized, by every Federación team's pre-publication account, as "deliberate" and "patient." She does not, in office, make decisions quickly. She does not, in office, refuse to make decisions. She makes them in, by her own standing description, "the time the question takes to answer itself." The Federación's most-cited line of hers, written in a letter to Bogotá Bears Tank Capitán Toribio in Year 32 after a three-year delay on a particular procedural ruling: <em>"the question, capitán, has, by my reading, been the same question for three years. the answer has, in those three years, changed twice. I am writing now because the answer is, by my reading this morning, the answer it was the first time you asked it. I do not, by Federación rule, owe you an explanation of the changes. I am giving you one anyway. The mountain has, by every cordillera-season's read, been moving more than we credit it with. I have, in three years, been listening to the mountain. The mountain has now, by my reading, settled. The answer is yes. Begin the protocol."</em> The protocol Toribio began that day was the formal request to amend the Federación's six-balloon contract to a seven-balloon contract for one specific category of match (the deciding round of the Federación's annual cross-team friendship tour). The Federación voted on the amendment six months later. The amendment did not pass. Doña Inés did not, on the failure, characterize the failure publicly. The mountain, by every Bogotá-side reading, was still moving on this matter. The mountain has not, in four subsequent years, settled.</p>
        <p>She has met Inkbeak Sr. seven times across his seven post-Year-33 visits. She has met Whittlestone in person once, by remote-link only, in a Year-35 cross-continental conference held with the Caucus and the Federación's senior delegation simultaneously connected through the Cartagena harbor's Quetzal-relay. The conference ran four hours. Whittlestone's pre-conference summary characterized Doña Inés to the Caucus as "the smartest person I have, in three years of remote correspondence, encountered, and the patient-est person I have, in any year, encountered. she is, by every read I can apply, the right Federación commissioner for this period of contact." Doña Inés's parallel pre-conference summary to her own delegation characterized Whittlestone as <em>"la única norteamericana que, por mi lectura de su correspondencia, no me trata como una novedad. me trata como un colega. esto es, por mi lectura, suficiente. los demás aprenderán, en su debido momento."</em> ("the only North American who, by my reading of her correspondence, does not treat me as a novelty. she treats me as a colleague. this is, by my reading, enough. the others will learn, in their own due course.")</p>
        <p>She has not, as of Year 36, named a preferred successor.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library bio · "Doña Inés de la Niebla" · drafted from Inkbeak's communiqué notes and the four published Federación-Caucus joint conference transcripts · the entry is the canonical North American summary; the Federación's own canonical bio is held in Bogotá and includes, by Federación convention, materials the Foundation Library has not been authorized to translate</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Saira Capytlán</h3>
        <div class="meta">Capybara · b. Manaus river-quarter, age uncertain · Manaus Capybaras (MNS), Captain since Year 33, Healer-class</div>
        <p>Saira is the Capybaras' captain, third in the role since the Federación's founding. She is also, by every Foundation Library report from Inkbeak's communiqués, the most-decorated active Healer in the Federación — winner of the Federación's annual Healer of the Year award in five of the last seven seasons, and nominee in the other two. She is the only Capybara-class Healer in either league's recorded history; the position is, on the North American side, dominated by Hedgehogs, and on the Federación side, by various rotational Lowland-Tapir, Spectacled-Bear, and Sloth Healers, who collectively form what the Federación calls "the Cordillera-Selva diagonal" — a coaching-staff-rotated tradition of moving Healers between northern Andean and Amazon-basin teams to share technique. Saira does not rotate. She has been a Capybara, in Manaus, in the Healer's slot, for fourteen seasons. Her stated reason: <em>"el río ya rota suficiente. yo no necesito rotar."</em> ("the river already rotates enough. i don't need to rotate.")</p>
        <p>Her technical reputation rests on what the Federación's tactical analysts call <em>la curación-en-grupo</em> ("group healing") — a Capybara-specific Healer-beam technique that, instead of focusing the beam on a single teammate, distributes the beam's restorative effect across all teammates within a five-meter radius simultaneously, at reduced per-target throughput but, on the right formation, at higher total throughput than single-target healing. The technique is, by every analyst's read, possible only because Capybaras are, by their species' standing pre-League social structure, accustomed to operating in groups of indeterminate size and composition. The Capybaras' default group, by Manaus river-quarter convention, is "however many capybaras are sitting in this particular pond at this particular hour." A Capybara Healer, on the field, treats the Capybara line as the same kind of group. The beam goes to the pond. The pond is, by Capybara reading, what the line is.</p>
        <p>Saira has been beam-target for one Federación-canonical eleven-second silence — the Federación's own ceremonial silence, distinct from the four canonical North American silences but operating on the same eleven-second standard the Whittlestone Address established. The silence was held at the Manaus venue at the close of the Year-34 Federación final, in which the Capybaras lost to the Cusco Vicuñas in a deciding round in which Saira had, in the round's final seventy seconds, beam-healed three of her four surviving teammates back from the brink of their first-balloon pop, only for the Vicuñas' final striker to flank-engage and pop her own three balloons in approximately fifteen seconds. The Vicuñas' captain, on the post-match line, walked the perimeter of the Manaus pitch alone in silence for eleven seconds before speaking the standard Federación post-match-victory greeting. Saira, watching from the bench, raised one paw in acknowledgment of the silence at its midpoint. The Vicuñas' captain returned the gesture. The Manaus crowd, by venue-staff report, did not cheer until the silence was over. The eleven-second silence is, by Federación archival convention, the only post-match silence held in honor of a defeated Healer in Federación history.</p>
        <p>She has, in Inkbeak Sr.'s personal communiqués (a separate series from the official seventeen-page communiqué; these are private pages Inkbeak shares with the Murder's elder council and which have, by the Murder's standing rule, not been published), been characterized as "by my reading the single Federación knight a North American Healer would, on a sanctioned cross-continental match's first encounter, immediately recognize as a peer. she is what the Hedgehogs would be, by my read, if the Hedgehogs were also a river. she is also a river. these things are not, by my read, in conflict."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library bio · "Saira Capytlán" · drafted from Inkbeak's published and personal communiqué materials, with Federación-side approval for the published portions · Saira has, by Manaus standing tradition, never given a public interview to a non-Federación journalist; the Foundation Library has, by Federación protocol, not requested one · she remains the Capybaras' captain as of Year 36 · she has not, in three Federación seasons since the Year-34 final, returned to a Federación final · the Capybaras have not, since, contended for the title</div>
      </article>

      <article class="bio lore-wide">
        <h3>Pell Whittlestone — chemist, Counsel, forge-keeper, address-author</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver · b. Boise (a small commune at the edge of the Treasure Valley salt flats) · age forty-three as of Year 36 · current titles: Foundation Counsel emeritus · Foundry chief chemist (still on the masthead, semi-retired from active inspection duty) · Caucus chair-emeritus · keeper of the founding-bell forge · author of the canonical Whittlestone Address · this bio is the canonical Foundation Library bio; she has, in twelve years of public service, declined every other authorized-bio request</div>
        <p>Pell Whittlestone is the single most-consulted living person in League institutional memory. She has not, in twelve years of public service, sought a single one of the offices she has held. She has been asked, by Caucus or Foundation protocol, to take each one in turn, and she has, in each case, accepted by saying the same four words at the formal-acceptance moment: <em>"on this matter, yes."</em> The four words are, by Foundation archival convention, recorded verbatim in the minutes of every appointment vote she has been the subject of. They are also, by her own pre-publication permission, the only direct quotes from any of those acceptance moments that the Foundation Library is authorized to print. She has otherwise, on every such occasion, sat in silence for the remainder of the meeting and gone home.</p>
        <p>Her training is in chemistry — specifically, the molecular composition of float-gas, which is the working medium of the sport. The Boise Float Gas Foundry hired her at twenty-one (Year 24, four seasons before the founding bell) on the strength of a single technical paper she had written for an upper-Idaho regional engineering quarterly: <em>"On the Three Pressures: A Working Theory of Float-Gas Stability Under Combat Stress."</em> The paper proposed, against the then-prevailing theory of single-pressure stability, that the gas operates under three distinct pressure regimes which transition at predictable thresholds, and that the dominant balloon-engineering practice of the time was optimizing for the wrong regime. The paper was, on first publication, rejected by the regional engineering board for being "speculative beyond the available evidence." The Foundry hired her anyway. Three years later her three-pressure model was the Foundry's working standard, and the regional engineering board had, in two subsequent papers, retracted the rejection without naming her. She has not, in two decades since, asked them to.</p>
        <p>Her tenure at the Foundry is the foundation of her reputation. She wrote the outgoing-inspection protocol that has, in twelve seasons, prevented every documented float-gas exploit except the one Tinkerbarrel of the Tampa Sharks managed in Year 30 R3 (the disclosed-Year-33 flat-batch incident). Her response to that disclosure, when Featherquill of the Wing Standard interviewed her three days after the column's publication, was: <em>"the Foundry has not, in seven years, shipped another flat batch. The Sharks have not, in seven years, asked us to."</em> She declined to elaborate. The non-elaboration is, by Featherquill's own published assessment, "the most precisely calibrated refusal-to-comment I have, in nineteen years of sportswriting, received from any subject." Featherquill also wrote, in the same column, that Whittlestone's refusal "is, in my reading, not silence. it is, in my reading, the second pressure." The line passed into League shorthand. To this day, when a Caucus member declines to elaborate on a procedural matter, the standard recognition phrase is "the second pressure." Whittlestone has not, in three years since, commented on the shorthand.</p>
        <p>Her transition into Foundation Counsel happened in Year 30 in a way that has, by every Foundation archivist's account, never been adequately explained. The previous Counsel — a senior Owl named Sundip Hootington Sr., who had served two seasons in the role and had been planning a third — passed unexpectedly in his sleep at the Owl Hall dormitory in Seattle. The Caucus's emergency working session named Whittlestone to the role two days later, in a vote of fourteen to zero with one abstention (her own, by procedural requirement). She was thirty years old. She had no legal training. She had no prior Caucus experience. She was, by every account, the most surprising appointment in the League's institutional history. When asked, in the days after the vote, why she had accepted the role, she said the four words. She has not, in thirteen years since, elaborated.</p>
        <p>As Counsel, she drafted the Year-31 Address (the canonical Whittlestone Address; see separate glossary entry); she designed the founding-bell convocation format that every Caucus chair has since used without amendment; she ratified the Heat Clause, the Crash Rule, and the Antlerwood Rule (named for L'Ancrage and Théodred III, the only player-named rule in League standing language); she sat on the contested Reno Open Court deed for two weeks until a settlement was reached; and she forged, in her off-season, the brass crown for the inaugural Coronation Cup. The crown was billed to the League at a price of one lobster. The bill remains unpaid as of Year 36 mid-season. Whittlestone has, on three separate occasions, declined to discuss the bill. The lobster vendor, on those same occasions, has provided, by her own standing custom, a single sentence: <em>"the bill is, by my own reading, not mine to collect on. it is, by my own reading, also not the Foundation's to settle. the bill is, by my own reading, between Pell and Pell. it will, in due course, be settled. it is not yet."</em></p>
        <p>Her current arrangement, since stepping down from active Counsel work in Year 35, is a semi-retired hybrid role she designed herself in collaboration with the incoming Counsel (a younger Beaver named Glaze Quartzfinger, who took the office at her recommendation). The arrangement: she retains advisory standing on every Caucus working session that touches the founding-bell traditions, the Address, the standing eleven-second silences, the Foundry's outgoing-inspection protocol, or any matter the active Counsel formally asks her to advise on. She does not, in any other matter, attend Caucus sessions. She does, by her own pre-arrangement preference, continue to forge ceremonial trophies for inaugural events as they arise (the Cold Stones trophy for the Polar Bears–Lynx friendly, the in-progress Quetzal-affiliate ceremonial whistle for the Yucatan canopy elders' annual exhibition, and one private commission she has, by her own preference, declined to characterize publicly). She also, by every Foundation Library account, continues to read every published Caucus minute, every Foundation Drawer filing note, and every Foundation Library bio as they go to press. She does not, on receiving them, comment.</p>
        <p>She is unmarried. She has, by her parents' own pre-publication account, no surviving siblings. Her two parents — both still living in the Boise commune as of Year 36 — are, by their own report, "fine, slowly aging, and increasingly bemused by the daughter we apparently raised." Pell Whittlestone visits them, by her own standing routine, twice per year at the founding-bell convocation week (when she travels to whichever venue is hosting that season's bell) and at the off-season turn (when she returns home for what her parents call "the silence week"). The silence week is named for the parents' own observation that during the visit, Pell speaks an average of "perhaps fourteen sentences per day." The parents do not, by their own report, find this concerning. <em>"Pell has always been, by our raising, an economical speaker. We are economical speakers. Boise is, on the whole, an economical city. We do not, in our family, take additional speech to be evidence of additional thought. The thought is, in any speaker we know personally, where the speaker keeps it. Pell is, by every available read, the economical-est speaker we have ever known. The thought is, by every available read, exactly where it should be."</em></p>
        <p>She has, by her own pre-publication arrangement with the Foundation Library, two standing requests for any future bio update: (1) that the bio not name a successor before she has formally named one herself, and (2) that the bio's signoff line, whatever else it says, include the lobster vendor's standing comment about the brass-crown bill. The first request the Library has agreed to. The second is honored below. She has, in twelve years of public service, asked the Foundation Library for nothing else.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library bio · "Pell Whittlestone" · the canonical bio · drafted Year 36 mid-season at her own pre-publication permission, in the longest-form authorized version she has, in twelve years, signed off on · the lobster vendor's standing comment about the brass-crown bill is included by her standing request: <em>"the bill is, by my own reading, between Pell and Pell."</em> · she has not, as of this writing, named a Counsel-emeritus successor · the founding-bell forge remains, by her own keeping, in continuous operation</div>
      </article>
      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Marisol Cumbralta</h3>
        <div class="meta">Andean Condor · Federación Sudamericana long-distance scout · twenty-nine years old · the first northbound oceanic arrival at the Pittsburgh Visiting Perch · Year 36 mid-season</div>
        <p>Marisol Cumbralta was born in the Cordillera Real, on a ledge in the upland Bolivian massif her family has occupied without break since at least the second generation after the Long Quiet — a ledge the Federación's high-cordillera ornithology bureau classifies as <em>"posición ancestral confirmada,"</em> a designation reserved for nesting sites with at least four documented generational continuities on file. She is, by every Federación register, the Condor scout with the most complete flight log on the Federación's active roster: nine hundred and forty-one sanctioned scouting flights between Year 20 and Year 36, three confirmed Caribbean-basin southbound crossings (Years 32, 33, and 35, all completed without incident), and one confirmed northbound crossing (Year 36 mid-season, the dispatch that carried her to the Pittsburgh Visiting Perch on its forty-seventh day of vacant standing).</p>
        <p>The Federación selected her for the first northbound dispatch in a working session held at Cartagena in the third week of Year 36's calendar. Doña Inés chaired the session. Six other Condor scouts were on the considered list. The session's deliberation took, by Bears' minutes, four hours. Cumbralta was selected on the strength of a single working-session statement made by the Federación's senior bureau-Bear Don Alfonso de la Cordillera Pampabajo, who said, on the matter: <em>"el primer arribo será leído por la Manada de Pittsburgh con la atención que la Manada aplica a todo testimonio aviar. nosotros, por nuestra propia regla, hemos clasificado el testimonio aviar como menos confiable de lo que nuestros Osos preferirían. la Cóndor que envíemos por primera vez al norte debe, por toda lectura honesta, ser aquella cuyo registro pueda ser leído por la Manada y, en cualquier referencia cruzada, no encontrar margen para corregirlo. esa Cóndor es, por mi propia lectura, Marisol Cumbralta. esto no es debate. esto es, por toda lectura honesta, lo correcto."</em> The session concluded without further deliberation. Cumbralta was notified that afternoon. She accepted the dispatch in writing the same evening, in a one-sentence reply transcribed by the Bears' courier: <em>"He recibido el encargo. Volaré. — M.C."</em></p>
        <p>Cumbralta is, by her own pre-flight description, <em>"not a narrator. i am a scout. the scout's job is to fly the route, observe the conditions, and return with what i have observed. the narration is, by my read, the work of the bureau that receives the report. i am, on this matter, willing to answer questions. i am not, on this matter, willing to embellish. if a question asks for what i do not know, i will say i do not know. if a question asks for what i do know, i will give the answer in the smallest correct number of words. this is, by my read, what the bureau receiving me has, in six years of operation, been built to receive."</em> The Pittsburgh Murder's Roost, on receiving this pre-flight description (relayed by Inkbeak Sr. on Flight 9 northbound, three weeks before her arrival), is reported to have replied, in the standing one-sentence format the Roost uses for inter-bureau acknowledgments: <em>"the Roost has read the description. the Roost is, on this matter, ready."</em></p>
        <p>Her interview at the bureau, conducted by Sigridweave on the first afternoon of her four-day Pittsburgh stay, produced one hundred and forty-one pages of transcript. The bureau's pre-publication summary characterizes the interview's content as covering <em>"the Federación's standing roster of fifty-three sanctioned teams, the seventeen-year operational history of the cordillera scouting program, the Federación's working classification of seven trans-Pacific bird-relay sources (which the bureau has never, in six years, had any direct evidence of and which Cumbralta confirms in detail with what is, by every cross-reference, the same careful precision the Year-34 albatross applied), the standing relationship between the Cartagena Bears and the Bogotá Spectacled Bears, and a single passage of approximately fourteen pages on the cordillera's prevailing wind patterns at the equatorial crossing — a passage the bureau has, by curator's standing recommendation, marked as a separate sub-file for distribution to the Murder's Roost on Roost-vote."</em> The Roost has, by Year 36 mid-season vote, accepted the sub-file and begun internal review. The Roost's standing position on the sub-file's content, after two working sessions: <em>"the wind information is, by every cross-reference Inkbeak Sr. can apply from his own eight crossings, accurate. the information also extends our existing crossing-route knowledge by a margin we have not, in twenty-seven years of crossing operations, had access to. we will, in due course, integrate the information into the Murder's standing crossing protocols. we will not, by Roost vote, alter the protocols immediately. integration of new information into long-standing protocols is, by Roost convention, undertaken slowly. we are, on this matter, undertaking it slowly."</em></p>
        <p>Cumbralta, on departing Pittsburgh on the morning of her fifth day, was asked at the harbor wall by a Wing Standard reporter (Talia Featherquill, who had flown to Pittsburgh for the occasion on Foundation expense) whether she would be returning. She answered, in League Common, which she does not speak natively but had used carefully for the four days of her visit: <em>"i will return when the Federación dispatches me to return. i do not, on the matter, dispatch myself. the dispatch is the bureau's. the flight is mine. these are different roles. they have, by my read, been kept separate by every careful flier on either continent for the entire history of the program. i will keep them separate."</em> Featherquill's column, published the following week in the Wing Standard, characterized this answer as <em>"the most professionally careful answer i have, in eleven years of column-writing, been given by any source on either continent. the answer is, by every reading, exactly the answer the Federación selected her to give. the Federación selected well. the Murder, by every reading, knows it. the bureau, by every reading, knows it. we should, by my reading, also know it."</em> The column ran without revision.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Wing Standard cultural feature, "The First Arrival" · Year 36 mid-season · by Talia Featherquill · the column is, by Foundation Library standing acquisition, on permanent file in the Northeast Coast Bureau's curator-recommended reading drawer · Cumbralta has not, in the four months since departure, been re-dispatched · the Federación's standing position on the timing of any second northbound dispatch is, in Doña Inés's hand: <em>"el primer arribo se ha hecho. el segundo será cuando el segundo deba ser. no hay calendario. hay vuelos. los vuelos vendrán cuando los vuelos sean correctos."</em></div>
      </article>

        <h3>Estelle Roiseau-Manchot</h3>
        <div class="meta">Penguin · LMG broadcast booth, translator · b. uncertain · Year 36 — present</div>
        <p>The booth's first translator, hired specifically for the Year 36 Continental Expansion. Estelle is, by her own preference, paid in lobster — at a rate that her contract pegs to "one Concession Row premium-vendor day's take" per matchday worked. The Foundation has not, on the matter, ever balked. The senior commentator has, on the matter, in private, said that Estelle is the best decision the booth has made in eight seasons.</p>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>The Concession Row Lobsterer</h3>
        <div class="meta">Beaver · Boston, Concession Row · est. Year 24 · the License Wall, prominently</div>
        <p>The vendor's name is on the License Wall and is, by Foundation tradition, withheld from broadcast — she requested this in Year 28 and has, every season since, renewed the request. She is the senior vendor on the Row by margin of two decades. Her stand, by Foundation revenue records, takes the highest single-day total of any concession on Concession Row except the rare championship-final Sundays, when the cider stand briefly overtakes her.</p>
        <p>Her prices have not changed in eight seasons. Her lobster has not changed in eight seasons. The Wolves have, every December, sent her a small dressed-cedar plank with the words <em>"The Pack Eats. — WLF"</em> burned into it. She has, every December, returned a small parcel of crab claws. The exchange is, by both sides' read, complete.</p>
        <p>She does not, on the matter, smile at customers. She has, by reliable record, smiled twice in eight seasons: once on the morning Mira Pawington died, and once on the afternoon the Year 36 Andean Condor landed. The smiles were, by both witnesses' accounts, identical.</p>

        <h3>Briarwing Hootington</h3>
        <div class="meta">Owl · scent-tracker, freelance · daughter of Hawkeye Hootington (deceased Y29) · paid in lobster</div>
        <p>Briarwing's profession does not, by League roster, exist. She is, by her own card, a "scent-tracker, working consultant." The Foundation retains her on a freelance basis to interpret marks left at training facilities, locker tunnels, and (twice) bathroom stalls. She has, in seven seasons of intermittent work, never been wrong about a captain's mark. She has, on the Whitefang scribbles, said only that they are "made by at least three different individuals, none of whom are using a name they were born with."</p>
        <p>Her fee is, by long-standing arrangement, two units of lobster per consultation. The Foundation has tried to renegotiate this twice, both times unsuccessfully. Briarwing has, both times, simply not returned the second telegram. The Foundation has, both times, sent the lobster.</p>
        <p>Her father Hawkeye died in Year 29 R4 holding the same bow Vela Hootington would later die holding. Briarwing has, on the matter, never carried a bow. She has, on the matter, said that her work "does not, by my read, require one."</p>

      <article class="bio">
        <h3>Referee Cob Stoneholt</h3>
        <div class="meta">Tortoise · senior arena official · 14 seasons of officiating · the slowest reflex in the League</div>
        <p>Stoneholt is, by every team's quiet acknowledgment, the slowest referee the League has ever fielded — and the most accurate. His observation method is, by his own admission, "I see what I see and I see it for as long as I see it." A Stoneholt call takes (per match-clock measurement) an average of 4.7 seconds to deliver. A Stoneholt call has, in fourteen seasons, been overturned exactly twice. Both overturns were, on subsequent review, returned to Stoneholt's original ruling.</p>
        <p>He has officiated every Coronation Cup since Year 31. The Raccoons have, every Coronation Cup, attempted exactly one stunt that hinges on Stoneholt's perceived slowness. They have, every Coronation Cup, been caught. They have, every Coronation Cup, complimented him on the catch. He has, every Coronation Cup, returned the compliment with a single nod. The Raccoons consider this their actual prize.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— League official roster · Stoneholt, senior · still active</div>
      </article>

        <p>Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. is the senior flying Raven of the Pittsburgh Murder and the only Murder member to publish under his own name in the Wing Standard. He has, on the matter, declined the title of "columnist" — he prefers <em>"observer."</em> His Year 36 column on the Andean Condor's arrival ran 2,400 words and contained, by Featherquill's own annotation in the same issue, "the only sentence I have ever read by a Raven that I have, on the matter, been jealous of." Slatequill's response was, by his own copy, three words: <em>"On the matter."</em></p>

The Bears have, by Federación protocol, never disclosed the contents of those letters. Slatequill has not, on the matter, complained.</p>

        <h3>Doña Inés of the Federación</h3>

Doña Inés has, on the matter, not commented.</p>

Her decision to send Marisol was, by every read, the decision to send someone she trusted with the question of whether the north was worth a second flight. Marisol's first dispatch back has not yet, by Foundation record, been written. The Foundation has, on the matter, set aside an empty file folder labeled <em>"Cumbralta — first dispatch — pending"</em> on the assumption that one will, in due course, exist.</p>

        <h3>The Pew-Pew Ewe</h3>
        <div class="meta">Sheep, female · anonymous fan · Section 14, Row M (every Brewer's Reach match) · also seen at Reno, Olympia, and Helena · handle by acclamation</div>
        <p>The Pew-Pew Ewe is, by Foundation broadcast staff's quiet consensus, the loudest single fan in the League — and the most consistent. She has, by usher records, occupied the same Brewer's Reach seat (Section 14, Row M, third in from the aisle) for at least twenty-six consecutive home matchdays. She is, on the matter, not a season-ticket holder; the seat is sold weekly and she purchases it weekly. The Foundation does not, on the matter, know how she manages this.</p>
        <p>Her handle was given to her by the Section 14 regulars. Her catchphrase, yelled in unison every time any Sniper anywhere on the field releases a shot, is two syllables: <em>"PEW! PEW!"</em> The yell is, by Foundation booth measurement, audible from the broadcast booth on calm days. Her broadcast nickname predates her appearance in any printed Wing Standard letters page by two seasons; the letters page, when she finally wrote in (Year 35 mid-season), opened with <em>"EXTRA! EXTRA! Read all about a fan what's been waitin' two whole seasons to write in!"</em> and the editor printed it without correction.</p>
        <p>She has not, by Foundation conviction, ever been photographed. The Section 14 regulars know her. The Foundation has, on the matter, decided to let the regulars keep her. Her writing is recognizable across at least eleven pieces of stadium ephemera in the archive — every one of them in the same exuberant 1920s-newsboy cadence, every one signed (when signed at all) <em>"— the Ewe what cheers"</em> or some variant.</p>

He has not, on the matter, ever paid for a ticket. He has, on the matter, also never tried to enter the stadium proper. The embankment is, by his own quiet preference, the seat.</p>
        <p>The Foundation has come to know him by sight. The senior usher at Gate Three has, by quiet arrangement with Concession Row, kept a thermos of weak tea on hand on cold matchdays. The thermos is, on the matter, never empty when the boy arrives, and is, on the matter, refilled by the usher's own paw before each match. The boy has, in three seasons, never asked for it. The thermos is, on the matter, simply there.</p>
        <p>His writings have appeared in the Wing Standard letters page once (Year 36 R4, at Featherquill's own request and over the boy's gentle protest). Three of his ephemera are in the Foundation archive — all in pencil, on scraps of paper of various provenances, in the same earnest hand. He has, on the matter, never asked for them back.</p>
        <p>The boy's name is, by long-standing Foundation discretion, not in any broadcast roster. The Foundation has, on the matter, decided that the boy will be, on the matter, named when he chooses to name himself. The boy has not, on the matter, chosen to. The League is, on the matter, in no hurry.</p>

The note is, on the matter, hers to keep refreshing. She has, on the matter, kept refreshing it.</p>
