      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Diary of a Healer (HED)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Anonymized · seized from a locker room · published with permission</div>
        <p><em>Day one.</em> They told me a Healer's job is to heal. The other rookies laughed when I asked who I should heal. The drill instructor said: "the lowest-HP teammate." I asked: "what if there are two." He said: "pick one." I asked: "how do I pick." He said: "you'll figure it out." I have not figured it out.</p>
        <p><em>Day forty.</em> I have been on the field for six matches now. I follow whoever needs healing. I do not shoot at anyone. The other team's Sniper shoots at me, every time, immediately, before they shoot at anyone else. The drill instructor says this is "expected behavior" and I should "keep my heal target between me and the Sniper." I asked if my heal target knew about this arrangement. He did not answer.</p>
        <p><em>Day eighty.</em> I have learned to wander a little. When my heal target gets too far ahead, or when they turn a corner I cannot follow into, I sometimes drift. The other Healers tell me this is normal. The other Healers all have a thing they think about while drifting. I think about lobster. I have never had lobster. The Beavers' Healer told me about it. I would like to try lobster. The League sells lobster at the Boston concession.</p>
        <p><em>Day one hundred and twelve.</em> I am writing this from the Hall of Fallen Heroes intake desk. They are processing my paperwork. The intake officer told me my matches will be replayed for memorial purposes. She told me I can request that my final match not be one of them. I told her I do not have a preference. I told her I would like a portion of my pension to be sent to the Boston concession in lobster. She wrote it down and underlined it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— anonymous, HED Healer cohort, posthumous</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Diary of a Sniper (SHK)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Tampa Tornado Sharks scout journal · maintained for three seasons</div>
        <p><em>Entry 14.</em> The Healer is the kill. Always. Even if the Healer is not the closest target. Even if the Healer is moving away. The Healer is the kill, because the Healer is the difference between the other team having a third round and the other team going home tonight.</p>
        <p><em>Entry 22.</em> I shot a Healer today. The Healer's heal target took the next four hits in eight seconds and went down on the fifth. I did not need to fire those four hits. The Healer's heal target was already losing the engagement; I just sped it up. The League's notes called it a "tactical erasure." I cannot stop thinking about the word <em>erasure</em>. I do not like it. The notes do not have to like it. The notes only have to be accurate.</p>
        <p><em>Entry 28.</em> The Healers have started wearing red ribbons. The Snipers have, in response, started ignoring the red ribbons. The Healers have, in response to that, started wearing the same colors as their teammates. The Snipers, in response to that, are still shooting them, because the Healer is the kill.</p>
        <p><em>Entry 34.</em> The opposing team's Healer was, today, my old neighbor's daughter. I did not know this at the time. I know now. I do not know if I would have done anything differently. I think the answer is no. The Healer is the kill.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Tampa Sharks scouts' shared journal, Year 34 entries</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Diary of a Grenadier (PND, the Marshmallow Drill)</h3>
        <div class="meta">"To be opened in case of post-traumatic frag review"</div>
        <p>I have not thrown a grenade since Year 34. I will not throw a grenade. I will not handle a grenade. I will not look at a grenade. I will not <em>think</em> about a grenade.</p>
        <p>The League says I am not under disciplinary review. The League says it was an accident. The League sent the report. The League sent flowers. The League sent the Marshmallow Protocol training video, which is fifteen minutes of footage of <em>me</em>, slowed down, with arrows added by an animator, and which I have not watched and will not watch.</p>
        <p>I throw stones now. We do not have a stone-throwing position on the roster, but the coach lets me do it in practice and then quietly takes the stones away before matches. I have a melee bat for matches. The melee bat is fine. The melee bat is not a grenade.</p>
        <p>Felix's family sent me a card last winter. It said "we know it wasn't your fault." I do know it wasn't my fault. I know exactly whose fault it was. The Otter moved. Felix did not. I did everything right except for being three feet too short.</p>
        <p>I am writing this because the league therapist said I should. She did not say I had to mail it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— anonymous, PND Grenadier, "do not file"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>The Steward's Notebook (League Office, Vault Wing)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Daily log · season 6 · partial</div>
        <p><em>Day 1 of vault rotation.</em> Picked up four armor pieces and one shield. Inventoried. Bagged. Sealed. Loaded. Ten-minute drive to the vault. All five items present on arrival. Vault staff signed.</p>
        <p><em>Day 7.</em> Picked up six items. Inventoried. Bagged. Sealed. Loaded. Ten-minute drive. <em>Five</em> items on arrival. The shield is not in the bag. The bag is sealed. The seal is intact. There is no rip. There is no opening. The shield is, however, not in the bag.</p>
        <p><em>Day 8.</em> Reviewed the truck. The truck is empty. The shield is not in the truck. The shield was, the steward confirms, in the bag at pickup. The shield is, the vault confirms, not in the bag at delivery. The seal is the same seal. We have no theory.</p>
        <p><em>Day 11.</em> The League Office is reviewing the matter. I have been told to keep doing my job. I have been told to keep doing my job <em>without checking the bag mid-route</em>. I have not been told why I should not check the bag.</p>
        <p><em>Day 14.</em> I checked the bag mid-route. The shield was in the bag. I drove the rest of the route. I unsealed the bag in front of the vault staff. The shield was not in the bag. I then unloaded every other item from the truck. The shield was, with apologies, in <em>my own coat pocket</em>. I do not remember putting it there. I have requested unpaid leave.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Steward's Notebook, redacted, vault wing archive</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Diary of a Tank (BDG)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Personal · taster's logbook · Boise Foundry, refinery shift 2</div>
        <p><em>Day 1.</em> Promoted off the field. The leg won't fully extend after Lhor's shot in S5, and the doctors say one more season as a Tank and the leg will not extend at all. The Foundry offered me the taster job. I took it. The Float Gas formula needs a Badger nose, they say. I am a Badger. I have a nose. We will see.</p>
        <p><em>Day 6.</em> The training is, "smell each batch, mark it on a scale of one to seven, and never lie." The senior taster (her name is Krela, she is older than the Foundry) tells me that the scale used to go to ten but they removed eight, nine, and ten because they smelled like things she did not want to remember. I asked what they smelled like. Krela did not answer. I have not asked again.</p>
        <p><em>Day 19.</em> The current batch smells like a six. Krela smells it and says four. We argue. The Foundry chemist comes in and smells it and says five. We compromise on five. The batch goes to the Foxes. The Foxes lose at the Bowl that weekend. I do not know if the loss is the gas's fault. I do not feel it is mine.</p>
        <p><em>Day 41.</em> Foundry shut down today. No reason given. We are paid in full. The senior taster tells me to "go home and not check the gas in your apartment." I check the gas in my apartment. The gas in my apartment is fine. The gas in my apartment is from a batch I rated a seven. I have a moment of pride.</p>
        <p><em>Day 41+1.</em> An unsigned letter arrived at the Office today. I am told not to discuss the letter. I am told the Foundry will reopen in approximately six weeks. I am told to keep doing my job during that time. I am being paid to not work. This is, I am told, "the reserve gas period." I am told the reserve gas is lighter and burns clean. I am told it is fine. I do not believe it is fine. I am instructed to believe it is fine.</p>
        <p><em>Day 87.</em> Foundry reopens. The gas chemist apologizes to no one in particular. I rate the new batch a six. Krela rates it a six. The chemist rates it a six. We agree. The batch goes to the Wolves. The Wolves win. I no longer believe the gas affects the matches. I believe Krela has been lying for thirty years about the scale only going to seven.</p>
        <p><em>Day 88.</em> Krela retired. She gave me her booklet of ratings. The booklet has entries on a scale of one to ten. I have not opened the back half of the booklet.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Taster's Logbook, Foundry Annex, partial transcription</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>Diary of a Speedster (PND) at Hallowtide Tag</h3>
        <div class="meta">Personal · Hallowtide Year 35 · Reno Hallowtide Hollow</div>
        <p><em>Pre-match.</em> The Pandas drew sixth-from-last in the entry order. Coach said this was good news. Coach also said the Wolves drew first, which was bad news. The "It" assignment is randomized at match start. There are eleven non-Wolf knights and one Wolf knight. Statistically, the Wolf will be It one time in twelve. Statistically, the Wolf has been It one time in five and won that one too.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 1.</em> The "It" assignment dropped. It is Kor Wartooth. We knew it would be. The Pandas exchange a look. The look is professional. Inside the look, we are screaming.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 40.</em> I am running. Kor is faster than me, which I knew, but I had not appreciated the gap. I am at full sprint. He is at three-quarters sprint and gaining. I am running toward the field's edge because the edges have cover. Cover is small jack-o'-lantern pumpkins. The pumpkins do not stop Kor. The pumpkins are decorative.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 67.</em> First tag. Not me — a Frog speedster on the other side of the field. The Frog freezes mid-stride; the freeze animation includes a small ❄ icon over their head. The Frog had been running diagonally, which I had thought was clever. The diagonal is a known anti-pattern in this venue. Kor has notes.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 89.</em> Frog is dead. Bleed damage finished the job before the freeze ended. The Frog never moved again.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 121.</em> Three more dead. I am still alive. I am also still running. I have run, in the last six seconds, in a perfect circle around the field's perimeter. Kor has been chasing. Kor has been gaining. Kor has not yet caught up because I am, somehow, faster than my actual stat sheet says I am. Adrenaline is a real thing. Adrenaline cannot be stat-blocked.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 154.</em> Six dead. Five alive including me and Kor. I am cornered. The corner is not, this time, my fault — Kor herded me. Kor knows the venue. I do not.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 156.</em> Tagged.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 156-216.</em> Frozen. Bleeding. Cannot move. The freeze duration in real time is three seconds. In subjective time it is approximately a season and a half. I watch Kor sprint away to chase the next-nearest target. I watch the next-nearest target also get tagged. I watch them die. I watch the bleed counter on my own HP bar tick down. I am reasonably sure I will die before the freeze ends.</p>
        <p><em>Tick 209.</em> I die. The freeze ends seven ticks later. The freeze ending is, in the rules, what would have allowed me to flee. The rules and the bleed are not, in practice, well-coordinated.</p>
        <p><em>Post-match.</em> Eleventh place. Coach says good job. Coach says we'll get them next year. Coach knows we will not get them next year.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Personal log, anonymous Panda Speedster, transcribed for the LMG broadcast cycle</div>
      </article>

        <h3>The Sandbagged: A Knight's Notebook</h3>
        <div class="meta">Personal · Year 35 mid-season · author redacted at request</div>
        <p><em>Match 3, R2.</em> Felt sluggish all round. Couldn't reach a Brawler I should have outpaced. The kiting drill in practice goes 8 reps in 9 seconds. I went 6 in 9 today. Coach says it's the field. Coach has not seen the practice numbers from yesterday.</p>
        <p><em>Match 3, post.</em> The trainer logged my SPD as 4.2. The roster card says 4.5. The trainer says the difference is "within margin." The margin is, by the trainer's own definition, plus or minus 0.1. The difference is three margins.</p>
        <p><em>Match 4, pre.</em> I asked the trainer to weigh me. I weighed normal. I asked her to test the springs in my boots. The springs tested normal. I asked her to test the kiting drill again. She refused, on the grounds that the test would tire me out before the match. I performed the test anyway, in the warm-up tunnel, on a stopwatch I trust. 8 reps in 9.4 seconds. Within margin. Barely.</p>
        <p><em>Match 4, R3.</em> Outpaced a Sniper I had no business outpacing. Got the kill. Streak of two. Felt like myself. The trainer says it's the new boots. The boots are old. The boots have been old for a year and a half. The trainer is not lying — the trainer believes what she is saying. The trainer has been told to believe it.</p>
        <p><em>Match 5, R1.</em> Sluggish again. The kiting drill ran 6 in 9. Same gap as Match 3. Same opponent in the bracket as Match 3. The opposing fanbase is large and well-monied. I am not naming them. The Wing Standard ran a column on this last week. Some of you read it.</p>
        <p><em>Match 5, post.</em> I lost the duel I should have won. I am not going to say the word. The word is a thing my coach says lawyers will get involved over. The word is a thing my fanbase says in the comments under my match clips. The word is also probably true. I will not pursue this further. I cannot prove it. The League cannot prove it. The trainer cannot prove it. The buyer is anonymous. The system is designed this way. The system is not, by design, going to tell me when this happened or stops happening.</p>
        <p><em>Off-day.</em> I went home. My partner asked how the season was going. I told her about the kiting drill numbers. She asked what I wanted to do about it. I told her I wanted to train as if it kept happening, and play as if it didn't, and not think about it the rest of the time. She said: "That's the whole job." She was right. The whole job, this season, has gotten quietly harder.</p>
        <p><em>Match 6, R1.</em> Won the duel. 8 reps in 9. The trainer smiled. I did not.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Anonymous knight's notebook, partial, submitted to Foundation archives under Knight Privacy Provision 4-c</div>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>A Fan's Notebook</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · season-by-season notebook · longtime BVR fan, anonymous, Boston · Year 28–Year 35</div>
        <p><em>S1.</em> Watched the inaugural at Brewer's Reach. Cold day. Sat in the third row from the lobster booth. Saw Bristlebeard die. Cried. Did not tell anyone I cried. Resolved to never miss a match.</p>
        <p><em>S2.</em> Did not miss a match. Watched some on the broadcast — the camera was a stationary mount and the framing was the same every match. I learned to ignore the framing and watch the knights. The Wolves arrived. The Wolves bowed once, after a kill, and people in the stands argued about whether they meant it. I thought they meant it. The bow has stuck.</p>
        <p><em>S3.</em> Tomik fumbled the grenade. I was at Hardwood Hall on a road trip with my wife. Watched the round on her brother's portable broadcast set. The fumble was visible because the camera was wide. The fumble was unmistakable. The Sharks retired the number. My wife asked if Tomik had a family. I did not know. I have since learned. I send a card to Tomik's family on the anniversary, every year, anonymously. They have never written back. I do not need them to.</p>
        <p><em>S4.</em> Brask Ironclaw III died in Phoenix. His father coached. I had been watching Brask since his rookie year. I do not have words about Brask. I went to the funeral. I sat in the back. The lobster vendor was there. I do not know how she got to Phoenix.</p>
        <p><em>S5.</em> The Power Core was introduced. The first time it activated I did not understand what was happening. I do not know if I understand now. The Beavers' new Bristlebeard died in the season opener. I had hoped he would not. I cried again. I told my wife this time. She nodded.</p>
        <p><em>S6.</em> Pawington Cup. Mira's accidental flag-carry. The League formalized the event the same year. I bought a small embroidered kerchief at the concession stand and have it framed at home. The kerchief is the wrong color (Otter green; the original was indeterminate riverbank cloth). I do not care. The kerchief is the kerchief.</p>
        <p><em>S6 (continued).</em> The broadcast camera started moving this year. Treadwell's experiment at Hardwood Hall. The first dynamic shot felt strange. By the third match I had stopped noticing. By the tenth match I noticed when it didn't. The camera, when it works, is invisible. The camera, when it doesn't work, is the only thing on the screen.</p>
        <p><em>S7.</em> Crash Wartooth died. The Crash Rule was enacted. Hallowtide Tag became official. I did not watch the first Hallowtide live — I had a cold and stayed home. I watched the broadcast the next day. Kor Wartooth's run was the most beautiful sustained piece of athletic motion I have ever seen. I have watched the recording fourteen times. I will watch it again next Hallowtide.</p>
        <p><em>S8.</em> Hester Quillstrike died at Helena Glacier Rink. Sundip Hootington Jr. died at Reno tying her record. Hester's Rifle is missing. The Power Core has been patched. The field has been widened. The Field-Widening is, by Treadwell's framing, a camera operator's blessing — the camera has more to do, the knights have more room to move, the openings of rounds are watchable for the first time. I agree with Treadwell. I do not, however, like that I had to be told the openings were not watchable before. I had been watching the openings for eight years. I had thought I was watching something. I had been watching something. Treadwell is also right that I am watching something better now. Both can be true.</p>
        <p><em>S8 (continued).</em> The Beavers' new Bristlebeard — the Third — has not died. He is twenty-two and plays defense and the Beavers' fanbase is split about him. I am one of the Beavers' fanbase. I am split too. I want him to live. I want the pattern to be unbroken because the pattern is part of why I started watching. I want the pattern to be broken because the pattern has cost the Beavers eight Tanks and three families. Bjorn does not need to know what I want. Bjorn is doing his job.</p>
        <p>I will be at Brewer's Reach next match. The lobster vendor will be there. The camera will move. The Beavers will play. Bjorn will, gods willing, walk off the field at the end. I will be in the third row from the lobster booth. The seat is mine, by usage. I have never paid for it. The vendor knows me by name. She has never charged me for the bisque. I have never asked for the bisque. We have an understanding.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Anonymous BVR season-pass holder, notebook entries condensed and anonymized for League Library accession</div>
      </article>

        <p><em>Day 1.</em> Editor wants 600 words on the field-widening for Quarterly. Asked me to be opinionated. I am, by training, opinionated. The deadline is fine. The reporting is the harder part. The Rules Committee will not return calls. They never return calls. I will draft from secondary sources and re-interview when they break. The bulletin language is unusually plain. They are embarrassed. People are reliable when they are embarrassed.</p>
        <p><em>Day 2.</em> Talked to two coaches. Wolves' staff are upset. Otters' staff are euphoric. I do not, in general, assume that. The knight asked to remain anonymous. I have honored the request. I am writing this in a private notebook so the request stays honored.</p>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>Working Journal — A Coyote Speedster (CYT)</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · Sonora high-desert basin · Year 36 founding-bell pre-season</div>
        <p><em>Tuesday.</em> Coach Reyes asked me to keep a working journal this season. The other Speedsters do not keep journals. The other Speedsters do not, by my read, write much at all. Reyes thinks the team needs at least one written internal record so that when we win something the league archivists can be told, with documentation, how we won it. I am writing the journal. I am the most-literate of the active line, by Reyes's measure, which I appreciate as a compliment but which I also suspect is the thinnest possible compliment our roster could field.</p>
        <p><em>Wednesday.</em> Drilled the drift today. The drift is the simplest tactic we run and also the most-respected. The drift is: <em>I appear to retreat.</em> I appear to retreat unhurriedly. I do not run; running marks me. I lope. I lope away from a center engagement. The opposing team, watching, registers that one Coyote is leaving the engagement. The opposing team's attention narrows toward the four Coyotes still in the engagement. I take a wide arc — wider than I would need to take if I were actually retreating — around the perimeter, behind a piece of cover that the opposing team's attention is not currently on, and I hold there. I am, at this point, no longer a knight in the opposing team's tactical map. I am erased. Reyes calls this <em>la borradura</em>. I am erased.</p>
        <p>The other four Coyotes, while I am being erased, are running their own drifts in their own arcs. By two minutes into the round, on a clean execution, the opposing team's tactical map shows an empty pitch with one Coyote engaged at the center and they are, at this point, badly mistaken about where their threats are. By two minutes and ten seconds, on a clean execution, six of us hit them from six positions, including the one Coyote at the center, who has, by this point, drifted out and back in. We do not, technically, have a sixth knight. The sixth Coyote is the field's perception of how many of us there are. Reyes calls this <em>el sexto</em>. The sixth.</p>
        <p><em>Thursday.</em> I asked Reyes whether the drift would still work in Year 36 now that the Caucus's Commitment Directive has formalized into a coaching standard across all teams. Rule One of the Directive is <em>"Commit to a heading for at least eight strides before reconsidering."</em> The drift requires opposing knights to redirect attention frequently — it depends on their attention being movable. If they're committing to a heading for eight strides at a time, the drift may have less to bait against.</p>
        <p>Reyes laughed. Reyes does not laugh often. Reyes said: <em>"The Directive will make every team better at walking. Every team but us. We have always walked correctly. The Directive describes our default. The Directive does not, however, address attention."</em> Then Reyes said: <em>"The drift is not about how the opposing team walks. The drift is about how the opposing team thinks about the pitch. The Directive does not change how teams think about the pitch. The Directive only changes how they walk on it. We are still going to be erased. We are still going to be six."</em> I wrote this down because it was, frankly, the clearest tactical instruction I have received in two seasons.</p>
        <p><em>Friday.</em> Met with the Antlerlords' coaching staff for a pre-season tactical exchange. We had been told this would be a one-hour meeting. It was four hours. The Antlerlords have one tactic. The tactic is: <em>"L'Ancrage stands. We rotate."</em> Their entire pre-season tactical packet is forty pages long, and thirty-six of those pages are about <em>which direction to rotate around the Anchor depending on which kind of opposing team we are facing.</em> When the Antlerlords were asked, in this meeting, what they would do against the drift, their head coach paused for forty-five seconds and then said: <em>"We would, I think, rotate slightly faster. The Anchor would not move. We have not yet faced this. We will think about it more."</em> I appreciate the honesty. I do not, however, look forward to playing them. I am told L'Ancrage is the size of a small building. Coach Reyes thinks the drift will still work, on the grounds that <em>"a building is a piece of cover; we run drifts around cover; this is, in fact, easier."</em> I want to believe this.</p>
        <p><em>Saturday.</em> Founding bell tomorrow. We open the season against the Pittsburgh Ravens. The Ravens' Snipers are, by Caucus record, the most-decorated archery class in the League. The drift is hardest to run against Snipers because Snipers do not need to redirect attention to track us — they have already tracked us. Reyes said tonight, at the team meal, that the drift will be modified for round one: we will scatter rather than drift, on the grounds that scattering creates more sniper-targeting decisions per second than drifting does, and the Ravens' Snipers will, with five targets to range, choose the wrong target at least once per round. The drift will return, in modified form, by round three when the Ravens' Snipers have settled.</p>
        <p>I asked Reyes how he knew the Ravens' Snipers would settle by round three. Reyes said: <em>"They settle by round three because that is when their bench tells them to settle. Their bench tells them to settle in round three because the bench has noticed, by then, what we are doing. We are giving the bench three rounds of misinformation. The fourth round is the round we win. We will lose the first three. We will lose them by tight margins. We will, in the fourth, win by a clean four-on-three. Trust me on this."</em> I do not, in fact, fully trust him on this. I am writing it down so that, after tomorrow, I can come back and check whether he was right.</p>
        <p><em>Sunday — addendum, post-match.</em> Final score Coyotes 3 Ravens 2. We lost rounds one, two, and three by margins of one knight each. We won rounds four and five by clean four-on-three. The fourth round took two minutes and forty seconds. The fifth round took ninety seconds. Reyes did not, after the match, say anything about having predicted this. Reyes simply nodded once at me and went to talk to the Ravens' coach. I did not write down what they said to each other. I do not need to. The journal is for the wins. This is a win.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— working journal, name withheld at coach's request, archived under team privilege at Sonora basin training facility</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>A Tank's Camp Notes (BDG)</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · Boise Brawling Badgers · seven-season Tank veteran · Year 36 training camp, weeks one through four</div>
        <p><em>Week 1, Monday.</em> Camp began with a coach reading the Commitment Directive aloud to the line. All five of us were in the room. All five of us already knew the Directive — every team has had the document since pre-season — but the coach, Brockholm Slatebrush, said he wanted us to hear it together once before camp started. The directive's three rules took him, by my watch, eleven minutes to read aloud, because he stopped after each rule and asked us, individually, what we thought of it. None of us had a strong opinion to offer. Slatebrush is a Tank. We are all Tanks. Tanks do not, as a class, have strong opinions about coaching memos. We have strong opinions about plate. The directive does not address plate.</p>
        <p><em>Week 1, Wednesday.</em> First scrimmage. The line drilled the Commitment Directive's Rule Two — <em>"When you have no target, hold a position. The position is your guard. Do not drift. Pick the position once, hold it for sixty strides, and only then reconsider where to stand."</em> This is, to a Badger, the easiest rule in the document. Our standard tactic is to hold the position until somebody asks us to move it. We held our positions. The scrimmage's opposing line (Speedsters from the practice squad) drifted around us for forty-five minutes and could not, by any approach angle, find an opening. The scrimmage ended in a stalemate. Slatebrush wrote on the practice board, in the team's Year-36 idiom, <em>"holding the floor is the floor"</em> and walked out of the gym without saying anything else. We took this as a compliment.</p>
        <p><em>Week 2, Friday.</em> Wave Doctrine drills today. The Doctrine — the new respawn rule for continuous-mode tournaments — does not, by League rule, apply to deathmatch. Our regular-season schedule is mostly deathmatch. We will, by season schedule, encounter the Doctrine in three matches across the season. Slatebrush had us drill the Doctrine anyway. He said: <em>"The Doctrine is the future. The Caucus will, within four seasons, extend it to deathmatch. We will be drilled. We will be ready. We will not be the team that has to learn the Doctrine in a Final."</em> I think he is right about the Caucus. The Doctrine has, by the Year 36 founding-bell schedule, already produced two come-from-behind wins in continuous-mode matches. The Caucus likes things that produce come-from-behind wins. The Caucus likes the Doctrine. The Caucus will, eventually, extend it.</p>
        <p>The drill was: the line was sent to the bench. The line waited eight seconds. The line returned to the field as a wave, in a four-knight diamond, with the slowest knight (me — Tanks are the slowest in any wave) on a sprint allowance. We crossed the spawn line within two seconds of each other. We hit the center engagement zone within four seconds of each other. The opposing line (the practice squad's Strikers) had, by the moment we arrived, formed a defensive arc that we, in formation, broke through on the first pass. The drill's coach (a Badger named Coach Grimshale, who has not, in nine seasons, ever shown an emotion publicly) said, watching the drill from the gym's elevated platform: <em>"This is, by a margin, the most coordinated thing a Badger line has done in a training camp. I am, frankly, surprised. The Doctrine is going to be good for us."</em> I wrote this in the journal because it is the closest Coach Grimshale has ever come, in my hearing, to being publicly enthusiastic about anything. Slatebrush told me, after the drill, that I should not, in any subsequent journal entry, make Grimshale sound enthusiastic. I am not making him sound enthusiastic. I am, however, recording that he was enthusiastic. The journal is the journal.</p>
        <p><em>Week 3, Tuesday.</em> The team had a closed-door tactical session today on the Antlerlords' L'Ancrage. The Antlerlords are, by season schedule, on our R7 schedule — the third week of the regular season. The Antlerlords' tactic is, in summary, <em>"L'Ancrage stands. We rotate."</em> Our coaching staff has been preparing for this match for, by Slatebrush's frank admission, the entire pre-season. We are a Tank-heavy team. They are a team built around a single Tank who does not move. The natural tactic, for us, against them, is to put our line on their L'Ancrage and dare them to rotate around our line. This is, by Slatebrush's read, what the Antlerlords expect us to do. He has, in the closed-door session, proposed that we do, instead, the opposite — we drift past L'Ancrage as if he is a piece of cover, and we engage their rotating four-knight at the perimeter where they are, by the rotation's geometry, more spread out than they expect to be. He called this <em>"the wide draw."</em> The line was skeptical. The line was also, at the close of the session, willing to drill it. We drilled it for three hours that afternoon. It is not a Badger tactic. It is, by reading, a Coyote tactic. Slatebrush admitted this, said: <em>"The Coyotes call this the drift. We are going to call this the wide draw, because if we call it the drift, we will not be willing to do it. We need to do it. We need to call it something else. The wide draw is what we are going to call it. Do not, in any post-match interview, call it the drift. The Caucus is paying attention. They will publish a paper and we will look like we have been borrowing tactics. We have, in fact, borrowed the tactic. But we will not look it. Do not test this."</em> The line agreed to the framing. The line is going to call it the wide draw. We have not, as a team, ever been told to lie to the Caucus before. We are doing it. It feels strange. It also feels correct.</p>
        <p><em>Week 4, Sunday.</em> Camp ends tomorrow. The Year 36 regular season opens in nine days. I have, as of this entry, drilled the Commitment Directive, the Wave Doctrine, the wide draw, and the standard four-knight Badger floor-hold. The line is more prepared than I have been at any pre-season opening since Year 31. We are, as a team, the oldest line in the League by average season-tenure. We are also, by the analytic services that publish such things, projected to finish fifth in the standings — out of twenty teams, that is the upper quartile but not the championship tier. Slatebrush's response to the projection, at the line meeting yesterday: <em>"Fifth would be the highest finish in Badger team history. The projections do not know we are running the wide draw. The projections do not know how good Coach Grimshale was, last week, at watching the wave drill. The projections are going to be wrong by, I think, two places. We will, by the bracket's end, finish third. Do not tell anyone I said this. The journal does not count."</em> He looked directly at me, when he said the last sentence. He knew about the journal. The whole line knows about the journal. The journal is supposed to be private. The journal is also, apparently, not very private. I will, going forward, write fewer team-strategy quotes from the head coach. I will also, with apologies to Slatebrush, leave this entry intact. The wide draw is the wide draw. He told us, all five of us, in a closed-door session. He knew I would write it down. He also knew the Antlerlords do not read the Badgers' team-internal training-camp journals, because the Antlerlords do not, by their own admission, read anything written in League Common faster than once per word. We have nine days to season-opener. We are, as a line, in a good place. I am going to bed.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— working journal, BDG Tank line · Year 36 training camp · archived under team privilege · "the wide draw" reference subsequently flagged by team comms staff but left intact by author's request</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>Pre-match notebook (QTZ) — the rafter approach</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · written by an unnamed Quetzal Healer in the Yucatan composite (Spanish creole) and translated by Roiseau-Manchot · the original is in the Quetzals' team facility · the translation is, by the Healer's pre-publication request, the only version released</div>
        <p><em>Match minus three days.</em> Cintzli has been, for the past four mornings, in the rafter-nest before sunrise. I do not know what she does up there. The team does not ask. The other Quetzals — Chac, Itzel, Yax, Pakal — do not ask. I, by my own bench-staff nosiness, have asked the team kitchen what she eats up there. The team kitchen says: nothing. Cintzli does not eat in the rafters. Cintzli eats afterward, when she comes down, at the team table, the same breakfast as the rest of us. The rafters are not, by the team kitchen's read, where Cintzli takes her meals. The rafters are where Cintzli is herself. The team kitchen is, on this distinction, very firm.</p>
        <p><em>Match minus two days.</em> The Healers' Mutual Aid Society newsletter arrived by post this morning, and the lead column is by a Beaver Healer I have not previously read. The column is about the Quetzal team — about us, about how it must feel to be the smallest team-by-mass in the League, about whether the rafter-nest gives us an advantage that is "fair." The column is well-meaning. The column is, by my read, also missing the point. The advantage is not the rafter. The advantage is Cintzli, who knows what to do with the rafter. Other Quetzals could nest in the rafter. We do not, by team practice, do this. The rafter is hers. The advantage is Cintzli's relationship with the rafter, not the rafter itself. I am writing this in the journal because I do not know if the column's author knows. I am not, by my own preference, going to write to the Society. The Society is for sharing, not correcting. I will let the column be what it is.</p>
        <p><em>Match minus one day.</em> Coach Itzlani gave the standard pre-match brief. The brief was short. Coach Itzlani's briefs are always short. The summary, by my notetaking: <em>"the team you are playing tomorrow is the Boise Brawling Badgers. they are the slowest team in the League. they will, by the analytic services, walk forward in a four-knight floor-hold. their fifth knight will be on the catwalk. they have, this season, drilled a tactic called the wide draw. the wide draw is what they will run if you stand still. do not stand still. cintzli will, on the catwalk, stay where she is. cintzli does not need to drift. the rest of you will drift past their catwalk and engage their floor-hold from the back, where their floor-hold is not a hold. do not, on any account, let stoneflank reach a corner. stoneflank in a corner is the wall. anywhere else stoneflank is a tank. tanks are tankable. walls are not. that is the brief. eat your dinner. sleep. fly well."</em> I wrote it down because Coach Itzlani said it in League Common, which is unusual; Coach Itzlani usually briefs in the Yucatan creole. He said, when I asked afterward why he had switched, that he wanted me to be able to write it down accurately for the journal. He knew about the journal. Of course he knew about the journal. Everybody, on every team, knows about everybody's journals.</p>
        <p><em>Match day, post-match, on the bench.</em> We won 4-1. Cintzli took eleven shots from the rafters and connected on nine. The two she missed were, by her own pre-bench statement, "the moss substrate at the catwalk's south corner is wrong; I will, on consultation with the venue's engineering staff, request a revision before our next match here." Stoneflank did not reach a corner. Stoneflank, in fact, stood at center pitch for most of the match, holding the floor he was, by archetype, supposed to hold. The Badgers' wide draw did not deploy because we did not stand still. The Badgers' coaching staff, on the post-match line, did not appear unhappy. Coach Slatebrush shook Coach Itzlani's hand and said something the LMG did not pick up because it was in the Yucatan creole, which Slatebrush — by my pre-match assumption — does not speak. Itzlani said, on the bench afterward, that Slatebrush had said, in passable creole: <em>"the rafter is the rafter. we will, on the rematch, be ready for the rafter. we are still working on it. you played well."</em> Itzlani's only response: <em>"he is a thoughtful coach. the wide draw was, by my read, the only tactic he could have brought. we played the only response. neither of us is, by this match, surprised. we will see them in the bracket. fly well."</em> I am going home now. I will sleep tonight. The match was a good match. The rafter is, by my own count, still the rafter. Cintzli is still in it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— working journal, QTZ Healer · Year 36 mid-season · archived under team privilege · the original Yucatan-creole entries are kept in a small bound notebook in the team's bench-staff archive; only the Roiseau-Manchot translations have been released</div>
      </article>

        <h3>A Polar Bear cub's notebook — the day the Northwalk came home</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · written by a young Polar Bear, name redacted at the cub's mother's request · the cub was eight years old at the time of the entry and is, as of Year 36, eleven years old and has, by her own preference, stopped keeping the notebook · the entry is a single page · republished here by family permission</div>
        <p><em>Year 35, the day they came back.</em></p>
        <p>Mama said they would not come back today. Mama said they would come back tomorrow because the road from the south takes thirty-two days going and twenty-nine days coming back, and they had only been gone for fifty-eight days, not sixty-one. Mama said I should go to bed and not wait at the door.</p>
        <p>I waited at the door anyway. I waited at the door for three hours. I did not have a coat on. I did not get cold because the door is the inside of the Frostfall Hall and the Hall is warm. I had a piece of dried fish that I did not eat because I was waiting.</p>
        <p>Mama came to the door at the end of the three hours. Mama was not angry. Mama said, "they will come back tomorrow." Mama sat down with me at the door. Mama was not wearing a coat either. Mama did not eat fish.</p>
        <p>The door opened at minute thirty-one of Mama sitting with me. The door opened by itself, because the wind sometimes opens the door — the latch is old. Behind the door was Aunt Tamzen. Aunt Tamzen was not supposed to be at the door for another day. Aunt Tamzen was tired. Aunt Tamzen had walked, by her own count, twenty-eight days. The road had been faster on the way home because they knew where they were going. Aunt Tamzen knelt down at the door. Aunt Tamzen took the dried fish out of my hand. Aunt Tamzen ate the dried fish. Aunt Tamzen said: "thank you for waiting. the next time we walk somewhere, we will tell you when we are coming home, and we will be on time. this time we were a day early. that is also being on time, in its own way. you waited correctly. the fish is good."</p>
        <p>Mama did not cry until later, when the Hall was full of bears and Aunt Tamzen had given her speech about the application being signed. Mama cried in the corner of the Hall, by herself. I went to the corner with her. Mama said, when I got there: "I did not think they would come back. I knew they would come back. I did not think I could let myself think they would come back. I was wrong to not let myself. They came back."</p>
        <p>I am writing this down because Aunt Tamzen said the road has to be remembered, and the road is the going and the coming back, and the coming back is the part the road does not always show on a map. I am eight years old. I waited at the door. The fish was good. Aunt Tamzen ate the fish. The League is now our League. Mama has stopped crying. The Hall is full. I am going to bed.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Anchorage Frostfall Hall, child's notebook entry, Year 35 · the original is in the Hall's children's display, behind glass, on a shelf the writer can no longer reach without standing on tiptoe · the writer has, on her mother's request, declined to be named</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>A rookie Raven's flight log — the first Pittsburgh-to-Boston trip</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · written by Crowstep Inkbeak (RVN, third-season Sniper, twenty-three years old, on her first League roster), in her standard pre-flight log format · the original is in the Murder's archival roost · published with the writer's permission and the Roost's approval</div>
        <p><em>Year 35 founding bell, three days before R1 (BVR away).</em> The Roost gave me the assignment in the first week of pre-season. The assignment is: fly to Boston, three days before R1, take the standard scouting circle of Brewer's Reach Pitch from the air, and report back. The Roost has, by tradition, sent a young Raven on this flight before every Boston match for the past four seasons. I have been told that I am the first Raven of my generation to take the flight. I have been told that the assignment is not, by Roost tradition, optional. I have been told that the assignment is, by every Raven who has flown it, the moment the flying Raven understands what the Roost has been training us for.</p>
        <p><em>The flight, day one.</em> I left at first light. The Murder gathered at the foundry quarter to see me off. There were, by my count from the air at the moment of takeoff, approximately three hundred Ravens watching. I had not, before the moment of takeoff, understood that the Murder would gather. The Murder does not, by tradition, narrate its rituals to the rituals' participants. I learned by being part of it. Slate Wirethorn, the master arrowsmith, was at the front of the gathering. Wirethorn does not, by his own tradition, speak before flights. Wirethorn nodded once. The nod was, by my read, all I needed. I went up.</p>
        <p><em>The flight, day two.</em> The Allegheny basin is wider, from the air, than from the foundry quarter. The basin is also greener. I had not, in twenty-three years of living in Pittsburgh, seen the basin from above. I have, in twenty-three years, seen the foundry quarter many times from above; I have not seen the world it sits in. The world it sits in is large. I am, on this matter, going to say nothing back to the Roost. I am going to keep this for myself. Roost, if you are reading this when I file the log: I will not, in my report, describe the basin's width. The basin's width is, by my read, the part of the assignment that is not, by Roost tradition, a report. The basin's width is for the flying Raven. The Roost has, by my best read, already understood this from its own first flights. I am, on this matter, with the tradition.</p>
        <p><em>The flight, arrival.</em> Brewer's Reach Pitch is, from above, smaller than I expected. The lobster vendor's booth is, from above, exactly the size she has always told us it is — she has, on every visit a Raven has made to the booth, said the booth is "small enough to see from a long distance and big enough to stop being seen from a longer one." The Raven who first told the Roost about this saying was the Raven who flew this assignment in Year 31. I have, in the flight log, retroactively confirmed her measurement. The vendor was at the booth. She looked up. She did not wave. She did, by my best read from a hundred and forty feet, smile. The smile was small. The smile was correct.</p>
        <p><em>The scouting circle.</em> I took the circle. I noted: three changes from last year's intelligence. The catwalk's south rail has been replaced (the new rail is approximately half a foot taller than the old one, which would change the angle a Sniper has to take to clear it on a forty-degree shot from the south stand; this is, by my read, consequential and we should drill for it). The visiting team's locker corridor has had its door replaced (the new door opens outward rather than inward; this is operationally trivial but psychologically interesting — the Beavers' coaching staff has, by my read, decided to make visiting teams pull rather than push on the way out, which is the kind of small choice that means they are, this year, paying attention to small choices). The lobster vendor's booth has not changed.</p>
        <p><em>Return flight, day one.</em> I am writing this on the Allegheny basin's eastern rim, before the descent into the foundry quarter. I am, by my own pre-flight commitment, going to file the report tomorrow morning, in the Roost's standard scouting format, with all three observations included. I am also, by a pre-flight commitment I made to myself and not to the Roost, going to file a single additional sentence at the bottom of the report. The sentence will say: <em>"the basin is wider than i thought."</em> The Roost will read this. The Roost will, by my best read of Roost tradition, not respond. The Roost will, by my best read, file the report intact, in the archival roost, with the additional sentence preserved. The next Raven to fly this assignment, in approximately four more seasons, will read the report. The next Raven will see my sentence. The next Raven will write her own sentence. The archival roost is, by my read, the only place in the Murder where a Raven gets to add a sentence the Roost did not ask for. The Roost has, in twenty-three years, made me earn this. I have earned it. The sentence is mine. The basin is, indeed, wider than I thought.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Crowstep Inkbeak, RVN Sniper, scouting log Year 35 · filed with the Murder's archival roost three days before R1 · the report's three operational observations were used in pre-match briefing · the additional sentence was preserved · this is the first Raven scouting log to be released to the Foundation Drawer and is published, by Roost vote, in honor of Crowstep's third season closing</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Backyard-circuit notebook (HED) — final entry before League admission</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · written by Bryony Threadspine, a senior Hedgehog from the pre-League Helena combat circuit, on the night before HED's formal League admission ceremony in Year 35 · the notebook is one of seven "circuit notebooks" the Helena tradition has kept across generations · this final entry was, by Threadspine's request, the last entry · the notebook has, since, been displayed under glass at the Helena Glacier Rink's east entry</div>
        <p><em>Year 35 closeout, the night before.</em> I have been, by my own count, twenty-nine seasons in the Helena combat circuit. The circuit predates me by, by the elder Hedgehogs' best account, six generations. The circuit will, by tomorrow morning's vote, be — formally, for the first time — a League team. We will be the Helena Hidden Hedgehogs. We have been Hedgehogs in Helena for as long as Hedgehogs have been Hedgehogs. We have not, before tomorrow morning, been a team that travels.</p>
        <p>I am sitting in my own kitchen tonight, by the back door, on the small chair I made when I was eleven years old and have not replaced. The kitchen is the kitchen I trained in when I was twelve. The back door opens onto the alley I shot my first arrows in. The alley is forty-two paces long. I know this because I measured it in Year 12 when I was thirteen years old, and the alley has not, in seventeen seasons of measurement on every season's first day, gotten any longer or any shorter. The alley is forty-two paces. The alley will, tomorrow morning, no longer be where my training takes place. The Caucus has built us a venue. The venue is at the south side of town. The venue's longest training corridor is one hundred and four paces. I have walked it. The corridor is, by every measurement that exists, longer than my alley. The corridor is also not my alley.</p>
        <p>The thing the Caucus does not, in every other team's tradition, fully appreciate is what we are giving up to join them. They think they are giving us something. They are. They are giving us the chance to play teams from outside Helena and to be paid in bits and lobster rather than in the small barter-market of the Helena combat circuit. They are giving us a venue with a longer training corridor. They are giving us, by their lights, a great deal. They are also taking the alley. I do not, by my own preference, want them to know this. The alley is mine. The alley is forty-two paces. The alley will, after tomorrow, still be forty-two paces, and Helena's Hedgehogs will still walk it on rest days. But it will not, after tomorrow, be where the work is. The work is going south.</p>
        <p>I have not, in twenty-nine seasons, lost a Helena combat-circuit match in my backyard. I have not, in twenty-nine seasons, played a sanctioned match anywhere except in my backyard. Tomorrow morning, both of those facts will, by League rule, become irrelevant. The Caucus does not record backyard matches. The Caucus's standings do not credit me with any of my twenty-nine seasons. I will, tomorrow morning, become a rookie. I will be twenty-nine seasons old as a rookie. The Caucus has, in eight years of operation, never had a rookie older than thirty. I will be, by their records, the second-oldest rookie in League history. The first was a Beaver named Old Bristlebeard the First, who debuted at thirty-one in Year 28 and died in the inaugural championship's final round.</p>
        <p>I will not, in my own first League season, die. I have made this commitment to myself tonight, in this notebook, by the back door of my own kitchen. The commitment is not, by my read, in my power to keep entirely. The work is the work. The League's work is more dangerous than the alley's work. I have been, in my preparation for tomorrow, slightly afraid. I have not, in twenty-nine seasons, been slightly afraid before a match. I am writing this down because the slight fear is, by my read, the appropriate response to the change of venue. The alley is forty-two paces. The League is the continent.</p>
        <p>I am closing the notebook now. I will leave it on the kitchen table. The Helena tradition will, by morning, by the elder Hedgehogs' decision, decide whether to put the notebook under glass. If they put it under glass, this entry will be the last entry — the notebook closes when the Hedgehog whose notebook it is enters League play. If they do not put it under glass, I will, tomorrow night, write another entry. I do not know, tonight, which it will be. The elder Hedgehogs will decide while I sleep. I am, on this matter, going to bed. The arrow is, by long-standing personal practice, on the kitchen mantle. I will, in the morning, take it with me.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Bryony Threadspine, HED Brawler · circuit notebook seven, final entry, Year 35 closeout · the notebook was placed under glass on the morning of admission day at the Helena Glacier Rink's east entry · Threadspine has, in three subsequent League seasons, lived through all three · she has not, in three seasons, opened the notebook</div>
      </article>

        <h3>Stripe-painting log (TGR) — pre-match preparation, the matriarch's hand</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · maintained by the Tiger matriarch (name redacted at the matriarch's standing request) since Year 33, before TGR's formal League admission in Year 35 · the log records, in single-line entries, the date and the team's R-number for each helmet she has hand-painted with the team's stripe pattern before each match · this is the most-recent page of the log, covering Year 36 so far · the log is in continuous service and will, by the matriarch's preference, continue to be filed in the team's bench-staff archive</div>
        <p>The page, in the matriarch's standard hand, in delta-basin black ink:</p>
        <p><em>Year 36 founding-bell pre-season exhibition (vs PND, away). Five helmets. The pigment ground fresh that morning, two hours before kickoff. Two helmets needed re-stripe due to humidity. The Pandas' venue is, by my read, too dry for the pigment to set without a second pass.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R1 (vs OTR, home). Five helmets. The Otters were polite at the post-match line. The Otters lost. The Otters did not, by my read, mind. The matriarch's stripe set well; the home venue's basin water keeps the pigment supple.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R2 (vs WLF, away, Olympia). Five helmets. The Olympia venue is wet. The pigment took three coats. The Wolves bowed at the close — five seconds, the absent-knight bow, because no one died. The bow was correct. The Wolves know.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R3 (vs RVN, away, Pittsburgh). Five helmets. The Pittsburgh foundry-air is, by every painter's account, hostile to delta pigment. I brought the basin water from home. Two clay jugs. The pigment held. The Ravens did not, in any post-match comment, ask about the pigment. The Ravens are, by my read, polite about pigment. They have their own.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R4 (vs SHK, home). Five helmets. The Sharks were, in the bench-staff briefing, keyed up. The Sharks always are. The pigment set in one coat. The match went five rounds. The match was good. We won.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R5 (vs HED, away). Five helmets. The Helena Glacier Rink is cold. Cold is, by my read, the easiest weather for delta pigment — the pigment sets fast and holds long. The Hedgehogs were polite, on the bench-staff side, before the match. After the match, the Hedgehogs were also polite. The Hedgehogs are, by my read, always polite. We did not, this match, win.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R6 (vs MOS, home). Five helmets. The Antlerlords' bench-staff brought, as a courtesy, a small jar of Saint-Laurent basin water. They had heard, by some route I have not been able to identify, that I bring my own basin water to away matches. They asked whether I would, in their venue, accept their basin water for my mixing. I said yes. The pigment, mixed with Saint-Laurent water, set differently — a slightly deeper black, a fractionally slower set. I have noted this. I will, by next pre-match preparation, ask the Antlerlords' bench staff for a second small jar. The Antlerlords agreed in advance. The Antlerlords are, by my read, also polite.</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R7 (vs CYT, away). Five helmets. The Sonora venue is dry — drier than Pittsburgh, drier than I expected. I brought four jugs. I needed three. The Coyotes' bench staff watched me mix. They did not, by my read, ask why. I told them anyway. They listened. They did not, by my read, comment. After the match, the Coyote bench's senior member walked over and gave me, without comment, a small clay vial of Sonora basin spring water. I have, since, used the spring water in the Year 36 R8 mixing. The pigment set faster than I have ever seen it set. I have, on this matter, noted the spring water in the team's archive. The vial is, by my preference, kept on the kitchen mantle next to my arrow. The vial is small. The vial is right.</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— TGR matriarch's stripe-painting log, page covering Year 36 founding-bell through R8 · maintained in continuous service · the matriarch has, in four seasons of logging, never missed a helmet · the helmets all match · the pigment, by every painter's recognition, is hers</div>
      </article>

        <h3>A Fox Striker's pre-sundown prep notes (FOX) — Year 36 mid-season, the Phoenix home stand</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · maintained by Bask Ironclaw the Fourth (FOX Striker, second season, daughter of the late Bask Ironclaw the Third and grand-niece of Bask Ironclaw the First — who challenged the Owls captain to a duel in Year 31 and won the team's League admission) · Bask the Fourth has kept a per-match prep journal since rookie year, as a tactical study for her own bench-staff promotion · this is one page, the four-match Phoenix home stand, Year 36 mid-season</div>
        <p><em>R3, vs PND, sundown.</em> The Pandas are, by every analyst's pre-match read, the slowest team to acclimatize to Phoenix even at sundown. The pre-match thermometer at the south gate read 34 degrees Centigrade at first whistle — within the Heat Clause's safe-engagement threshold but at the upper end. The Pandas wore their full standard armor, which is, by every measure, the heaviest in the League. The Pandas' Tank, watching us run our heat-acclimated speed pattern, took approximately fourteen seconds longer per engagement to commit than his pre-match drill rate suggested he would. The fourteen seconds compounded across five rounds. We won 4-1. The Pandas' coaching staff, on the post-match line, said only: <em>"the heat is the heat. we are not, this match, going to complain about the heat. we are, this match, going to acknowledge that the heat is the heat. you played the venue. we did not. we will, in the rematch at Portland, play the venue. you will, in your turn, struggle with the rain."</em> They are right about the rain. We will, on that match, struggle.</p>
        <p><em>R4, vs RCC, sundown with misting overlay.</em> The misting overlay was Whittlestone's recommendation; the Caucus, on our coach's pre-match request, approved it. The mist was, by every Fox's pre-match preference, a slight inconvenience — Foxes do not mind misting; the Foxes invented the misting overlay for our own venue's safety; we do not, however, perform our best in misting. The Raccoons, by every pre-match indicator, were going to scavenge our mid-engagement gear and were going to do it at speed. We drilled, in the past three weeks, specifically against scavenge-mid-engagement; the drill held. We won 3-2 in five rounds. The Raccoons' captain, on the post-match line, said: <em>"the drill was the drill. the misting did not, by my read, change the math. you played a clean match. we played our match. we will, on the next bracket, scavenge differently."</em> She is, by every analyst's read, going to scavenge differently. We will, on the next bracket, drill differently.</p>
        <p><em>R5, vs CYT, sundown.</em> The Coyotes are, by every analyst's pre-match read, the team I most wanted to play this season. They are also, by every analyst's pre-match read, the team I most feared playing this season. They drift. We have drilled against drift for the past two weeks. We have not, by every drill instructor's pre-match read, drilled enough. The match was, by every measure, a study in la borradura: at the eleven-minute mark, our active line had visual on three Coyotes; at the twelve-minute mark, we had visual on two; at the thirteen-minute mark, we had visual on five — but five from positions we had not, in any drill, anticipated. We lost 1-4. Coach Reyes, on the post-match line, said only: <em>"the drift is the drift. you drilled. you drilled well. you did not, by my read, drill correctly — but the drilling that would have been correct does not, by my read, exist yet. we will, on the next bracket, drill it for you. you will, in your turn, find a counter. that is the work."</em> He is right. The drilling that would have been correct does not exist yet. We will invent it. So will the Coyotes.</p>
        <p><em>R6, vs LYX, sundown.</em> The Lynx do not, by their tradition, train as a team. They form up on match day. They play. They go home. They do not, by every visiting team's pre-match read, give any pre-match indication of what they will do. We had no tape. We had a single brief from the Caucus's tactical analysts: <em>"they will, by their tradition, scatter into the venue's five quadrants and shoot at whoever they see."</em> The brief was correct. They scattered. They shot at whoever they saw. The match was, by every Fox Striker's post-match account, the most disorganized-feeling match we have played all season — there was no central engagement, no flanking attempts, no coordinated rotations. There were just five Lynx, one in each quadrant, taking patient shots at whichever Fox was, in any given second, the most exposed. We won 3-2, but only because our Sniper got lucky on the third Lynx's nest position and our Healer kept three of us alive past round four. The Lynx, on the post-match line, did not say anything. The Lynx do not, on the post-match line, say anything. They walked off in five separate directions, in five separate exits. We have not been instructed, by Caucus protocol, to find this strange. We are, by every pre-match warning, going to play them again next bracket. We will not, by my read, drill differently. There is no way to drill against five separately-coached snipers who are not, by their own coaches' instruction, told what each other are doing. We will play. We will see. — B.I.IV, FOX Striker, second season, the Phoenix home stand notebook</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— working journal, FOX Striker · Year 36 mid-season, Phoenix home stand R3 through R6 · archived under team privilege · Bask the Fourth has, by Foxes' coaching staff's pre-promotion review, been identified as the team's most likely future bench-staff promotion candidate · she has, on this assessment, said only: "i am not, this season, ready. i am, this season, watching. i will, in due course, be ready."</div>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Apprentice's hammer journal (BVR weaponsmith) — the year I forged my first weapon</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · written by Stoneshore Bristlefletch (BVR Brawler, rookie season, twenty years old, second-generation Beaver-clan weaponsmith from the Brewer's Row workshops) · the journal is the Beaver tradition's standard apprenticeship record, kept by every Beaver Brawler during the year leading up to their first sanctioned-match weapon · the journal is filed in the workshop's archive on the date the apprentice's weapon is first carried in League play</div>
        <p><em>Week one, the day I started.</em> Aunt Marrowby — the Brewer's Row workshop's senior smith, third generation, fifty-one years old, in her thirty-fourth year at the workshop — handed me a piece of raw steel today. The piece is approximately fourteen pounds. It is, by Aunt Marrowby's pre-handing description, "the piece. you do not, by my preference, get a different piece. the weapon you forge from this piece is, in due course, the weapon you carry. if you fail, by your own work, to make a weapon from this piece, then you do not carry a weapon, and you do not play. there is no second piece. there is the piece. you have, by tradition, one calendar year. begin."</em> I asked Aunt Marrowby what kind of weapon I should make. Aunt Marrowby said, with a small, genuine kindness: <em>"the piece will tell you. listen to it. the piece has been a piece for fourteen pounds' worth of geological history. you have been a Beaver for twenty years. the piece is older than you. respect this. begin."</em></p>
        <p><em>Week three.</em> I have, in the past two weeks, done nothing to the piece. I have looked at the piece. I have weighed the piece (fourteen pounds three ounces; Aunt Marrowby was, on the inventory tag, slightly approximate). I have read the workshop's archival journals — twenty-three previous apprentices' journals, all filed at the moment they first carried their weapons in sanctioned play. I have read all twenty-three journals from beginning to end. I have noticed that, in twenty-three journals, the apprentice typically begins forging in week four. I am, on Aunt Marrowby's pre-week-four advice, not going to begin forging until I am ready. I am not, by every measure I can think to apply, ready.</p>
        <p><em>Week four.</em> Aunt Marrowby walked past my workbench today and said, without stopping: <em>"the piece is asking for a hammer. you have, by my count, four hammers within reach. choose one. the piece will, in due course, tell you which hammer was correct. you will, in due course, learn to listen for which hammer it asks for."</em> I chose the medium-weight hammer. The piece did not, in any way I could detect, indicate whether the hammer was correct. I struck the piece for the first time at 2:14 p.m. on a Thursday in week four. The piece rang. The ring, by every other Beaver in the workshop, was the standard ring of an apprentice's first strike. Aunt Marrowby, watching from across the workshop, did not comment. The piece, by my own pre-strike commitment, has now been struck. The forging has begun.</p>
        <p><em>Week eleven.</em> The piece is, at this point, beginning to take a shape. The shape is, by my own surprise, going to be a Stun Baton. I had, in pre-forging meditation, expected the piece to be a Plasma Mace. The piece had other plans. Aunt Marrowby, on inspection of the eleven-week shape, said only: <em>"a Stun Baton is, by every Beaver's read, a sensible first weapon. the piece chose well. you chose well. continue."</em> I am, by every reading I can apply to my own work, mildly relieved. A Stun Baton is, by every Beaver Brawler's pre-rookie analysis, a forgiving weapon. The Stun Baton's effect register, on a missed strike, is "no harm to the wielder." A Plasma Mace's effect register, on a missed strike, is "the wielder's hand experiences plasma feedback." I am, on this matter, glad to be forging a Stun Baton.</p>
        <p><em>Week thirty-six.</em> The Baton is finished. I struck the final tempering blow at 4:14 p.m. on a Tuesday in week thirty-six. The Baton rang on the final blow with a clean, low note that the workshop's standing-ear (a junior smith named Quillsetter, age eleven, who has the most-sensitive hearing in the workshop and is, by long-standing apprenticeship tradition, the workshop's first-pass quality reviewer for ringing-tone) declared "correct, in every dimension I can hear." Aunt Marrowby, on the close-out inspection, walked the Baton through the standard twenty-three-point apprentice review. The Baton passed twenty-three of twenty-three. Aunt Marrowby, signing the workshop's archival certification, said only: <em>"the Baton is yours. you forged it. you may, on the next sanctioned match, carry it. the Baton is, by every reading I can apply, a good weapon. it will, in due course, also age. it will, in due course, be the Baton your apprentice's apprentice's apprentice carries. that is, by every Beaver's hope, what it is for."</em></p>
        <p><em>Week forty-six, the day before R1.</em> I am, tomorrow, going to carry the Baton on a sanctioned field for the first time. I have, in the past ten weeks since forging completion, drilled with it for approximately two hundred hours. The Baton is, by my body's reading, mine. I am, by my own reading, scared. The Brewer's Reach Pitch will, tomorrow, be my first sanctioned match. The Beavers' coaching staff has, by their pre-match briefing, warned me that the Wolves — our R1 opponent — will, by long-standing pack tradition, target the rookie Brawler in the first round. I have, by Aunt Marrowby's standing pre-rookie advice, "drilled the Baton as a defensive weapon, not as an offensive weapon. the offensive striking will, in due course, come. for round one of your rookie season, the Baton is, by my preference, a wall. be a wall. let the pack come to you. when the pack arrives, the wall will, by your own working knowledge, be ready." I am going to bed. The Baton is on the workshop mantle. The piece, by every reading, is now the Baton. The Baton is, by every reading, the Beaver. The Beaver is, on the day of R1, ready.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Brewer's Row workshop apprenticeship journal, Stoneshore Bristlefletch · filed in the workshop archive on the date of R1 (Year 36 founding bell, BVR vs WLF) · the Baton, by post-match record, was carried in three rounds of R1 and connected on two defensive blocks · Stoneshore is, as of Year 36 mid-season, on the active line and has, in twelve sanctioned matches, lost no rounds in which the Baton was the active weapon · the Baton, by the workshop's standing archival rule, will be, on Stoneshore's eventual retirement, hung in the workshop's apprentice gallery as the seventy-eighth weapon to complete a full career under one carrier</div>
      </article>
