        <h3>Foundry-quarter elder's commonplace book (RVN, Pittsburgh) — entries spanning two seasons</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · written by an unnamed Roost elder, in the Roost's standard commonplace-book format · the book contains short observations, photographs, and notes the elder has thought worth keeping but which are not, by the Roost's silent-deliberation rule, formally archived in the Roost's photograph collection · the book is, by long-standing personal tradition among Roost elders, kept in the elder's own residence and inherited at the elder's death by the next-named seat-holder · this excerpt covers Year 35 admission through Year 36 founding bell · the elder is the senior of the nine and is, by Roost convention, never named in writing</div>
        <p><em>Year 35, week of admission.</em> The League is now ours. The League is, by my reading, also not ours — the League will, in due course, ask things of us that we have not, in centuries, been asked. The Roost has voted unanimously to accept the asking. The Roost has, in a vote conducted in silence by the standard means, also voted unanimously to ensure that the asking does not, in any of its asking, take from us what we are. The two votes are not, by my reading, in conflict. They will, on certain days, feel like they are. The young Ravens will not, by my reading, always understand the votes' coexistence. We will, in due course, teach them. We have, in the foundry-quarter, taught harder things.</p>
        <p><em>Year 35, two weeks after admission.</em> The Beavers refused to sell us new arrows last week. The young Ravens are, by general locker-room report, angry about this. The Roost is not. The Beavers are, by every reading I can apply to a Beaver, being Beavers. They are not, by my reading, refusing the arrows out of malice. They are, by my reading, refusing the arrows because they want us to make our own. This is, by my reading, also Beaver. The Beavers, in their inaugural year, made their own. They are, on this matter, asking us to be like them. We can be like them. We can also be more than like them. We will make better arrows than the Beavers. The young Ravens will, in due course, see this. The young Ravens will, in due course, also see that the Beavers were, by their own internal logic, paying us a compliment. The compliment is hard to recognize. The compliment is real.</p>
        <p><em>Year 36 founding bell.</em> Slate Wirethorn finished the buffer commission for the Saint-Laurent Antlerlords last week. The buffer, by every Roost member's read, is the best piece of work Slate has done in three years. The Antlerlords paid in clams. The clams are good. Slate has, in his thirty years at the foundry, never been paid in clams before. He is, by his own quiet account, pleased with the clams. He is, by my reading, also pleased that the work is being asked for from outside the Murder. The Roost has, in eight days since the commission's completion, voted unanimously to allow Slate to take a second commission, this one for the Foxes — Bask the Fourth's father, the late Third, broke his ceremonial sword in his final career engagement; the Foxes have asked Slate to forge the replacement. Slate has accepted. The Roost has approved. The replacement will be, by Slate's standing pre-design commitment, "in the Fox style, not the Raven style. I am, on this matter, not building a Raven sword. I am, on this matter, building a Fox sword as a Raven would build it. the Foxes will, in due course, recognize the difference. they will, in due course, also recognize that the difference is, by my hand, a kindness."</em> The Murder is, by my reading, growing.</p>
        <p><em>Year 36, mid-season.</em> Crowstep Inkbeak filed her scouting log this morning. The log included the additional sentence at the bottom — <em>"the basin is wider than i thought."</em> — that the Roost has, in twenty-three years of pre-match Boston scouting flights, allowed every flying Raven to add. The sentence is, by my reading, exactly the sentence Crowstep needed to add. The sentence is, by every Roost elder's reading, also exactly the sentence we needed her to add. The young Ravens are, by my reading, on the path. The path is, by every reading I can apply, the right path. The Murder will, in due course, fly to other places. The basin will, in due course, be even wider than Crowstep thought. The Roost will, in due course, vote on whether to send the next-flying Raven to a place farther than Boston. We have not, by my reading, made that decision yet. We will make it when the right Raven asks for the right reason. We have, in twenty-three years, never made a decision for any other reason.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Roost elder's commonplace book, senior seat · entries Year 35 admission through Year 36 founding bell · the book is at the elder's residence in the foundry-quarter · the Roost has, by long-standing rule, accepted the publication of these specific entries on the elder's pre-publication review · the elder is not named, by Roost convention, and will not, on her eventual death, be named — only her seat will, by Roost archival practice, be assigned to the next holder, who will, in due course, begin her own commonplace book</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary">
        <h3>Drift training notebook (CYT) — Coyotes' rookie Speedster, Year 36 pre-season</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · maintained by Tachi Sandshine (CYT Speedster, rookie season, eighteen years old, third-generation Sonora desert-runner) · the notebook is the Coyotes' standard rookie training record, kept through the eight weeks between admission acceptance and first sanctioned match · the Coyote coaching staff requires every rookie to keep one but does not, by long-standing tradition, ever read them · this excerpt is from week six of eight</div>
        <p><em>Week six, day one.</em> Coach Reyna had me run the drift pattern eleven thousand times today. That is, by her own pre-day clarification, an exaggeration. She had me run the drift pattern two hundred and thirty-eight times, and at the end of the day she said, by way of feedback: <em>"you have, by my count, run the pattern eleven thousand times less than the senior line. continue."</em> I am, by my own honest assessment, exhausted. The pattern is, by my own honest assessment, working. I can, on the third repetition of the day, vanish for approximately one full second from the senior line's visual field. By repetition two hundred, the duration is closer to three seconds. By repetition two hundred thirty-eight, the duration is, by Coach Reyna's stopwatch, four-point-six seconds. The senior line, watching me on the last repetition, did not, in any of their post-drill notes, indicate they thought the time was meaningful. They are, by my own reading, being kind. Four-point-six seconds is, by every metric Coach Reyna has shared with the cohort, the threshold at which a rookie Coyote stops being a rookie Coyote.</p>
        <p><em>Week six, day three.</em> The veteran on the line opposite mine today was Cazador Dunecourse, twelve seasons in. He is, by every Coyote tradition, the standing benchmark for la borradura — the disappearing — and is, by his own pre-drill clarification, "going to make you visible by every means I have spent twelve seasons developing. you will not, on the drill floor, hide from me. you will, in due course, learn what hiding looks like by being unable to do it." I was, by Cazador's count, visible for two hundred and thirty of two hundred and thirty-eight repetitions. The eight in which I was, by his measurement, briefly invisible were, by his post-drill assessment, "accidents of the sand. the sand was, on those eight, helping you. the sand will not, on the field, always help you. you will, in due course, learn to make the sand help you on purpose. that lesson is — by every honest reading — eight or nine seasons away. continue."</em> I am, on this matter, going to continue.</p>
        <p><em>Week six, day five.</em> Coach Reyna, at the end of today's session, made an unusual call. She had the entire rookie cohort — six of us — sit down in the shade of the venue's south wall, and she said, by way of a speech I had not been led to expect: <em>"the Coyotes have, in eight years of regional combat circuit and now in our first League season, learned one thing about the drift that the Foxes' tactical archive does not contain. the drift is not, in its essence, a movement skill. the drift is, in its essence, a respect skill. you do not learn to disappear from the senior line by becoming faster than the senior line. you learn to disappear by understanding, in your own body, what the senior line is actually looking at when they look at you. you understand this by being looked at, repeatedly, by senior knights who know how to look. cazador has, this week, looked at each of you. you are, on this assessment, not yet ready. you will, by my count, be ready in approximately three more weeks. continue."</em> I am, on this matter, sitting with the speech. The cohort, sitting in the shade, has not yet stood up. We will, in due course, stand up. We will, in due course, drill. The drilling is the work. The respect is, by every Coyote's standing reading, what makes the drilling matter.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Tachi Sandshine, CYT Speedster rookie notebook · week six of eight · pre-season Year 36 · Coach Reyna has not, by long-standing tradition, read this notebook · Cazador Dunecourse has, by Coyote rookie tradition, signed the front cover with a single mark of his thumb in dust from the venue's south wall · the dust is still on the cover · Tachi has, in twelve sanctioned matches since week eight closed, hit the four-point-six-second threshold against five different teams</div>
      </article>

        <h3>The lobster vendor's deferred ledger (Brewer's Reach Concession Row, Years 28–36)</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary, of sorts · maintained by the lobster vendor at Brewer's Reach Pitch Concession Row, in continuous service since the founding bell · the ledger records every transaction at her booth across nine seasons of League play · published here for the first time, with the vendor's pre-publication permission · the Foundation Drawer's curator has, on the publication, written: "this is the most-cited document in the League's institutional record that has, in nine seasons, never been read by anyone other than its author"</div>
        <p>The ledger is a single bound book, eleven by fourteen inches, with hand-ruled lines on each page and a leather cover the vendor's grandmother (also a lobster vendor; the grandmother's booth was at Brewer's Reach before Brewer's Reach was a Pitch) bound for her in Year 27. The book has, in nine seasons, been refilled with new pages once — at the end of Year 33 — when the original pages ran out. The vendor's grandmother's binding is still on the cover. The vendor has, by her own pre-publication account, never considered replacing the cover. The cover is, by every reading, the book.</p>
        <p>Each entry is a single line: a date (in the vendor's own dating system, which uses match-day numbering rather than calendar days), a customer (by appearance or, if the vendor knows them, by name), a count of lobsters sold, a price paid, and — on a small minority of entries — a single additional note in the right margin. The notes are the diary part. There are, by the curator's count, four hundred and seventy-three notes across the ledger's nine seasons. Three of them are reproduced below, with the vendor's permission.</p>
        <p><em>Year 28, founding-bell day, entry 412 (the four hundred twelfth lobster sold that day): "the bell rang. i sold the lobster. the bell rang because of the match. i sold the lobster because of the customer. neither of us, by my reading, was ringing the bell or selling the lobster for the other. we were, by my reading, doing our own work. the work was, on this day, the same work two of us were doing in the same place. that is fine. that is the day."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 31, the day Pawington dropped the kerchief: "a small otter came to my booth today and asked me how to play a game. she said the game was, by her own pre-question explanation, 'capture the flag, but with no flag.' i said the game was, by my standing read, called capture the flag. she said the game was not, in her version, going to have a flag because the flag would not, on the field, be a flag. i said the version sounded fine. she paid for her lobster in clams. the clams were, by my count, three more than the booth's standing price. she said the additional clams were 'for the version of the game that does not yet exist.' i accepted the clams. i did not, by my standing practice, ask for further explanation. the version of the game has, in five years since, played four times. i still have the clams."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 mid-season, no specific match-day: "a Quetzal came to my booth today. she did not speak League Common. i did not, by my standing limitations, speak the trees' language. she pointed at the lobster. i nodded. she paid in two small wooden tokens of a kind i had not, in nine seasons, seen before. i accepted the tokens. she ate the lobster at the booth without seasoning, in approximately twelve seconds, with what appeared to be considerable enjoyment. she nodded once before she left. the tokens are, by my reading, currency from somewhere. the somewhere is, by my reading, not Brewer's Reach. the Foundation has, in three subsequent inquiries, asked me what the tokens are. i have, in three subsequent responses, answered: 'the tokens are payment for one lobster, accepted by me, on the day described in my ledger. the tokens are, by my own standing practice, not for sale. they are, by my own standing practice, also not for review.' the Foundation has, in three subsequent acknowledgments, accepted my answer. the tokens are in the booth's lock-box, beneath the bowls of unground sea-salt. they are, by every reading available to me, fine where they are."</em></p>
        <p>The vendor's ledger contains four hundred and seventy other notes the curator has not, on the vendor's pre-publication review, been authorized to publish. The vendor's stated reason: <em>"the ledger is the booth's. the notes are the booth's. three of them are, by my own preference, fine to share. the rest are, by my own preference, not. the booth has, in nine seasons, kept its own counsel. the booth will, in nine more, continue to keep its own counsel. that is, by every reading, what booths are for."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Brewer's Reach Concession Row · the lobster vendor's deferred ledger · Years 28 through 36 · published with the vendor's permission · the ledger remains, by the vendor's standing rule, in the booth's lock-box · the booth, by long-standing personal preference, has not been moved · the construction crew that built the Pitch around the booth was, by every contemporaneous account, "fine with this arrangement"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>The Inkbeak Pocket-Diary — Caribbean basin crossing pages, Years 33 through 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · maintained by Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. (PIT Murder, senior flying Raven) on the eight oceanic flights he has made between Pittsburgh and Cartagena · these are the pocket-diary pages, distinct from the official seventeen-page communiqués and the personal communiqués Inkbeak shares with the Murder's elder council · the Murder's Roost has, by Year-36 vote, authorized publication of approximately one-third of the pocket-diary pages, on the grounds that the pages "describe the flight, not the flights' counterparts, and the flight is, by our reading, more our story to tell than anything that happens at the destinations" · the pages below are excerpts arranged chronologically across the eight flights · the pocket-diary is bound in standard Murder archival cloth, kept in a small reinforced pouch Inkbeak carries on his right leg, and has, in eight crossings, never been opened in flight · the entries are written upon landing</div>
        <p><em>Flight 1, Year 33, day 4 (mid-passage). The wind has held east-southeast for ninety hours. The sun has risen four times and set three. The water below is, by my fourth-day measurement, the same color it has been since day two. I have not, in twenty-two flight years, looked at one color of water for ninety consecutive hours before. The color is, by my standing internal vocabulary, "the deeper blue." There is no shallower blue available, on this passage, for comparison. The deeper blue is, by my reading, the only blue. The reading is wrong, by every Pittsburgh-coastal cross-check I am capable of, but it is, by the four days' immersion, what my eyes are honest about. I will, on landing, recalibrate.</em></p>
        <p><em>Flight 1, Year 33, day 7. A pod of dolphins, eight or nine of them, surfacing approximately fifty meters below me at the four-hour mark this morning. They saw me. I saw them. There was, by my reading, a sustained mutual acknowledgment for approximately twenty seconds. They did not, by my reading, slow their passage. I did not, by my reading, slow mine. They were going east. I was going south. We were both, by every honest read, in the same ocean for the same reason: we live here, and we are passing through. The dolphins were, by every reading I can apply, the first non-bird non-fish living creatures I have shared an ocean with. I will not, by Murder protocol, characterize them in the official communiqué. I will say only, in this pocket-diary, that they appeared to be, by every read available to me, in good health and good spirits. I do not know whether spirits is the right word for dolphins. I have, in the four years since, not learned. The Foundation Library's marine biology fragments are, by every Library archivist's pre-publication acknowledgment, very thin on this question.</em></p>
        <p><em>Flight 3, Year 34, day 9, at the moment of crossing the equator. I am told by Federación-side meteorological consultation that there is, on the equator, no detectable atmospheric difference from the air ten kilometers north or south of it. I have, on three crossings, found this not to be true. The air at the equator is, by every flight, slightly heavier on the wing. The heaviness is not large. The heaviness is, by my own measurement, approximately the difference between flying at noon and flying at three in the afternoon. The Federación-side consultant's response, when I noted this in correspondence on returning from Flight 2: "Sr. Inkbeak, the heaviness you describe is real. It is not, by our instruments' detection, atmospheric. It is, by our reading, a thing the long-distance flying body does in response to crossing a line the body has, in its evolutionary record, never been at peace with. The body remembers what the instruments do not. We trust the body. We have, in our own pre-flight Condor briefings, included this observation as standard expected experience for the equatorial passage." I have, in three subsequent crossings, continued to feel the heaviness. I have, in three subsequent crossings, also continued to fly through it.</em></p>
        <p><em>Flight 5, Year 35, day 3. A Manx shearwater, southbound, crossed my path at low altitude at approximately the eleventh hour of the day. We had perhaps four seconds of mutual awareness before the bird, by every appearance, deliberately steered to avoid eye contact. The shearwater is one of the long-distance fliers the Murder has, by Roost vote, formally classified as "narrators of indeterminate reliability." Shearwaters are not, by Roost reading, dishonest. Shearwaters are, by Roost reading, prone to embellishment in a way the ordinary listener has difficulty separating from honest description. The Roost classifies them as indeterminate rather than untrustworthy, which is a finer distinction than the casual listener might credit. I respect the Roost's classification. I have, on this Flight-5 encounter, no information to add. The shearwater did not, on the four-second encounter, characterize anything. The shearwater simply went around me. Going around me is, by every Roost-vetted criterion, not embellishment. Going around me is, on a four-day passage, just what we do.</em></p>
        <p><em>Flight 6, Year 35, day 11, last entry of the flight. Approaching Cartagena. The harbor wall is in sight at approximately twenty-eight kilometers. The visiting-Raven roost is, by my flight-six approach angle, just visible in the gap between the harbor wall's two southern towers. The wax on the senior perch is, on every flight's approach, visible from approximately fifteen kilometers out, because the wax catches the late-afternoon Cartagena sun in a particular way that the Bears' wax-makers have, by their own pre-publication acknowledgment, optimized for visibility on a Pittsburgh-bound flight's return approach. The Bears' Healer-Capybara confirmed this on Flight 4: "Sr. Inkbeak, we wax the perch the way we do because we want you to see it from far. We want you, at the moment you first see it, to know you are home. We know that home is not Cartagena. We have not, by any pretension, asked the perch to be your home. We have asked the perch to remind you that you have, on this flight, found the place you flew toward. That is, by our reading, a kind of home for the duration of the visit." I have, on every flight since, watched for the wax. I have, on every flight, seen it at the predicted distance. I have, on every flight, felt, at the moment of seeing it, the thing the Healer-Capybara described. The thing is real. I do not, in the official communiqués, characterize it. I will, in this pocket-diary, characterize it: the thing is what the Murder has not yet, in its institutional vocabulary, given a name to. The thing is, by every standing read I have, the right thing for the Federación to have given us. We have not, in four years, given them an equivalent thing on our side. We should. I have, on this flight, drafted a Roost-vote proposal for an equivalent thing at the Pittsburgh harbor wall, for the day the first Federación Condor lands northbound. The Roost will, in due course, vote on the proposal. The Roost has, on every prior such proposal, voted slowly. The Roost will, by every honest read, vote slowly on this one too. I have, in the proposal, asked the Roost to be, on this matter, slightly less slow. The Roost has, on receiving the proposal, made no acknowledgment. I expect, by Murder convention, no acknowledgment will be made until a vote is held. A vote will, in due course, be held.</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library archival diary · the Inkbeak Pocket-Diary, Caribbean basin crossing pages, partial publication authorized by Roost vote Year 36 mid-season · the published pages are approximately one-third of the diary's total content · the unpublished two-thirds remain in the Murder's archival roost custody · Inkbeak Sr.'s Year-35 Roost-vote proposal for a Federación-equivalent visiting-perch arrangement at the Pittsburgh harbor wall was, by Year-36 mid-season Roost vote, ratified · construction of the perch is underway · the Bears of the Cordillera have, on receiving Inkbeak's relayed news of the ratification, sent a small ceremonial gift northward via Flight 8: a sealed jar of the wax used on the Cartagena senior perch, with a note in Doña Inés's hand reading <em>"para el día"</em> ("for the day")</div>
      </article>
      <article class="diary lore-wide">
        <h3>Sigridweave's pencil-marginalia, the morning the Condor lands</h3>
        <div class="meta">A diary · Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau · the senior curator's working desk-pad · pencil throughout · Year 36 mid-season, the forty-seventh day of the Pittsburgh Visiting Perch's vacant standing · transcribed with the curator's permission · only the pages relevant to the dispatch decision are reproduced</div>
        <p><em>Forty-fifth day, evening.</em> the perch has stood empty forty-five days. the Roost is, by every account from Inkbeak Sr.'s side, calm about the wait. i am, on my own side, also calm. the calm is not, by my read, the right word. the calm is the working state. i have not, in two years, drafted a second draft of the response. the first draft is, by my read, the response. the file is, on the desk this evening, where it has been for two months — in the drawer, second from the top, between the Federación bulletins and the Murder's Roost-minutes folder. the desk is clean. the snowfall is, by the calendar, not yet on us. the calendar is, by my read, the only thing in the office that is on schedule.</p>
        <p><em>Forty-sixth day, evening.</em> Inkbeak Sr. has sent word from the harbor watch: a southerly arrival has been sighted at twenty-eight kilometers, on the standard approach angle, at the standard fifth-day pace. the bird is a Condor. the bird is the Cóndor. the Federación's working calendar puts the dispatch at eleven days four hours from Cartagena; the bird is, by Inkbeak's range estimate, on schedule for the forty-seventh-day morning. i have, on receiving this word, gone to the drawer. the file is in the drawer. the draft is in the file. the draft has not been altered since i last read it on the eighteenth day of the perch's standing. the draft is the same draft. the dispatch decision is, on this evening, the same dispatch decision it has been for two years.</p>
        <p><em>Forty-sixth day, late.</em> the bureau's working position on the dispatch decision is, in the standing-rules document, that the dispatch decision is the senior curator's. the senior curator's standing position on the dispatch decision is that it has not been settled. the position has held for two years. the position is, on this evening, going to be tested by the morning. i have, by my own preference, not let the position be tested by any prior morning. i have, on this matter, used the perch's standing emptiness as the reason for not testing the position. the perch will not, by tomorrow morning, be empty. the reason will not, by tomorrow morning, be available. i am, on the matter, going to have to decide.</p>
        <p><em>Forty-sixth day, midnight.</em> i have read the draft three times this evening. the draft is the draft. the draft has not asked, in two years, to be revised. the draft has asked, in two years, only to be dispatched or not dispatched. the dispatch question is the only question the draft has had since the morning of its drafting. i have not, in two years, settled the question. i am, on this evening, alone in the office, with the file open on the desk, and the snowfall not yet here, and the perch waiting and the Cóndor flying, and the question is, by my own honest read, settled.</p>
        <p><em>Forty-seventh day, dawn.</em> the dispatch decision is to dispatch. i have, this morning, not amended the draft. i have, this morning, written one cover note. the cover note is, on the standing-rules document, what the bureau attaches to a draft on dispatch. i have written the cover note in pencil. the standing-rules document, by long convention, asks for the cover note in ink. i have, on this dispatch, declined the convention. my reason, written at the bottom of the cover note in the same pencil: <em>"the draft is in pencil. the cover is in pencil. the dispatch is in pencil. the bureau will, on this dispatch, accept the dispatch as it is. the bureau will not, on this dispatch, ask the senior curator to convert the pencil to ink. the senior curator has, on this dispatch, exercised the senior curator's standing prerogative. the dispatch is, on this matter, what it is. the bureau will receive the prerogative. the bureau will, in due course, file the dispatch in the standing way. the dispatch is, on this morning, on its way."</em></p>
        <p><em>Forty-seventh day, dawn-plus-one-hour.</em> the Cóndor is at the perch. Inkbeak Sr. has signaled from the harbor wall. the Roost has completed the four-second acknowledgment. the perch has, on its forty-seventh day, done the work it was built for. i have, on the desk, the cover note finished. i have, on the desk, the draft from the drawer. i will go to the harbor at noon, in my own working capacity, with the file. i will, at the close of the interview the bureau and i are about to begin, place the file in the Cóndor's care for southbound carriage. the Cóndor will, by every Federación standing protocol, deliver the file to Cartagena on her return crossing. Doña Inés will, in due course, receive it. the Albatross — if she ever returns to Pittsburgh harbor — will, by every Federación-side standing protocol, receive the file in the manner the Federación uses for forwarded correspondence: which is to say, when the Albatross is next on the Federación side and accessible, and not before. i do not know, on this morning, when that will be. i have not, on this matter, asked. the dispatch-ledger is, on this morning, no longer open. the dispatch-ledger is, on this morning, settled. the writing-ledger is also, on this morning, settled. both ledgers are, on this morning, the same ledger. they have, by my own pre-publication acknowledgment, been the same ledger since the morning the draft was written. i was wrong, in the draft's last paragraph, to call them different. i was wrong on the matter of the ledger. i was right on the matter of the writing. these are, on this morning, the corrections i owe my own draft.</em></p>
        <p><em>Forty-seventh day, evening.</em> the Cóndor has the file. the interview's first session is finished. the interview will, by long-standing protocol, conclude tomorrow morning at the second sitting. the file is, on this evening, in the Cóndor's pouch — a small reinforced courier-pouch the Federación issues to all northbound and southbound dispatch-bearers, of the same construction as the pouch Inkbeak Sr. carries on his right leg on every Caribbean-basin crossing. the Cóndor accepted the file with the standing four-word Federación dispatch-receipt: <em>"recibido. lo llevaré. — M.C."</em> i nodded. she nodded. the nod was, on the matter, sufficient. the desk is, this evening, clean again. it is the cleanest the desk has been in two years. the cleanness is, on the matter, not the absence of work. the cleanness is the absence of the work that has, for two years, been on the desk. there will be other work. there is always, by the bureau's standing description of the bureau's purpose, other work. but the desk is, this evening, clean of this work. the work is, on this evening, on its way.</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— senior curator's working desk-pad, Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau · pencil throughout · Year 36 mid-season · the marginalia have been transcribed for the bureau's own archives by the junior bureau-Owl Pellic Snowcrest, with the senior curator's express permission · the curator's standing pre-publication note on the transcription, in pencil at the head of Snowcrest's clean copy, reads in full: <em>"this is what the morning looked like, by my own read. it is not the only thing the morning was. it is what the desk-pad held. the rest is, by my own preference, not in the file. the rest will, in due course, settle in the same way the wax on the small ledge of the perch is settling. we will not, on the matter, refresh the wax. we will, on the matter, not transcribe the rest of the morning either. — sgw."</em></div>
      </article>

        <h3>Match Log: Year 33 Final, BVR vs WLF (Boston, Brewer's Reach)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Official sportscaster transcript · 22:14 game time · partial · the round-three Loambright shot</div>
        <p>22:14 — Bristlebeard the Second engages Crash Wartooth at center pitch. BST takes first swing.</p>
        <p>22:18 — Wartooth counters with Stun Baton. BST stunned, drops to one balloon.</p>
        <p>22:22 — Wartooth's three-Wolf rotation closes from the south side. BST recovers stance, falls back toward the Beaver line.</p>
        <p>22:31 — BST's bench substitutes him out for the standard Beaver Sniper rotation. The Wolves' line presses; the Beavers' line holds.</p>
        <p>22:48 — Round 2 closes 1-1. Round 3 opens with Wartooth retreating across center pitch under pursuit by a Beaver Brawler. The Wolves' Healer, Avery Loambright (Hedgehog, on Year 32 inter-team Healer-shortage loan), steps out from behind cover to open a heal beam on Wartooth.</p>
        <p>22:52 — Bristlebeard the Second, returned to the line for round 3, takes a railgun shot at Wartooth at twenty-three paces. The kinetics tracker's read: a clean line at Wartooth's chest. The line passes through the spot Loambright steps into at the moment the shot is leaving the rifle. Intersection time: nineteen frames between trigger pull and line-cross. Bristlebeard could not, by mechanical possibility, have aborted the shot.</p>
        <p>22:53 — The shot lands. Loambright is dead before she hits the pitch. The Beavers' bench substitutes Bristlebeard the Second out immediately; he walks off the pitch under his own power, into the dugout, and does not return for the remainder of the match.</p>
        <p>23:08 — Wartooth, in the round's remaining minutes, mounts a solo charge through the Beaver line. The broadcast booth, watching, calls it <em>"the most controlled grief any of us have ever watched in this sport."</em> The Wolves win round three.</p>
        <p>23:24 — Rounds 4 and 5 are played without a single Wolf attempt to retaliate against the Beaver Sniper position. The Wolves' line targets active line, not Healers, not Tanks. They win both rounds clean.</p>
        <p>23:36 — The Wolves win the match, the championship, and the Year 33 final. They do not celebrate. They walk to the chalk mark where Loambright fell — her body has been removed and prepared for transport per protocol; a Foundation steward has chalked the spot. Six Wolves form a small circle around the chalk mark. The Wolf captain — Halfmoon Greylane, then in her third season as captain — bows once, deeply. The bow lasts, by the broadcast's stopwatch, eleven seconds. The crowd is silent. The Beaver bench is silent. Bristlebeard the Second, watching from the dugout, is visibly weeping. This will later be called "The Bow."</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Boston Sportscaster Booth, Year 33 final · the broadcast feed of the round-three shot is, by Caucus archival classification, "do not edit" · the LMG has, in eight subsequent broadcasts, never re-cut it</div>

        <p>06:24 — Sundip walks to the Power Core to celebrate. Sundip <em>climbs onto</em> the Power Core to celebrate. Sundip's celebration is interrupted by the Power Core's overload sequence, which has not been seen in eight seasons. Sundip does not survive the celebration.</p>

        <p>14:16 — Felix Marshmallow is no longer with us.</p>

        <p>14:19 — The Otter Speedster, in the locker room afterward, says: "I was just trying not to get shot." The Otter Speedster is correct. The Otter Speedster is also haunted.</p>

        <h3>Match Log: Year 35 R8, OWL vs FRG (Reno Open Court) — the 412-pace match</h3>
        <div class="meta">LMG broadcast transcript · 17:02 game time · uncut</div>
        <p>16:58 — End of round 4. OWL leads 2-1. Frogs take the next round and force a deciding fifth. Sundip Hootington Jr. (OWL Sniper) is the only OWL knight at full HP. He is carrying Hester Quillstrike's Railgun Rifle, which has been on his back since Year 35 R3.</p>
        <p>17:00 — Round 5 begins. Frogs adopt a four-Speed flank formation; OWL holds center. The Power Core, which has been quiet for eight seasons, is showing its standard pre-spawn glow. Coach Bristlewren of OWL has just been visible on the sideline cam saying "stay off the core" — he has been saying this every match for two years and the camera operator has stopped considering it newsworthy.</p>
        <p>17:01:15 — A Frog Speedster breaks left along the court's diagonal. Sundip tracks them. He is two hundred and forty units away, well within his railgun's effective range, and waiting for the line. The Speedster is moving fast.</p>
        <p>17:01:23 — Sundip fires. The shot is read live by the LMG kinetics tracker as having traveled four hundred and twelve paces along the diagonal of the Reno court. The Speedster's head balloon pops. The Speedster's body balloon pops a frame later from inertia. Two-balloon kill. Sundip has, by the kinetics tracker's official measurement, exactly tied Hester Quillstrike's longest-shot record. The crowd does not yet know this. The kinetics tracker tells the LMG broadcast booth, which tells the announcer.</p>
        <p>17:01:25 — Sundip's stat panel updates: the 412-pace co-record is now formally his. The League's Records Committee will, in the morning, confirm. The shot is recorded with the rifle Hester carried first.</p>
        <p>17:01:30 — Sundip walks to the Power Core. The remaining three Frogs are at the south wall and visibly retreating. OWL's other knights are pursuing. There is no immediate combat threat. Sundip is alone in the center of the field. He climbs the Core's outer rim — a customary celebration that has been done by perhaps four Snipers in League history.</p>
        <p>17:01:32 — The Power Core overloads. The overload is uncontained. The Core had been latent for eight seasons. The League had not, in its eight-season memory, had the Core do this. The game systems engineering team will, in the offseason, release a report identifying the latent fault as a charge accumulation that had no release valve.</p>
        <p>17:01:33 — Sundip is killed by the overload. The dying Frog Speedster, who had been wounded by Sundip's shot, is also killed by the overload (the Speedster was within the blast radius and did not have time to retreat). Hester's Rifle falls at the base of the Core, on top of Sundip's body. Two of the three remaining Frogs are wounded but survive. OWL's other three knights are far enough away to be unaffected.</p>
        <p>17:01:55 — Round resolves with one OWL knight standing and two FRG knights standing. The round is declared a draw under the post-overload safety rule. The match goes to OWL on a 3-2 round count from the previous rounds, but the post-match writeup will note the draw round explicitly because the math depends on it. The Frogs will, the next morning, be given partial credit for "posthumously denying Sundip his celebration."</p>
        <p>17:03 — The OWL bench is silent. The FRG bench is silent. The Reno crowd is mostly silent. The lobster vendor in the concession area is, by sideline reporter account, weeping. The reporter does not name the vendor in the dispatch. The vendor is not the Brewer's Reach vendor. The vendor is a Reno concession worker on her first season of Cup-cycle work. She is recorded as saying, after composing herself: "I didn't know him. I just hate when this happens."</p>
        <p>17:04 — Hester's Rifle is photographed at the base of the Power Core by an LMG production assistant who has been told to retrieve it as soon as the field is cleared. The Rifle is retrieved at 17:11 and added to the post-match drop pile.</p>
        <p>17:30 — Cleanup begins. A vault steward, in the process of cataloging dropped gear, notices Hester's Rifle and recognizes it. The steward signs the dropped-gear ledger but does not turn the rifle in to the vault. The steward will, the next day, request unpaid leave. The League will grant the leave without comment. The Rifle has been at large since.</p>
        <p>17:45 — The League patches the Power Core overload latency in the post-season. The patch reduces the Core's charge accumulation cap by approximately forty percent and adds an audible warning at ninety percent. The patch is not retroactive. Sundip's death stands.</p>

        <h3>Match Log: Year 36 R2 Crown — RCC vs PLR (Boise Frosthold Pitch)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Official sportscaster transcript · 14:38 game time · Crown-bracket continuous-mode · the Wave Doctrine's second sanctioned application</div>
        <p>00:00 — Crown match opens. Standard Crown rules apply: brass crown spawns at the center pitch; whoever wears it scores team points per second; first team to fifty wins. Wave Doctrine in effect — downed knights return together as a wave on a fixed delay rather than as individuals on rolling timers.</p>
        <p>00:31 — Both teams advance to center. The crown spawns at the eight-second mark; Pell Whittlestone's standard placement. Pickup contest is a four-on-four melee. PLR Brawler Saltgale takes the crown at the 49-second mark via a clean shoulder-into-shoulder against an RCC Tank. Saltgale begins scoring.</p>
        <p>02:12 — Score PLR 18 RCC 0. Saltgale is in mid-court, shielded by his three teammates rotating around him in the standard Polar Bear wall pattern. RCC Brawler Trash Tinker engages the wall from the south. Trash absorbs three plate hits and is downed at 02:18. RCC's first wave-pending knight on the bench.</p>
        <p>02:46 — Score PLR 22 RCC 0. RCC Speedster Drift Brittlepaw, attempting to flank Saltgale from the east, is shot at extreme range by PLR Sniper Frosttooth. Speed-archetype kit absorbs nothing; Brittlepaw down at 02:51. Two RCC knights now wave-pending. The Caucus's Wave Doctrine clock starts.</p>
        <p>03:08 — Score PLR 28 RCC 0. RCC's remaining three knights — captain Trashbright, Healer Featherquill (no relation), and Striker Roundeye — adopt a defensive arc at the south wall. They are not pushing the wall. They are waiting. The crown is, by the LMG broadcast booth's read, a lost cause this minute. The bench is the play.</p>
        <p>03:34 — Score PLR 32 RCC 0. RCC's first wave releases. The wave is the two downed knights — Trash and Brittlepaw — accompanied by Trashbright and Roundeye, who have, on the wave's release, fallen back to spawn to consolidate. (Captain Trashbright's read of the play, per his post-match interview: <em>"the snowball was running. We had to break the snowball. The way to break a snowball is to stop fighting downhill. We fell back. We re-formed. We came up the hill together."</em>) Featherquill, the Healer, remains in the field as RCC's lone defender.</p>
        <p>03:34:08 — The wave forms at RCC's spawn line in a four-knight diamond. Trashbright leads. Trash anchors the rear. Brittlepaw and Roundeye flank. The slowest knight in the wave is Trash, the Tank; the Wave Doctrine grants him a sprint allowance to keep the wave's pace consistent. The wave begins its advance.</p>
        <p>03:48 — Score PLR 38 RCC 0. The wave crosses the eighth-pace line. PLR's wall, having seen the wave form on the broadcast tactical map, is already adjusting. Saltgale (still wearing the crown, still scoring) cannot move; his crown is anchoring his score. The other three Polar Bears begin to spread to engage the wave's flanks.</p>
        <p>04:02 — The wave hits the center engagement zone. Trashbright leads with shield raised. Trash hits the line at full sprint with the Wave Doctrine's allowance still active — he hits PLR Brawler Snowtread square at four-foot range and Snowtread is, by the engagement camera, knocked clean off the crown's outer ring. Snowtread is down at 04:04. PLR's first wave-pending knight.</p>
        <p>04:14 — Brittlepaw and Roundeye engage Frosttooth from two angles. Frosttooth's railgun has tracking time; she is not built for two-target close engagement. She catches Roundeye but Brittlepaw closes the angle and downs her with a paired pistol burst. Frosttooth down at 04:16. PLR's second wave-pending.</p>
        <p>04:23 — Featherquill, the lone RCC Healer, has been steadily moving up the field at a Healer's pace and is, at this point, in mid-court. She does not engage. She stays in cover. She is, per Healer protocol, waiting for a teammate to need her. Trashbright takes a hit from PLR's last standing line knight (Coldcoat, the Tank) and falls back. Featherquill closes to him and heals. Trashbright re-engages.</p>
        <p>04:31 — Saltgale, alone now and still anchoring the crown, recognizes the situation. He has lost three teammates in twenty seconds. He drops the crown. He retreats. The Caucus's Wave Doctrine has, in this engagement, delivered exactly the snowball-break the doctrine was designed for. Score PLR 41 RCC 0 — but the score is no longer ticking. The crown is unattended.</p>
        <p>04:34 — Trash, the RCC Tank, picks up the crown. Trash begins scoring for RCC. Score PLR 41 RCC 1.</p>
        <p>04:48 — PLR's wave forms. Snowtread, Frosttooth, and Saltgale (who has fallen back to spawn to consolidate, the same tactical move RCC made at 03:34) wave-up together in a three-knight wave. Coldcoat and the remaining PLR knight Whitesong are still in the field, contesting Trash. Whitesong is, at this point, in close engagement with Featherquill, who has switched from Healer to defensive harasser — a non-standard role for a Healer but one the Caucus permits when the Healer is the only available defender.</p>
        <p>05:02 — PLR's wave crosses center. The wave is a three-knight chevron with Frosttooth in the rear. The slowest in the wave today is Saltgale, the Brawler, who is on a sprint allowance from the Wave Doctrine. The wave hits the RCC line at full pace. The engagement is short and close.</p>
        <p>05:14 — Featherquill is downed by Whitesong. RCC's first wave-pending knight. Trash drops the crown to engage. Score frozen at PLR 41 RCC 4.</p>
        <p>(transcript continues — abbreviated for archive)</p>
        <p>13:08 — Score PLR 47 RCC 38. Both teams have, over the intervening eight minutes, executed three more wave returns each, with progressively cleaner formations and progressively more decisive engagements. The match has, by the broadcast booth's read, become a back-and-forth contest of wave-vs-wall, neither side able to maintain a sustained crown lead.</p>
        <p>13:42 — RCC's fourth wave forms with all four downed knights plus Trashbright. The wave is, at this point, the largest single return of the match. Wave Doctrine sprint allowance activates on Trash. The wave crosses center as a five-knight phalanx — wider than the diamond, wider than the chevron, the formation Trashbright has personally drawn up on the bench in the prior 80 seconds.</p>
        <p>14:03 — The phalanx engages PLR's depleted line (PLR has, at this moment, three knights on the field; Saltgale has the crown). The phalanx splits the line. Saltgale is, for the second time in the match, knocked off the crown — this time by Roundeye, who has been waiting for this exact engagement angle for, by his post-match recount, "the entire match." Trashbright picks up the crown.</p>
        <p>14:18 — Score PLR 47 RCC 47. Trashbright is, at this moment, the most-attended-to knight in the venue. PLR's three remaining line knights converge on him. RCC's other four knights form a defensive ring around him. The crown ticks up.</p>
        <p>14:22 — Score PLR 47 RCC 48. The defensive ring holds. PLR's line takes one knight down (Coldcoat, by Trash) and is now two-on-five at the crown.</p>
        <p>14:28 — Score PLR 47 RCC 50. RCC wins. The Wave Doctrine's second sanctioned application produces the second consecutive comeback in Crown match — both matches the trailing team won, in both cases via wave-formation re-entry and sustained late-match crown contest.</p>
        <p>14:38 — Match over. The Polar Bear bench is silent. The Raccoon bench is, in the broadcast booth's mic, audibly cheering. Whitepaw the Steady, captain of PLR, walks to Trashbright at the post-match line and shakes his paw. Whitepaw says, on the open mic: <em>"You came up the hill together. We had won the hill four times. The hill is, today, yours. We will see you next bracket."</em> Trashbright nods. The post-match interview is brief. The Caucus's tactical analyst Pell Whittlestone, on the broadcast feed, calls the match <em>"the second confirmation of the doctrine's intended effect; we have, in two matches, seen the snowball not snowball; we will, I expect, see this become the new shape of Crown."</em></p>

      <article class="log">
        <h3>Match Log: Year 36 R7, BDG vs MOS (Boise Highland Pitch — the Wide Draw debut)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Official sportscaster transcript · 21:14 game time · the first sanctioned use of the Badgers' Wide Draw tactic · the post-match Caucus tactical-archive entry that has, by Featherquill's read, "ended the era in which Tank teams played slowly because they had to"</div>
        <p>00:00 — Match opens. Best-of-Five deathmatch on the Boise Highland Pitch, the Badgers' home venue. Teams: Boise Brawling Badgers (BDG, all five active line returning) versus Saint-Laurent Antlerlords (MOS, founding-bell roster, Théodred Brisefer III "L'Ancrage" anchoring center). Pre-match consensus, by every analyst's read: a slow, grindy match. Both teams favor stationary tactics. The over-under on round length is set at six minutes and ten seconds.</p>
        <p>00:42 — Round 1. Antlerlords open in their standard L'Ancrage formation: Théodred III at center pitch, motionless; the four perimeter knights in concentric arcs, rotating clockwise around him at a measured walking pace. Badgers open in a four-knight floor-hold at the south end of the pitch with their fifth knight (the line's Sniper, Quartzbreaker) holding the high ground in the eastern catwalk. Standard Badger opening. The booth's commentators settle in for the expected slow round.</p>
        <p>01:38 — Round 1, 56 seconds in. Badger Tank Stoneflank breaks formation. He does not advance toward the L'Ancrage. He drifts west along the pitch's perimeter, in the slow loping gait the Coyotes call <em>la borradura</em>. The Antlerlords' rotating arc adjusts to track him; the rotation widens slightly to maintain the same arc-radius around the now-displaced threat. The booth's commentator, watching this, says on the broadcast: <em>"That is a Coyote tactic. The Badgers do not run the Coyote tactic. We are watching, by my read, a thing the Badgers are not supposed to be doing."</em> The commentator's read is wrong. The Badgers are doing this on purpose. The Antlerlords' coaching staff has not, at this moment, identified the tactic.</p>
        <p>01:55 — Round 1, second drift. Badger Brawler Coalfist drifts east. The Antlerlords' rotating arc now has two displaced threats and is, by the rotation's geometry, beginning to spread. L'Ancrage, at the center, does not move. The two Antlerlord knights still in the standard rotation are now twenty paces from the center on either side; the two displaced Antlerlord knights tracking the drifters are now thirty paces from center, at the perimeter, in an arc Théodred III cannot, by sight line, support without rotating his stance.</p>
        <p>02:18 — The wide draw closes. Both Badger drifters, on a coordinated signal from the bench (the bench used a small bell, audible on the LMG sideline mic; the Antlerlords' coaching staff has, in their post-match write-up, formally requested the Caucus investigate whether the bell counts as in-game communication; the Caucus has, in its preliminary response, declined to investigate), reverse direction simultaneously. The Antlerlord knights tracking the drifters are now caught in mid-perimeter, twenty paces from the L'Ancrage, with no cover. The Badger Sniper Quartzbreaker, on the catwalk, takes both Antlerlord perimeter knights in two shots over four seconds. Score: BDG 2 MOS 0 in active line. The Antlerlords now have two perimeter knights and L'Ancrage. The Badgers have all five.</p>
        <p>02:34 — The Antlerlords' coaching staff calls a tactical pause (a thirty-second mid-round pause permitted under Year-36 rules for major formation breakdowns). Théodred III is told, on the bench-to-pitch comm, to abandon the L'Ancrage stance and join the perimeter rotation as a fifth knight. The order is, by Antlerlord historical record, the first time L'Ancrage has been ordered off-anchor in a sanctioned match. Théodred III complies, slowly, in the way of his species. The Badgers, watching this on the field, do not press while the Antlerlord rotation reforms. They wait. The booth's commentator, watching the wait, says: <em>"That is — that is, frankly, sportsmanship. The Badgers are letting the Antlerlords reform. They could be pressing. They are not. The Badger coaching staff is, by every account I have ever heard, the most ruthless in the League. We are watching a thing I did not, in my career, expect to ever watch."</em> The commentator's read, here, is also wrong. The Badgers are not letting the Antlerlords reform out of sportsmanship. They are letting the Antlerlords reform because they have, in pre-match scouting, determined that the Antlerlords' five-knight perimeter rotation (without L'Ancrage at center) is, by tactical analysis, weaker than the four-plus-one rotation. The Badgers want the Antlerlords in the weaker formation. They are letting the Antlerlords get there.</p>
        <p>03:42 — Round 1 resumes. The Antlerlords' new five-knight perimeter rotation is, in execution, exactly as compromised as the Badger pre-match scouting predicted. Théodred III, in motion for the first time in the match, is the slowest knight in the rotation by a wide margin (he is, by the Caucus's mass register, the heaviest knight in the League; the rotation's pacing assumes a walking speed L'Ancrage cannot sustain). The rotation drags. The Antlerlords' coaching staff, watching the drag, calls another tactical pause to substitute Théodred out for a backup Tank. The Badgers, again, do not press. The substitution is made. The Antlerlords' new rotation, with the backup Tank in L'Ancrage's slot, is faster but lacks the gravitational mass — the new Tank cannot, by his own weight, hold the center. The rotation now has a center that drifts. The Badgers know this. The Badgers have been preparing for this for nine weeks of pre-season camp.</p>
        <p>04:18 — The Badgers' line advances, for the first time in the match, in a coordinated push. The push is the team's standard four-knight floor-hold, advancing one stride at a time, with the Sniper still on the catwalk providing covering fire. The Antlerlords' drifting center cannot, by formation geometry, repel a wall advance. The wall arrives. The Antlerlords lose two more knights in the engagement. Round 1 final: BDG 5 MOS 1 active. The Antlerlords have one knight standing — their captain, Marc-Olivier Brisefer, who at this point is in slow retreat toward the bench. He is permitted to walk off. The round resolves at 4:51 game time. Round 1 took, by stopwatch, three minutes and twenty-three seconds. The pre-match over-under was wrong by two minutes and forty-seven seconds.</p>
        <p>(Rounds 2 through 4 are reproduced in the official transcript and abbreviated here for archive.)</p>
        <p>16:38 — Round 4 closes. Score: BDG 3 MOS 1. The Badgers are one round away from the match. The Antlerlords have, across rounds 2 through 4, attempted three separate counter-tactics to the wide draw. The third counter — putting Théodred III in motion full-time as a roving anchor rather than a stationary one — was, by the LMG kinetics tracker's read, the closest the Antlerlords have come to a sustainable response. The roving anchor is, by every Caucus analyst's pre-existing tactical literature, an experimental formation. The Antlerlords had not, by their own coaching staff's frank admission, drilled it before this match. They drilled it in real time, in front of forty thousand spectators, on the most important regular-season match of their inaugural League run. The drill went, by the line's morale read, "fine, but not better than fine. We need eight more weeks of camp on this, and we have, instead, the Year 36 R8 schedule. We will be drilling it on the road."</p>
        <p>20:45 — Round 5 opens. The Antlerlords open with the roving anchor. The Badgers open in a five-knight floor-hold (the standard formation, no wide draw). The Antlerlords have, by visible bench instruction, decided to fight the match the Antlerlords' way and accept the loss if the loss comes. The Badgers — who have, by Slatebrush's pre-match commitment, drilled the wide draw for nine weeks — have, in this round, decided to give the Antlerlords the courtesy of a Tank-on-Tank match. The crowd notices. The crowd is, by the broadcast booth's read, completely silent. They have been watching tactical innovation for twenty minutes. They are now watching, in round 5, two Tank teams playing each other Tank-style. The crowd has not, in fifteen years of Boise home games, seen this kind of round.</p>
        <p>21:08 — Round 5, 23 seconds in. Théodred III, in his roving-anchor stance, walks directly toward Stoneflank. Stoneflank walks directly toward Théodred III. They meet at center pitch. They engage. The engagement is, by the kinetics tracker's read, a six-second exchange of plate-on-plate impacts that produces, on the official damage register, exactly equal damage to both Tanks. Stoneflank, who by archetype has slightly higher base HP, survives by a margin of one balloon. Théodred III is downed. The crowd erupts.</p>
        <p>21:14 — The Antlerlords' remaining four knights, watching their captain go down to a clean Tank engagement, do something the LMG broadcast booth has, in eight years of coverage, never seen. They walk forward in a single line. They engage the Badger line head-on. They do not rotate. They do not anchor. They fight. The round ends in a four-on-four melee that takes ninety seconds to resolve. The Badgers win, 4-1, on the strength of the Sniper still on the catwalk. The match resolves. Final: BDG 4 MOS 1.</p>
        <p>22:55 — Post-match line. Marc-Olivier Brisefer walks to Slatebrush. They shake. Brisefer says (the LMG mic captures this in Saint-Laurent creole; Estelle Roiseau-Manchot translates): <em>"You drilled this. We did not. We will drill. We will see you in the off-season exhibition. The wide draw is a good tactic. I am, frankly, glad it was not the Coyotes who debuted it on us. I would have, in that case, been less gracious. The Badgers we expected. The wide draw we did not. The combination was unfair, and the unfairness was the work. Well played."</em> Slatebrush nods. Slatebrush does not, in this moment, attempt to translate the wide draw's origin. Slatebrush has been told, by the Badgers' line, to not in any post-match interview call it the drift. Slatebrush calls it, on the post-match interview tape, only <em>"a Boise tactic, drilled in pre-season."</em> The Caucus, watching the tape, does not press. Coach Reyes of CYT, watching the tape from the Sonora basin training facility, sends Slatebrush a single private letter that reads, in its entirety: <em>"Well drifted. — Reyes."</em> Slatebrush has the letter framed in his office. He has not shown it, by his own commitment, to anyone outside the team.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG broadcast transcript · Year 36 R7 BDG vs MOS · Boise Highland Pitch · expanded into formal match record at the Caucus's tactical archive request · the Wide Draw debut</div>

      <article class="log">
        <h3>Match Log: Year 28 R5 (Inaugural Championship Final), BVR vs WLF (Boston, Brewer's Reach)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Foundation archive reconstruction · the broadcast era's earliest preserved match transcript · partial · pieced together from the Brewer's Reach Reader's match-day column, the Beavers' coaching staff's session notes, the Wolves' captain's hand-written post-match letter, and Pell Whittlestone's mother's eyewitness account (Whittlestone's mother was, that day, at Concession Row buying a lobster)</div>
        <p>00:00 — Match opens. Best-of-five championship deathmatch on the Brewer's Reach Pitch. Teams: Boston Brisk Beavers (BVR, founding roster, Old Bristlebeard the First anchoring as Tank) versus Wichita Wild Wolves (WLF, founding roster, Hardvein Quickstep as captain, the team six weeks old). The Beavers are the heavy favorite by every measure available; the LMG's predecessor (the Tampa coastal salvage crew, broadcasting via field-test tower) gives the Wolves no better than 5-to-1.</p>
        <p>00:02 — The lobster vendor, on Concession Row, sells her four hundredth lobster of the season approximately as the founding bell rings. (This is the only match-day datum, by Foundation archive reconstruction, that the lobster vendor herself has ever volunteered. Asked, decades later, what she remembered of the inaugural match, she said: <em>"i sold a lobster at the bell. the bell was the bell. the lobster was the lobster. the match started. that is what i remember."</em>)</p>
        <p>00:14 — Round 1 opens. The Wolves run a tight pack-formation press at the Beaver line. Bristlebeard the First, anchoring the Beaver Tank position, takes the press head-on. The press fails. Two Wolves are downed. The Wolves retreat in formation. Round 1 to the Beavers.</p>
        <p>03:51 — Round 2 opens. The Wolves, having watched the failed press, change tactics. They split into two sub-formations and engage the Beaver line at oblique angles. The Beaver Healer (a Beaver named Marrowby — no relation to the Reno night steward of the same surname) is caught between the two sub-formations and downed by a Wolf Sniper. The Beavers' line, briefly without a Healer, falls back. Round 2 to the Wolves.</p>
        <p>09:22 — Round 3 opens. Both teams reset. The Beaver coaching staff, by hand-written note relayed to the bench, calls for Bristlebeard the First to hold the center while the rest of the Beaver line works the perimeter. The First holds. The Wolves cannot break the center. Round 3 to the Beavers.</p>
        <p>14:36 — Round 4 opens. The Wolves run their pack-formation press again, this time with all five Wolves committed. The Beaver line breaks at the perimeter. Two Beavers are downed in the first six seconds. The First, holding the center alone, watches the perimeter collapse. Quickstep (Wolves Captain) closes the distance with the First. They engage. The First takes a Wolf Brawler down before the engagement resolves. The First is downed. Round 4 to the Wolves. The match is now 2-2.</p>
        <p>22:14 — Round 5 opens, the deciding round. Both teams' active lines are at three knights apiece (the wave-doctrine respawn protocol does not yet exist; Year 28's respawn is the original three-life-per-match system). Bristlebeard the First has one life left. The Wolves engage immediately. The Beaver line is, by every analyst's pre-round read, on the verge of losing.</p>
        <p>22:46 — Bristlebeard the First, watching the engagement at center pitch and seeing three of his teammates clustered in a tight defensive formation around him, makes a decision the Beaver coaching staff has not, in eight subsequent reconstructions, been able to read into his pre-match notes. He pulls the pin on a high-yield grenade he has been carrying since round one. The grenade is, by the Foundry's pre-League testing rig (the rig Whittlestone's mother and aunts had been calibrating in their workshop for the past six months), at maximum charge. The First holds the grenade against his own chest plate.</p>
        <p>22:48 — The grenade detonates. The First is destroyed in the blast. Three Beavers in the immediate radius are also destroyed. The Wolves' active line, which had been closing on the Beaver formation, is at the blast's outer edge — the blast does not kill the Wolves but knocks Quickstep and one Wolf Sniper off their feet. The Beaver line, by the explosion's mechanics, is now down to one knight: a Beaver Brawler named Stonewright Bristlecomb, who had been twelve paces from the blast and survives with two balloons remaining.</p>
        <p>22:54 — Stonewright, on the field with one teammate-less knight remaining, walks forward into the dust. The Wolves, recovering, see one Beaver. They do not, by Quickstep's later letter, immediately understand that this is a one-vs-three engagement they should already have won. The grenade has, by every reading, broken the round's geometry.</p>
        <p>23:11 — Stonewright engages the closest Wolf Brawler. The engagement is, by the LMG predecessor's mid-engagement spotter call, "the cleanest single-knight engagement in the match's twenty-three minutes." Stonewright wins. Two Wolves remain. Stonewright walks forward.</p>
        <p>23:34 — Stonewright engages Quickstep. Quickstep, the Wolf captain, has been watching Stonewright's approach for twenty seconds and is, by his own letter, "unprepared for the engagement in a way I have not been unprepared for an engagement before or since. The Beaver was small. The Beaver was bleeding. The Beaver was, by every measurable metric, ours to finish. We did not finish him. The Beaver finished me. I have never been able to explain this." Stonewright kills Quickstep. One Wolf remains.</p>
        <p>24:02 — The remaining Wolf — a Sniper named Lerebrook — does not engage Stonewright. Lerebrook, by Wolf-pack tradition, walks off the field. The Wolves do not, by long-standing Wolf tradition, fight a one-vs-one with the captain dead. Stonewright, by Beaver scoring rule, wins the round and the match by walk-off forfeit. The Beavers win the inaugural championship 3-2.</p>
        <p>24:14 — Stonewright, at center pitch, sits down. He does not stand back up for nine minutes. The Foundation steward, eventually, walks the championship trophy to him and places it on the pitch beside him. Stonewright, asked later why he did not walk to the trophy, said only: <em>"the First was at the center. the center is where the trophy goes. i did not, by my own preference, want to walk away from the center."</em> The trophy has, in eight subsequent Final ceremonies, been brought to the surviving knight rather than walked to by the surviving knight; the Caucus codified this practice in Year 30. The Bristlebeard Pattern (the ratified term for tactical self-sacrifice in which a knight uses an explosive on themselves to take opposing knights with them in the blast) is named for the First. The Pattern is, in eight subsequent seasons, observed twice — once by the First's son in Year 32, once by Felix Marshmallow in the Year 34 incident that produced the Marshmallow Protocol. The Pattern is not, by Caucus standing, encouraged. The Pattern is, by Caucus standing, also not prohibited.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Archive reconstruction · Year 28 R5 inaugural championship final · pieced together from four contemporaneous accounts · the Brewer's Reach Reader's match-day column is the only complete play-by-play and was, by the Reader's senior columnist's standing tradition, written without a byline · the column is on display at the Brewer's Reach Pitch lobby under glass</div>
      </article>

      <article class="log">
        <h3>Match Log: Year 36 R4 (QTZ vs WLF, Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall) — Cintzli's home debut</h3>
        <div class="meta">LMG broadcast transcript · 21:18 game time · partial · the match described in the ZUNUN-probable Year 36 R4 ticket stub on file in the Foundation Drawer · the only Quetzals home match in which the Wolves performed the five-second absence-bow at close</div>
        <p>00:00 — Match opens. Best-of-five at the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall. The venue is, by every visiting team's pre-match acknowledgment, the most thoroughly elevated venue in the League — the rafters extend approximately forty feet above the pitch surface, and the Quetzals' Sniper has, by Caucus terrain registration, full access to the rafters as personal terrain (no formal designation, by the Caucus's three repeated declinations on the matter). Teams: Yucatan Vibrant Quetzals (QTZ, home, Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy as captain; the team's first sanctioned home match) versus Wichita Wild Wolves (WLF, away, Halfmoon Greylane as captain; the team's first match at a Continental Expansion-era venue).</p>
        <p>00:02 — The Wolves enter via the visiting-team locker corridor. The corridor is, by the Yucatan venue's standard layout, lit only by the natural canopy filter — the corridor is dim. The Wolves' active line emerges onto the pitch in their standard formation. Cintzli is not on the pitch. Cintzli is, by Quetzal tradition, in the rafter-nest, and has been since approximately 7:14 a.m. (per the team kitchen's morning-shift staff observation). The Wolves' line, looking up, locates her. The LMG broadcast booth's pre-match analysis has, in pre-match coverage, told the Wolves to expect this. The Wolves have, by Greylane's pre-match commitment, drilled for the rafter sight-line for the past three weeks. The drilling has been, by every Wolf Brawler's post-drill comment, "useful but not sufficient — the rafters are bigger than we drilled for."</p>
        <p>00:14 — Round 1 opens. Cintzli takes her first shot from the rafter at fourteen seconds in. The shot is, by the kinetics tracker, a clean line at the Wolves' Healer (Pinedrift). Pinedrift is, by his own pre-match commitment to Greylane, three steps ahead of the schedule he had drilled for the rafter angle. The shot misses by approximately one foot, hitting the pitch surface eighteen inches from Pinedrift's left flank. Pinedrift does not, by his own subsequent statement, react visibly; he continues his pre-drilled lateral movement. The shot is, by every analyst's read, the closest miss of Cintzli's inaugural season to date.</p>
        <p>00:51 — Cintzli takes her second shot, this time at the Wolves' lead Brawler (a Wolf named Sapphire Pinedrift, no relation to the Healer). The shot connects. The Brawler is downed. Wolves' line falls back to regroup; the Quetzals' ground line presses forward.</p>
        <p>04:38 — Round 1 ends. Quetzals win 1-0 via Cintzli's two-shot opening (one miss, one kill) and the ground line's clean perimeter coverage.</p>
        <p>06:14 — Round 2 opens. The Wolves, by Greylane's pre-round bench call, run a different tactic — three Wolves stay tight at the perimeter, two work into the rafter access (a single ladder at the south corner, which the Quetzals' coaching staff has, by venue-design choice, not removed). The Wolves' two ladder-climbers reach the catwalk by minute one. Cintzli, in the rafter-nest at minute zero, is by minute one in a different rafter-nest. The Wolves, in the catwalk, look at an empty nest. They do not, by their pre-round drill, know which rafter-nest she has moved to. The catwalk is empty. The catwalk has, by Quetzal venue tradition, eleven possible rafter-nests; only one is in use at a time; the choice is Cintzli's.</p>
        <p>09:22 — Cintzli takes a shot from a different rafter-nest. The shot connects with one of the Wolf catwalk-climbers. The climber is downed. The remaining Wolf in the catwalk retreats; the round resolves on the ground level with the Quetzals winning 4-on-3.</p>
        <p>11:51 — Round 3 opens. The Wolves, by Greylane's third bench call of the match, abandon the rafter approach entirely. They commit five-on-four to the ground level and try to overwhelm the Quetzals' ground line. The Quetzals' ground line, having drilled exactly this scenario, holds. Cintzli takes one shot from the rafters and downs the Wolves' Sniper (a Wolf named Brownwillow Wolfsbane, on her third season). The round resolves at 14:18; Quetzals win 5-3 in active-knights ratio at round close.</p>
        <p>14:42 — Match resolves. Quetzals 3, Wolves 0. The match has not produced a permadeath on either side; all downed knights have been recovered to active rotation per the standard wave-doctrine respawn. Cintzli has not, in the entire match, descended from the rafters. The match's final-shot kinetics-tracker register: 11 shots taken from rafter-nests, 9 connections (8 kills, 1 miss-then-bench-resolve), 2 outright misses. The shooting accuracy is, by every analyst's post-match reading, the highest single-match Sniper accuracy ever recorded at the Yucatan venue.</p>
        <p>15:14 — Post-match line. The Wolves, on the pitch, walk to the chalk mark where, had any knight fallen, the body would have been. No knight has fallen. The Wolves form their standard small circle anyway. Greylane, at the chalk mark, bows. The bow lasts, by the broadcast's stopwatch, five seconds, not eleven.</p>
        <p>15:21 — Greylane straightens. The bow is over. The Quetzals, on the pitch, watch the bow without moving. Cintzli, in the rafter-nest, watches the bow from above. After the bow, the Quetzals' captain — Cintzli — descends from the rafter for the first time in the match. She walks, by the canopy's narrow ladder, to the pitch surface. She walks across the pitch to Greylane. She does not speak. She nods, once, deeply, in a gesture the Quetzals' coaching staff has, in three subsequent matches, formalized as the Quetzals' return-to-the-bow. The nod takes, by the broadcast's stopwatch, five seconds. The two captains are, for those five seconds, by every camera angle, perfectly aligned. The crowd is silent.</p>
        <p>15:26 — Greylane, after the nod, says one sentence. The Wolves' bench mic captures it: <em>"Thank you for the rafter."</em> Cintzli, in response, says one sentence in the trees' language. The LMG broadcast booth has not, in the eight months since the match, attempted to translate it. Roiseau-Manchot, on consultation, said only: <em>"the trees' language is the trees' language. i do not speak it. i will not, on the broadcast, render what i do not speak. the captains have understood each other. that is, by my read, sufficient."</em> The match is over. The Wolves walk off. The Quetzals, by team tradition, do not celebrate.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— LMG broadcast transcript · Year 36 R4 QTZ vs WLF · Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall · the absence-bow at five seconds is the first formally-recorded Wolves bow of less than eleven seconds · Cintzli's return-nod has, in three subsequent matches, been performed at every Wolves-Quetzals close-of-match · the trees' language sentence has not been translated and is, by Cintzli's preference, not in the public record</div>
