      <article class="musing">
        <h3>Featherquill on the Question of the 412-Pace Shot</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · Featherquill · The Wing Standard, mid-Year-36 · the column ran 1,400 words; here is the kernel</div>
        <p>I have been asked, on the matter, four times this year alone, whether the 412-pace shot is the longest sniper kill in League history or whether it is, on the matter, the most-witnessed. These are not, by my read, the same question. The longest is a measurement. The most-witnessed is a memory. The longest is, on the matter, a fact. The most-witnessed is, on the matter, a story.</p>
        <p>Hester Quillstrike's shot is, by the Foundation's measurement record, the longest. Sundip Hootington Jr.'s shot, the same season, is by the Foundation's record the second-longest by exactly zero paces — both shots measured at 412. The Foundation has, on the matter, ruled the shots co-records. Sundip Jr. and Hester have both, on the matter, died holding the record. The record will, on the matter, never be broken. It will only, on the matter, be tied.</p>
        <p>The most-witnessed sniper kill in League history is, on the matter, neither shot. It is the Year 32 R3 finishing kill on Bristlebeard the Second, made by a Wolves' Sniper at 89 paces, in front of a Brewer's Reach Pitch crowd of 14,400 — the highest single-match attendance in eight seasons. The 412-pace shots were, by Foundation count, witnessed live by 8,200 and 8,100 respectively. The longest shot is, on the matter, not the most-witnessed. The most-witnessed shot is, on the matter, not the longest. The story is, on the matter, the witness count. The fact is, on the matter, the measurement. They are, on the matter, both true.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Featherquill, The Wing Standard, Y36 R5 column</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>An Open Letter from a Coach Who Has Asked Not to Be Named</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · The Wing Standard, Year 36 · the editor has confirmed the letter's authenticity but agreed to anonymity</div>
        <p><em>"I have coached in this League for nine seasons. I will not, on the matter, name my team. I have a question that the post-match press conferences do not, by their format, allow me to answer honestly: do you, the readers, understand that we — the coaches — meet?"</em></p>
        <p><em>"We meet four times a season. The Caucus does not call the meetings. The Foundation does not pay for them. We pay for them ourselves, in lobster, by long-standing arrangement with a Concession Row vendor who sets the per-coach rate and does not, on the matter, negotiate. We meet at her stand, after her stand has closed for the night. We meet at the picnic table she does not put away because she likes us, on the matter, occasionally. We do not, on the matter, take notes."</em></p>
        <p><em>"What we discuss is, on the matter, not for publication. What I will say is this: every Marshmallow Protocol began at one of these meetings. Every grievance the Caucus thinks it heard from one team alone was, on the matter, brought up by all of us at the same table the night before. The League is not, on the matter, run only from the Office. The League is, on the matter, also run from a picnic table outside a vendor's stand at midnight."</em></p>
        <p><em>"Print this if you will. The vendor has agreed, by my own arrangement, to deny everything if asked. — A coach"</em></p>
        <p>(Editor's note: the Foundation has, on the matter, declined comment. The vendor has, on the matter, also declined comment. The picnic table is, on the matter, still there.)</p>
        <div class="signoff">— The Wing Standard, anonymous coach's letter, Y36</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>On the Continental Expansion's Quiet First Year</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · Featherquill · The Wing Standard, Year 36 closing column</div>
        <p>The Caucus's Geography reclassification opened the door for the Lynx, the Antlerlords, the Coyotes, and the Quetzals. The four expansion teams have, in Year 36, made the bracket but not the final. They have produced, between them, two Promoted Legends and zero perma-deaths. The League has, on the matter, gained 220 knights and lost zero. This is, by my read, the quietest expansion season in the Caucus's possible plan.</p>
        <p>The pattern will not, on the matter, hold. The Continental Expansion's full impact will arrive, by my read, in the second season — when the four expansion rosters are, on the matter, no longer protected by the senior teams' instinctive caution toward newcomers. Year 37 will, on this read, be a perma-death year for at least one of the four expansion teams' founding rosters. I will not name which one. I do not know. I do, on the matter, hope to be wrong.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Featherquill, closing column, Year 36</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>Letter to the editor · The Wing Standard, Year 35 mid-season</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · a fan letter, printed without correction · the writer is, by handwriting cross-reference, the Pew-Pew Ewe</div>
        <p><em>"EXTRA! EXTRA! Read all about a fan what's been waitin' two whole seasons to write in! Folks, I have been hollerin' from Section 14 since the Year 33 closeout — Brewer's Reach Pitch, Row M, third seat in, ya can spot me by the green wool scarf and the 'PEW PEW' I'll be hollerin' every time a Sniper draws — and I am here to tell ya, by jingo, that this league has GOT IT, every season, and the editor of this here paper has been UNDERSELLING IT! Not the writin', folks! The writin' is dandy! I'm talkin' the SCOPE!"</em></p>
        <p><em>"The Wolves bowed eleven seconds and you printed it once. ONCE! The Beavers built their own arrows because the Beavers wouldn't sell em — that's a story you SELL on the corner, not file under 'columns received.' The Pawington Cup brings out the Reno crown thieves every season and you call it a 'recurring incident' — that's news, folks! That's HOT off the press!"</em></p>
        <p><em>"Stop the presses, Featherquill, the people what fill the seats are LIVIN' for this stuff and the people what fill the SECTION-14 seats are livin' for it LOUDER. Get yerself out to a matchday some time. Section 14 will save ya a seat. Bring three cents. We'll get ya a program. — the Ewe what cheers"</em></p>
        <p>(Editor's note: we have, on the matter, taken the suggestion. Featherquill attended a Section 14 matchday in Year 35 R6. He has, on the matter, written a follow-up musing. He has not, on the matter, agreed to bring three cents to the next one. The Pew-Pew Ewe has, by usher report, forgiven him.)</p>
        <div class="signoff">— The Wing Standard letters page, Y35 mid-season · printed without correction</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>A young fan's letter · The Wing Standard, Year 36 R4</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · printed at Featherquill's request, over the writer's gentle protest · the writer is anonymous; the editor's introduction is included</div>
        <p>(Editor's introduction: I have, on the matter, asked the young writer of this letter for permission to print it. He gave permission only after I assured him his name would not appear. I have, on the matter, kept that assurance. The letter is in pencil, on the unprinted side of a discarded matchday program. — F.)</p>
        <p><em>"Mr. Featherquill, sir,"</em></p>
        <p><em>"I watch from Gate Three. The embankment is fine for me. I can see the corner where the Owls Striker comes in. I cannot see the far corner. The crowd tells me what happens in the far corner. They cheer different for different things. I have, in three seasons, learned to read the cheer."</em></p>
        <p><em>"You wrote in a column once that the most-witnessed sniper kill is not, on the matter, the longest one. I have been thinking about this for a month. I think you are right. I think the people who watch a thing are part of the thing. The people on the embankment are watching too. I think we are part of the thing also. I do not know if this is, on the matter, true. I am ten. But I have been watching for three seasons and I think it is true."</em></p>
        <p><em>"Thank you for writing what you write. The boy at the Concession Row stand reads me your column. He does not have to. He does it because the column is good. The column is good. I will, in due course, learn to read the column on my own."</em></p>
        <p><em>"— a fan, Brewer's Reach, Gate Three"</em></p>
        <p>(Editor's afterword: I have, on the matter, written back. I sent the letter through the senior Brewer's Reach usher with the request that it be passed to the boy without ceremony. I have not, on the matter, asked the usher whether it was received. I trust, on the matter, that it was. — F.)</p>
        <div class="signoff">— The Wing Standard letters page, Y36 R4 · with editor's notes</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>Featherquill's Section-14 Visit</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · Featherquill · The Wing Standard, Year 35 R6 closeout column · this is the kernel of a 1,100-word piece</div>
        <p>I went to Section 14, as the Pew-Pew Ewe asked me to. I brought, by my own concession, the three cents she demanded. The matchday-program vendor accepted the three cents without comment. The program was placed in my paw. The Ewe was already in seat 3 by the time I arrived (I am, on the matter, slow to arrive at any matchday — a habit I will, in due course, address). She greeted me with an incredulous <em>"BY JINGO! THE EDITOR HIMSELF! FOLKS, MAKE ROOM!"</em> and the four regulars in Row M shifted left. There was, on the matter, a seat for me.</p>
        <p>I had thought I was, on the matter, attending to take notes. I took, by my own count, no notes. The Ewe hollered "PEW PEW" at every Sniper shot — both teams' Snipers, both directions — and I, somewhere in the third round, heard my own voice join hers. The cheer is, on the matter, contagious. I will not, in this column, undersell what that means. I have written about the broadcast booth's view of a sanctioned match for eleven seasons. I had not, in any of those columns, accurately conveyed the Section 14 view. The Section 14 view is the view from inside the cheer. The cheer is, on the matter, the match.</p>
        <p>I will, in due course, return. The Ewe knows this. The seat knows this. The senior usher waved at me on my way out and I waved back. I think the wave is, on the matter, a kind of seat ticket. I read this line in a young fan's letter the following season; the line was, on the matter, his. I do not believe in coincidence. I believe in conventions that the gate gives to people who keep showing up. I am, on the matter, glad to be a person who keeps showing up.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Featherquill, The Wing Standard, Y35 R6 closeout column</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>The Wing Standard's Year 34 Editor's Note · "On the Embankment Tradition"</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · Featherquill · The Wing Standard, Year 34 R6 column · the first published mention of the Gate-Three handoffs, two seasons before he would write about them again</div>
        <p>The League's stadiums have, in the eight seasons of my reporting, been written about almost exclusively from the inside. I have written about the broadcast booth's view, the Caucus delegates' lounge, the senior commentator's chair, and (twice) the Hall of Fallen Heroes' archive room. I have not, in eight seasons, written about the gates.</p>
        <p>I have learned, this season, that the gates are, on the matter, also part of the venue. There are kits — kits, plural, by Foundation usher's confirmed count, at three venues — who watch from the back-gate embankments rather than the seats. They cannot, on the matter, afford the seats. They have not, on the matter, asked the League for seats. They are, on the matter, simply there. The League has not, on the matter, formally addressed this. The League's individual Knights have, on the matter, addressed it personally — by handing matchday programs to the embankment kits as they walk their gear-bags to the parking lot through the back gates.</p>
        <p>I am, on the matter, told the convention started at Brewer's Reach Pitch, R3 of this season, with an Owls Striker whom the Owls' bench staff have, on the matter, asked me not to name. The convention has, since R5, traveled to Reno. It will, by my own read, travel further. I will, in due course, write about the embankments themselves — but I am, on the matter, not yet ready. The embankments deserve, by my read, more than a column. They deserve a season of careful watching.</p>
        <p>I will, on the matter, watch carefully. I will write about them, on the matter, when I have, on the matter, earned it. The kits, on the matter, are owed careful writing.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Featherquill, The Wing Standard, Y34 R6 column · "the first mention of the embankments"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>The Wing Standard's Year 33 closeout column · "On the New Voice in Section 14"</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · Featherquill · The Wing Standard, Year 33 closeout · two paragraphs, in passing, in a column otherwise about the Bristlebeard-vs-Loambright incident</div>
        <p>(Excerpt — the column's main subject was the Y33 R5 final, the Loambright shot, and the first Bow. The Section 14 paragraph appears as a closing aside.)</p>
        <p>And I would be, on the matter, derelict not to mention: there is, this season, a new voice at Brewer's Reach. Section 14, Row M, third in. A single sheep, by usher's report, female, green wool scarf. The voice has been hollerin' "PEW PEW" at every Sharks Sniper draw I have, in three closeout matches, witnessed. The voice is, on the matter, both completely sincere and (I cannot, on the matter, deny this) somewhat absurd. The crowd's reaction has been, in three matches, the same: the regulars in Row M cheer her, the regulars in the surrounding rows tolerate her, and the visiting fans look briefly puzzled and then, on the matter, also tolerate her. By the third match, three rows of Section 14 had joined her on the catchphrase. By the closeout match, six rows had.</p>
        <p>I am, on the matter, going to write more about Section 14, in due course. The Section 14 voice has, on the matter, the cadence of a fan who has been waiting two full seasons to find her voice and has, on the matter, found it. I am, on the matter, glad she has found it. I will, on the matter, watch the Section 14 row count grow. I will, on the matter, also stay, by my own preference, in the broadcast booth — I am, on the matter, slow to attend matchdays in person. This is, on the matter, a habit I will, in due course, address.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Featherquill, The Wing Standard, Y33 closeout column · "the new voice at Brewer's Reach"</div>
      </article>

        <div class="meta">Musing · the Beavers' Caucus delegate · Y35 mid-season · the memo was not circulated; it was, on the matter, an internal Beavers'-bench-staff note that surfaced when the bench staff cleaned out the captain's office</div>
        <p>(Editor's note: The memo's author has, on the matter, given permission to print on condition that her name is, on the matter, not included. The Wing Standard has, on the matter, kept the condition.)</p>
        <p><em>"To the Beavers' bench staff, in confidence,"</em></p>
        <p><em>"I sat in the Caucus's annual stadium-revenue review yesterday. The review covered the Year 35 mid-season figures. The review did not, on the matter, mention the back-gate embankments at any of the four venues that have them (Brewer's Reach, Reno Open Court, Olympia Harbor, Helena Glacier Rink). The embankments are, by Foundation venue convention, not part of any revenue model. The kits on them are, on the matter, not paying customers."</em></p>
        <p><em>"Two delegates raised the question of whether the embankments should, on the matter, be ticketed. The question was, on the matter, raised quietly. The Commissioner did not, on the matter, respond. Stripewhisker did not, on the matter, respond. The lobster vendor (whose Caucus consulting seat she has, in eight seasons, attended twice) was, on the matter, not present. The two delegates' question was, on the matter, allowed to die in the silence."</em></p>
        <p><em>"I am, on the matter, writing this for the bench-staff record because I want it on the bench-staff record that the question was raised and that the Office, on the matter, declined to entertain it. The Beavers will, on the matter, never vote to ticket the embankments. The Beavers will, on the matter, also never propose it. We have, on the matter, our position. — the Beavers' Caucus delegate"</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Beavers' bench-staff archive · "the embankments are, on the matter, not for sale"</div>
      </article>

      <article class="musing">
        <h3>Featherquill's Year 36 closeout column · "On Inheriting a Voice"</h3>
        <div class="meta">Musing · Featherquill · The Wing Standard, Year 36 closeout column · the kernel of a 1,400-word reflective piece</div>
        <p>I have, in three Wing Standard columns this season, written about the Pew-Pew Ewe and the boy at Gate Three. I will, on the matter, keep writing about them, until they ask me to stop. I am, on the matter, also old enough to know that I will, in due course, be replaced as the editor of The Wing Standard. The replacement will be, by my preference, someone who has been, on the matter, watching the embankments and Section 14 longer than I have.</p>
        <p>I am, on the matter, training her now. I will not, in this column, name her. She is, by my own read, ready to take the column when I am, on the matter, ready to give it up. I will, in due course, give it up. The column is, on the matter, not the matter. The matter is, on the matter, the watching.</p>
        <p>The boy at Gate Three has, by his own quiet practice, been keeping a notebook of cheer-cadences for three seasons. The Ewe has, by her own bonafide assertion, been hollerin' for four. They have, between them, accumulated more careful observation of what makes a Float Knights match a Float Knights match than any single Foundation file in the archive. They are, on the matter, doing the work the column should be doing. I am, on the matter, simply paying attention.</p>
        <p>If you are reading this column on a matchday and you are, on the matter, in a stadium seat: notice, in the next round, what the cheer for a Sniper kill at the far corner sounds like. Two beats. The cheer for a Brawler tag-out is, on the matter, one long beat. The cheer for a Healer save is three short beats and then a hush. The cadences are not, on the matter, mine. The cadences are the boy's. I have, on the matter, simply made them visible.</p>
        <p>The Ewe would, on the matter, holler at me for "stealin' the kid's bit." I would, on the matter, agree. I have, on the matter, given the kid full credit. The credit is, on the matter, his. The cadences are, on the matter, his.</p>
        <p>The matter is, on the matter, the watching. — Featherquill, closing.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Featherquill, The Wing Standard, Y36 closeout column · "the matter is, on the matter, the watching"</div>
      </article>

    <!-- A grab-bag of ephemera that the Foundation Archive has, over the years,
         scooped up, transcribed, photographed, or simply written down before
         it blew away. Graffiti, scent-marks, advertisements, overheard
         conversation, betting slips, lost-and-found notices, half-burned
         pages, recipe cards, fan letters, kid's drawings described in prose,
         and damaged transcripts in which the missing words are noted as such.
         Most are short. None are canonical. All are real. -->
    <div class="lore-section lore-grid" data-loresection="found">
      <article class="history lore-wide">
        <h3>The Found Papers Cabinet</h3>
        <div class="meta">A working archive · Float Foundation Ephemera Drawer · contents added on a rolling basis · transcribed by a rotating staff of three</div>
        <p>What follows is the contents of the Foundation's Ephemera Drawer, transcribed in the order it was filed. Some entries are graffiti taken down before the wall was repainted. Some are scent-marks that an Owl scent-tracker rendered into prose for our records. Some are betting slips, lost-and-found notices, advertisements clipped from publications nobody can identify, fan letters, complaint letters, recipe cards, and one (1) child's drawing. The drawer is open to public submissions. We will, in general, accept anything. We do not, in general, attest to its truth.</p>
      </article>

        <p><em>"WHITEFANG WAS HERE — Y31 — and so was a regrettable amount of beer"</em></p>

I am not certain Whitefang exists. I am certain that someone, repeatedly, wants me to think they do."</em></p>

        <h3>Scent-mark transcription · Olympia training facility, gym wall, three feet up · Year 34</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · a scent-mark was rendered into prose by a Foundation-retained Owl scent-tracker (Briarwing Hootington, daughter of Hawkeye, freelance) · the original mark has since faded</div>
        <p>Briarwing's rendering, on Foundation letterhead: <em>"The mark is, by my professional read, a Wolves' captain mark, made by Hardvein Quickstep approximately three weeks before his retirement. The mark contains four readable layers. Layer 1: territorial — 'this is Wolves' territory.' Standard. Layer 2: personal — 'this is Quickstep's mark.' Standard. Layer 3: a date-stamp, in the manner the pack uses for important transitions — 'this mark was made on the day Quickstep decided to retire.' This is, by my read, the actual point of the mark. Layer 4: a single short instruction, addressed to Greylane, who would inherit the captaincy three weeks later. The instruction is, in scent-language, untranslatable into League Common with confidence. My best rendering: 'the pack will be heavier than you expect; carry it anyway.' This is, by my read, what one captain leaves another. The mark is, in its way, a will."</em></p>
        <p>The mark was, by Briarwing's note, allowed to fade naturally. Greylane was informed of the rendering and declined to comment.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · scent-tracker fee paid in lobster, two units, recorded</div>

The gauge had been… for six weeks before… so we did not, at the time, …trust the gauge. …if it had not been Whittlestone, we would have. …the trust was, by the time the smell came, the only thing the floor still… and Whittlestone was the floor. The other tanks were fine. The fourth tank's batch is, by my own count, not in any League team's reserves and never will be. Whittlestone… we are not ever going to… and I have, this morning, decided to write this and burn it. The burning will not, by my read, succeed. Someone will find this. Someone will read it. They will not, on the strength of this single page, learn what happened. They will learn that something happened, and that the Foundry handled it. The handling was, by my read, the right handling.       <article class="found">
        <h3>Children's drawing · Boston, post-Year-35-Final · pinned to the Foundation Hall lobby corkboard</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · crayon on butcher paper, approximately 18 inches by 24 inches · signed in the lower right by a child who has printed her name as "ELLE" with a small heart</div>
        <p>The drawing is, by the Foundation lobby steward's description: <em>"two figures crossing a green field. The figure in front is gray with a purple cloak — the colors are, by my read, the Wolves' game-day colors. The figure being carried in the front figure's arms is smaller and yellow, with a small white cap that I think is meant to indicate the Healer position. There are, in the upper background, three figures with bows. There are not three; there were two; the child has added a third, who is, by my best guess, a representation of how scary the moment felt. The drawing's caption, in the upper margin, reads in block letters 'GREYLANE CARRYS THE HEALER. DONT YOU EVER STOP. — ELLE.'"</em></p>
        <p>The drawing has been on the Foundation lobby corkboard since the Year 35 quarterfinal. Greylane has, on three known occasions, walked through the lobby and not commented on it. The drawing has not, in Foundation steward's running record, been moved. The corkboard has been refreshed twice. The drawing has, both times, been pinned back up first. ELLE has not, by Foundation knowledge, ever returned to claim it.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Hall lobby corkboard, ongoing display · Year 35 to present</div>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Bathroom-stall poetry · Reno Open Court, women's washroom · ongoing collection across Years 32-36</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · pencil and gel-pen on stall door, accumulated · the door has been transcribed three times, photographed twice, and explicitly preserved by the venue's coaching staff against repainting</div>
        <p>The door, in chronological order of additions, reads (each line has been added by a different hand at a different time, identified by ink type and dating; the verses build on each other in a way the venue's curator describes as "informal collaborative drafting"):</p>
        <p><em>(Year 32, pencil)</em>: <em>"the crown will go where the crown will go"</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 32, blue gel-pen)</em>: <em>"the crown does not, in fact, decide"</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 33, red gel-pen)</em>: <em>"the crown decides nothing. the crown is decided."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 34, black gel-pen)</em>: <em>"deciding is for those who have not been crowned. those who have been crowned are simply, after, in the place the crown puts them."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35, pencil)</em>: <em>"i was, after, in the pawn shop. i did not decide that. i decided to be there. there is a difference."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36, gold gel-pen)</em>: <em>"the difference is the door."</em></p>
        <p>The door has, by Reno Open Court's coaching staff's standing order, been left intact since Year 32. The venue has been repainted three times in the intervening seasons. The door has, on every painting, been removed, stored, and reinstalled.</p>

        <h3>Fan letter · Year 35, addressed to the Beavers' coaching staff · forwarded to the Bristlebeard family</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · single sheet, careful printing · the writer has identified themselves only by initials · the letter has been forwarded with the family's permission</div>
        <p><em>"Dear Beavers' coaching staff,</em></p>
        <p><em>I have been a Beaver fan since Year 28. I watched the First charge into Phoenix in his last match. I have his commemorative button. I have, in fact, three of his commemorative buttons. I am writing about Bjorn.</em></p>
        <p><em>The fanbase has, since Bjorn took the Riot Shield, been split. I have read the columns. I have, in person, attended the discussions at the Brewer's Reach lobby. I have, by my count, sat through eleven separate explanations of why Bjorn should die in his second season the way the First and the Second did. I have not, on any of those occasions, agreed.</em></p>
        <p><em>The First died well. The Second died well. The pattern was, by every account, the pattern. I am not asking the Beavers to break the pattern. I am asking the Beavers to consider whether the pattern, by Bjorn's eighth season, has changed. Bjorn has lived. The First and the Second did not. Bjorn carries the Shield. The Shield is, by every account, the Shield. The pattern is the pattern. The pattern can, sometimes, be that the Shield outlasts the wearer. It is also possible that the pattern is, sometimes, that the wearer outlasts the Shield. I would like the Beavers to consider this.</em></p>
        <p><em>I am, on a personal note, very glad Bjorn is alive. I will continue to be a fan whether he dies in his ninth season the way his ancestors did, or whether he dies, eventually, of old age, in a Boston rocking chair. The Beavers are the Beavers. The pattern is the pattern. The fan is the fan. We will all be the things we are. — D.M., Boston, lifelong fan."</em></p>

        <p><em>"…the Long Quiet, by my read, was not a single event. The dating range — three to five hundred years — is not a margin of measurement error. The range is a range because the event itself was distributed. The Old Ones did not… in a single moment. The Old Ones, in different settlements, ceased to be present at different moments. Some settlements emptied first. Some emptied second. Some emptied third. The settlements that emptied first are, today, the settlements with the most…of the Old-Ones-era artifacts intact, because the next settlement's emptying preserved them.       <article class="found lore-wide">
        <h3>Letter from the south · postmarked Lima, delivered Year 35 to the Yucatan League outpost</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · two-page letter, formal Spanish · the writer has identified themselves only as "a representative of the basin coordinating council" · the letter has been translated by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot at the Foundation's request</div>
        <p>Translated text, with formal Spanish formality preserved where it survives translation:</p>
        <p><em>"To the Yucatan League outpost, with greetings,</em></p>
        <p><em>The basin coordinating council has, in receipt of your Year 34 inquiry regarding southern continental participation in the Float Knights League, deliberated for two seasons. The deliberation has, regrettably, not produced an affirmative response. The reasons follow.</em></p>
        <p><em>The southern animal communities — comprising, by our register, twenty-three settled lizard-line communities, eleven alligator-line communities, fourteen serpentine-line communities, and an indeterminate number of tropical bird communities (the bird communities do not, by their own preference, register their numbers; we have estimated forty, but the estimate is, by every honest reading, low) — have, on consultation, declined to send delegations northward. The reasons are three.</em></p>
        <p><em>First: travel distance. The continent's central rail does not connect south of the Yucatan extension, and our communities are not, in the aggregate, willing to fund a connecting line. The funding shortfall is structural, not ideological. We have not the surplus.</em></p>
        <p><em>Second: predator-prey unease. The northern League has, by our review of your existing roster, several teams whose species lines are predator species in our jungle ecology — the Foxes, the Wolves, the Lynx, and the Sharks all register as threats to specific southern lines. Our serpentine communities, in particular, have indicated that they would not, in good conscience, send athletes into a venue where they would be required to share a locker tunnel with a Lynx. The unease is not, by our read, irrational. The Lynx have not, by your own League's record, eliminated the predator instinct from their working lives. We do not blame them. We do not, however, ask our communities to room with them.</em></p>
        <p><em>Third: climate adaptation. Our jungle communities are not, by physiology, suited to the venues your League routinely plays in. The Helena Glacier Rink would, by every honest assessment, be lethal to a basin lizard within forty minutes of arrival. We do not have a counter-proposal that would shift your venue rotation to accommodate us; we recognize that your continental venue distribution is the venue distribution and that we are asking for a substantial accommodation if we ask it.</em></p>
        <p><em>We thank you, formally, for the inquiry. We extend, equally formally, an invitation: should the League ever wish to play exhibition matches at one of our southern venues — the Lima Highlands Pitch, the Caracas Canopy Hall, the Buenos Aires Wetlands — we will host. The hosting will be hospitable. The hosting will not, on our part, include the dispatching of teams northward in return. We hope this is acceptable. We hope, in any case, that the Float Knights League prospers in its current form, and we will, with respectful interest, follow it from here.</em></p>
        <p><em>With respect,</em><br/>
        <em>— a representative of the basin coordinating council, by signature redacted at the council's request"</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Yucatan League outpost · letter file Year 35 · translated by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot, fee paid in clams · Foundation has not, formally, responded</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found">
        <h3>Note · folded inside a Lynx coach's playbook · Year 36 founding bell · returned with the playbook</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · single sheet, in the Lynx language (Foundation translation provided by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot, who has, on the Lynx's preference, declined to render certain phrases for which the Lynx language has no neutral League-Common equivalent) · the playbook itself was returned to the Lynx coaching staff with the note left intact</div>
        <p>Translation, with untranslatable sections noted in italic prose rather than rendered (Roiseau-Manchot's standard practice for words she has chosen not to render):</p>
        <p><em>"To the next coach who reads this — I am the third coach to write a note here. The first coach was — the Lynx pronoun used here is not 'I' or 'we' and has, by Roiseau-Manchot, no neutral League-Common rendering — and the second coach was, in the same fashion, untranslatable. I am, in the same fashion, untranslatable. We do not, in the language we use when we have to speak, use the same word for ourselves twice. This is what makes the language right for us. The League will not understand this. The League does not need to. The League needs only to understand that the playbook works. The playbook is, in the Lynx way, written by an untranslatable hand and read by an untranslatable hand. We do not, between us, share the playbook the way the other teams share their playbooks. We share it the way the Lynx language allows itself to be shared. The next coach will know what this means. The next coach will be untranslatable. We will, on the day of the next match, be on the field together for the first time. We will run together, untranslatably, for the first time. We will play, together, in the Lynx way. The other teams will not understand what they are watching. We do not, on this point, owe them an explanation. We owe ourselves the playbook. The playbook is here. Read it. — untranslatable signature, in the Lynx hand."</em></p>
        <p>The note is, by Roiseau-Manchot's professional read, <em>"the most fully realized expression of Lynx team culture I have, in four months at the LMG, encountered. I have rendered it as fully as I can. The untranslatables are not failures of translation. They are the Lynx language refusing to be turned into League Common. I have honored the refusal. The note is, in League Common, what is left after the refusal. The League is welcome to it."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Lynx coaching staff · returned to team possession after Foundation transcription · the playbook is, by Lynx custom, kept in a different unmarked location each week</div>

The paint is the long pattern because the long pattern is what tonight's match calls for. The Sharks have, by every scout's read, six knights they think of as their first line. We have, by the matriarch's read, five knights and a stripe pattern. The pattern is the difference. Walk slow. Strike when the moment is the moment. Bring the helmet home. — the matriarch, by hand, before dawn."</em></p>
        <p>The note was found by a Bayou Tigers equipment manager during post-match locker breakdown. Stripeshoulder, asked about it later, declined to comment except to confirm the helmet was, indeed, painted in the long pattern that night. The Tigers won the match 3-2. The helmet has been retired and is, by Bayou tradition, in a small glass case in the matriarch's home.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · Bayou Tigers locker note Year 35 R5 · provenance: post-match locker breakdown</div>

        <p>Page 11 (Sniper kill-chains): <em>"this assumes the sniper picks the target. the wolf sniper does not pick. the pack picks. this is why our sniper hits more often than yours. you are training the sniper. we are training the pack. — Greylane"</em></p>

        <p><em>(Year 35 R3, two hours later, different hand)</em>: <em>"and the shooter is gone."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R3, dawn, a third hand)</em>: <em>"the line is not gone. the line stays."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R8, the night Sundip tied the mark)</em>: <em>"the line was tied. the line is now two lines. the lines stay."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R8, two hours later)</em>: <em>"and now the second shooter is gone too."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 35 R8, the next morning)</em>: <em>"the lines stay. the shooters do not. the lines remember the shooters. — a Helena fan, no team affiliation"</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36 founding bell, the day Hester Quillstrike's twin took the field for the first time wearing Hester's old number)</em>: <em>"the lines stay. the third shooter is on the field. the third shooter is the first shooter's twin. the lines are watching."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36 R3, after the twin's first sanctioned kill)</em>: <em>"a new line. shorter than 412. it counts anyway."</em></p>
        <p><em>(Year 36 R6, after the twin's first long-distance shot — 287 paces, well short of the mark)</em>: <em>"the twin is the twin. the twin is not the sister. the line is its own line. — H., a Helena fan, sister to a different shooter (yes). i hope the twin understands."</em></p>
        <p>The wall has not been repainted. The Helena venue's coaching staff has issued a standing instruction that it be left as-is. The cleaner has been told that her weekly transcription is, by the staff's read, the official record. She has, in private, told the Foundation Drawer's curator that she has been adding her own line each week — in pencil, very small, in the bottom corner — and has not, in any of her transcriptions, included her own additions. <em>"They are not for the public,"</em> she said. <em>"They are for the wall. The wall knows what I have written."</em></p>

        <p>The drawing, by the Foundation lobby steward's description: <em>"a single figure mid-flight, in green and red — quite plainly Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy, drawn with the wing-coverts in the iridescent shifted-green that the child has rendered with, by my read, an unusual amount of care for an eight-year-old. The board is also, by my read, exactly the right amount of full."</em></p>

We have, on consultation with A., agreed to leave the notes where they are. They are part of the thesis now, in the way the unwritten paragraphs of any rejected thesis are part of it. We are not, by A.'s preference, going to publish them. We are also, by A.'s preference, not going to remove them. The Foundation library has agreed to the same. The notes are in the book.         <h3>Letter to the Commissioner · Year 36 mid-season · received by Foundation general correspondence box · author age 7</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · single page, lined notebook paper, pencil, careful printing · forwarded by the Office of the Commissioner to the Foundation Drawer for archival on the strength of the Commissioner's handwritten note <em>"file this; reply pending"</em></div>
        <p>The letter, in full, with original spelling preserved: <em>"Dear Commissioner Wiskerstone, my name is Penn and I am 7. I have a question about the wave. when the team is downed and they come back as a wave, do they get to talk on the way? my brother says yes because they are walking together. my dad says no because they are still respawning and respawn is silent. who is right? please write back. I will tell my brother and my dad whatever you say and we will stop fighting about it. thank you. — Penn, age 7, Boston, brewer's row, the small house with the green door."</em></p>
        <p>The Commissioner's reply, in the Foundation correspondence log, in her own hand and forwarded with the original letter to the Drawer for completeness: <em>"Dear Penn, the wave does talk on the way. They walk together; they may speak quietly. The respawn ends at the bench, not at the spawn line. Your brother is right. Your father is, by the formal rule, also right — but not in the way he meant; he is right that respawn is silent, but the wave is not respawn. The wave is the formation that follows the respawn. Show this letter to your father. He may be cross. Show it to him anyway. — M. Whiskerstone, Office of the Commissioner. P.S. Tell your father to come by my office at his convenience. I would like to discuss the rule with him personally; he sounds like a careful reader, and the Office is, on careful readers, always recruiting."</em></p>
        <p>Penn's father came by the Office, by the steward's log, six weeks later. He did not, by the Foundation's subsequent personnel records, accept the recruiting offer; he did, however, by the same records, accept the bowl of bisque the Commissioner sent down to her own office that afternoon. He has, in the four months since, returned twice. The bisque, on both subsequent visits, was waiting.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · Year 36 mid-season · Penn's letter and the Commissioner's reply have, by the Foundation's standing policy on under-eighteen correspondents, been published only with the parents' explicit written permission, granted by both parents and Penn himself, who says he is "fine with the letter being in the book, because the answer was right and my brother now does the dishes for the rest of the month"</div>

        <p>A second page, dated nineteen days later: <em>"Day 19 of shutdown. The new rig has arrived from Pittsburgh. The slight under-specification is, by my read, the cause of the Year 30 R3 flat batch, the Year 31 batch-3 inconsistency that the Foxes' coaching staff complained about and which we corrected at our own expense, and possibly two other batch issues we did not catch in time. I will, in the next forty-one days, take three. The forty-one-day shutdown is, by my read, the longest unscheduled production interruption in the Foundry's twenty-six-year history. The Foundry has, in forty-one days, lost approximately twelve thousand bits in revenue. The Foundry will, in the next twelve months, recover the loss.         <h3>Reno academy thesis defense transcript · Year 35 closeout · the rejected Long-Quiet thesis</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · single page from the Reno academy's standard thesis-defense transcript format · this page is the closing exchange of the four-hour defense session for the rejected Year-35 thesis on the distributed-emptying hypothesis (cross-reference: Found Papers entries "Fragment · torn page from a Reno-academy thesis" and "Bookmark · folded inside a Reno-academy graduate thesis") · the thesis author, by her own pre-publication request, is identified only as "A."</div>
        <p>The page reads, in standard transcript format, with the defense committee's questions marked Q and the candidate's answers marked A:</p>
        <p><em>"(3:47 PM) Q (Committee Chair, Dr. M. Shellbark): The committee has, in deliberation, decided to advance to closing questions. A., we have, in three hours of defense, raised our concerns about the thesis's methodology. We have not, in those three hours, raised our concerns about the thesis's framework. The framework — the distributed-emptying hypothesis — is, by every committee member's reading, the most-promising new framework the field has produced in a decade. The committee is, by my standing read of the room, going to vote against advancement on methodological grounds. The framework is not, by any committee member's vote, the reason for the rejection. I want, on the record, to ask you: what is the framework's next step, in your own working plan, after this defense?</em></p>
        <p><em>(3:48 PM) A: I am, on this question, going to give the committee an honest answer. I do not, by my own pre-defense planning, have a next step that depends on this defense's outcome. The framework is mine. The framework will, by my own working commitment, continue to be mine after this defense. The committee's vote, by my reading, is on the methodology. The methodology can be improved. I will improve it. The framework, by my reading, is going to need approximately ten more years of work before it produces a publishable monograph. I am, on this matter, twenty-six years old. I have time. I am not, by my own reading, in a hurry.</em></p>
        <p><em>(3:49 PM) Q (Committee Chair, Dr. M. Shellbark): A., I am going to ask one more question, off the formal record but in the transcript by my own request. Will you, after this defense, continue to deposit your work in the Foundation Library's open stacks?</em></p>
        <p><em>(3:50 PM) A: Yes. The thesis is, by my own pre-defense decision, going into the open stacks regardless of the vote. I am, on this matter, asking the Foundation Library not to remove my name from the catalog but to redact it on the catalog card itself. The work will be findable. The author will not. This is, by my reading, the right arrangement. I am, on this matter, going to keep working. The bookmark notes I have, in the past three months, started writing inside the thesis are, by my own pre-publication arrangement with the Foundation Library, going to stay in the thesis. The Library's volunteers will, in due course, find them. The volunteers will, in due course, write to me through the Library's anonymous-correspondence system. We will, in due course, correspond. The work will continue. The framework will, in due course, be ready. I am not, by my reading, in a hurry.</em></p>
        <p><em>(3:51 PM) Q (Committee Chair, Dr. M. Shellbark): A., for the formal record: the committee will, on its scheduled vote, almost certainly reject. I am, on the formal record, going to vote to advance to revision. I will, on this vote, lose 4-1. I want, on the formal record and in this transcript, to say that the loss is, by my reading, the right loss. The framework deserves the rejection because the methodology is not yet ready. The framework also deserves to live, because the framework is, by my reading, the right framework. These two readings are not, by my reading, in conflict. They will, in due course, be the same reading. I am, on this matter, glad you are twenty-six.</em></p>
        <p><em>(3:52 PM) A: Thank you. I will, in due course, see you at the next defense.</em></p>
        <p><em>(End of formal defense transcript. Vote: 4 to reject, 1 to advance to revision. Thesis status: rejected. Author's standing notice to the Library: 'redact name on catalog card; deposit thesis in open stacks; preserve bookmark notes.' The Library has, in eight months since deposition, complied.)"</em></p>
        <p>The Foundation Drawer's curator's filing note: <em>"This is, by my read, the most hopeful piece of paper the Drawer has ever filed about an academic rejection. A. is still working. Shellbark has, in retirement, written a column ('On the Long Quiet,' Reno academy quarterly review, Year 35) that defends, in retrospect, the rejection vote and the work both — and that is, by my read, also addressed to A. without naming her. A. has, by the Foundation Library's anonymous correspondence records, received Shellbark's column. A. has, by the same records, replied. The reply is, by Shellbark's pre-retirement permission, in the Library's anonymous-correspondence file under restricted access. The reply is, by every reading available to me, kind. The work continues. The Drawer is glad to file this transcript."</em></p>

        <p>The Foundation Drawer's curator's filing note: <em>"The tokens were tendered as payment for one lobster on a non-specific match-day in Year 36 mid-season by a Quetzal who did not, by the lobster vendor's report, speak League Common. The Quetzal nodded once before leaving. The tokens are, by every reading available to the Library, currency from somewhere — but the somewhere is not, by every reference-collection check, on the post-Long-Quiet North American continent in any way the Library currently understands. The vendor has, by her own pre-publication explanation, declined to speculate on the somewhere. Her stated reason: <em>'the tokens are payment for one lobster, accepted by me, on the day described in my ledger. that is, by my standing read, the only fact about the tokens that is properly mine to share. the rest is the somewhere's. the somewhere will, in due course, share what it wants to share, or not.'</em> The Drawer accepts the vendor's framing. The tokens stay in the lock-box. The photograph is the entry. The somewhere is, by every reading, fine where it is, which is not where we are."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · the two wooden tokens · Brewer's Reach Concession Row lock-box · Year 36 · the only photograph on file · the tokens have not been removed from the lock-box · the Quetzal has not, in the eight months since, returned to the booth</div>

        <h3>Apprentice's notebook · Sonora Drifting Coyotes pre-League regional combat circuit · Year 26 (pre-Foundation)</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · single-page extract from a longer notebook · the original notebook is in the Coyotes' team archive at the Sonora venue · this page was donated to the Foundation Drawer by the notebook's author's granddaughter on the occasion of the Coyotes' League admission in Year 36 · the author was a Coyote drift-coach in the pre-League circuit, two generations before Coach Reyna · the page describes a drill the modern Coyotes still run, with one notable continuity</div>
        <p>The page reads, in a careful older hand, in the Sonoran composite-creole the modern Coyote coaching staff still uses for drift instruction: <em>"the four-point-six-second mark is, by my count this season, hit by approximately two of every five rookies in the cohort. the threshold is not, by my reading, the right metric — the metric is too easy. the metric should be, by my reading, the seven-second mark. but the seven-second mark is, by my count this season, hit by zero of fifteen rookies in the cohort. that is too hard. the four-point-six-second mark is, by my reading, what the cohort can be reasonably expected to hit. the seven-second mark is, by my reading, what the cohort should aspire to. the cohort is told, on the drill floor, only the four-point-six. the seven is, by my own pre-coaching commitment, kept private. it is mine, until a rookie hits it. when a rookie hits it, the seven will be hers, and i will, in due course, retire."</em></p>
        <p>The Foundation Drawer's curator's filing note: <em>"This page is, by my read, a small but extraordinary document. The Coyotes' modern drift-coach Reyna uses the exact same four-point-six-second threshold the author used two generations ago — and, on consultation with the Coyote coaching staff after this page's deposition, also the same private seven-second aspiration. Reyna confirmed, on the consultation, that the seven-second mark has, in the seventy-two seasons since the page was written, been hit by no rookie. The mark remains, by the coaching staff's standing tradition, private. Reyna did not, on the consultation, indicate she had any plans to retire if the mark were hit. She did say, by way of clarification: <em>'the mark will be hit. the rookie who hits it will, by my read, be one i have not yet trained. that rookie may not, in any way i can predict, ever know that the mark was hers to hit. the mark is the mark. the rookie is the rookie. the work is, on this matter, the work.'</em> The Drawer files this page with profound respect."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · Coyote pre-League circuit notebook page · Year 26 · the page is on display, by the family's permission, behind glass at the Sonora venue's south corridor · the four-point-six is the cohort threshold · the seven is, by tradition, private · this Drawer is, by Coyote coaching-staff request, the only public reference to the seven outside the coaching staff itself · the rookie who hits the seven will, on her hitting it, learn whatever the coaching staff at that time chooses to tell her</div>
      </article>

        <h3>Photograph · Théodred III at center pitch · Year 34 Final · 31:00 mark · the Antlerwood Rule's evidence</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · photograph · LMG broadcast capture · the canonical photograph used by the Year 35 Caucus wave-doctrine review committee in their deliberations on what would become the Antlerwood Rule · the photograph hangs, by Caucus archival decision, on the wall of the Caucus's tactical-archive review chamber</div>
        <p>The photograph, by the LMG's broadcast-capture metadata: <em>"timestamp 31:00 of the Year 34 Final, frame 1860 (at 60 frames per second). The frame shows, at center pitch of the Saint-Laurent venue, the Antlerlords' L'Ancrage knight (Théodred III) in the standing-anchor position. The composition is, by the broadcast booth's framing choice, near-symmetric: Théodred III occupies the exact center of the frame, with the venue's center-line markings extending equally to the left and right of his position. He is, in this frame, in the same posture he held at minute 0:00. He is, in this frame, in the same posture he will hold at minute 31:14 when the match resolves. The frame is, by every analyst's read, indistinguishable from any other frame in the match in which Théodred III is visible at center pitch — except for the timestamp, which is, by Caucus archival convention, used to anchor the photograph in the Final's broadcast record."</em></p>
        <p>The Year-35 Caucus wave-doctrine review committee's filing note, attached to the photograph in the tactical-archive review chamber: <em>"This photograph was, by committee resolution, the deciding evidence in the Year 35 Antlerwood Rule deliberations. The committee — over forty-seven hours of deliberation, with three formal recesses — was unable to determine whether Théodred III's stillness during the Year 34 Final constituted a wave-doctrine violation. The argument against (filed by the committee's three more-junior members) was that the wave-doctrine's ten-second movement-mandate is, by its drafting language, applicable to all knights at all times during sanctioned play, regardless of position or posture. The argument for (filed by the committee's six more-senior members, including chair Margaux Whiskerstone) was that the photograph showed, in its composition, a knight occupying the position the moose has held for ninety-three years and which the species, by long-standing biological commitment, considers home — and that the wave-doctrine could not, by any reasonable reading, be applied against home. The chair's deciding vote, on the seventh and final ballot, was for the latter. The Antlerwood Rule was drafted that same day, ratified at the Year 35 closeout Caucus meeting, and entered into the standing-rule book in language specific to the L'Ancrage and no other position. The photograph is hung in the review chamber, by the chair's standing instruction, 'so that future committees considering similar cases will, before deliberating, look at the photograph for as long as they need to look at it. the photograph is, by my read, the answer. the language we wrote is, by my read, the explanation of the answer. both should be available to future committees in equal measure.'"</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · Year 34 Final broadcast-capture photograph · the canonical Antlerwood Rule evidence · the photograph hangs in the Caucus's tactical-archive review chamber · Théodred III continues to hold L'Ancrage as of Year 36 mid-season · the Rule remains in standing language · no committee has, in two seasons since ratification, found cause to amend it</div>
