        <h3>The First Inkbeak Communiqué — pages 1–4 (of 17) · Year 33 · oceanic crossing observation log</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · the canonical first-contact document between the North American League and the Federación Sudamericana · seventeen pages of folded archival shorthand handwritten by Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. (PIT Murder, senior flying Raven, then in his twenty-second flight year) during his Year-33 oceanic crossing and forty-one-day stay in Federación territory · the full document is in the Foundation Library's archival roost custody; only the first four pages have been authorized by the Murder for transcription into the public Drawer · this is the standard-edition four-page extract, with the Murder's Roost-vetted footnotes intact</div>
        <p><em>"Day one, dawn departure. Two hundred and seven flap-cycles to clear the Caribbean coast at Tampa, by my own count, which is, by the Murder's standing methodology, the count that matters. Wind from the east-southeast at what an old-Atlas reader would call eight or nine knots. The Sharks' coast watchman waved as I cleared the last home thermal. I dipped one wing in acknowledgment. The watchman waved twice. Sharks are, on this matter, kinder than the Murder generally credits them with being. The Murder will, on my return, hear this from me."</em></p>
        <p><em>"Day three, sunset. The first land-bird I have encountered on this passage is a sooty tern, who is, by my best read, lost. We exchanged perhaps twelve seconds of mutual circling, in silence. I have not, in twenty-two years of recorded flight, seen a sooty tern before. The bird's wing condition is, by my read, fine. Its bearing is wrong. I asked, in the airborne sign-language the Murder has, in three centuries, refined for cross-species cordiality, whether it required assistance. The bird, by its own response in equivalent sign, said no, then said the word 'home' three times in three different bearings, then resumed flight to the south-southwest. I have noted the encounter in the standard format. The bird is, by my read, lost. The bird is also, by its own read, going home. Both are true. The Murder will, on my return, hear this from me as well."</em></p>
        <p><em>"Day eleven, midday. Cartagena coast in clear sight from approximately sixty kilometers out. The Federación delegation that met me at the harbor wall — three Spectacled Bears, one Lowland Tapir, two Capybaras of, by my read, considerable seniority — were standing at the end of a stone breakwater that had been, by their own pre-arrival announcement (relayed via the Quetzal-canopy network in Yucatan), prepared with a tier of three perches for a Raven of the Murder. The middle perch was the senior perch. The Bears had, on their own initiative, polished the middle perch overnight with a wax of, by their post-landing explanation, 'the same composition our Cordillera council uses for the senior perch in the Bear-council chamber.' I landed on the middle perch. The Bears bowed. I returned the bow at the depth the Murder uses for foreign senior councils. The Tapir said, in League Common with the audible Bogotá accent the Cintzli briefing had prepared me for: <em>'welcome, senior. the council is in session in three days. you are invited. you are also, by our hospitality protocol, free to decline.'</em> I accepted the invitation. The Capybaras escorted me to the visiting-Raven roost, which is an actual roost, in an actual tree, in the actual harbor square, that the Federación had pre-built for the contingency of a Murder visit. The roost has been, by Bogotá-side records, ready for four years. They had, on three previous occasions, been ready for nothing in particular. They were, on this occasion, ready for me. I have not, in twenty-two years of flight, been more honored."</em></p>
        <p><em>"Day fourteen, the Cordillera Council. The Bears' chamber is dug into the cliff-face above Bogotá at an altitude my Pittsburgh-trained lungs found, on first arrival, more difficult than the Bears had been led to expect. They paused the council for one full hour, by their own clock, to allow me to acclimatize. I drank a tea their Healer prepared, which was made of a leaf I have not, in any pre-flight scouting, encountered, and which restored me to my usual level of bearing within forty minutes. The Healer is a Capybara. I had not understood, before this trip, that Capybaras are physically capable of the surgical precision Healing requires. I was wrong about this. The Murder will, on my return, hear this also."</em></p>
        <p><em>"The council itself ran four hours. The agenda was, in the Federación's standard order: (1) the visiting senior's report on his own League's standing condition; (2) the Federación's report on its own standing condition; (3) any matters of mutual interest. I delivered the Murder's standard delegation report — twenty-six minutes of Pittsburgh-side history, current twenty-team-roster, the Whittlestone Address as I understand it, the Foundation Library's structure, the four canonical eleven-second silences (the Bow, the Address coda, and the two more recent additions Pell Whittlestone has acknowledged but not yet, by Foundation standing rule, entered into the canonical list). Commissioner Doña Inés de la Niebla — a Spectacled Bear of, by every Bogotá-side description, considerable scholarly inclination — listened without interruption, then asked seventeen questions in a row, in League Common with no detectable accent shift across the seventeen. The first sixteen were factual. The seventeenth was: <em>'do you, by your own honest accounting, believe our two leagues should attempt, in either of our institutional lifetimes, to play a sanctioned cross-continental match?'</em> I answered: <em>'commissioner, I am, by every Murder rule, not authorized to answer that question on behalf of my Caucus. I am also, by my own honest accounting, going to answer it on behalf of myself: I do not yet know. I would like, before I know, to watch your league play.'</em> The Commissioner nodded once. She said: <em>'that is the honest answer. that is also, by every Bogotá-side hospitality protocol I am aware of, the right answer. you will watch our league play. we will speak again on the matter when you have. you are welcome here for as long as that takes.'</em> The forty-one-day stay was set, in that moment, as the answer to the seventeenth question. I am, in this communiqué's drafting, on day forty-one. I am ready to fly home tomorrow. I have an answer to the question. I will not, by Murder protocol, give the answer in this communiqué. I will give it to the Roost, in the chamber, on the standard format. The Roost will, in due course, decide what to do with my answer."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · the First Inkbeak Communiqué (pages 1–4 of 17) · Year 33 · Slatequill Inkbeak Sr.'s handwriting in the Murder's archival shorthand, transcribed by the Drawer with the Roost's vetted footnotes (which are not reproduced in this public extract; the footnotes correct three minor weather observations and one Cartagena-harbor measurement, all in directions that strengthen the communiqué's overall accuracy) · pages 5–17 remain in the Murder's archival roost custody and are, by Roost-vote standing rule, "not yet" public · Inkbeak's seventeenth-question answer to the Roost has not, in three subsequent years, been disclosed to the Foundation Library · the answer is, by Roost convention, the Roost's · Inkbeak Sr. continues to fly the Caribbean basin annually · the Cartagena visiting-Raven roost remains, by Federación standing protocol, in service · the wax on the senior perch is renewed, by the Bears' standing rule, on the day after each Inkbeak departure</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found lore-wide">
        <h3>The Old World File · five entries from a working folder · Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau · Years 30 through 36</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · the canonical North American archive of bird-relayed claims about animal leagues operating on the European, Asian, and African continents · the file contains, as of Year 36 mid-season, fifty-eight entries collected over six years from twelve distinct birds (eight gulls, two terns, one Arctic skua, one albatross who landed at Pittsburgh in Year 34 and stayed three days before flying onward) · the Foundation Library's filing convention is to record the entry verbatim, then attach a single-line curator's annotation indicating the relative confidence the Library assigns to the claim · five representative entries are reproduced below; the full fifty-eight are available to scholars by formal request · the Library's standing position on the entire file is that it is, in aggregate, "of cultural and historical interest, of speculative entertainment value, and of approximately zero confirmed factual content. We file the folder anyway. We file folders. That is what the Library does."</div>
        <p><b>Entry 7 (Year 30, gull, name not given, observed at Boston harbor for fifteen minutes):</b> <em>"there is a league in the place that used to be France. they play in the ruins of a great cathedral that has, in the centuries since, become a sort of bowl. the floor is grass. the knights are red foxes and they are, by my eyewitness account, larger than any fox you have on this continent. their captain is named Jean-Bertrand and he has, by reputation, never lost a duel. they play with seven balloons not three or six. the balloons are made of a fabric we do not have a word for in League Common."</em> <b>Curator's annotation:</b> the gull was paid in fish-scraps for a fifteen-minute interview. the fish-scraps were not contingent on the content of the interview. the gull's accuracy on Boston-harbor matters that the bureau could independently verify (tide times, weather conditions over the previous forty-eight hours, the gull's own arrival route) was checked at approximately 60 percent. confidence in the claim above: low. confidence that the gull saw something: medium. confidence that what the gull saw is, in any meaningful sense, what the gull described: very low.</p>
        <p><b>Entry 19 (Year 32, tern, named "Wave-Counter," observed at Tampa harbor for two days):</b> <em>"there is a league in the islands that used to be Japan. they play on platforms of stone built over water. the knights are macaques and tanuki and one team of red-crowned cranes. the macaques' team has been undefeated for nineteen of their seasons, which I think are shorter than yours. their captain is a macaque named, in their language, something that translates approximately as 'the one who waits.' the cranes' team is, by everyone's account in the island chain, the most-feared team because they are, by their species, both Snipers and able to fly above the platforms. no one has, in nineteen seasons, beaten them in a sanctioned match held over water. they only play sanctioned matches over water. they have, by their own choice, never played a sanctioned match held on land."</em> <b>Curator's annotation:</b> Wave-Counter was paid in shrimp-paste for the two-day interview. her accuracy on Tampa-harbor matters that we could verify independently was checked at approximately 70 percent, which is unusually high for a long-distance tern. she said three things during the interview that we found, on cross-check with the Foundation Library's pre-Long-Quiet geographic fragments, to be plausibly accurate descriptions of cultural patterns the Old-Ones recorded for the relevant region. confidence in the claim above: low-to-medium. confidence that the league exists in some form: medium. confidence in the specific names, season counts, and team compositions: low. <em>(Curator's marginal note, hand-written rather than typed, in pencil: "Wave-Counter is, by my own honest read after two days, a very serious tern. her seriousness is not, by every Library standard, evidence. her seriousness is, by my standing read, also not nothing. I have, on filing, marked the entry medium-confidence rather than low. I will defend the marking, if asked. — sgw")</em></p>
        <p><b>Entry 31 (Year 33, Arctic skua, name not given, observed at Anchorage harbor for two hours):</b> <em>"there is a league in the place that used to be Russia. they play on the frozen rivers in winter and on the steppes in summer. the knights are wolves and bears and a team of sables and a team of golden eagles. the wolves' captain is a Siberian wolf named, by his own pack, 'the Cold-Carrier.' the eagles' captain is, in their language, a name that translates as 'the one who is not afraid of the steppes.' there is also, by reputation, a team of moose, but they are not, by every other team's standing avoidance, a team that is invited to many away matches. the league has, by my own three-year flight count, twenty-two teams. the league plays year-round. the league does not, by my own observation, take a winter break. they take, by my own observation, a summer break, because the steppes in summer are, by every other species' assessment, a worse problem than the rivers in winter."</em> <b>Curator's annotation:</b> the skua was, by its own first-statement, "not interested in payment." we offered fish-scraps anyway, which the skua accepted at the end of the interview. the skua's accuracy on Anchorage-harbor matters was checked at approximately 50 percent, with the inaccuracies clustered in matters of recent weather (which the skua appeared to genuinely have not observed, having just arrived). confidence in the claim above: low. note that the existence of a moose team is, by Saint-Laurent Antlerlords' standing comment on the entry (relayed via Caucus inquiry in Year 33): "yes, there is a moose team in the place that used to be Russia. it is, by every conceivable read, our cousin team. we have not, in our institutional memory, made any contact with them. we are, by Théodred III's standing personal pre-publication preference, not yet ready to. we will, in due course, be. we are not yet."</p>
        <p><b>Entry 44 (Year 35, gull, name not given, observed at Boston harbor for forty minutes):</b> <em>"there is a league in the place that used to be Britain. they play in eight separate venues across the islands. the knights are badgers and foxes and red squirrels and one famously bad-tempered team of hedgehogs. their captain — the badgers' captain, the senior captaincy of the league as a whole — is named Lord Brock, and he has, by his own reported claim, won every championship in the league's history. the league has been operating for, by Lord Brock's reported claim, eleven hundred years."</em> <b>Curator's annotation:</b> the gull was paid generously in fish-scraps for the forty-minute interview. the gull's accuracy on Boston-harbor matters was checked at approximately 30 percent, which is low even for gulls. the eleven-hundred-year claim is, by every standard the Library applies, not credible — pre-Long-Quiet records for the relevant geography do not support a continuous tournament-organized sport tradition older than approximately two centuries, and a Long-Quiet-spanning continuous tradition would be, by every available archival method, the largest historical claim in any species' working record on the planet. confidence in the claim above: very low. <em>(Curator's marginal note, hand-written, in pencil: "the gull was, by my read, lying. I do not file gulls who are lying. I am filing this gull because the Helena Hedgehogs requested, by formal letter, that any claim involving British hedgehogs be filed regardless of confidence. they want, on the matter, a record of every such claim. I respect the request. I am filing. — sgw")</em></p>
        <p><b>Entry 53 (Year 34, albatross, name not given, observed at Pittsburgh harbor for three days, the only confirmed long-stay albatross visit in the bureau's six-year operation):</b> <em>"there is a league in the place that used to be South Africa. they play on the savannah at sunset, by tradition. the knights are meerkats and warthogs and one team of cheetahs that have, by everyone's account in the southern hemisphere, the fastest Speedsters of any league on the planet. there is also, by reputation, a team of African Wild Dogs whose pack tactics are, by everyone's account, more sophisticated than the wolves' on this continent. the league has been organized for approximately fifty years and has, in that time, played a sanctioned match against a Madagascar-based league four times. all four matches were held on neutral ground in what used to be the Comoros. the lemur-and-fossa-led Madagascar league won three of the four. the cheetahs' captain has not, by reputation, taken the loss well in any of the three losses."</em> <b>Curator's annotation:</b> the albatross's accuracy on Pittsburgh-harbor matters was checked at approximately 80 percent, which is the highest accuracy figure the bureau has recorded for any visiting bird in six years of operation. she gave the interview without payment, declined fish-scraps, declined the Murder's standing visiting-bird hospitality. she said she had flown from "very far south" and was going "very far north" and had stopped at Pittsburgh because she had "heard the harbor was a place that asked questions of visiting birds." she answered every question in three days of interviews with what appeared to be, by every interviewer's note, careful precision. she did not embellish. she said, when she did not know a thing, that she did not know it. the bureau's standing-rule note on this entry: <em>"this is the only entry in the file the Library is, by curator's recommendation, willing to call 'medium-to-high' confidence. the albatross was, by every standard the bureau applies, a careful narrator. we do not know whether the things the albatross described are, in fact, accurate; we know only that the albatross did not, by every measurable standard, lie or embellish. we are, in this entry, accepting an albatross's testimony as our least-bad available source. we acknowledge the limitation. we file the entry. — Library Northeast Coast Bureau, Year 34 mid-summer, on the senior curator's review."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau · the Old World File · five representative entries of fifty-eight on file as of Year 36 mid-season · the Library's standing position is that the file is, in aggregate, of speculative interest only · the senior curator's standing position (in pencil, in the file's flyleaf) is that the albatross of Entry 53 is, by every available read, the only narrator in the file the Library should consider responding to in any official capacity, and that the Library has not, in two years since the entry's filing, drafted a response · the Library's working title for any future response, if drafted, is "to a careful narrator, from a careful library" · the title has been on the curator's draft list for two years · the draft itself does not yet exist</div>
      </article>

      <article class="found lore-wide">
        <h3>"To a Careful Narrator, from a Careful Library" — first-draft response to the Year-34 albatross · Year 36 mid-season · senior curator Sgw, in pencil</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · the long-deferred draft response to Entry 53 of the Old World File · drafted by the Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau senior curator (initialed "Sgw" — Sigridweave, the Owl who has held the curatorship since Year 31) on a single sheet of unbleached library-stock paper, in pencil, on the morning of the first sustained snowfall of Year 36 · the draft is not, as of this filing, dispatched · the Library's standing position on whether to dispatch is "we have not, in two years, decided. we are, on this draft, closer to a decision than we have been. we have not decided yet" · the draft is filed in the Foundation Drawer at the senior curator's request because, in her own marginal note: "if I do not file this, I will continue to draft it, and the drafting is, by my own honest read, no longer the productive part" · the response below is the full text of the draft, transcribed with permission</div>
        <p><em>"to the careful narrator who landed at Pittsburgh harbor in the late summer of Year 34 and gave three days of careful interviews to my colleagues at the bureau — and who has, in the two years since, been the standing exception to every working assumption this Library holds about bird testimony:</em></p>
        <p><em>"i will write this as i would speak it, in the office, on the first afternoon of the snow. the snow is, this morning, the first sustained snowfall of the season. it is, by my own habit, the morning i clean my desk. cleaning my desk has, in the two years since you visited, included pulling your file out of the drawer, reading the bureau's notes again, putting the file back, and not yet drafting this response. i am drafting it this morning because the snow is here and the desk is clean and the only thing left to clean is, by my own honest read, this draft.</em></p>
        <p><em>"first: the bureau owes you an honest acknowledgment. you gave us three days of testimony in conditions of considerable physical strain (you had, by every Pittsburgh-harbor-watch report, just completed an oceanic crossing of perhaps the longest single passage any bird in our records has documented), and you accepted no payment, no hospitality, no fish-scraps, no roost-time. the bureau's standing protocol assumes payment because payment establishes a contractual reciprocity that the bureau finds easier, on the bureau's side, to interpret. you declined the protocol. the bureau, in its own slowness, took two years to write down what we should have written down on the third afternoon of your visit, which is: the protocol assumed payment because we did not yet have a vocabulary for what you were giving us instead. you were giving us, by my own subsequent reading, a gift of a kind the bureau does not have institutional shape to receive without ambiguity. we received it ambiguously. we are, in this draft, attempting to receive it more cleanly. i do not know whether we have succeeded. i am, on the matter, going to keep trying.</em></p>
        <p><em>"second: the contents of your testimony. you described a league of meerkats, warthogs, cheetahs, and African Wild Dogs in the place that used to be South Africa, organized for approximately fifty years, with a quadrennial sanctioned exhibition against a Madagascar-based league of lemurs and fossas, played on neutral ground in what used to be the Comoros. four exhibitions, three of which the Madagascar league won. the cheetahs' captain unhappy with all three losses. the bureau has, in the two years since, applied every cross-reference tool we have to your testimony. we have not, by any cross-reference, been able to either confirm or refute it. we have, however, found one passage in a pre-Long-Quiet geographic fragment recovered from the Helena archive that mentions, in passing, that the islands of the Comoros were "of long-standing diplomatic significance to communities on both shores of the Mozambique Channel." this is not, by any reading, evidence of your specific claim. it is, by my own read, the kind of structural pre-condition under which your specific claim could plausibly have arisen. i am noting it. i am not, in this draft, claiming it as confirmation. you would not, by my read of your testimony's standards, want me to.</em></p>
        <p><em>"third: a question, if you ever return to Pittsburgh harbor and the bureau is, on that occasion, available. you said, on the second afternoon, that you had been told the harbor was 'a place that asked questions of visiting birds.' the bureau has, in the two years since, asked itself who told you. we have not, in our institutional records, found the answer. the bureau has, in the relevant period, given that description of itself to no visitor we have a record of. we are not, by this question, accusing you of anything. we are, by my own honest read, asking because the answer would be, in the bureau's working theory of how reputations propagate among long-distance fliers, useful to know. it would tell us something about how the bureau is read at distance, which is a thing we do not, in our usual operations, have any way to learn. we would, if you ever returned, like to learn.</em></p>
        <p><em>"fourth, and last, by my own preference: thank you. the bureau has, in six years, filed fifty-eight entries from twelve birds. seventeen of those entries are, by every standard we apply, lies. thirty-three are, by every standard we apply, embellishments of varying severity. seven are, by every standard we apply, of indeterminate reliability. one is, by every standard we apply, careful. that one is yours. you have made the file, by your single contribution, more honest than every other contributor combined. we owe you, on that arithmetic, more than the file format permits us to owe in our standard annotations. this draft response is, by my own pre-publication acknowledgment, an attempt to owe you that more without altering the file format. i do not, on this matter, intend to alter the file format. you would not, by my read of your standards, want the format altered for one entry, even yours. you would, by my read, want the format kept and the format read with the entries it contains, and the careful entry recognized as the careful entry, and the entries that are not careful recognized as what they are. that is what the file is doing. that is what the bureau is doing. that is, by my own read, what we owe each other on this matter, and what i am acknowledging this morning, in pencil, on this draft.</em></p>
        <p><em>"i will keep the file. i will keep the draft. i may, in due course, dispatch the draft. i may, in due course, not. you will, by every honest measure available to a bureau on this side of the ocean, never know, with any certainty, which of those choices i made. i am writing this last paragraph aware of that. i am writing it anyway. the writing is, on my own read, what i owe the file. the dispatch, if it happens, will be what i owe you. these are different debts. they are, by my own preference, kept on separate ledgers. the writing-ledger, this morning, is settled. the dispatch-ledger remains, on this matter, open.</em></p>
        <p><em>"with careful regard,</em></p>
        <p><em>"— Sigridweave (Sgw), senior curator, Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau, on the morning of the first sustained snowfall of Year 36."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Ephemera Drawer · "To a Careful Narrator, from a Careful Library" · first-draft response · Year 36 mid-season · the draft is, as of this filing, not dispatched · the senior curator has, by her own pre-filing arrangement, asked that the draft be filed in the Drawer rather than kept on her desk because, in her marginal note, "the desk is, this morning, clean. i would like, by my own preference, to keep it clean. the draft is not, by my honest read, going to settle on a dispatch decision in the next year. the file is, by my honest read, the right place for the draft to settle while the dispatch decision waits" · the dispatch decision continues to wait · the draft remains, by curator preference, the only document she has authorized for Drawer-filing in pencil rather than in ink · her stated reason: "ink is what we use for the file. pencil is what we use for the draft. the draft is, by my own read, still the draft."</div>
      </article>
      <article class="found">
        <h3>The cover note · pencil on bureau letterhead · attached to the Sigridweave dispatch · Year 36 mid-season, the morning of the perch's first occupation</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · the brief cover note that traveled south with Sigridweave's two-year-deferred response to the Year-34 albatross · written in pencil on standard Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau letterhead, in the senior curator's hand, on the morning of the forty-seventh day of the Pittsburgh Visiting Perch's vacant standing · the original is in the Federación's Cartagena bureau archive (filed there by Doña Inés on receipt) · this transcription is from the carbon-paper copy the Northeast Coast Bureau retained for its own files</div>
        <p>The full text of the cover note, transcribed verbatim:</p>
        <p><em>"to Doña Inés, in Cartagena —</em></p>
        <p><em>"the enclosed is the response i drafted to the Year-34 albatross. the draft has been on my desk, and in my drawer, for two years. i have, this morning, dispatched it. the dispatch is via the Cóndor (Marisol Cumbralta — your bureau's selection has been, by every read available to me on the receiving side, exactly correct).</em></p>
        <p><em>"i am asking, in this cover note, that the response be held by your bureau and forwarded to the Albatross only when the Albatross is, on the matter, accessible. i do not, on the matter, ask that you forward it on any schedule. i do not, on the matter, ask for a confirmation of receipt. i do not, on the matter, ask anything of the Federación in handling this dispatch except the standard Federación-side hospitality the Federación extends to all northbound-and-southbound forwarded correspondence: which is to say, hold it, file it, forward it when the right occasion forwards it, and consider the matter closed on your bureau's side once it is forwarded. that is the entirety of what i am asking.</em></p>
        <p><em>"the draft is in pencil. the cover note is in pencil. the dispatch is, on this morning, in pencil. the bureau's standing-rules document, on the matter of cover notes, asks for ink. i have, on this dispatch, declined the convention. my reason is, by my own honest read, that the draft is what it is, and the cover note is what the draft asks the cover note to be, and the convention has, on the matter, been wrong about the right ink for two years. the convention is wrong on this dispatch. the convention will, on the matter, be right again on the next dispatch. i am not, on this matter, asking the convention to change. i am asking the convention to accept that, on this one dispatch, in pencil, on bureau letterhead, the senior curator's standing prerogative has been exercised. the bureau will, in due course, file the carbon copy in pencil, in our drawer. you will, in due course, file the original in your drawer in whatever the Federación's standing convention asks. these are different drawers. they are, on the matter, the right drawers.</em></p>
        <p><em>"thank you for sending Cumbralta. she is, by every available read, exactly the Cóndor the dispatch needed. she has, on her arrival, given the bureau more institutional vocabulary than we had at the Albatross's visit. we will, in due course, do better at the receiving than we did. we will not, on the matter, do better immediately. better at the receiving is, by every honest read, the work of decades. we are, on this dispatch, two years and forty-seven days into it. the work continues.</em></p>
        <p><em>"with careful regard,</em></p>
        <p><em>"— sgw."</em></p>
        <p>Doña Inés's standing pre-publication note on the original, written in pencil at the bottom (in the same hand she uses for working notations on Federación working drafts; her own standing-rules document on ink and pencil is, by her own bureau's report, more permissive than the Northeast Coast Bureau's): <em>"recibido. lo guardaré. cuando la Albatros regrese, si regresa, lo enviaré. si no regresa, lo guardaré para siempre. esto es, por toda lectura honesta, lo que la curadora del norte está pidiendo. lo daré. — D.I."</em> The note is on the original, which is in Cartagena. The carbon copy in the Northeast Coast Bureau drawer carries no annotation in Doña Inés's hand; the Bureau's own standing-rules document does not, on the matter, ask for one.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau · cover-note carbon-copy · pencil on letterhead · Year 36 mid-season · the dispatch is, by every standing record on either continent, in transit · transit is, on the matter, indefinite · the bureau has, in three subsequent working sessions, declined to discuss the dispatch's expected arrival window with the Albatross · the curator's standing position on questions of timing: <em>"the Cóndor has the file. the Federación has the working protocol. the work is, on the matter, no longer ours. it is, on the matter, the Federación's. and beyond the Federación, it is the Albatross's, when the Albatross is on the matter accessible. we are, on this dispatch, finished. we will, on the next dispatch, when the next dispatch is the next dispatch, be ready. that is, by my own read, all the bureau owes the work. — sgw."</em></div>
      </article>
      <article class="found lore-wide">
        <h3>The Whitefang Scribblings · a working catalogue · Foundation cleaner-pool annual filing · Year 36 mid-season</h3>
        <div class="meta">Found Paper · the running collaborative graffiti catalogue maintained, on a rolling basis since Year 31, by the Foundation cleaner-pool that services Brewer's Reach Pitch and (on a quarterly inspection rotation) six other venues · this filing is the Year-36 mid-season annual cumulative · the catalogue is not, by any League standing rule, official; it is, by the cleaner-pool's standing internal practice, kept and added to as Whitefang scribbles are encountered, the way a baker keeps a sourdough starter</div>
        <p>The Foundation cleaner-pool's standing position on the Whitefang scribblings, in the catalogue's flyleaf note (in the hand of the senior cleaner Maurin Brushpaw, a Capybara who has serviced the Brewer's Reach Pitch since Year 30): <em>"we have, in five years of cataloguing, not identified the writer or writers. we have, in five years, identified eleven distinct handwritings, in red gel-pen, blue ballpoint, pencil, paint-marker, charcoal, and (once, in Year 34) what was, by the Foundation chemist's pre-publication acknowledgment, beet-juice. we have, in five years, never asked the writers to stop. they have, in five years, never asked us to keep them up. the matter is, by my own read, in equilibrium. the catalogue is, by my own read, the right working response to the equilibrium. we will, in due course, keep cataloguing."</em></p>
        <p>A representative selection of catalogue entries follows. The full catalogue runs to forty-seven pages and is on file in the cleaner-pool's working office on the south concourse, behind the lobster vendor's booth.</p>
        <p><em>Year 31 R7, Brewer's Reach men's washroom, fifth stall from the door, pencil on tile grout (the founding entry):</em> <em>"WHITEFANG WAS HERE — Y31 — and so was a regrettable amount of beer."</em> Cleaner's note, Brushpaw's hand: <em>"i transcribed this on the morning shift. i did not, by the cleaner-pool's standing rule on graffiti, immediately remove it. the standing rule, on Whitefang, has since been written. the standing rule is: most-recent only is, on the wall, until the next-most-recent appears; on the matter of every venue, only one Whitefang at a time."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 32 R3, Boise Foundry break-room, paint-marker on locker door:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG IS NOT, by every careful read, here today. — submitted in good faith."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"the foundry break-room is, by Foundry standing rule, not on the cleaner-pool's standing rotation. this entry was reported to the catalogue by a Foundry chemist on her own initiative. she removed it on her own initiative the same week. the catalogue thanks her."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 33 R5, Reno Open Court north corridor, charcoal on concrete:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG VOTED. — the ballot does not, on the matter, survive."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"appeared the morning after the Year 33 Coronation Cup. removed within four hours by the Reno Cultural Office, who did not consult the cleaner-pool. the catalogue retained the transcription. the Cultural Office has, on the matter, not commented."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 34 R2, Helena Glacier Rink visiting-team locker tunnel, beet-juice on whitewashed plank:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG, after a careful look, declines."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"the beet-juice was a first for the catalogue. the Foundation chemist confirmed the medium on a Wednesday. the writing was, by the chemist's pre-publication acknowledgment, executed with what was, on her own measurement, fresh juice — the Helena venue is six hundred kilometers from the nearest beet farm; the writer carried the beet. we have not, on the matter, asked. the writer was not, on the matter, available to ask."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 34 R8, Brewer's Reach Pitch upper concourse, third stall of the men's washroom, blue ballpoint on stall door:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG WAS HERE during the Marshmallow Drill. WHITEFANG IS, on the matter, sorry."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"this entry appeared the week after Felix Marshmallow's permadeath. it was, by my own subsequent retention vote, kept on the door for an extended period — i did not, on this entry, apply the standing most-recent-only rule. the entry remained on the door for fourteen weeks. it was eventually, by my own working judgment, transcribed and removed; i replaced it on the door, in pencil in my own hand, with the simple line 'WHITEFANG IS, on the matter, still sorry.' that line has been, in the eight subsequent quarters, refreshed by an unknown second hand at every cleaning interval. it is, on the door, today. the catalogue does not, on the matter, ask whether this counts as Whitefang or as me. the catalogue files the entry under both."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 35 R1, Olympia Harbor Pitch east concourse, pencil on bench backrest:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG SAW Pawington's last match. WHITEFANG was, on the matter, in the third row."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"a note in a different hand, in the same pencil, in the same location, three days later: 'whitefang was not in the third row. i was in the third row. i did not, on the matter, see whitefang.' the catalogue files both."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 35 R12, Tampa Bay Salt-Air Stadium concession-row pillar, red gel-pen:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG, by every available read, prefers the Bay's chowder."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"the Tampa concession proprietor is reported to have framed this and to have hung it behind her cash register. she has, on the matter, not removed it. the catalogue retained the transcription only. the cleaner-pool's Tampa rotation has, on the matter, made an exception and not removed it from the pillar either; we transcribed it, photographed it, and left it. the proprietor's framed copy is, by every account, more durable than the gel-pen will be on the pillar. the gel-pen will fade. the framed copy will, on the matter, last. we have, in our own standing record, declined to call the framed copy a Whitefang. it is, by our own standing record, a copy of one. the original is on the pillar. it is fading. that is, by our own standing record, what Whitefangs do."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R3, Saint-Laurent Antlerlords' visiting-team mat-room, pencil on mat-board:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG IS, on the matter of the new teams, glad."</em> Cleaner's note: <em>"first Whitefang in a Continental Expansion venue. the entry was, by the Antlerlords' coaching staff's preference, photographed and left in place. the Antlerlords' standing position on Whitefangs, communicated by the team's cultural liaison: 'we do not, by our own custom, have an equivalent. we are, by our own read, glad to host. we will, on the matter of when to remove, defer to the cleaner-pool's standing rule. we will not, on the matter, ask.' the catalogue thanks the Antlerlords. the entry remains on the mat-board as of this filing."</em></p>
        <p><em>Year 36 R5, Brewer's Reach Pitch men's washroom upper concourse, third stall, red gel-pen:</em> <em>"WHITEFANG WAS NEVER HERE — and was here anyway."</em> Cleaner's note, Brushpaw's hand: <em>"this is, by the standing most-recent-only rule, currently the active Whitefang at Brewer's Reach. it has been on the door for nine days. the previous Brewer's Reach Whitefang — a Year 36 R3 entry reading 'WHITEFANG checked the lobster — and confirms, on the matter, the price has not changed' — was, by the standing rule, removed on the morning the new entry was discovered. the previous entry is in the catalogue. the new entry is on the door. the door is, on the matter, what the door is."</em></p>
        <p>Brushpaw's standing closing note, written at the bottom of every annual cumulative filing in the same pencil: <em>"the catalogue does not, by my own read, need to identify Whitefang. the catalogue does not, by my own read, need to know who the writers are or how many of them there are or whether the writers know each other. the catalogue's job is, by my own read, only to keep faith with the writing. the writing is, by my own read, a thing the venues have been doing on themselves for five years and which the Foundation has, by long-standing institutional habit, not been able to quite stop. the not-quite-stopping is, by my own read, on this matter, correct. the catalogue is the not-quite-stopping in working format. the not-quite-stopping is, by my own read, what the venues have been telling us they want. we are, on the matter, listening. — m.b."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Foundation Cleaner-Pool annual cumulative · Year 36 mid-season · the catalogue is on file in the cleaner-pool's working office on the south concourse, Brewer's Reach Pitch, behind the lobster vendor's booth · the catalogue is not, by Foundation standing rule, available to non-cleaner-pool staff except on Brushpaw's standing-rules permission · the lobster vendor has, on three documented occasions, been observed reading the catalogue in the working office while the cleaner-pool was on shift · she has not, on the matter, commented · she has, on the matter, also not borrowed it · the cleaner-pool has, on the matter, never refused her access · the lobster vendor's reading habit is, by Brushpaw's own pre-publication note, "the most welcome reading the catalogue has, in five years of operation, received."</div>
      </article>

        <p>The text, burned into the wood: <em>"The Pack Eats. — WLF — Year (year)"</em>. There are, by Boston Concession Row archive, eight planks on the wall.         <p>The vendor has, on the matter, never spoken about the plank to any reporter. The Wolves have, on the matter, also never spoken about the crab claws. The transaction is, by all readable accounts, the most efficient ongoing diplomatic relationship in the League.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Boston Concession Row archive · vendor's wall, plank ephemera</div>
      </article>

    <div class="lore-section" data-loresection="timeline">
      <article class="history">
        <h3>The League Timeline</h3>
        <div class="meta">A working chronology · Float Foundation Archive · entries drafted, in each instance, by whoever was on duty the week the event was filed</div>
        <p>The events below use League Years (LY), counted from the founding of the Boston Brisk Beavers and the inaugural match at Brewer's Reach. The Long Quiet — formerly called the Collapse, in older League documents — is in the unstated past, three to five centuries before the founding bell. The League's current season is Year 36. The chronology that follows is not exhaustive; we have written down what we could remember, and what the team archives would let us write down, and what the lobster vendor confirmed when we asked.</p>
        <div class="lore-timeline">
          <details class="lore-timeline-era" open>
          <summary><span class="era-name">Pre-League</span> <span class="era-count">1 entries · Before the founding bell · the continent reorganizes itself</span></summary>
          <ol class="lore-timeline-era-list">
            <li><span class="yr">Pre-League</span><div class="ev">The continent reorganizes itself. Boston rallies around the workshop floor. Tampa rallies around the salvage tide. Reno rallies around the one slot-machine power line that, by Year 8 of the post-Long-Quiet calendar, has not stopped humming. The Hedgehogs of Helena have already been running backyard tournaments for three generations and pay no attention to anyone else's chronology. The lobster vendor takes up the booth at the Brewer's Reach pitch site three years before the pitch is built. She is asked, by the construction crew, whether she will move while they work. She says no. They build around her. She is still there.</div></li>

        <h3>Speculations on the Long Quiet</h3>
        <div class="meta">A working compendium · the question that is, on the matter, never asked formally · Float Foundation Cultural Office, refreshed annually</div>
        <p>The Old Ones are gone. They have, by the most careful Reno-academy dating, been gone for between three and five centuries. They left their cities, their machines, their painted runes. They did not, on the matter, leave themselves. The League does not require any animal to have an opinion on what happened. The League does, however, allow itself to wonder. Below are the wonderings the Cultural Office has, in eight seasons of intermittent collection, found worth recording.</p>

        <h4 style="color:var(--gold);margin-top:18px;">Theory the First — They Walked Away</h4>
        <p>The dominant Reno-academy view, as set down in the Year 32 working paper <em>"Walking Hypothesis"</em> by an anonymous senior researcher: the Old Ones simply, on the matter, left. The theory holds that they were a species capable of long-distance travel — they built machines that flew, they built machines that floated, they built (per the Reno power-line evidence) machines that drew lightning out of the air at will. A species with that toolkit could, by the Walking Hypothesis, have decided to relocate. The theory does not, on the matter, speculate where. The theory holds only that they went.</p>
        <p>Counter-evidence: the cities were left intact. The runes were freshly painted. The machines were, in many cases, mid-task. The Foundry's earliest Year-13 inspection logs note that several Old-Ones devices were still drawing power from extant lines when the Foundry's first chemists arrived. No civilization, by the senior researcher's own subsequent doubt, walks away in the middle of running its own machines. The Walking Hypothesis is, on the matter, not the Cultural Office's preferred reading.</p>

        <h4 style="color:var(--gold);margin-top:18px;">Theory the Second — They Were Made Smaller</h4>
        <p>The minority but persistent Helena-academy view, championed by a Hedgehog scholar named Mossquill Sharpfoot (currently the Hedgehogs' senior coach; the academic position was earlier in her career): the Old Ones did not, on the matter, leave. They were, by some process the theory does not specify, reduced. The Helena view holds that the modern animal kingdom — every species the League fields, every species in any city — is, in some non-trivial sense, descended from the Old Ones themselves. We are, by this read, what the Old Ones became.</p>
        <p>The theory is, on the matter, not popular. It is, on the matter, also not easily refuted. The League's Cultural Office has noted, in a quiet appendix to the annual compendium, that the Helena view is the only theory that neatly explains why the Old Ones' machines fit our paws so well, why the runes use letter-shapes our eyes can read, why the cities were built at scales our cohorts could re-inhabit without modification. <em>"The cities fit us,"</em> Sharpfoot wrote in her one published paper on the subject, <em>"because the cities were, on the matter, built for the bodies we are now wearing. The transition is, in this read, the answer to the question of where they went. They are, on the matter, here."</em></p>
        <p>The League does not, on the matter, take a position. Most Knights, asked, do not have one either. A small but determined minority finds the theory, in their own private words, "comforting." A larger minority finds it "disturbing." The largest group, by the Cultural Office's own informal poll, simply has not thought about it.</p>

        <h4 style="color:var(--gold);margin-top:18px;">Theory the Third — They Were Taken</h4>
        <p>The fringe but enduring Tampa-academy view, which the Cultural Office records out of duty rather than endorsement: the Old Ones were, on the matter, removed. By what or whom is not specified. The Tampa view's leading text is a single half-page broadside posted on a Tampa Bay venue concourse in Year 31 by an anonymous author, signed only with a small drawing of a fish. The broadside has, in five seasons, been re-posted every season, by a different hand each time, on the same wall. The Foundation has, on the matter, declined to interfere. The fish has, on the matter, also evolved — the Year-36 fish has fins the Year-31 fish did not.</p>
        <p>The theory's strongest piece of supporting evidence is, by the Cultural Office's own admission, atmospheric: there are, in the Old Ones' cities, certain rooms that look as if their occupants stepped out for a moment and never returned. The Office has documented thirteen such rooms across four cities. The rooms are, on the matter, not part of any guided tour. The Office does not, on the matter, comment on what one feels in them.</p>

        <h4 style="color:var(--gold);margin-top:18px;">Theory the Fourth — There Was No Long Quiet</h4>
        <p>The Reno-academy's contrarian view, which has the smallest following but the loudest single voice (a retired Coyote scholar named, by her own preference, only "Reyna" — no relation to the current Coyote coach): the Long Quiet did not, on the matter, happen. The Old Ones are, on the matter, still here. We have, by this view, simply lost the ability to perceive them. The cities, the machines, the runes — all are evidence that they continue to exist around us. We do not see them. They do not see us. We have, by this read, been sharing a continent for three to five centuries without overlap.</p>
        <p>The theory is, on the matter, untestable. Reyna acknowledges this. Reyna has, on the matter, also said in her one public lecture: <em>"the untestable hypothesis is not, on the matter, the same as the false hypothesis. We have, on the matter, simply not yet developed the perception. We will, in due course, perhaps. The Old Ones may, on the matter, be patient."</em> The Cultural Office has filed Reyna's lecture transcript and, on the matter, declined to extend funding for further investigation.</p>

        <h4 style="color:var(--gold);margin-top:18px;">Theory the Fifth — A Coyote's Theory, Held Quietly</h4>
        <p>This entry is included by the request of a sitting Coyote coach, who has, on the matter, asked not to be identified. Her theory, in her own paraphrase: the Old Ones built things they could not, on the matter, ultimately steward. The things continued to work. The things will, on the matter, eventually stop. The Old Ones either left because they knew this, or were left behind by their own machines, or both. The story is, by her read, neither tragic nor sinister; it is the story of a species whose tools outlasted them. We, on the matter, are using the tools now. We will, in due course, also be outlasted by something. The Cultural Office should, by her read, take this as a working assumption rather than as a question.</p>
        <p>The Coyote coach concludes: <em>"the question 'what happened to them' is, by my read, a question we should be asking about ourselves. The Old Ones are us, on a delay. Plan accordingly."</em></p>

        <div class="signoff">— Float Foundation Cultural Office · Working Compendium on the Long Quiet · refreshed annually · the compendium is, on the matter, in no danger of being completed</div>
      </article>

        <h3>The Continental Expansion's Standing Bracket</h3>
        <div class="meta">A working ledger · the four expansion teams' admission and current status · Caucus Geography Committee · Year 36 mid-season</div>
        <p>The Year 36 founding bell admitted four expansion teams under the Caucus Geography Committee's reclassification of "the continent" to include territories north of the Yukon, south of the Sonora, and west of the Sierra Nevada. The four teams — the Yukon Hunting Lynx, the Saint-Laurent Antlerlords, the Sonora Spectacular Coyotes, and the Yucatan Quetzals — were admitted on a unanimous Caucus vote, in that order. The vote on the Quetzals was, by Caucus secretary's note, the first unanimous Yucatan vote in eight seasons; the previous three Yucatan candidacy proposals had failed by various margins.</p>
        <p>The expansion teams' Year 36 records, as of mid-season: Lynx 1-7, Antlerlords 4-4, Coyotes 5-3, Quetzals 6-2. The Quetzals are currently the second-best record in the League, behind only the Wolves. Cintzli has, on the matter, declined to comment on the standings. Marc-Olivier Brisefer has, on the matter, said only that <em>"we are, on the matter, exactly where the bracket put us. The bracket is, by my read, fair. We will, in due course, win the matches the bracket gives us."</em> Coach Reyna has, on the matter, not been seen by any LMG broadcast camera all season; the Coyotes' bench staff continue to relay her instructions. The Lynx have, on the matter, won the only home match they have played all year.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Geography Committee · standing ledger, refreshed weekly</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Federación Sudamericana — A Sister League, Across the Equator</h3>
        <div class="meta">A working profile · the southern continent's parallel league · Caucus liaison file · Year 36 onward</div>
        <p>The Federación Sudamericana de los Caballeros Flotantes — by the Caucus's official liaison register, "the Federación" — is the parallel league operating across the southern continent. It has been operational, by every Murder cross-reference, since Year 22 — six seasons before the founding of our own. The Federación admits twelve teams. The teams are based, by published roster, in cities the Caucus's geographic atlas does not yet contain accurate maps of: the cordillera, the highland plateau, the river-mouth, the patagonian flats, and others.</p>
        <p>The Federación's senior councillor is Doña Inés of the Andean Condors. The Federación's contact with the League proper has, until Year 36, been mediated entirely by the Pittsburgh Murder, which has been the only set of fliers in the northern hemisphere with the long-distance range to reach the southern continent and return within a single season. The Year-36 arrival of Marisol Cumbralta on the Pittsburgh Visiting Perch is, by every Caucus liaison reading, the formal opening of bilateral correspondence. The Foundation has, on the matter, set aside an empty file folder labeled <em>"Federación — first dispatch — pending"</em> on the assumption that one will, in due course, exist.</p>
        <p>What the Foundation knows about the Federación is, by liaison file, this: it is real. It is older than ours. Its teams play under different rules. The rules differ on the points of (1) balloon altitude, which is set lower in the Federación to accommodate the higher-altitude flying species native to the cordillera, (2) match duration, which is set longer to allow for the longer recovery times of the Federación's largest species (the Capybara teams in particular), and (3) the role of currency, which is — by the Federación's preference — not lobster but a regional shellfish the Foundation has not yet identified. The Foundation has, on the matter, requested a sample. The Federación has, on the matter, not yet sent one.</p>
        <p>An exhibition match between the two leagues is, by Murder's quiet record, on the table. The match would, by Caucus discussion, be played at a neutral altitude on a neutral continent — likely a venue at sea level on the southern shore of the Yucatan or the northern shore of the Federación's cordillera. The match has not, by either side's official record, been scheduled. The match will, by Featherquill's own confident column, happen within five seasons. He will not, in this column, name a date.</p>
        <div class="signoff">— Caucus Liaison Office · Federación working profile · refreshed annually</div>
      </article>

      <article class="history">
        <h3>The Rumored Overseas League</h3>
        <div class="meta">A speculative profile · oceanic-circuit rumors · Caucus liaison file, conditional · Year 36 mid-season · "everything below is, on the matter, hearsay"</div>
        <p>The Cultural Office's working file on the Overseas League is, by the file's own first paragraph, "a collection of rumors held together by, on the matter, the consistency of the rumors themselves." The League has not, on the matter, ever received a formal communication from any overseas counterpart. The League has, however, received seven separate informal communications, all from different sources, all describing the same set of facts.</p>
        <p>The composite picture, per the rumors:</p>
        <p>— There is a competitive league operating, by every account, "across the great water" — formally unnamed in any of the communications received, but referred to colloquially as "the Overseas League" or "the Far Bracket."</p>
        <p>— It admits, by the most-cited rumor, somewhere between sixteen and twenty-four teams. Species rosters include lineages this continent does not field: pangolins, fennec foxes, ibex, snow leopards, marmots, and (per the most sensational rumor, which the Cultural Office files with appropriate skepticism) a species described only as "the larger primate."</p>
        <p>— It has been operational for "longer than ours and, possibly, longer than the Federación's" — every account agrees on this point but no account specifies a founding year.</p>
        <p>— Its currency is not, on the matter, lobster. The currency is reported variously as "salt," "spice," "amber," and "a kind of stone we do not have here." No two accounts agree.</p>
        <p>— Its rules, by every rumor, are different from ours, but no rumor has yet specified how. The Caucus has, on the matter, asked.</p>
        <p>The Foundation's standing position, per the file's working header: <em>"the Overseas League may, on the matter, exist. The Overseas League may, on the matter, not. We will, in due course, find out. The water is, on the matter, wide. The wait is, on the matter, the wait."</em></p>
        <p>Featherquill's own private column on the matter, run as a closing-paragraph aside in his Year 36 R7 column: <em>"if they are out there, they are, on the matter, also wondering whether we are out here. The first formal communication will go from one to the other. I will not, in this column, predict which direction. I will, on the matter, predict only that whoever sends it first will, by the act of sending, end the long mutual wondering. I am, on the matter, in favor of the wondering ending."</em></p>
        <div class="signoff">— Float Foundation Cultural Office · Overseas League working file · "everything within is, on the matter, hearsay" · refresh quarterly</div>
      </article>
    </div>
