        <h3>Glossary of Terms</h3>
        <div class="meta">Reference · maintained by the League Office Editorial Board</div>
        <dl>
          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">-</span> <span class="bucket-count">1 term</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The 412-Pace Mark</dt>
              <dd>The League's longest single-shot kill on record, named for the LMG kinetics tracker's measurement of the firing distance — four hundred and twelve paces along the diagonal of the venue. Set by Hester Quillstrike, HED Sniper, at the Helena Glacier Rink in HED's inaugural season — the same shot was, in the moment of its making, the shot that took her life, by the coordinated four-Otter rush at the next round's open. Tied — exactly, never broken — by Sundip Hootington Jr., OWL Sniper, at the Reno Open Court later that same year, on a shot taken with the Rifle Hester had carried first. The mark is now jointly held, posthumously, by both shooters. The mark's measurement is contested, in colloquial usage, by a small but persistent Reno-academy faction that refers to it as "the 412-pixel mark" — a piece of slang that originated in a Year-36 graduate-thesis presentation in which the student, having spent six weeks in the Cultural Office's Old-Ones-screen archive, used the wrong word for the unit and was, mid-presentation, gently corrected by her advisor. The slang escaped the seminar room. The slang has not, in two seasons, escaped the Reno-academy. The Records Committee uses paces. The Foundation uses paces. The fans who care about the figure use paces. The slang exists. We are noting that it exists. We are, for clarity, calling it the 412-Pace Mark in this glossary. The slang is fine. The pace is the unit.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">A</span> <span class="bucket-count">2 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Antlerwood Rule</dt>
              <dd>League rule, ratified Year 36 founding bell. Designates non-removable bony growths — specifically antlers, horns, and tusks — as <em>attached weapons</em> for the purposes of melee resolution. Named for Bertaud Antlerwood, whose six-foot-four-inch antler span at the Year 36 Caucus's pre-season measurement triggered the original ruling. The rule applies League-wide but, in practice, governs primarily the Moose and the Bison (the latter through a separate clause for horns). The Sharks, who proposed an analogous rule for teeth, were politely deferred on the grounds that teeth are removable.</dd>

              <dt>The Antlerwood Rule</dt>
              <dd>The single Caucus standing rule that, by ratified Year-36 protocol, applies only to one team and one position. The Rule states that a Saint-Laurent Antlerlords knight in the L'Ancrage stance (the team's standing-anchor position, held since Théodred I in the founding regional circuit and currently held by Théodred III) is exempt from the wave-doctrine respawn protocol's ten-second movement-mandate. Antlerlords' L'Ancrage may, by the Rule, remain stationary at center pitch for the entire match, by which they mean the entire match. The Rule was ratified in Year 35 closeout after the Year 34 Final, in which Théodred III stood at center pitch for the full thirty-one-minute match without moving and the wave-doctrine review committee was unable to determine whether his stillness constituted a rules violation. The committee's eventual finding — which became the Rule — was that Théodred III's stillness was, by every measurable kinetic standard, "in fact a position the moose has held for ninety-three years and which the species, by long-standing biological commitment, considers home." The Rule is, by Caucus standing language, "specific to the L'Ancrage and no other position. the Rule is, by intent, narrow. the Rule is, by long-standing precedent, also correct." Other Antlerlord knights are subject to the standard wave-doctrine. So is every other moose in the League (currently zero, but the Rule's drafting committee wanted the language explicit).</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">B</span> <span class="bucket-count">14 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Balloon Contract</dt>
              <dd>The standard agreement signed by every Knight before joining a roster. Specifies that a Knight is allotted three balloons per match, popped one-per-knockout. The third pop ends the Knight's match (and, after enough cumulative pops across their career, ends the Knight). Allegedly proposed by Splinter Tooth in Year 28.</dd>

              <dt>Balones de Honor</dt>
              <dd>"Honor balloons" — the three reserved balloons that distinguish a Federación Sudamericana balloon contract from a North American League contract. The Federación uses a six-balloon contract (versus the North American three-balloon), with the first three popped by the standard popping rule and the last three reserved as <em>balones de honor</em> that may not be popped except in the deciding round of a deciding match. The Federación's stated rationale, drafted by Espinaobscura at the Federación's founding bell and ratified without amendment ever since: <em>"el contrato de seis globos preserva la dignidad de la línea visitante haciendo imposibles ciertas formas de eliminación a mitad de partido"</em> ("the six-balloon contract preserves the dignity of the visiting line by making certain forms of midmatch elimination impossible"). North American Caucus tactical analysts have, in three working sessions, characterized the Federación rule as "a different game from ours, in the same way that the Wolves' Brawler-pack and the Antlerlords' L'Ancrage are different games from each other within our own league. it is not, by our reading, a worse game. it is also not, by our reading, our game. we play three. they play six. neither side has, in twenty-four seasons, formally proposed bringing the other rule to either bracket."</em> The Caucus's working note: <em>"if a sanctioned cross-continental match ever occurs, the balloon-rule question will be the first the rules-committee has to resolve. the rules-committee has not, in three working sessions, proposed a draft answer. we have not, in three working sessions, also proposed a draft question."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Bayou Bench</dt>
              <dd>A specific bench at the Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue, located in the visitors' locker tunnel approximately twelve paces from the visitors' bench access door. The bench is unremarkable in construction — standard cypress board, four standard cypress legs, no markings or carvings — and is, by the Tigers' coaching staff's standing acknowledgment, "by deliberate intention, not on any of our facility tours." The bench's significance is that Mossleaf Underbrush (WLF Healer, retired Year 32 R5 due to unrecoverable spinal injury) was, by the venue's own incident-recovery records, sitting on this bench when the Wolves' coaching staff confirmed her injury was non-recoverable, in the seventeen minutes between her removal from the field and the team bus's departure. She was, by Wartooth's own private statement to a Foundation interviewer in Year 34, "the third-best person who has ever sat on that bench, by my read. the first being her. the second being Avery, on the night Avery was loaned to us and we drove from Helena to Olympia and made a stop in the Bayou. Avery sat on that bench because Mossleaf had sat on that bench. Avery did not, by her own report, know this when she sat. Avery learned it from me later. Avery did not, on learning, change anything in her face. Avery just nodded once. Avery understood. that bench is, by my read, where the Wolves keep certain things. those things are not, in any official record, what the bench is for. the bench is, in the official record, a bench." The bench is, in the official record, a bench.</em></dd>

              <dt>The Bayou Walk</dt>
              <dd>The Tigers' pre-match ritual, first introduced at the Year 36 founding bell. The four Tiger knights of the active line walk the perimeter of the Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue once before the opening bell, in a single column, slowly, without speaking. The matriarch (Stripeshoulder, as of Year 36) walks at the front. The Walk is not, by the Tigers' own account, a strategic element. It is a way of greeting the field. The Tigers continue the practice at away matches when the host venue permits it; most do.</dd>

              <dt>Bird Testimony</dt>
              <dd>The class of historical and geographic claims that arrive at the North American League and the Federación Sudamericana through long-distance flying birds, principally gulls, terns, skuas, and (rarely) albatrosses. Bird testimony is, by both leagues' standing institutional position, the only available source of information about animal-organized activity on the European, Asian, and African continents — the Land-Bridge Problem prevents non-flying species from making the journey, and the journey across the Atlantic or Pacific basins is reliably survivable only by certain long-distance flying species. The two leagues differ slightly in their classification of bird testimony reliability. The North American Pittsburgh Murder, who serve as the de facto custodian of the question, classify long-distance fliers along a four-tier scale: <em>confirmed-trustworthy</em> (one Raven only — Slatequill Inkbeak Sr.), <em>indeterminate reliability</em> (most shearwaters, Manx specifically; certain individual gulls who have, in repeated cross-checks, demonstrated honest reporting; the Year-34 albatross of the Old World File Entry 53), <em>habitually embellishes</em> (most gulls; most terns; the Arctic skua class, with one or two individual exceptions), and <em>known to lie outright</em> (a small number of named individuals the Murder's Roost has, in working sessions, formally identified). The Federación uses a similar but not identical scale, with three tiers (<em>de fiar</em>, <em>de fiar parcialmente</em>, <em>de embellecimiento conocido</em>). Both leagues' working position is that bird testimony about overseas leagues is, in aggregate, of cultural and historical interest, of speculative entertainment value, and of approximately zero confirmed factual content. Both leagues file the testimony anyway. Both leagues' archives consider this filing a matter of institutional honor.</dd>

              <dt>The Bow</dt>
              <dd>See <em>The Bow</em>, further down (the longer entry under W-after-The-Wide-Draw). The bare term is the in-locker-room shorthand; the entry below has the full version with its eleven-second duration, Greylane's standing commitment, and the canonical fan-letter explanation.</dd>

              <dt>The Bow</dt>
              <dd>The Wolf-pack post-kill ritual, originated at the Year 33 Brewer's Reach Final. After a fallen opponent goes down — either in match or in subsequent visits to the Hall of Fallen Heroes — the Wolves on the field briefly form a circle around the body or the chalk mark and the captain bows. The bow lasts eleven seconds. The duration was set on its first observation and has not, by Wolves' captain Halfmoon Greylane's stated commitment, ever varied. Not adopted by any other team. The Wolves themselves consider it a form of acknowledgment, not apology. The canonical explanation, from a fan letter <em>"On the Bow"</em> reprinted in <em>The Long Bow</em>, vol. 2, is that the bow is wolf physics — the fallen opponent is, briefly, part of the pack's pattern, and the pattern requires acknowledgment. Greylane has never publicly explained the bow. She has, when asked, said only: <em>"The bow is a Wolf thing. It is not for me to explain. It is for the body to receive."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Brass-Crown Bill</dt>
              <dd>The unpaid invoice for the Coronation Cup's brass crown. Forged by Pell Whittlestone in her own off-season at the Boise Foundry's ceremonial-trophy bench in Year 31, in time for the inaugural Coronation Cup's first event that summer. Whittlestone billed the League at a price of one lobster. The bill remains unpaid as of Year 36 mid-season — six seasons. Whittlestone has, on three separate occasions, declined to discuss the bill. The lobster vendor, on those same occasions, has provided the same single sentence: <em>"the bill is, by my own reading, not mine to collect on. it is, by my own reading, also not the Foundation's to settle. the bill is, by my own reading, between Pell and Pell. it will, in due course, be settled. it is not yet."</em> The Foundation Library files the bill in the Standing Unpaid Ledger, a one-entry register that has, in the Library's institutional record, never had any entry except this one. The Ledger is, by the Library's own pre-publication acknowledgment, kept open primarily because the Library is, on this matter, "extremely curious to see what 'in due course' turns out to mean." The lobster vendor, asked by the Library in Year 35 whether she would be willing to characterize "in due course" further, declined politely. The Library has not, in the year since, asked again.</dd>

              <dt>Brewer's Reach Pitch</dt>
              <dd>The Boston home venue of the Boston Brisk Beavers and the host venue of every annual Foundation Day. The Pitch is the oldest sanctioned-League venue on the continent — it predates the League itself by approximately three years (the lobster vendor's booth, on Concession Row at the Pitch's eastern boundary, was established before the Pitch's construction crew arrived; the Pitch was, by the construction crew's own subsequent admission, built around the booth). The Pitch's central feature is a low brass bell at the south concourse, originally installed (by Foundation working theory) as a fire-station call-bell during the late Old-Ones era. The bell is rung once by the Commissioner at every season's founding bell. The Pitch's standard configuration is open-air; weather contingencies are managed by the Whittlestone overlay catalog (Foundry, Underdig, Submerged, Nightwoods, Hallowtide, Petalfall, Frostfall, Neonspark, Bramble, Aurora, Harvest, and the default Stock). The Pitch holds, by Foundation seating-records, approximately eighteen thousand seats; the Concession Row vendor stalls add capacity for approximately four thousand standing fans. The single most-photographed object at the Pitch is, by the LMG broadcast booth's photo-archive count, the lobster vendor's booth.</dd>

              <dt>The Brewer's Reach Reader</dt>
              <dd>The Boston-based weekly newspaper of record for the Brewer's Reach Pitch district. Founded Year 27 (one year before the inaugural match), originally as a workshop-floor newsletter for the Beaver-clan engineering community in Brewer's Row. The paper's senior columnist — by long-standing house tradition, never named on byline — has held the senior columnist's chair since Year 27 and is the only Reader staff member to predate the League itself. The senior columnist's column on the lobster vendor (the running series, of which "On the Bell at the Booth" is one entry) is, by every Reader subscriber's pre-issue expectation, the paper's most-read column; subscribers' polling has, in six separate years, asked for the column to be increased from weekly to daily, and the Reader has, in six separate years, declined the polling. The senior columnist's stated reason, transmitted through the Reader's editorial intern's response cards: <em>"the column is weekly. the column has been weekly since the booth opened. the booth and the column move at the same pace. neither will, by mutual standing arrangement, be accelerated."</em> The Reader maintains the only complete archive of every match-day column from the Brewer's Reach Pitch since Year 28. The archive is, by Reader convention, available to the Foundation Library on request and to no other archival body. The Reader is, by every reading, the League's institutional memory's most-trusted parallel record.</dd>

              <dt>Briarwing's Renderings</dt>
              <dd>The set of scent-mark transcriptions produced by Briarwing Hootington (Owl scent-tracker, freelance, daughter of Hawkeye), commissioned by the Foundation Drawer on a per-mark basis at the rate of two lobsters per mark. Briarwing's working method, by her own description, is to <em>"render the meaning, layer by layer, into League Common, and to mark the layers I cannot translate as untranslatable rather than guessing."</em> Her catalog includes, as of Year 36 mid-season: the Year 34 Hardvein Quickstep retirement-and-instruction mark on the Olympia gym wall (the four-layer mark addressed to Greylane, the closest thing the pack has to a will), the Year 35 Pinedrift recovery mark Greylane left on the Olympia training-room door after the carry (rendered as <em>"the Healer is alive; this is enough; we will continue"</em>), and four other marks the Foundation Drawer has retained but not, on Briarwing's professional advice, published. Briarwing is paid in lobster. She has, by her own statement, never asked for bits.</dd>

              <dt>Bristlebeard Pattern</dt>
              <dd>The well-documented Beaver Tank tradition in which the team's anchoring Tank takes the surname Bristlebeard, charges directly at the first enemy line they see, and dies in their first or second season. The First died in Year 28 R5, eating a grenade in the inaugural championship final and taking three Beavers with him in the blast — the founding instance of <em>tactical self-sacrifice</em>. The Second died on the opening kickoff of Year 32. The Third — Bjorn Bristlebeard, currently active — has, as of this writing, broken the pattern by playing a defensive back line and surviving eight matches into Year 35. The Beaver fanbase is split between those who want the pattern restored and those who want Bjorn to live. Bjorn is twenty-two. Bjorn carries the First's Riot Shield. The Foundation has offered to vault the Shield. Bjorn has declined. The fanbase notices.</dd>

              <dt>Bristlebeard's Riot Shield</dt>
              <dd>The most-traveled item in League history. Originally carried by Old Bristlebeard the First (BVR Tank, deceased Year 28 R5, the founding instance of tactical self-sacrifice). Entered scavenge circulation following his permadeath and has since been carried by seven knights across six seasons, including (in order) two unnamed Beavers reserves in Year 29, an Otter Brawler in Year 30 who lost it back to the Beavers in the next season's pre-season exhibition, the Beavers' starting Tank for the entire Year 31 bracket, Wikrai Wartooth Sr. (Wolves Speedster, briefly, in Year 32 — the Wolves were, at the time, scavenging into Beaver positions), Mok Mok of the Raccoons in Year 34 (the post-Reno-Heist period; Mok Mok claimed the seven tally marks on the inner rim were "from training"), and Wikrai Wartooth Jr. in Year 33 (briefly, before his death in the Final, which is the Shield's seventh and final scavenge of record before its disappearance during transit to the neutral vault — see <em>The Reno Heist</em>). The Shield is, at this writing, somewhere on the continent. The Beavers continue to look. The Beavers are tired.</dd>

              <dt>Buenos Aires Wetlands</dt>
              <dd>A southern continent venue, located in the river-delta wetlands south of what the Old Ones called Buenos Aires. Maintained by the wetlands alligator-line community. The venue is, by the southern coordinator's description, <em>"a venue where every match would be played in approximately ankle-deep water, regardless of season. The water is the venue. The northern teams will, on visiting, need to plan accordingly. We are honored, in any case, to host."</em> The Sharks' coaching staff has, on receipt of the invitation, expressed informal interest. The Sharks have not formally requested the exhibition match; the Caucus has not, in any case, scheduled one. The Sharks are, by Caucus analyst's read, the most likely League team to eventually visit, on the grounds that they are the only team currently rostered whose archetype-line is comfortable in standing water. The alligators are, by every available account, comfortable hosting them; the Sharks are, by every available account, comfortable visiting; the trip is, by either's account, expensive.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">C</span> <span class="bucket-count">16 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>Caracas Canopy Hall</dt>
              <dd>A southern continent venue, located in the upper canopy of the tropical jungle north of what the Old Ones called Caracas. Maintained by the Caracas tropical-bird community (multiple species, organized by canopy level rather than by team). The Hall is, by the southern coordinator's description, <em>"more rafters than venue. The northern teams' Snipers would, by canopy structure, find the venue accommodating. The northern teams' Tanks would, by canopy structure, find the venue impossible. We are, in extending the invitation, suggesting that the League consider a Sniper-roster-only exhibition match at the Hall. We will, in such a match, host with our own Snipers; the matchup would be, by every honest reading, lopsided in our favor; we are willing to accept this asymmetry as the cost of hospitality. The League is welcome to decline."</em> The League has, as of Year 36, neither accepted nor declined.</dd>

              <dt>The Caribou Standard</dt>
              <dd>The Yukon Boreal Council's preferred currency for postal and small-trade transactions, used by the Lynx in lieu of bits or lobster. Cured caribou strips, dried to a standard moisture content the Council's elder women set in the founding-era and have not, in living memory, varied. One large strip equals approximately three bits at the Whitehorse postal hub's exchange rate; smaller strips trade at fractional rates the postmaster will calculate on request. The standard does not, by Council policy, fluctuate with hunt yield — the Council adjusts the strip-size standard rather than the exchange rate, on the grounds that <em>"a Lynx hunting in a thin year should be paid the same as a Lynx hunting in a fat year for the same letter."</em> The League has, in formal correspondence, accepted caribou as payment on three Lynx-related transactions to date (all three at Tessik Snowstep's request, all three for postal-fee reimbursement on courier traffic between the Lynx team and the Yukon Boreal Council). The Foundation accounting office has, in private, expressed mild discomfort with the practice. The Foundation has, in public, accepted it.</dd>

              <dt>The Clam Ledger</dt>
              <dd>The freshwater secondary currency, used primarily in cities along major river systems — Pittsburgh (Allegheny basin), Saint-Laurent (the entire freshwater outflow), Helena (glacier-runoff streams), and Boise (Snake River tributaries). The Clam Ledger trades at approximately four to six clams per lobster, depending on shucking status, source water, and seasonal availability. The Saint-Laurent freshwater clam — smaller than the Pittsburgh variety, six per lobster — has, since the Antlerlords' Year 36 admission, become the dominant in-League freshwater currency by volume, on the strength of a single decision by the Foundation accountancy to accept the smaller variety at par with the Pittsburgh variety for vendor-staff payroll purposes. The Pittsburgh Ravens' equipment foundry has, since Year 36 R3, accepted Saint-Laurent clams as payment for League-spec arrows; the Antlerlords, in turn, have accepted Pittsburgh-foundry arrows as payment for visiting-team lodging at the Saint-Laurent venue. The arrangement is, by every Foundation accounting officer's read, "the cleanest cross-team freshwater barter the League has ever produced. We are not, formally, recognizing it. We are, in practice, paying half our Saint-Laurent venue payroll in Pittsburgh arrows."</dd>

              <dt>The Coalbroke Stop</dt>
              <dd>A bathroom break in transit between the Year 33 final and the League's neutral vault, during which Bristlebeard's Riot Shield is generally agreed to have disappeared from a sealed bag in a parked truck. The truck driver bought a soda. The gas station camera does not point at the truck. Three reporters and one detective have asked. None of them have answers. Locker-room shorthand for "the moment the thing was actually stolen, even though officially nothing was."</dd>

              <dt>The Cold Stones</dt>
              <dd>The trophy awarded for the Frostfall Friendly, the annual pre-season exhibition match between the Anchorage Polar Bears and the Yukon Hunting Lynx. Established at the Year 36 founding bell, when the Caucus suggested the two northern teams meet in advance of the regular season; neither head coach was sure that "friendly" was the right word. The trophy is, by Whittlestone's design, two flat river-stones — one from the Anchorage settlement, one from the boreal stronghold north of Whitehorse — bound at the seam with brass wire. The stones are not, by Whittlestone's frank admission, anything special. <em>"They are stones from the two places. The trophy is the bringing-together. The trophy is not the stones."</em> The winner keeps the trophy until the next pre-season. The Polar Bears took it in Year 36 by a single round; the Lynx, by their head coach Tessik Snowstep's only public comment on the result, were "unsurprised, but not, in the way the League might assume, displeased." The match itself was held at the Boise Frosthold Pitch on the grounds that Boise was the only neutral venue with a working ice surface that pre-season, and the trophy is currently at the Anchorage Frostfall Hall, on the wall opposite the entry, at a height a Polar Bear can reach without having to bend.</dd>

              <dt>The Cold Stones (continued)</dt>
              <dd>See <em>The Cold Stones</em>, earlier in the glossary, for the trophy's full description (Whittlestone's design, the two river-stones bound in brass wire, the Bears' Year 36 single-round win). One additional detail of record: the Lynx, after the inaugural Friendly, formally requested visitation rights to the Stones during their year of Bears' custody. The Polar Bears, by their coaching staff's reply, have <em>"in good humor, declined,"</em> on the grounds that <em>"the Stones are at the Frostfall Hall, on the wall opposite the entry, at a height a Polar Bear can reach without bending. The Lynx are welcome at the Hall during all match-day hours. The Stones do not, by our reading, require a separate visitation. The Lynx are welcome to look at the Stones from the entry, which is the same view we have when we walk in. We have not, by our reading, denied them anything. We have, by our reading, declined to formalize what does not require formality. The Lynx have understood this. The Lynx have, by Tessik's quiet reply, accepted it."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Commitment Directive</dt>
              <dd>League coaching standard, ratified Year 36 founding bell alongside the Wave Doctrine. Establishes a formal expectation against the dither — the tactical pattern in which an indecisive bench staff leaves their active line frozen mid-engagement while the bench debates the call. Under the Directive, a head coach has a maximum of four seconds to issue a call once an engagement has begun; the call is, after the four-second window, assumed by League rule to be the call the active line's captain would have made on the field, which the captain may then execute without bench confirmation. The Directive is, by every coaching staff's frank admission, controversial; the Wolves' coaching staff supports it (because Greylane, by tradition, makes her own calls anyway), the Pandas' coaching staff opposes it (the Pandas' bench has historically taken six to nine seconds to confirm a call, and the Pandas' captain has, in three matches since the Directive's ratification, been forced to act without bench confirmation, which the captain has, by post-match interview, called "uncomfortable but, on reflection, correct"), and the rest of the League is split. The Directive will, by the Caucus's standing review process, be re-evaluated at the Year 37 founding bell.</dd>

              <dt>Concession Row</dt>
              <dd>The strip of food vendors along the eastern boundary of Brewer's Reach Pitch, Boston. Notable for the lobster vendor who has been there since before the inaugural match (Year 28) and has not, for any reason, ever moved her booth. Her prices have not changed since the League's founding. She is the Float Foundation's sole lobster supplier.</dd>

              <dt>The Cordillera-Selva Diagonal</dt>
              <dd>The Federación Sudamericana's coaching-staff-rotated tradition of moving Healer-class knights between northern Andean and Amazon-basin teams to share technique. The "diagonal" — named for the cartographic line from Bogotá's high country (cordillera) southeast through the lowland jungle (selva) to Manaus and Iquitos — is the Federación's principal mechanism for cross-team Healer development. Healers loaned through the diagonal serve a half-season at the receiving team and return at season's end with technique exchange documented in the Federación's standing Healer-development log. Eight of the Federación's eleven teams participate; the three exceptions are the Caracas Sloths (whose Healer rotation operates on a slower-than-half-season timescale by the team's own standing description, "because Sloths do, on this matter, what Sloths do"), the La Paz Chinchillas (whose extreme-altitude home venue makes Healer-loans physiologically impractical for non-altiplano species), and the Manaus Capybaras (who, by their own captain Saira Capytlán's pre-publication explanation, "do not, by Capybara reading, rotate; the river already rotates enough"). The diagonal has, by every Federación analyst's read, produced the strongest Healer-class development program in either league's combined record. The North American Caucus has, in three working sessions, considered drafting an equivalent program for the North American League; the working sessions have, in three years, declined to draft. The principal obstacle, by Whittlestone's pre-decision summary: "we are, by every standing North American Healer's pre-consultation position, not yet a continent that asks Healers to rotate. the Hedgehogs would, by every Helena consultation, accept rotation in principle; the Hedgehogs would also, by every Helena consultation, prefer that they not be the only team that does. the diagonal is, by Federación standing, an everyone-rotates program. we are not, by our own standing, an everyone-rotates continent. we may, in due course, become one. we are not yet."</dd>

              <dt>The Coronation Cup</dt>
              <dd>The League's annual single-match crown event, held at the Reno Open Court on Foundation Day. A brass crown (forged Year 32 by Pell Whittlestone of Boise) spawns at the center of the arena; whoever wears it scores team points per second but cannot fire a weapon. First team to fifty points wins. RCC has won six of eight. The crown has been reported "missing for inspection" the morning after every RCC win and recovered, every time, in a Reno pawn shop. The League's Atlas Committee has stopped commenting.</dd>

              <dt>The Crab Standard</dt>
              <dd>The Tampa Bay vendor district's preferred currency unit, alongside but distinct from the lobster. The Crab Standard is, by Foundation accountancy informal practice, treated at a floating rate against the lobster — the Year 33 Tampa ledger records 1.4 fresh-caught crabs per lobster as a typical week's rate, with day-old or ice-stored crab dropping to 0.9. The Crab Standard is the operating currency for the Tampa Bay venue's concession row, the Olympia harbor canteen (which imports Tampa-caught crab weekly), and three Reno restaurants of repute. The Foundation does not officially recognize cross-currency exchange; the Foundation's accountancy office, when asked about the practice, has on three occasions said only that it "does not officially recognize" the exchange. The accountancy office uses the exchange table every Friday. Splashfang &amp; Sisters of Tampa (est. Year 24) supply approximately seventy percent of the in-circulation Crab Standard. The remainder is informal — backyard catches, fishing-cooperative submissions, and a small but steady contribution from a single Olympia harbor docker who goes out alone most Sunday mornings and is, by every honest account, the source of the highest-quality crab in the entire continental supply chain. He has, on multiple occasions, declined to scale his operation. He has said, when asked: <em>"I am one otter with one boat. I will, by my own commitment, remain one otter with one boat. The crab will be what the crab is. I do not want the work."</em></dd>

              <dt>Crash Rule</dt>
              <dd>See <em>The Crash Rule</em>, further down. The bare name is the in-locker-room shorthand; the entry below has the full version with the named knight, the year, and Wartooth's later comment on it.</dd>

              <dt>The Crash Rule</dt>
              <dd>An equipment standard adopted League-wide after Year 34, requiring all Wolves Brawlers to wear heavy plate. The rule is named for Crash Wartooth, who, in Year 34 R3, was stunned three times in twelve seconds by an Owls' bench-coach-coordinated focus-fire engagement that exposed a gap in the Wolves' Brawler kit. Wartooth survived the round but tore a knee tendon, missed eight matches in recovery, and returned the next season, by his coaching staff's careful management, in heavier plate than the kit he had left in. The rule was proposed by the Wolves' coaching staff at the Year 34 off-season working session and adopted by the Caucus as a Wolves-only standard within four hours of submission — the fastest single rule-change ratification in League history. The rule does not apply to other teams' Brawlers; the Wolves do not, by their own coaching staff's preference, want it to. <em>"It is our rule. The plate is our plate. The pack is the pack. The other teams will, in their own time, decide what their Brawlers need to wear. We will not, on the record, recommend."</em> Wartooth, asked years later about the rule, said only: <em>"It is heavier. I am older. The two adjustments fit together. I do not, on the matter, have a stronger opinion. The rule is the rule. I am still on the line."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Crawfish Pile</dt>
              <dd>The Bayou Tigers' export currency, formalized as a unit at the Year 33 first-export volume of six crawfish per pile. The crawfish-pile-of-six trades at approximately 1.2 lobsters by Year 33 ledger; the rate has held within ten percent across the three years of formal export. The Crawfish Pile is the operating currency for the Bayou Cypress-Hollow venue's concessions, all of New Orleans' delta-basin food markets, and (informally) the Tampa Bay vendor district's late-season trade when the local crab catch is short. The Tigers' export operation is run by a single bayou cooperative — the Stripeshoulder family's extended household, which maintains the catch traps along the bayou's outer rim — and the cooperative has, in three years, never missed a weekly export shipment to Tampa. Stripeshoulder herself has, in interviews, declined to discuss the export operation in any detail; her stated reason is that <em>"the crawfish are the bayou's. The bayou gives them. We pass them along. The discussion of how, frankly, would not be a discussion. It would be the bayou's, not ours. We are not, in this matter, qualified to speak."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Crown's Engravings</dt>
              <dd>The Coronation Cup crown was forged by Pell Whittlestone (BDG, retired Year 31) at the close of Year 31 and engraved at her workshop in Boise vernacular script. The League's calligraphers can identify the script as Boise but cannot fully translate it beyond the obvious team-emblem motifs. Whittlestone has declined three formal League requests to translate the engravings, on the grounds that the engravings "are not for the League." A new sigil is added to the rim each season, between Cups. The crown is mailed to Whittlestone after the season closes; she returns it before the next Cup. The League pays in lobster. The accounting is sealed. The current crown carries six sigils — one for each Cup champion — and an additional set of small marks along the inner band that have never appeared in any photograph.</dd>

              <dt>Curación-en-Grupo</dt>
              <dd>"Group healing" — the Capybara-class Healer-beam technique developed at Manaus by Saira Capytlán (Capybara, captain of the Manaus Capybaras since Year 33) and the only documented Healer technique in either league's combined record that is species-specific to a non-Hedgehog Healer. The technique distributes the beam's restorative effect across all teammates within a five-meter radius simultaneously, at reduced per-target throughput but, on the right formation, at higher total throughput than single-target healing. Possible only because Capybaras are, by their species' standing pre-League social structure, accustomed to operating in groups of indeterminate size and composition; the Capybara Healer treats the line as the same kind of group the Capybaras' default river-quarter pond contains. The technique has been studied, by Federación tactical analysts, across nine seasons of Saira's career; it is not, by their analysis, transferable to non-Capybara Healers. North American Caucus tactical analysts have, in three Inkbeak-relayed correspondences, requested a technical demonstration; Saira has, in three responses, declined politely on the grounds that "la técnica no se demuestra. la técnica se hace. la técnica es de la línea, no de la cámara" ("the technique is not demonstrated; the technique is done. the technique belongs to the line, not the camera").</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">D</span> <span class="bucket-count">3 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Denver Stand</dt>
              <dd>The Bison's home-match tradition: the patriarch (Yellowhide, as of Year 35) stands at the south end of the Highland-Plains pitch in full ceremonial harness for the duration of every home match. Not a coaching role. The herd-rotation tactical style requires every Bison knight to know where the herd's center of gravity is at all moments; Yellowhide is, by tradition, that gravity. Opposing teams have learned to orient on him too — by the third pre-League exhibition match, every visiting knight had unconsciously adjusted their positioning relative to his standing point.</dd>

              <dt>The Desert Pattern</dt>
              <dd>The Sonora Drifting Coyotes' signature engagement tactic, in which one Coyote appears to retreat — repeatedly — drawing opposing knights into believing the Coyote position is collapsing, until six Coyotes engage simultaneously from positions the opposing team had thought were already cleared. The pattern requires precise timing across the entire pack, and has been drilled (per the Sonora pack's training records) eleven thousand times. Coined by Featherquill in her Year 36 founding-bell preview feature; the Coyotes themselves describe the tactic as <em>"asking the desert."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Drift / la borradura / el sexto</dt>
              <dd>The Sonora Coyotes' signature tactical pattern. A Coyote Speedster, mid-engagement, appears to retreat — unhurriedly, in a wide arc, in a manner that the opposing team's tactical attention reads as <em>"that knight has left the engagement"</em>. The Coyote then drifts behind cover at the perimeter and, by the opposing team's perception, ceases to exist on the tactical map. Coach Reyes of CYT calls this <em>la borradura</em> ("the erasure"). With four Coyotes drifting simultaneously across an engagement, the opposing team's perception of the field collapses to one or two visible Coyotes — and, when the drift reverses and the Coyotes re-engage from their drift positions, the opposing team's tactical map registers a sixth Coyote that was not, in fact, ever there. Reyes calls this <em>el sexto</em> ("the sixth"). The Coyotes have, by Caucus statistical record, never fielded more than five active knights in a sanctioned match. The opposing team always counts six.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">E</span> <span class="bucket-count">3 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Eleven Federación Teams</dt>
              <dd>The eleven-team roster of the Federación Sudamericana, in two phases of admission. <b>The original seven (Year 12 founding):</b> the Bogotá Cordillera Bears (Spectacled Bears, Andean highlands; the Federación's standing senior team and home to its commissioner's office), the Manaus Capybaras (Capybaras, Amazon basin; the Federación's largest fan community by attendance), the Cusco Vicuñas (Vicuñas, Andes; high-altitude specialists, six-time Federación champions), the Buenos Aires Maned Wolves (Maned Wolves, Pampas; the Federación's southernmost original-seven team), the Caracas Sloths (Three-toed Sloths, Venezuelan coastal range; deliberately and by every account the slowest team in either league's combined history), the La Paz Chinchillas (Chinchillas, Andean altiplano; the Federación's smallest knights by mass and the team that has, by Federación record, fielded the most Speedster-class knights per match-day in the league's history), and the Iquitos Lowland Tapirs (Lowland Tapirs, Amazon basin's western reaches; the Federación's most-decorated Healer-development program, by way of the Cordillera-Selva diagonal). <b>The Year-22 Expansión del Cono Sur (Southern Cone Expansion):</b> the Asunción Howler Monkeys (Howler Monkeys, Paraguay; the only team in either league's combined record whose pre-match ritual is acoustic — the team's senior knight calls the line in by howling at a frequency the visiting team has never, by any account, been able to anticipate the response timing of), the Belém Giant Anteaters (Giant Anteaters, Amazon mouth; the Federación's tank-class specialists), the Montevideo Coatis (Coatis, Uruguay coast; nimble, omnivore-strategy), and the Santiago Pampas Foxes (Pampas Foxes, Chilean cordillera; the Federación's youngest team and the second team in either league's combined roster to use a "fox" species classification — distinct from, and not formally related to, the Phoenix Furious Foxes, though the two teams have exchanged a single goodwill correspondence via Inkbeak in Year 35).</dd>

              <dt>The Eleven-Second Bow</dt>
              <dd>See <em>The Bow</em>. The duration is the duration. The bow is the bow. The pack is the pack.</dd>

              <dt>The Expansión del Cono Sur</dt>
              <dd>"The Southern Cone Expansion" — the Federación Sudamericana's Year-22 (League Common dating) admission of four new teams, expanding the Federación from its founding seven to its current eleven. The four admitted teams: Asunción Howler Monkeys, Belém Giant Anteaters, Montevideo Coatis, and Santiago Pampas Foxes. The Expansion is parallel in concept and timing to the North American League's Year-30 and Year-36 expansions (Tigers/Polar Bears/Bison/Ravens in Year 30; Lynx/Moose/Coyotes/Quetzals in Year 36) but did not, by every Federación-side account, draw on any North American precedent — the Federación had completed its own admission process for the four new teams approximately two seasons before Inkbeak Sr.'s Flight 1 brought first-contact between the leagues. The two expansions arriving at similar mathematical structures (founding-seven plus four-team blocks) is, by every Caucus-side and Federación-side analyst's read, a matter of independent institutional convergence rather than influence. The Federación's stated reason for the four-team block: "Espinaobscura's standing position, in pre-publication notes available to his successor, was that any expansion should add at least four teams in a single admission cycle, on the grounds that fewer than four creates dynamics in which the new teams are perceived as 'an addition' rather than 'a peer admission.' the four-team block makes the new teams, by their own reading and by the Federación's, peers from the founding bell of their first season."</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">F</span> <span class="bucket-count">14 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Federación Sudamericana</dt>
              <dd>The Federation of Floating Knights of South America — the parallel league operating on the South American continent, founded Year 12 (League Common dating) at Bogotá by Mateo Espinaobscura (Spectacled Bear, first Federación commissioner). Currently eleven teams, founded in two phases: the original seven (Bogotá Cordillera Bears, Manaus Capybaras, Cusco Vicuñas, Buenos Aires Maned Wolves, Caracas Sloths, La Paz Chinchillas, Iquitos Lowland Tapirs) plus the four-team Year-22 <em>Expansión del Cono Sur</em> ("Southern Cone Expansion": Asunción Howler Monkeys, Belém Giant Anteaters, Montevideo Coatis, Santiago Pampas Foxes). The Federación and the North American League share the substantive rules of the sport — five-knight teams, balloon contracts, perma-death, position archetypes — and share the canonical Whittlestone Address as their convocation speech in a Bogotá-drafted Spanish-and-Inca-composite-creole translation ratified at the Federación's founding-bell convocation. The two leagues differ on several matters of detail, the most notable of which is the six-balloon contract (versus the North American three-balloon) with three reserved <em>balones de honor</em>; see the separate entry. The two leagues are connected via the Pittsburgh Murder's flying-Raven correspondence program, established Year 33. The leagues have not, as of Year 36, scheduled a sanctioned cross-continental match. The Federación's current commissioner is Doña Inés de la Niebla, a Spectacled Bear of, by every Bogotá-side description, considerable scholarly inclination, who took the office in Year 28 (Federación dating; also Year 28 in League Common dating, by chronological coincidence the two leagues' calendars happen to share for this season).</dd>

              <dt>Felix Drills</dt>
              <dd>See <em>The Felix Drills</em>, further down. The shorthand "Felix Drills" is the in-locker-room name; the formal Caucus name is <em>The Marshmallow Protocol's grenade-safety training</em>; the entry below uses the locker-room name as the headword on the grounds that, in eight seasons, no knight has ever, in the locker room, called it the Marshmallow Protocol's grenade-safety training.</dd>

              <dt>The Felix Drills</dt>
              <dd>The unofficial in-locker-room name for the grenade-safety training that became mandatory across the League after the Year 34 Marshmallow Incident. The drills are named for Felix Marshmallow, the Pandas' Tank who was killed by friendly grenade fire in mid-match — the formal protocol bears the team's name, the drills bear his. Pre-season camp, every team, every year: a Grenadier-class knight stands at the center of the practice circle holding a defused training grenade. The line walks past in single file. Each knight, on passing, repeats the same four words aloud — <em>"the grenade is yours."</em> The Grenadier responds, also aloud — <em>"the grenade is mine."</em> The line continues. The drill takes, by stopwatch, roughly four minutes per team per season. The drill has not, in three subsequent seasons, prevented every grenade incident; it has, by Caucus statistical record, reduced friendly-grenade casualties by approximately seventy percent. The Pandas' coaching staff continues to attend the drill in person every season. They do not, in attendance, run the drill themselves; they observe. Felix's family has, every season since Year 34, sent the Pandas' bench a small plate of marshmallows on the morning of the drill. The marshmallows are eaten. The plate is returned. The plate has been returned, by tradition, with a single sentence written on its underside: <em>"the grenade is ours."</em> The plate has, in three years, never come back blank. The family has, in three years, never asked who is writing on it.</dd>

              <dt>The Field-Widening</dt>
              <dd>The Year 35 mid-season expansion of the standard match field from 960×540 units to 1280×720 units. The change was announced by Rules Committee bulletin in plain, mildly embarrassed language. Its purpose was to eliminate spawn-camping (see above) and restore a tactical opening phase to each round. The Wolves were unhappy. The Otters were euphoric. Talia Featherquill wrote a column for The Wing Standard. The LMG broadcast team adapted their camera framing within one match. Knights adapted their opening positioning within one season. The field-widening is, by general consensus, the single most consequential rules change in League history that did not require a death to motivate it.</dd>

              <dt>The Float Foundation</dt>
              <dd>A neutral non-profit jointly funded by the League and the LMG. Operates the Hall of Fallen Heroes, pays out benefits to surviving family of permadeath Knights (often in lobster, by family request), and runs the Foundation Hall venue for Foundation Day events.</dd>

              <dt>Float Gas</dt>
              <dd>The proprietary lifting gas that fills League-spec balloons. Distilled at the Boise Float Gas Foundry. Each team receives a different formula: Boise gets the heaviest batch (with regulators); Olympia gets the lightest; Phoenix gets the desert formula (high-altitude expansion); etc. Composition is patented and undisclosed. The Foundry shut down for 41 days in Year 33 with no explanation.</dd>

              <dt>The Float Gas Tasters</dt>
              <dd>A small group of (allegedly non-Badger) individuals retained by the Foundry to taste each batch of Float Gas before it ships. Paid in cured salmon. Their job is to detect "the song" — an undefined sensory quality of approved Float Gas.</dd>

              <dt>Focus Fire</dt>
              <dd>A team tactic, descended from competitive shooter and MOBA play, in which all team members coordinate to attack a single enemy target at the same time. The League's broadcast booth introduced the term in Year 34 after the Owls demonstrated it in a semifinal against the Beavers — five Owl knights independently selected the same wounded Beavers Tank and converged on him within a single round. The Tank had 38 HP. The kill resolved in 1.4 seconds. The Beavers' coach called it "uncomfortably professional." The League's response was to let it happen.</dd>

              <dt>Foundation Day</dt>
              <dd>Annual league holiday celebrating the inaugural match at Brewer's Reach. The Holiday Festive (League Foundation Hall) biome is in rotation during this event.</dd>

              <dt>The Founding Bell</dt>
              <dd>The opening of each League season — formally, the moment the brass bell at the south concourse of Brewer's Reach Pitch is rung once by the Commissioner to signal the beginning of pre-season practice. The bell itself is older than the League; it was, by the Foundation's working theory, installed in the Brewer's Reach concourse during the late Old-Ones era for unrelated purposes, possibly as a fire-station call-bell, and was kept by the Beavers' founding-era coaching staff "because it sounded right." The Commissioner rings it personally on the first Tuesday of each season's pre-season window. The ringing is broadcast live by the LMG. The ringing has, in eight seasons, never been delayed for any reason — including the Year 33 Foundry shutdown (the ringing went on schedule; the gas did not), the Year 35 Helena admission (the bell rang in Boston while the Hedgehog delegation was still arriving by rail), and the Year 36 founding bell itself (which is the term that has, by general adoption, displaced "season opening" in League usage). Featherquill's column on the Year 36 ringing closes with the only line that has, in three subsequent ringings, been quoted from memory by the broadcast booth: <em>"The bell is older than we are. The bell will be here when we are not. The bell does not, on any of our matches' outcomes, have a vote. The bell rings. The season begins. We play."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Founding Years</dt>
              <dd>League Years 1 through 8 — the period during which the League's twelve formal teams were progressively admitted (BVR in Year 28, HED in Year 35). Most of the heroes in the Hall of Fallen died during these years, and most of the league's institutional rules (the Crash Rule, the Marshmallow Protocol, the Stadium Wars settlement, the Riot Shield's seven-carrier saga) were established in this period.</dd>

              <dt>The Fourteen-Second Window</dt>
              <dd>(1) The duration of the Pelt's Reading's pre-knowledge advantage in heat-affected matches. (2) The window during which Bristlebeard the Second's Year 33 Loambright shot, by every kinetics-tracker reconstruction, could not have been aborted between trigger pull and line-cross — nineteen frames of mechanical delay, approximately one-third of one second. (3) By coincidence, also the duration of the gap between the south-corridor security walk-by (9:31 p.m.) and the Foundation transit officer's arrival at the cage (9:47 p.m.) during the Reno Heist — the window in which the original Riot Shield was substituted for a forgery. The Caucus's tactical-archive footnote on the three usages, written by the procedural archivist on the third Caucus member to ask whether the recurrence was meaningful: <em>"the recurrences are coincidence. fourteen seconds is a useful interval to humans, knights, and architects of corridor security. the interval is, by every reading, not symbolic. the interval is the interval."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Frostfall Friendly</dt>
              <dd>The annual pre-season exhibition match between the Anchorage Polar Bears and the Yukon Hunting Lynx, contested for the Cold Stones trophy. Established at the Year 36 founding bell at the Caucus's suggestion, after the Geography Caucus's reclassification opened League recruiting to the Yukon. The match is, by Caucus rule, played under Frostfall overlay regardless of host venue; the inaugural match was hosted at the Boise Frosthold Pitch because no other neutral venue had a working ice surface that pre-season. The Friendly is the only pre-season match that produces a trophy; both teams have, by mutual silent agreement, treated it accordingly. The Polar Bears took the inaugural Cold Stones by a single round in a match that ran four rounds longer than the over-under and ended, by every account, in a small ceremony of antler-touching at center pitch that neither team's coaching staff had drilled in advance and which has since been entered, without comment, into the LMG broadcast highlight reel.</dd>

              <dt>The Frosthold Pitch</dt>
              <dd>The Boise venue selected by the Caucus as the official neutral-ground for the Cold Stones Frostfall Friendly. Distinguished by its central feature: a long ridge of low ice that runs north-south down the middle of the pitch, which deteriorates over the course of a match into a series of low pillars, then into a flat surface, depending on how heavily the round has trampled it. The ridge is not, by League rule, considered a permanent terrain feature; it is, in practice, the most influential single piece of cover on any League pitch, on the grounds that it is constantly changing under play. The Caucus has discussed regulating the ridge. The Caucus has, on each occasion, decided not to regulate the ridge, on the grounds that <em>"the ridge is the venue; we cannot regulate the venue without rebuilding the venue; we are not in the rebuilding-venues business this season."</em></dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">G</span> <span class="bucket-count">1 term</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>Greylane's Carry</dt>
              <dd>The Year 35 quarterfinal in which Wolves' captain Halfmoon Greylane carried a downed Healer (Pinedrift) across forty-eight paces of open pitch under sustained fire from two opposing Snipers and a Brawler. Greylane took fourteen separate hit registers, three of which dropped her HP into the red, and did not return fire during the carry. Pinedrift survived. The match playback is in the Caucus's tactical archive under the file name <em>"Greylane carry — do not edit"</em> — the most-viewed playback in the archive, by Foundation steward measurement. Greylane has refused to allow the Wolves' coaching staff to use it as a training video. Her own statement on the record: <em>"That was not a teaching moment. That was the only thing I knew how to do. The Healer's name is Pinedrift. The Healer is alive. That is the lesson, if you need a lesson. I would prefer you did not need a lesson."</em></dd>
