          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">H</span> <span class="bucket-count">8 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Hall of Fallen Heroes</dt>
              <dd>A long, narrow room in the Foundation Hall (Boston) maintained by the Float Foundation. Lists, in order of permadeath, every Knight who has ever been recorded as permadeceased on a sanctioned League field. Eight rows of names, at this writing, with room for forty more rows. Visited by every Wolves' active line at the start of every season's Brewer's Reach match — the captain bows for eleven seconds at Avery Loambright's name (third row from the door, sixth name) and the line follows. The Bears, the Antlerlords, the Lynx, and the Quetzals have, since their respective League entries, observed similar visits with their own teams' fallen — the Bears' visit takes the form of a single shared minute of held breath; the Antlerlords' visit takes the form of a slow, deep nod from L'Ancrage that lasts (by Foundation steward measurement) twenty-three seconds; the Lynx visit individually, in rotation across the whole pre-season, never as a group; the Quetzals have not, as of Year 36, lost a knight to permadeath, and so do not yet have a Hall ritual. The Foundation has set aside, against the Quetzals' wishes, a row for them anyway. The Quetzals have not protested.</dd>

              <dt>Hallowtide</dt>
              <dd>League-wide week-long autumnal event. The Halloween (Reno Hallowtide Hollow) biome is the host venue. Wichita Wolves famously play their best games during Hallowtide.</dd>

              <dt>Hallowtide Tag</dt>
              <dd>The League's only projectile-banned event. Played at the Reno Hallowtide Hollow during Hallowtide week. One knight is "It"; the others flee. Tagging requires a melee strike and freezes the target for three seconds, during which they take heavy bleed damage. The "It" role does not pass — the tagger keeps it. The match ends when only one knight remains alive; ranking is by death order. The Wolves have won every official Hallowtide Tag (codified Year 34). Kor Wartooth is the two-time defending champion. The Pandas have entered every year and have never finished above tenth.</dd>

              <dt>The Healers' Mutual Aid Society</dt>
              <dd>The professional association of certified Healers operating across the continent's regional combat circuits and (since Year 32) within the League itself. Founded by Dr. Lopecora Plumstone in Year 28, originally as an informal sharing-circle among non-League Healers; expanded to formal Society status in Year 30 with the writing of the Healers' Creed (the working manual that Plumstone's "Notes Toward a Healer's Manual" eventually became); expanded again in Year 32 to include League-roster Healers when Plumstone's standing roster of certified non-League Healers was used to staff the Year 32 Healer-Shortage Exemption. The Society maintains the standing roster of certified non-League Healers (thirty-one names, as of Year 36, available for inter-team exemption loans), distributes the annual Healer's Creed prayer cards (one per Healer per year, hand-pressed at the Society's print shop), and convenes a single annual general meeting at the Reno academy's medical wing (the only annual non-League gathering that the Reno academy hosts). The Society's standing publication is a quarterly newsletter that has, in seven years, never missed an issue. Plumstone, the Society's founding director, is in her pre-retirement period as of Year 36; she has not yet identified a successor and has, on three formal Society inquiries, declined to begin the succession process. Her stated reason: <em>"the Society is, by every reasonable read, working. we will not, by my preference, change directors until the Society is no longer working. it has, in eight years, not stopped working. we will, in due course, see."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Hedgehog Tradition</dt>
              <dd>The informal Helena combat circuit that predates HED's formal League admission by several generations. Backyard ranges, neighborhood three-on-three brawls, and mountain-pass exhibition matches gave Hedgehog snipers in particular a sustained training environment outside League oversight. This is why Hester Quillstrike, a rookie in HED's inaugural season (Year 35), was already capable of setting the league's longest-shot record (the 412-Pixel Mark) in her debut year.</dd>

              <dt>The Helena Tradition</dt>
              <dd>The pre-League Hedgehog combat circuit centered in Helena, predating HED's formal League admission (Year 35) by, by the elder Hedgehogs' best account, six generations. The Tradition operated as a barter-market tournament structure across Helena's neighborhood backyards, alleys, and the mountain-pass exhibition ranges, with senior Hedgehogs filing match results in their personal "circuit notebooks" — a private archival format kept in continuous service across families. Seven such notebooks are on display under glass at the Helena Glacier Rink's east entry; the most recent, Bryony Threadspine's, was closed on the morning of HED's admission ceremony in Year 35. The Tradition's training advantages — sustained sniper drilling at irregular range, and a culture of detailed circuit-notebook record-keeping — are, by every Caucus tactical analyst's read, the single largest reason HED's inaugural season produced (1) the longest-shot record in League history (Hester Quillstrike's 412 paces), (2) the highest rookie-Sniper accuracy rate in League history, and (3) the most Hall-of-Fallen entries from a single team in a single inaugural season. The Tradition has, since admission, continued informally — the alleys are still there, and Hedgehogs still measure them.</dd>

              <dt>Hold Range</dt>
              <dd>A Sniper's preferred firing distance, generally seventy to ninety percent of their weapon's maximum range. Closer than seventy and they're vulnerable to brawlers; further than ninety and damage falloff makes the shot unreliable. Snipers in Hold Range are said to be "in pocket." Snipers below it are said to be "out of pocket," which is the same expression the Beavers locker room uses to describe knights who are about to embarrass themselves.</dd>

              <dt>The Hollow's Hum</dt>
              <dd>The collective non-verbal sound the Hallowtide Tag's Reno Hallowtide Hollow crowd makes during the match's mid-engagement and final-pair circling moments — a low, sustained, multi-throated hum, distinct from a cheer or a gasp, that the LMG broadcast booth has, in three years of Hallowtide coverage, transcribed only by name. The Hum is, by long-standing Hallowtide tradition, the only sound the Hollow's crowd makes during the match's final-pair circling sequence — the crowd is asked, by long-standing Hallowtide protocol, to be quieter than at other matches, but the Hum is, by tradition, exempt from the quiet rule. The Hum is, by every Hallowtide attendee's pre-match expectation, going to happen at least twice during the match: once at mid-match (when a major engagement closes), and once at the match's resolution (when the final tag is taken). The Hum has, in three Year-36 Hallowtide Tag matches, lasted, on average, ninety seconds after the final tag — extending past the broadcast's cut-to-black and into the venue's natural ambient soundscape. The Hum is not, by Caucus standing rule, considered part of the broadcast. The Hum is, by Caucus standing rule, considered part of the venue.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">I</span> <span class="bucket-count">1 term</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>Ink and Pencil</dt>
              <dd>The Foundation Library's standing curatorial convention for distinguishing finished filings from working drafts. <b>Ink</b> is what the Library uses for canonical entries — published bios, ratified glossary entries, archived match logs, official Foundation Drawer findings, the Caucus working-session minutes after they have been ratified by the Caucus chair. <b>Pencil</b> is what the Library uses for working drafts, marginal notes, curator commentary, and any document the curator considers "still in motion." The convention is unwritten; it has been Library practice since founding and is enforced by senior curator preference rather than Foundation Library standing rule. Sigridweave's draft response to the Year-34 albatross is the only document filed in the Foundation Drawer in pencil rather than ink — her stated reason: <em>"ink is what we use for the file. pencil is what we use for the draft. the draft is, by my own read, still the draft."</em> The Foundation Library's archivists have, on three separate occasions over the past four years, requested that the Pencil/Ink convention be formally written into the Library's standing-rules document. The request has, on three occasions, been declined by the senior curator on the grounds that <em>"the convention works because it is unwritten. writing it down would, by my own honest read, be the kind of decision the convention itself instructs us not to make in ink without at least two years of drafting in pencil first. we have not drafted it in pencil. we are, on this matter, in pencil. the rules document remains, on this matter, in ink. that is, by my read, the right division."</em> The standing-rules document remains unchanged.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">L</span> <span class="bucket-count">12 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>L'Ancrage</dt>
              <dd>The Saint-Laurent Antlerlords' tank-class tradition: the team's anchoring Tank — currently Théodred Brisefer III — stands in the center of the pitch as a stationary tactical anchor while the other four Antlerlord knights rotate around him in concentric arcs. The position name translates from the Saint-Laurent native creole as "The Anchor." The role is, technically, just a Moose; the Antlerlords' tank assignment under League rules has no separate plate kit because the Moose's own mass and antler rack constitute the kit. The current L'Ancrage is approximately one and three-quarters of an Old-Ones cargo lorry by the Caucus's mass register; the Caucus has not been able to measure him precisely because their measurement scale ends at one cargo lorry. He has, by Antlerlords' coaching account, never lost a one-on-one engagement on a sanctioned field. Opposing teams have, by tactical necessity, started organizing their pitch geometry around his standing point — even when they intend not to engage him directly.</dd>

              <dt>La Borradura</dt>
              <dd>The Coyotes' tradition-name for the drift pattern, in their pre-League dialect of Sonoran composite-creole. Translates approximately as "the disappearing" or "the erasure of self from the field." The technical execution is, by Caucus tactical analysis, a coordinated rotation of all five Coyote knights through the venue's terrain features at irregular intervals, producing a "now-you-see-them, now-you-don't" effect on the visiting team's situational awareness; the pattern is most effective on venues with eleven or more discrete cover points. The cultural meaning, by every Coyote elder's standing explanation, is older and broader: the drift is a respect skill before it is a movement skill. A Coyote learning la borradura learns to disappear from a senior line by understanding what the senior line is actually looking at when they look at her — and the senior line learns, in turn, to look more carefully at every rookie on the cohort's drill floor. The drift, by its tradition's standing claim, has been drilled by Coyote ancestors for approximately eleven thousand seasons. The figure is, by every analyst's read, an exaggeration. The figure is, by every Coyote's standing read, also a kind of truth.</dd>

              <dt>The Land-Bridge Problem</dt>
              <dd>The cartographic and physiological obstacle that prevents non-flying species from traveling between the North American and South American continents — the modern, post-Long-Quiet condition of the Central American isthmus, which the Foundation Atlas Committee's Year-34 cartographic survey documented as a discontinuous chain of seventeen separate land-segments separated by a flooded basin, three volcanic-active high-temperature exclusion zones, an unbridged river system "approximately as wide as Lake Superior in pre-Long-Quiet measurements," a coastal swamp belt, and a final isthmus segment that is "geographically intact but chemically altered in ways the canopy elders are not, by our own diagnostic ability, prepared to characterize for non-Quetzal species." The committee's resolution: <em>"the isthmus is, in modern terms, an ocean. it is not, by our cartography, the same ocean as the Caribbean or the Pacific. it is its own ocean. the ocean has, by our naming, no name."</em> The practical consequence is that the North American League and the Federación Sudamericana, despite occupying continents that are technically connected by land, are connected only by air, and only via the Pittsburgh Murder's eleven-day Caribbean Raven crossing route. See also: the Federación's parallel framing, <em>"un problema del continente, no de la liga."</em></dd>

              <dt>Lima Highlands Pitch</dt>
              <dd>A southern continent venue, located in the high mountain plateau of what the Old Ones called Lima. Maintained by the Lima lizard-line community (basin variety, descended from a continuous population that survived the Long Quiet at altitude). The pitch is, by the southern coordinator's brief description in the standing invitation, <em>"a flat stone court at altitude, with mountain wind, and a sun the northern teams will need to acclimate to."</em> The League's pre-Year-37 exhibition schedule has the venue listed as a possible exhibition slot. No date has been set. The community has, in correspondence, indicated that they would be honored to host. The community has, in the same correspondence, indicated that they will not, in any case, send a team north.</dd>

              <dt>The LMG Translator</dt>
              <dd>The single staff position at the LMG broadcast booth dedicated to multilingual translation of pre-match, post-match, and sideline interviews from non-League-Common-speaking teams. Currently held by Estelle Roiseau-Manchot (Saint-Laurent goose), who handles Saint-Laurent creole (Antlerlords), the Lynx language (when Lynx captains consent to be interviewed at all), and the Yucatan Spanish creole half of Quetzals' interviews. Trees-language Quetzals interviews are not, currently, translated by the position; the LMG has not yet hired a trees-language translator. Roiseau-Manchot's working method is rigorous non-summarization: she renders the source ambiguity in the target language and lets the captain's own words do the talking. She is paid in mixed bits and lobster, with the lobster portion the largest individual lobster-payment line item in the Foundation's books — a fact the Foundation has, on three occasions, attempted to convert to bits for streamlining and which Roiseau-Manchot has, on three occasions, declined.</dd>

              <dt>The Loambright Correction</dt>
              <dd>A standard taught at the Caucus's annual sniper-class workshop: <em>do not, when shooting at a non-Healer target, choose a firing line that intersects the path of an opposing Healer at any point in the projectile's travel.</em> Named for Avery Loambright, the Hedgehog Healer who was killed in the Year 33 Brewer's Reach Final by a Beaver Sniper round meant for the Wolves' Striker Crash Wartooth. The shooter, Bristlebeard the Second, has not — in eight subsequent seasons — taken another shot whose line intersected an opposing Healer's path. The correction is, by every Caucus archery instructor's account, the single most-respected unwritten standard in the sport. The League has not, formally, written it down. The League's snipers do not, by an informal agreement that has survived three different head archery instructors, need it written down.</dd>

              <dt>Lobster Standard</dt>
              <dd>The Float Foundation's persistent practice of paying its larger settlements in lobster instead of bits. Treated as eccentric by outside observers and as accounting fact by the Foundation's bookkeepers. The Foundation has one supplier — the Brewer's Reach lobster vendor — and has, on three documented occasions, attempted to acquire a backup supplier; on three occasions the backup supplier has closed shop the next morning, with no explanation, and the lobsters in the secondary fridge have spoiled overnight. The Foundation has stopped trying. Pell Whittlestone (the crown forger) bills exclusively in lobster. So does at least one independent contractor at the Boise Foundry. So does, by implication and the records of three settled lawsuits, the Wing Standard's own publication office. The Lobster Standard is, by every reasonable measure, the League's secondary currency. The Commissioner has not formally acknowledged this. The Commissioner's ledgers have.</dd>

              <dt>The Lobster Vendor's Deferred Ledger</dt>
              <dd>The bound transaction record kept at the Brewer's Reach Pitch Concession Row lobster booth, in continuous service since the founding bell of Year 28. The ledger contains a single line per transaction (date, customer, count, price) plus, on a small minority of entries, a marginal note in the vendor's hand. The notes are the deferred-diary portion: four hundred and seventy-three notes across nine seasons, three of which were published in Year 36 with the vendor's permission and the rest of which the vendor has, by long-standing personal preference, declined to release. The original ledger volume runs from Year 28 through end of Year 33; a second volume (with the original leather cover, bound by the vendor's grandmother in Year 27) covers Year 34 onward. The Foundation Drawer's curator has, on the publication of the three released notes, called the ledger "the most-cited document in the League's institutional record that has, in nine seasons, never been read by anyone other than its author." The ledger remains in the booth's lock-box; the booth has not been moved.</dd>

              <dt>The Long Marketing Group (LMG)</dt>
              <dd>The League's exclusive broadcast partner — a post-Long-Quiet advertising consortium founded in Year 31 by a Tampa coastal salvage crew that recovered, intact, a working Old-Ones broadcast tower. Holds rights to all sanctioned-match coverage and operates the kinetics tracker (the official kill-line measurement system used to verify long-shot records). Slogan: <em>"If it's not on LMG, it didn't happen."</em> Funds approximately forty percent of the Float Foundation's operating budget. Famously antagonistic with the Commissioner's office and the Beaver coaching staff, who have in private accused the LMG of selective non-broadcast (see the unprinted musing <em>"On the Long Marketing Group"</em>); the LMG has not formally responded. Holds the only authorized set of cameras at every venue. Does not, by formal League rule, control which matches are broadcast — but does, by its own stated editorial discretion, decline to broadcast some matches per season for "format coherence" reasons that the LMG is reluctant to elaborate on. The Sharks have lost three matches that were, on paper, training matches. The Beavers have won two of those. The standings reflect what the LMG broadcast.</dd>

              <dt>The Long Quiet</dt>
              <dd>The centuries-ago event when the prior dominant species (the Old Ones) ceased to be present. Estimated three to five hundred years before the League's founding; the dating is contested by perhaps a hundred years on either end. Whatever happened to them did not, as far as anyone has been able to determine, leave physical evidence beyond the absence itself. Their cities, runes, machines, and a great many of their tools remain. The League does not require any Knight to have an opinion on the Long Quiet to play. The League does, however, require that you do not vandalize Old-Ones ruins. Formerly called "the Collapse" in older League documents — the term remains in use informally, though the Long Quiet is now the formally preferred term per the Year-36 Pamphlet revision.</dd>

              <dt>The Long Snatch</dt>
              <dd>The Olympia Outlaw Otters' pre-League exhibition tradition, predating the Pawington Cup by several seasons and the formal Capture-the-Pole bracket by considerably more. One Otter would carry a colored kerchief from one corner of the field to the other while the rest of the team escorted them, the goal being neither speed nor scoring but the unbroken delivery of the cloth. Pawington, in his Otter career, ran the kerchief in nine consecutive exhibitions and never dropped it; the Otters lost every actual scored match he played in the same span. The tradition was formally retired when the Pawington Cup was codified in Year 33 — the Otters' coaching staff, on the codification, simply stopped scheduling Long Snatch exhibitions, on the grounds that <em>"the League now has a flag event. We will play the League's flag event. The Snatch is over. The Snatch was, in its time, fine."</em> A faded, hand-stitched kerchief — black wool, eighteen inches square, with a small embroidered otter in the corner — hangs on the wall of the Olympia Harbor Pitch's locker corridor, behind a small glass plaque that reads, in the Otter coaching staff's own hand: <em>"Pawington's last carry. Year 32 R-final exhibition. The cloth went corner to corner. The match score was eight-three Otters lost. The Snatch was, that day, the only thing that worked."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Lynx Solitude</dt>
              <dd>The Yukon Hunting Lynx training tradition, in which each active knight trains alone with a single position-coach for the bulk of the season; the team only forms up on match day. The five active Lynx knights have five separate position-coaches; the team's senior coach (Tessik Snowstep, as of Year 36) reviews training but does not direct it. The League considers the practice unusual but compliant — the rule book requires teams to <em>have</em> training programs, not to specify what they look like.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">M</span> <span class="bucket-count">3 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Marshmallow Protocol</dt>
              <dd>League-wide grenade safety regulation enacted after the Marshmallow Incident in Year 34. Mandates pre-season grenade-safety drills for all teams. Officially named for Felix Marshmallow; informally called "Felix Drills."</dd>

              <dt>Mok Mok of the Raccoons</dt>
              <dd>Reno-resident Raccoon, fourth Coronation Cup year and ninth season on the active line as of Year 36. The Raccoon who, in Year 33 closeout, "found" the original Bristlebeard Riot Shield on a folding chair in the Reno Open Court's south corridor (the chair labeled in chalk: "for Mok Mok, with love, from someone who was not paying attention to the cage's lock") and immediately turned it in to the Foundation transit-officer at the security desk. The substitute Shield that arrived at the vault three days later is, by every Caucus inspection, a competent forgery; the original, at this writing, is not in Mok Mok's possession (the Caucus has, on three separate inspections of his Reno residence and his off-season storage locker, confirmed this) and is, by every reading, somewhere on the continent. Mok Mok is the only Raccoon to have carried the Shield in a sanctioned match (Year 34 R3, by Caucus scavenge-circulation rotation) and is the only person who has, on the record, claimed the Shield's seven tally marks on the inner rim were "from training." He has, in three subsequent interviews, declined to specify whose training. He has, by the LMG broadcast booth's running observation, smiled exactly once during this declination — at a press conference in Year 36 founding bell, when asked the same question he had previously declined to answer twice.</dd>

              <dt>The Murder of Pittsburgh</dt>
              <dd>The collective name for the Raven settlement built into the foundry ruins of post-Long-Quiet Pittsburgh. ("Murder" is the corvid collective noun; the Ravens use it without irony.) The Murder is governed by an elder-council known only as the Roost; major decisions require consensus among nine elders. The Pittsburgh Plundering Ravens are the Murder's official League representation. The Murder, as a body, does not bury its dead — cremation in the foundry-fires has been their practice for as long as anyone has counted, including back into the time the Old Ones still walked.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">N</span> <span class="bucket-count">1 term</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Northwalk</dt>
              <dd>The journey the Anchorage Polar Bears completed on foot in the Year 35 mid-season — from Anchorage to Brewer's Reach in thirty-two days — to deliver their inclusion application to the League in person. The Polar Bears do not consider the Northwalk a feat. They consider it the courtesy that an application of that gravity required. The League considers it remarkable. Whitepaw, on arrival, is reported to have asked only for water and a chair before reading the application aloud to Whiskerstone. Whiskerstone read the application in silence afterward. The audio of Whitepaw's reading, captured by Treadwell at Whiskerstone's request, is in LMG archive vault 2. It has been requested for public broadcast eleven times. It has been released zero times.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">O</span> <span class="bucket-count">3 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Old Ones</dt>
              <dd>The prior dominant species on this continent. Walked upright on two legs. Built the cities every animal community now lives in. Wrote the runes painted on every concrete wall, metal sign, and street pole. Have been gone, by the most careful Reno-academy dating, for between three and five centuries — the dating is contested but no scholar puts the Long Quiet at less than three hundred years ago. They lived alongside our great-great-great-grandparents at the most generous reading. Their physical artifacts (concrete, steel, glass, latex paint, foundry slag, the occasional intact dolly rig) persist where they were sheltered from rain. The League does not, formally, take a position on what the Old Ones were. Most animals do not, in daily life, think about them at all. Some scholars think about them more than is healthy.</dd>

              <dt>The Old World File</dt>
              <dd>The Foundation Library Northeast Coast Bureau's working folder of bird-testimony entries describing animal-organized leagues on the European, Asian, and African continents. Maintained since Year 30; contains fifty-eight entries as of Year 36 mid-season, collected from twelve distinct birds (eight gulls, two terns, one Arctic skua, one albatross). Each entry records the testimony verbatim and a curator's confidence annotation, which ranges across the file's six-year history from "very low" (most entries) through "low" and "low-to-medium" to a single "medium-to-high" entry (Entry 53, the Year-34 albatross who landed at Pittsburgh, declined payment, and gave three days of interviews of unusual carefulness). The Library's standing position on the file as a whole is that it is "of cultural and historical interest, of speculative entertainment value, and of approximately zero confirmed factual content." The senior curator's separate standing position, recorded in pencil on the file's flyleaf, is that the albatross of Entry 53 is the only narrator the Library should consider responding to in any official capacity. The Library has not, in two years since the entry's filing, drafted such a response. The Library's working title for the response, if drafted, is "to a careful narrator, from a careful library." The title has been on the curator's draft list for two years. The draft itself does not exist.</dd>

              <dt>The Oyster Tab</dt>
              <dd>The Yucatan-sourced tropical-ocean currency, used primarily at the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy venue's concessions and (since Year 36) at the Concession Row in-shell oyster cart that the lobster vendor herself sponsored, on the grounds that <em>"the lobster is one bit; the oyster is something else; the something else needs its own booth, and I am not adding the something else to my booth, but the something else is good and people should be able to buy it. I am introducing the Quetzals' supplier to the Foundation. The Foundation will handle it from here. I do not, on this matter, need to be involved further."</em> Oysters trade at approximately 0.7 lobsters per oyster, in-shell, requiring shucker — the rate is high on a per-unit basis because the Yucatan-sourced oyster is, by every culinary read, exceptional, and the shucking is, by professional oyster-shucker rate, additional. The Oyster Tab is the only currency in Foundation accountancy's books that has a formal supplemental fee for skilled labor (the shucking fee, paid in lobster, two units per dozen oysters). The fee was negotiated by the Quetzals' coaching staff on behalf of the supplier, who is a single Yucatan jungle-floor opossum named Rosalva Jirónsalado. Jirónsalado does not, by her own preference, ever travel to non-Yucatan venues. The shucking, when oysters are shipped to Concession Row, is done by a contracted shucker the Foundation has retained — by her recommendation — at the standard fee.</dd>

            </dl>
          </details>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">P</span> <span class="bucket-count">15 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Pawington Arc</dt>
              <dd>An unusually wide arcing run from flag-pickup back to home base, used by Reka Pawington (Mira's first cousin once removed) during Pawington Cup matches. The arc adds approximately 30% to the direct route distance but consistently evades defenders, who anticipate a straight-line return. Three other Speedsters across the League have attempted to copy the Arc. None have replicated Reka's cap rate. Reka has, on multiple occasions, attributed the Arc to advice received from her late cousin: "the corners watch you. The middle doesn't care." League historians do not know what this means.</dd>

              <dt>Pawington Arc</dt>
              <dd>An unusually wide flag-running route, named for Reka Pawington (KIT, rookie Year 35) who used it to set the Pawington Cup's single-match capture record at three captures. The arc takes the carrier near the field's edges instead of straight back to base, adding roughly 30% to the route distance. Defenders consistently fail to anticipate it. Three other Speedsters have attempted the arc; none have replicated the cap rate. Reka has declined to explain why the arc works for her and not for the imitators. Her stated reason is a quote from her aunt Mira: <em>"Mira always said the corners watch you. The middle doesn't care."</em> League historians do not know what this means.</dd>

              <dt>The Pawington Cup</dt>
              <dd>The League's flag-running team event, codified at the Year 32 founding bell by the Caucus's flag-event committee after a Year 31 Otters-vs-Kits exhibition in which Mira Pawington accidentally invented the format by dropping her team's standard Long Snatch kerchief and watching a Kit Speedster run it home. A flag spawns at center; teams compete to carry it back to their own base. The carrier cannot fire and moves at four-fifths speed. First team to five captures wins. Hosted on alternating years by KIT (Hardwood Hall) and BVR (Brewer's Reach Pitch). KIT has won five Cups. BVR has won two. SHK has entered three and won zero, having refused on principle to slow to four-fifths speed. Mira Pawington — the Scavenger Queen, the Cup's namesake — won the inaugural Year 32 Cup three rounds to one, dropped the kerchief once in round one (intentionally, on principle, "to demonstrate that the rules accommodate the dropping"), and died in a non-League hunting accident in late Year 32.</dd>

              <dt>The Pawington Tradition</dt>
              <dd>A Kits-only scavenging ritual where the scavenger kneels by the fallen and asks permission before taking gear. Originated with Mira Pawington. Bench officials have on at least one occasion claimed to hear the corpse <em>respond</em>; that bench official was sent home.</dd>

              <dt>The Pelt's Reading</dt>
              <dd>A Fox-specific physiological skill: the use of the pelt's air-temperature receptors to read venue conditions ahead of central thermoregulation. A heat-acclimated Fox, by approximately the third sanctioned match of her rookie season, learns to read the venue's air-temperature signature on her own pelt; the pelt's reading anticipates the body's core thermoregulation by approximately fourteen seconds. The fourteen seconds are, by every Fox's working assessment, the engagement-decision window in a heat-affected match. The Pelt's Reading is, by Caucus tactical analysis, the single largest source of the Foxes' home-match advantage at Phoenix venues; the Heat Clause was ratified explicitly with the Pelt's Reading in mind, on the grounds that visiting teams without the Reading could not, in mid-summer Phoenix, safely engage at peak match-temperatures. The Reading is not, by League rule, considered an unfair advantage; it is, by every Caucus tactical analyst's read, "what a Fox is" rather than "what a Fox does." The League regulates the venue's temperature; the League does not, by Caucus standing rule, regulate species-specific physiology.</dd>

              <dt>Permadeath</dt>
              <dd>The condition triggered when a Knight uses up the last of their three lives in a match. Permadeath is final. The Knight's gear drops on the field for survivors to scavenge; their helmet is placed in the Hall of Fallen Heroes; their family receives Float Foundation benefits.</dd>

              <dt>Personal Sandbag</dt>
              <dd>A storefront item, introduced Year 35, costing one hundred and fifty bits, applying a fractional speed reduction to one named opposing knight for the duration of a single match. Subject to a long-running ethics debate; the League's official position is that the item is legal sabotage, the Knights' Union's position is that it is sabotage that knights cannot defend against because they cannot detect it, and The Wing Standard's position is that both of these are correct simultaneously.</dd>

              <dt>The Phoenix Heat Clause</dt>
              <dd>A League scheduling rule, introduced Year 32, requiring that all Foxes' home matches be played at sundown or under the venue's misting overlay. Named for Phoenix's daytime ground temperatures, which the Caucus's pre-rule analysis confirmed could exceed the safe-engagement threshold for non-Fox species (specifically: Beavers, Pandas, and Polar Bears) in mid-summer matches. The clause was proposed, with characteristic directness, by the Foxes' captain Bask Ironclaw the Second at a Year 31 closeout working session: <em>"the heat is the heat. we like the heat. the visiting teams do not, by every reading, like the heat. we are not, by my preference, going to lose visiting teams to heat exhaustion. the schedule should reflect this. we will play at sundown. we will, by Foundry overlay, mist the venue when sundown is not feasible. the heat is still the heat. the visiting teams will, by my read, do better. we will, by my read, still win."</em> The Caucus ratified the clause unanimously. The Foxes have, in five subsequent seasons, lost approximately the same percentage of home matches as before the clause's introduction — a result that the Foxes' coaching staff has, in three separate post-season reviews, called "consistent with my read at the time of the proposal." The Caucus's continuity-planning office considers the clause one of the League's most successful safety regulations.</dd>

              <dt>The Phoenix Heat Clause</dt>
              <dd>A scheduling rule, negotiated Year 30 and revised Year 34, requiring Phoenix-hosted matches between June and mid-September to either start after 7:30pm local OR run under the misting system installed at Skyline Pitch. The clause is responsible for the orange-pink sky that appears in most Foxes home broadcasts, and for the faint soda smell at the field's edge.</dd>

              <dt>The Phoenix Sandstone Reader</dt>
              <dd>The Phoenix-based weekly newspaper of record for the Foxes' affiliate fan-club community. Founded Year 30, originally as a single-page broadsheet circulated at the Foxes' home venue ticket booth. The Reader's standing tradition, since founding, has been to publish exactly one column per active Fox knight per season — the column being written by the knight herself, on a topic of her choosing, in her own voice. Bask Ironclaw the Fourth's "On the Heat" column from Year 36 mid-season (a reply to Talia Featherquill's "On the Numbers" in the Wing Standard) was the second column she has written for the Reader; the first, in her rookie season, was on the proper care of a ceremonial sword inherited from a deceased parent. The Reader's circulation is small (approximately fourteen hundred subscribers as of Year 36) but its readership is dedicated; subscribers retain back issues at a rate the Foundation Drawer's curator has called "extraordinary even by the standards of small newspaper communities." The paper's offices are in a back room of the Phoenix Sandstone Pitch's south concession concourse. The senior editor is, by standing tradition since founding, an aging Fox who has retired from the active line.</dd>

              <dt>Pinedrift the Survivor</dt>
              <dd>The Wolves' Healer, on the active line since Year 32 and the only Wolves' Healer to have served continuously through both the Year 33 Loambright period (when the Wolves' Healer slot was held by Loambright on the inter-team exemption) and the post-Year-33 era (when the slot returned to Pinedrift). Subject of Greylane's Carry in Year 35 quarterfinal. Has not, in five subsequent seasons, been knocked down on a sanctioned field. The team's Olympia laundry-service annotation (<em>"the tabard came in worse than it left"</em> — see Found Papers) is the only known indirect criticism of his match performance on record; he has, on his own pre-statement, never read the annotation aloud and is, by the supply-room steward's account, satisfied with the team's response. The four bits in lobster credit Pinedrift personally walked to the laundry's back door before the next match are, by laundry-owner accounting, still the only debt the Wolves have ever paid in lobster on time.</dd>

              <dt>Pinedrift the Survivor</dt>
              <dd>A Wolves' Healer who, in the Year 35 quarterfinal at Olympia, was downed by Sniper fire and carried by Halfmoon Greylane across forty-eight paces of open pitch under sustained Sniper fire to the bench medical strip. Pinedrift survived. He has, in subsequent seasons, returned to the active roster as a healer. He has, in subsequent seasons, played in seventeen matches. He has not, in any subsequent match, allowed himself to be downed in open pitch — he plays a careful Healer's game, with cover priority, that the Wolves' coaching staff has, in private, called <em>"the Pinedrift adjustment"</em> and which the staff teaches to every new Wolves' Healer as a baseline habit. Pinedrift has, in five known interviews, declined to discuss the carry. He has said only, on the record: <em>"I was carried. I am alive. The captain did the carrying. The captain has, on this matter, said all that needs to be said. I will not, by my own preference, add to it."</em> He has, by his coaching staff's quiet record, sent Greylane a small handwritten card every year on the anniversary of the carry. The card, by Greylane's quiet record, is, in every year, the first piece of mail she opens that day.</dd>

              <dt>The Pittsburgh Harbor Wall Visiting Perch</dt>
              <dd>The North American counterpart to the Cartagena visiting-Raven roost — a tier of three perches under construction at the Pittsburgh harbor wall as of Year 36 mid-season, intended for the day the first Federación Sudamericana Andean Condor lands northbound. Proposed by Slatequill Inkbeak Sr. on Flight 5 (Year 35) in a formal Roost-vote proposal that was, by Year-36 mid-season Roost vote, ratified. Construction began Year 36 R3. The middle perch — the senior perch — is, by Murder protocol, sized and reinforced for an Andean Condor's wingspan and weight (which are, by every measurement available, considerably greater than a Raven's). The wax for the senior perch was provided by the Bears of the Cordillera, in a sealed jar carried north on Inkbeak's Flight 8, with a single-line note in Doña Inés de la Niebla's hand reading <em>"para el día"</em> ("for the day"). The wax is, by Murder standing rule, in the Roost's secure custody and will be applied to the senior perch on the day before any announced first Federación Condor arrival. No first arrival has, as of Year 36 mid-season, been announced. The Federación's three Andean Condor scouts have, by their own pre-publication caution, declined to commit to a date. The Murder's standing position: <em>"the perch will, by our reading, be there when they are ready. the perch is, by our reading, also a kind of message that we are ready. they will, in due course, read the message. we are not, by our reading, in a hurry."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Playbook Rotation</dt>
              <dd>Pre-season Caucus tradition codified in the Year 30 Playbook Rotation Rule. Each off-season, every head coach draws a numbered tile from the Caucus's season ballot bag and adopts the corresponding doctrine — one of twenty-five named playbooks ranging from BALANCED through BERSERKER, DOCTRINE, PHALANX, ANARCHIST, GLASS CANNON, etc. — for the upcoming year. Coaches must run their drawn doctrine "in good faith." The system has been challenged three times in formal protest (twice unsuccessfully, once successfully — the Frogs' Year 32 GLASSCANNON re-draw). The Caucus considers the surprise factor essential. Featherquill publishes the full season grid every founding bell.</dd>

              <dt>Project Neon Inheritance</dt>
              <dd>The Reno Cultural Office's internal working paper documenting how Reno's lower-Strip survived the Long Quiet. The paper's central finding: a single dedicated power line on the lower Strip stayed lit when the rest of the city went dark, because that line had been installed by the Old Ones' casino consortium specifically to keep slot machines spinning during outages — and the line had been chained to a sub-grid the rest of the city did not know about. Three blocks. Twelve buildings. The Raccoons moved in within "a season" of the Old Ones' disappearance, by the founding-generation oral account; food trade organized along the lit blocks shortly after; engineering guilds gathered in the slot-machine bays within a generation. The original Old-Ones hardware has been replaced and re-replaced across twelve generations of Raccoon engineers; what is unbroken is the continuity of light. The Cultural Office classified the paper internal-only. A junior intern photocopied it in Year 35 and leaked it to The Wing Standard. The Cultural Office has never commented. The intern is now a junior columnist at the same paper. The leak did not damage anyone, the League Library quietly accessioned a copy, and the Cultural Office continues to write polished sentences for orientation pamphlets.</dd>

            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Quetzal Nest</dt>
              <dd>The rafter-nest maintained personally by Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy in the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy venue's overgrown rafters. The nest is not formally registered as terrain but functions, in matches at the Yucatan venue, as Cintzli's preferred shooting position. The Caucus has discussed registering the nest on three separate occasions and has, on each occasion, declined to register it on the grounds that doing so would imply the League had built it (the League did not build it; Cintzli built it; the rafters were there before either). The Quetzals have not asked for the nest to be registered; the Caucus has not asked it to be removed; the matter is, by mutual silent agreement, not a matter.</dd>

              <dt>The Quetzal Rafter-Nest</dt>
              <dd>The personal nesting position constructed by Cintzli of the Yucatan canopy in the rafters of the Yucatan Jungle-Canopy Hall. Built by Cintzli, before the venue was registered as a League facility, from materials Cintzli gathered herself. Not formally registered as terrain (see the Caucus's repeated declinations to register the nest, on the grounds that registration would imply League construction). Functions, in matches at the Yucatan venue, as Cintzli's preferred shooting position. Cintzli brings her own moss to away venues; she has, in her inaugural season, declined to take exactly two shots for lack of an appropriate moss substrate at the away venue. The Quetzals have, in fourteen matches, not lost an aerial shot to nesting-position issues other than these two declinations. The nest is, by Cintzli's preference, untouched by her teammates and unphotographed by the LMG (the LMG's broadcast booth has, on three occasions, requested permission for an above-rafter camera angle; on three occasions Cintzli has declined). The Caucus respects the decline.</dd>

              <dt>Quickfingers' Reno Storage</dt>
              <dd>The Reno pawn shop owned by Moss Quickfingers (a beaver of unknown allegiance, sixteen-year shop-tenure), at which the Coronation Cup brass crown has, by the Raccoons' annual practice, been deposited overnight every Cup year the Raccoons have won. The shop's official function is general pawnbroking; the crown is the only item Quickfingers is on record as accepting from the same client every year, and the only item he has ever stored under the same pawn ticket-name (a member of the active Raccoon roster, varying by year). The shop accepts payment for storage in lobster only. Quickfingers has, in three separate interviews, declined to comment on whether the practice is technically pawning, layaway, or some informal hybrid. He has said only: <em>"The crown is at my shop. The Foundation knows where it is. The Raccoons know where it is. I am paid in lobster. The lobster is good. I have stopped asking questions."</em> The shop is on Reno's South Strip, between a tobacconist and a tea-and-coffee importer; it has not, in sixteen years, been moved.</dd>

          <details class="lore-glossary-bucket" open>
            <summary><span class="bucket-letter">R</span> <span class="bucket-count">8 terms</span></summary>
            <dl class="lore-glossary-bucket-list">
              <dt>The Raccoon Dignity</dt>
              <dd>The Raccoons' annual post-Coronation-Cup ritual, established by Dustpaw Trashbright at the inaugural Cup in Year 31 and continued by every subsequent Raccoon captain. On winning the Cup, the captain accepts the brass crown on the broadcast post-match line, makes a brief statement that includes the phrase <em>"I will be taking it home,"</em> and transports the crown — by team transport, at speed — toward Pittsburgh. The crown is then, on every winning year, recovered the following morning at Moss Quickfingers' Reno pawn shop, where it has been stored overnight in exchange for a small lobster fee. The Foundation has built a recurring annual budget line for the recovery. The line is called <em>"crown retrieval logistics"</em> and amounts, annually, to four lobsters and a small storage fee. The practice has, in six of eight Cup years, occurred on schedule. (The two non-Raccoon Cup wins did not, by the winning teams' respective decisions, involve any pawning.) The Foundation has stopped commenting on the practice. Featherquill has called it <em>"the cleanest sport I have ever covered."</em></dd>

              <dt>Rally Point</dt>
              <dd>The position toward which a wounded knight retreats when their team has a healer or a healthy Tank in the field. Distinct from "running away" — a rally point implies a destination, and a destination implies a plan. The League's broadcast team uses the term to distinguish controlled retreats from panicked ones. Coaches use the term to distinguish a knight who is doing their job from a knight who is not.</dd>

              <dt>Reef Tinkerbarrel</dt>
              <dd>The Tampa Tornado Sharks' bench-staff disclosure officer (a position the Sharks created in Year 33 specifically for this purpose, after Tinkerbarrel's testimony). In Year 33, Tinkerbarrel — then a junior bench-staffer with no prior official disclosure role — wrote a letter to the Office of the Commissioner detailing the Sharks' use of the Year 30 R3 flat batch in the Tampa-vs-Foxes match, a match the Sharks had won 5-0 by exploiting the under-pressure-spec ammunition the Foundry had shipped them. The disclosure was not, by Tinkerbarrel's own pre-letter expectation, going to result in the Year 30 R3 result being voided (and it didn't — the Caucus's working session voted 11 to 4 against voiding). The disclosure was, by Tinkerbarrel's stated intention, a matter of the record being right. He testified to the Caucus in person; he did not, in testimony, defend the Sharks' Year 30 conduct. He did, in testimony, note that the Sharks' coaching staff had, in Year 30, been in a regulatory gray zone the League's standards had not yet caught up to. The Caucus accepted this. Tinkerbarrel was, the next season, promoted to the Sharks' senior disclosure officer role — a position he still holds. The Foxes' captain, on the post-disclosure record, said only: <em>"We accept. We will see them next bracket. We will be paying very close attention to the inflation rig."</em> The phrase "paying close attention to the inflation rig" has, in three subsequent seasons, become the LMG broadcast booth's running half-joke for any Sharks match.</dd>

              <dt>The Reno Heist</dt>
              <dd>The presumed (officially: alleged, possibly imagined) theft of Bristlebeard's Riot Shield in transit to the vault after Year 33's final. The Shield has since been seen on a Raccoon roster, then stolen back, then re-stolen, then re-stolen. Its current location is unknown and is being looked for. The lookers are tired.</dd>

              <dt>Reserve Gas</dt>
              <dd>The lighter, alternative Float Gas formula the Boise Foundry distributed during the Year 33 forty-one-day shutdown. Reserve gas burns cleaner but lifts less; matches played on it have a slightly different feel that veterans claim to detect. The Badgers, who normally receive the heaviest formula and rely on it, finished the Year 33 season 2-12. Reserve Gas is not currently in production. Its formula is not, officially, known to anyone outside the Foundry's senior chemist; unofficially it is widely suspected of being known to whoever wrote the unsigned Foundry letter that arrived in Year 33.</dd>

              <dt>The Roost</dt>
              <dd>The elder council that governs the Murder of Pittsburgh, the corvid settlement that runs the Pittsburgh Plundering Ravens' affiliate community. Composed of nine elders, each holding a permanent seat for life. Major decisions require consensus among nine. The Roost's deliberations are, by long-standing tradition, conducted in silence — the elders communicate by the small head-tilts, throat-feather displays, and pre-known coded movements that the Murder has used since back into the time the Old Ones still walked. The Roost's archival records are, by Roost tradition, photographs (taken in the foundry-quarter's pre-Long-Quiet camera setup that the Murder has, by quiet accident, kept in working condition for centuries) — not transcripts. Decisions are recorded as the photograph of the Roost at the moment of consensus, with the date and the decision's subject noted in the Roost's hand on the photograph's back. The Roost has, in the post-Long-Quiet era, made approximately two hundred photographed decisions, including (in chronological order) the decision to admit Slate Wirethorn as the Murder's master arrowsmith, the decision to apply for League admission (Year 33), the decision to send a young Raven on a pre-match Boston scouting flight every season (Year 34, post-admission), and the decision to publish Crowstep Inkbeak's scouting log in the Foundation Drawer in Year 36. The photographs are in the Roost's archival roost. The Roost has not, in living memory, made a decision that was not unanimous.</dd>

              <dt>The Roost's Photographs</dt>
              <dd>The archival decision-record of the Murder of Pittsburgh, kept by the Roost in continuous service since back into the time the Old Ones still walked. The Roost does not transcribe its deliberations; the Roost photographs the moment of consensus. The photographs are taken on a pre-Long-Quiet camera setup (a fixed studio rig in the Roost's archival roost, mounted on a stationary tripod, with the Roost's nine elders arrayed in a fixed semicircle) and are developed in the foundry-quarter's shared darkroom by a Raven photographer who has, by Roost-appointed tradition, the Roost's standing trust. The photographs' backs are inscribed, in the Roost's hand, with the date and the decision's subject — a single short phrase per photograph. The Roost's archival roost contains, as of Year 36 mid-season, approximately two hundred photographs, the earliest dating to the late Old-Ones era. The photographs are, by Roost convention, never displayed outside the archival roost; the Foundation Library has, on three separate occasions, requested archival access, and the Roost has, on three separate occasions, declined. The Roost's stated reason, transmitted through the Murder's standing liaison: <em>"the photographs are the Murder's. the Murder is, by long-standing tradition, the Murder's. the photographs will, in due course, be the Murder's. the Foundation has, by every reading, our respect; we have, by the same reading, this matter for ourselves."</em></dd>

              <dt>The Roving Anchor</dt>
              <dd>An experimental Antlerlords tactical formation in which L'Ancrage (the team's anchoring Tank) abandons his stationary center-pitch stance and joins the perimeter rotation as a slow-moving fifth knight. By every Caucus analyst's pre-existing tactical literature, the formation is theoretically possible but practically compromised — L'Ancrage's mass is a feature of his stationary stance, and a moving L'Ancrage cannot, by his own walking speed, sustain the rotation's pacing. The formation was first deployed in a sanctioned match in Year 36 R7 (BDG vs MOS at the Boise Highland Pitch), in real-time response to the Badgers' Wide Draw tactical debut, with no prior team drill. The Antlerlords lost the match 4-1. The formation has not, by Antlerlords' coaching staff's pre-Year-37 commitment, been retired; it is being drilled into the team's off-season exhibition schedule and is, by Marc-Olivier Brisefer's stated intent, expected to debut in fully-drilled form in Year 37's regular season.</dd>
